title: SLIGHTED - Diamondbacks take series of slights into surprise series with Rangers
content:
SLIGHTED - Diamondbacks take series of slights into surprise series with Rangers

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 26 | Section: Sports 
 
 864
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ARLINGTON, Texas - Before opening the World Series, the Arizona Diamondbacks wanted to recount a series of slights.Overlooked by oddsmakers and angered by analysts, the Diamondbacks find themselves in a Surprise Series against the also unexpected Texas Rangers. But the mindsets couldn't be more different ahead of Friday night's opener in Major League Baseball's third all-wild card title matchup."We just put it on our list and keep those receipts and walk around with a little bit more of a chip on our shoulder," Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said Thursday. "It gives you a little bit more motivation. And when you can get a little bit more, you take it." Diamondbacks closer Paul Sewald has become keeper of the receipts, reminding teammates of what they consider disrespect."Maybe I found screenshots that maybe other people didn't," he said, wearing a T-shirt that proclaimed "Snakes Alive." "We took offense to that and we're excited that we're here and people are still not giving us that much credit here." The Diamondbacks are tracking closely what the public says, with MLB Network a clubhouse constant.Meanwhile, the Rangers insist they pay no attention."We don't listen to the outside noise that much," second baseman Marcus Semien said.Zac Gallen, a 28-year-old righthander coming off a career-best 17-win season, starts Game 1 for the Diamondbacks, in the Series for the first time since beating the New York Yankees for the franchise's only title in 2001. Texas starts Nathan Eovaldi, a 33-year-old righthander and a two-time All-Star who has overcome two Tommy John surgeries.Gallen, who grew up in a Philadelphia suburb, followed the pennant-winning Game 7 victory over the Phillies with a tweet highlighting the losing team's spring training and reminded Philadelphia fans to" make sure to get those tix for your next game." When the Phillies led the NLCS 2-0, backup catcher Garrett Stubbs talked about celebrating in the Chase Field pool. Gallen responded to what he said were online direct messages."I just figured if they want to talk junk to me, I'll say one back," he said. "And I feel like being from there, I knew how to hit them the hardest." Both teams worked out Thursday under a closed roof at Globe Life Field, where World Series logos were freshly painted on the turf.Both clubs are two years removed from 100-loss seasons, and the Diamondbacks could become just the second champion with a negative run differential after the 1987 Minnesota Twins.Arizona went 84-78 during the season and earned the NL's sixth and last postseason berth, finishing with what would be the second-fewest wins for a Series champion behind the 2006 St. Louis Cardinals' 83. The Rangers were 90-72 and got the fifth AL slot.Texas hasn't won a title since the franchise started play as the expansion Washington Senators in 1961, and odds of a Diamondbacks-Rangers Series were 1,750 to 1 when wagering for the 2023 season opened."We weren't concerned with what people thought of us," said firstyear Rangers manager Bruce Bochy who led San Francisco to three titles from 2010-14. "We thought we belonged and we thought we could win." Lovullo, excited about his first Series as a manager, opened his news conference by snapping a photo of assembled media "just to break the ice." He had a message for MLB Network's Chris "Mad Dog" Russo, who promised before Game 6 against the Phillies to "retire on the spot" if Arizona won the pennant."You can't back out of that one, Mad Dog. You've got to do something," Lovullo said. "I do like Howard Stern's thought about walking with a billboard saying that I am whatever, a liar in Midtown Manhattan for half a day.That will do it for me, but I ain't going to forgive you until you do something unbelievable, maybe show up here and say you're sorry to the entire team." BETTER NATE THAN NEVEREovaldi is 4-0 in this postseason.He was to have started Game 4 of the 2018 Series for Boston but instead relieved in the 12th inning of Game 3 and delivered a memorable performance before giving up Max Muncy's winning home run leading of the 18th for the Los Angeles Dodgers."I kind of had my moment there," Eovaldi said. "Having Game 1, trying to set a tone for the team, there's a lot of pressure with that, but also a lot of excitement." GREAT GLOVESArizona had the fewest errors in the major leagues during the season (56), one less than Texas.The Diamondbacks have allowed three unearned runs during the postseason and the Rangers one.MUTUAL ADMIRATIONLovullo, 58 and in his seventh season as a big league manager, effusively praised the 68-year-old Bochy, in his 26th. Lovullo recalled giving Bochy a gift during his last season with San Francisco in 2019."It's been an absolute honor to manage against you. I hope you find your way back to doing this one day," Lovullo recalled saying, adding Bochy responded: "If I do, it will be an honor to be managing against you, as well." "I couldn't believe he said that to me," Lovullo said. "I was just honored to be in his presence.And I will be for these next nine days."

title: Lions sweep into history - Top Parkside for volleyball program's first back-to-back conference titles
author: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com
content:
Lions sweep into history - Top Parkside for volleyball program's first back-to-back conference titles

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com | Page: 24A | Section: Sports

 Words

 CENTREVILLE - Queen Anne's County High's sports program has been riding a historic wave this autumn.Girls' head soccer coach Mike Kern became the school's alltime leader in career coach victories for one sport on Sept. 25, when the Lions logged a 5-0 shutout of North Caroline, giving him his 267th triumph Two days later, head field hockey coach Shana Corder notched her 100th career victory.Corder's crew continued that historic theme last Tuesday, when it defeated Pocomoke, 1-0 in double overtime for Queen Anne's first Bayside Conference field hockey championship in school history. A day later, junior Ben Marks smashed the conference and course records at Cambridge-South Dorchester while becoming the school's first boys' cross country champion since Mike Rea in 1997.Not wanting to be left behind, Queen Anne's volleyball team got in on the act Monday night, when it swept Parkside, 25-15, 25-16, 25-16 in the Bayside championship, giving the Lions their first ever back-to-back conference crowns in volleyball."They're just a complete package," Parkside head coach Greg Mallory said of the Lions. "They serve well. They can place the ball just about anywhere. Their setter (Kayce Titus) did an awesome job. She was rotating the ball. It really didn't matter where we sent our blocks to, she was just able to get the ball in the other direction. And they've got some fantastic hitters." Perhaps earning an assist in this second Lions' title run in as many years was North rival North Caroline, which handed the defending conference champions a humbling 3-0 loss on Sept. 14."That woke the girls up big time," Queen Anne's head coach Nevada Brice said of the Caroline loss. "We needed it. It was definitely a defining moment in our season this year. I think they came in a little overconfident to that North Caroline game, which I'm actually glad that they did." Since that loss, Queen Anne's (14-1) has won 11 straight matches, winning 33 games and dropping only four."I think that really opened our eyes to push farther and work harder the rest of the season," Lions senior outside hitter Caroline Taylor said of the loss. "Because we know we have more potential and that wasn't our game that we played. So ever since we've been practicing even harder and coming out for games more prepared." But it was Parkside (12-4) that grabbed early leads of 3-0 and 5-2 in Monday's Game 1. The Lions steadily reeled in the Rams, as Marylee Kline's ace, a stray Parkside return, and a Lions kill gave the hosts their first lead at 8-7.Parkside regained the lead at 9-8 before Queen Anne's rallied, then moved to a 13-9 lead behind Baillie Pinder's four-point service run.The Lions slowly widened their advantage before Baillie Pinder's kill capped a 25-15 Game 1 victory.The Rams managed small leads in Game 2, but at no time did the Lions ever seemed rattled, playing with a relaxed approach."'Don't get upset about it. It's a rally point,'" Brice said of a point she has stressed to her team throughout the season. "We can get it back within no time. It's just get your game going, and let's take on that next point."The big thing is stressing to stay in the moment," Brice continued."Start with that one pass and then move on. Don't worry about the score at the time. Sure, we need to worry about it sometimes, but we really need to focus on the present moment; what needs to be done." Game 2 featured eight ties before an errant Rams return and a booming kill from Bianca Baker (match-high 14 kills) gave Queen Anne's a 15-13 lead, prompting a Parkside timeout. After the teams returned, Taylor completed an 8-point service run, which included kills from Baker, Sydney Pinder (11 kills) and Titus, stretching the Lions' cushion to 20-13. Baillie Pinder added a kill before the Rams misplayed a return to close Queen Anne's 25-16 Game 2 win.After Sydney Pinder opened Game 3 with a kill, Taylor reeled off eight consecutive service points for a 9-0 lead that was never in jeopardy, as the Lions continued hammering kills - one off a Parkside player's chin and another off a shoulder - but also showed an ability for tapping kills into open spaces."It's being strategic, and that's what I talk to the girls about," Brice said. "On paper, a kill is a kill. It doesn't matter what it looks like.Your job is to get them out of system, or get the kill if you can. It's like chess. You have to be smart when you play. Don't just hit the ball." Helping to orchestrate that strategy was Titus, who finished with 36 assists."Most of the time I'm trying to set up my hitters and just draw the blockers," Titus said. "We definitely look for holes and we're a very strategic team. So I think putting that into play, and talking to my hitters and passers - I couldn't do it without my passers - definitely helps." The Lions were up nine before an errant serve and an ace from Parkside's Lainey Geiser pulled the Rams within 23-16, bringing Brice out of her seat for a timeout."We were not playing volleyball.At all," Brice said. "Just simple mistakes were being made. I needed to do a little snap out there and get 'em back into shape, and just finish the game." The Lions did, with Sydney Pinder driving a kill off a Parkside player's hands before Kaisa Hickson served an ace that just slipped over the net and fell for a 25-16 final."It's awesome," Taylor said of the second conference crown. "Especially as a senior. This is my last year and I really hope to go far this year.This was just the first part of the ride."

title: HALLOWEEN THRILLER
author: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com
content:
HALLOWEEN THRILLER

 Author/Byline: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com | Page: 24 | Section: Sports

 CENTREVILLE - Queen Anne's County High's boys' soccer team was less than a minute away from victory and a regional title Tuesday night.And then, boom.Parkside's Nick Pusey collected a ball in the middle of the field, streaked in alone on goal, and neatly tucked the equalizer into the right side of the net."We had momentum," Queen Anne's head coach Wade Hosler said. "We had possession, and then we lost possession and made a mistake in the middle. And wow. After all that work and being up, and then giving one up with that little time left It's hard to deal with." The Lions stood stunned.That empty feeling was vanquished almost 20 minutes later, when Ryan Lee scored off Nicolas Esper's well-placed pass in the second minute of double overtime to give Queen Anne's a thrilling 3-2 victory for the Class 2A East Region II championship on Halloween night.The top-seed in the Class 2A state playoffs, the Lions (12-2-1) will host eighthseeded Lackey on Friday in a state quarterfinal at 5:30 p.m."Completely different team," said Hosler comparing his team that was thumped 6-0 at Parkside on Sept. 20 to the one that earned Queen Anne's its first regional crown since 2012. "We were tired (in the first game - it was Queen Anne's third game in three days). We had some illness. We had guys who were not 100 percent."So we came into this game pretty healthy and we had done a little shifting with positions and players," Hosler added. "We felt like after that game we got our feet underneath us and made a good run." The Lions went unbeaten in their final seven regular-season games, which included a 1-1 double-overtime draw with perennial South Bayside power James M. Bennett."Got a tie against Bennett, which showed us who we could play with," said Hosler, whose team battled Bennett through a scoreless first half before losing 2-0 to the Clippers in the Bayside Conference championship Oct. 23.Queen Anne's and the second-seeded Rams (10-3-1) were scoreless through Tuesday's first half. But that scoreless stalemate ended, when Parkside's Douglous Bozman came in on the right side of the box and drilled a ground-hugging shot that glanced off the outstretched right hand of Queen Anne's keeper Ethan Keppler and into the left corner for a 1-0 Rams lead 2:35 into the second half.Parkside almost increased its lead 14 minutes later when it dropped a dangerous ball into the box that bounced up on Keppler, who controlled the rebound.Less than 90 seconds later, Queen Anne's captain Billy Schindler sent a rocket into the back of the net that was immediately waved off by officials. But the Lions pulled even with 17:19 remaining, when Adan Canales drove a corner kick toward goal that went off a Parkside player for a 1-1 tie.Then with a little over 7 minutes remaining in regulation, William Nagle launched a throw-toward the 6-yard line that Esper leaped and headed into the back of the net for a 2-1 Queen Anne's lead."He really has an incredible throw," Esper said of Nagle. "And we knew from the beginning, when he threw it. We both made eye contact and I just had to jump for it. It was the best feeling. It would have been good to end it there. But in OT, I guess that makes it better, right?" That feeling of joy was suddenly replaced by shock with under a minute remaining in regulation, when Pusey bolted down the field and knotted the game at 2-2, sending the game into extra time.Parkside came closest to scoring in the first 10-minute overtime, when Keppler dove to make a save at the right post with 6:06 left.Then with almost 2 minutes off the clock in the second OT, Esper found Lee making an outside-inside run from the left side and slid a beautiful feed to his teammate, who sent the game-winner inside the near post then sprinted toward the far flag where he was swallowed by a frenzy of teammates and fans."Didn't really think it was going to go through," Esper said of his winner. "I think that was a perfect pass, perfect diagonal run right in the corner. Just a great way to beat 'em. We lost 6-0 regular season. It's perfect to come back, take that win."Just amazing," Esper said of momentarily vanishing in the postgame celebration."Especially to end regionals.We're regional champs." Hosler agreed."Feels amazing," Queen Anne's head coach said."This is our first region championship since 2012.So it's been awhile. It feels great and these guys have worked extremely hard.They're such a great group of kids. They do everything for each other."

 CENTREVILLE - Shana Corder objects to a longstanding belief."The saying is, 'Every corner is a goal,'" Queen Anne's County High's longtime head field hockey coach said. "That is so so false in the game of field hockey. I don't know who came up with that, but it's not true." Corder's argument gained strength Tuesday afternoon as her top-seeded Lions went 0 for 11 on penalty-corner opportunities through 46 minutes of play against rival Kent Island.Then came the 12th corner."I looked at one of my assistant coaches (Kelsey Johnson) and said, 'OK, 12 years ago today we beat Kent Island (for the regional championship) with my first daughter, Logan, when she played,'" Corder said. "'First time we had beaten them in years.So I'm going with lucky number 12. It's going to go in.' And it went in. Kelsey's like, 'How did you know that?' I was like, 'I didn't. It just sounded good.'" Corder and the topseeded Lions were also feeling good yesterday, after Jordan Bilbo converted a pass from Haley Cole with 13:34 remaining, lifting Queen Anne's to a 1-0 victory over the Buccaneers in the Class 2A East Region I championship.Queen Anne's (14-0) is seeded second in the 2A state tournament, and will host No. 7 seed Centennial on Friday at 4 p.m. in a quarterfinal."We work so hard on our corners," Corder said. "All a corner usually goes down to is if the inserter's getting it down right. Sometimes that doesn't happen, or they fly too fast, or they mess up and it just breaks down. But that was a great executed corner.Jordan finished it off with that tap in. It was beautifully done." But Bilbo admitted her and her teammates were getting a bit frustrated with their missed opportunities.That was partly due to Kent Island making adjustments from the first time the two teams met 13 days earlier."We've watched them a couple of times since and they collapse on one side of the field," Bucs head coach Laura Harding said. "They keep everybody on their team on that side and that's why it's hard to get the ball up the line. So we worked on quick passing and getting the ball over to the other side and transferring the ball over. A lot of give and goes." Queen Anne's earned three corners in the first quarter and seven more in the second. It managed just one in the third before the 12th chance came early in the fourth.Cole got the ball off the insert and struck a shot that went off Bilbo's stick and over the left shoulder of Bucs' goalie Brynja Petursson."It was a dump to Haley Cole and I just happened to be at the perfect spot," Bilbo said. "We all just connected very well."In the third quarter we got a little frustrated with ourselves, but in our huddle after the third quarter, we said, 'Hey, we got this. We can do this.,'" Bilbo said. "We've been working on mental toughness so our mental toughness had to be where it needed to be to get that goal. We all just really wanted it." Queen Anne's finished with 13 corners to none for Kent Island (8-6)."My girls played amazing," said Harding, who started three freshmen and three sophomores.The Lions' defense delivered another outstanding effort, as goalie Cassidy Alexander and company posted their 13th shutout of the season."I have such a tremendous defense that keeps us strong, and keeps us out of trouble, that they just have to give the offense time to put it in," said Corder, whose defense has yielded just one goal all season. "And basically you can tell that by our scores (six one-goal wins). All our games are close. We are not an offensively strong team. We are a defensively strong team. I think it's just paying off. Sometimes it takes us to the third or fourth quarter to get that late goal.We just have to have patience with one another."

title: Eagles rally to oust Colonels - Mistakes, Granado's fourth-quarter TD end season for Colonel Richardson
author: Kyle Ingerson; Special To The Cecil Whig
content:
Eagles rally to oust Colonels - Mistakes, Granado's fourth-quarter TD end season for Colonel Richardson

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Kyle Ingerson; Special To The Cecil Whig | Page: 23A | Section: Sports 
 
 484
 Words

 CHESAPEAKE CITY - Despite being in the midst of a long offensive slump, Bohemia Manor High put together its best quarter of football in recent weeks Friday night, rallying in the fourth quarter to defeat Colonel Richardson in a Class 1A East Regional first-round playoff game.The Eagles advance to Friday's semifinals, traveling to top-seeded Perryville at 7 p.m.Trailing by a point with just under nine minutes to play, Bohemia Manor stopped Colonel Richardson on a fourth-and-2 to get the ball back in Colonel Richardson territory. Two plays later, Junior Council ripped off a 25-yard run to set the Eagles up with a first-and-goal. Xavier Granado then took it in from four yards out to give the Eagles their first lead of the game with 7:12 remaining.Granado credited his offensive line for helping him find the holes necessary to get the go-ahead score."I love my line," Granado said. "They got me anywhere I needed to go and that's all you can hope for in a playoff game." After another defensive stop on the ensuing Colonel Richardson possession, Bohemia Manor found its in familiar territory as its offense had the ball in the final minutes with a chance to seal the victory.The Eagles did just that as a key 18-yard run by Granado, followed by Chris Harris' quarterback keeper on a third-and-3 resulted in a first down. Harris' rushing touchdown in the second quarter put the Eagles within a point at the half."I just let my running back and my o-line do the work," Harris said. "Let them get the yards, burn the clock, get the first downs and seal the win." Colonel Richardson head coach James Jackson thought his team made too many self-inflicted mistakes down the stretch that cost them in a close game.Colonel Richardson led for the majority of the game after taking an early 7-0 lead in the first quarter on quarterback Tarron Hammond's 5-yard touchdown run."We were our own 12th man," Jackson said. "We had some bad snaps and got behind in the distance on drives and it hurt us. It's been like that for us all year but in a playoff game you can't have that." Bo Manor head coach Vince Ricci praised his team for its gritty performance and not letting the results from the previous two weeks carry into the playoff openere. The Eagles entered Friday's contest coming off back-to-back losses against Perryville and Fallston.Bohemia Manor scored a combined two points in the pair of losses.Perryville defeated Bohemia Manor 42-2 in the regular season three weeks ago."We knew coming in that we needed to get back to being gritty and playing Bo Manor football," Ricci said."It takes us back to those first couple weeks when we were winning by grinding out the end of game situations."

title: Stephen Ames looks to add more hardware at Charles Schwab Cup
author: Roberto Jozef

Stephen Ames looks to add more hardware at Charles Schwab Cup

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 The final stage of the PGA Tour Champions tour gets underway as the 34th annual Charles Schwab Cup Championship tees off Nov. 9-12 at the Phoenix Country Golf Club, with ESPN and CBS providing all tournament coverage.In what's been a year full of storylines and record-breaking performances for 59-year-old Stephen Ames, it's been a season like no other - an excellent way to enter this week's Charles Schwab Cup Championship.Now a six-time winner on the senior circuit, Ames, who is a citizen of both Canada and the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago, has won four of his past 13 starts, including shooting 9-under 63 at this year's Boeing Classic, for a record-dominating seven-stroke victory over defending champion Miguel Angel Jimenez. Ames managed to also tie the Boeing Classic record for the lowest score by a winner at 197.Clearly in the zone, Ames is well aware of his strong play throughout but with all the noise, the Canadian keeps his focus on simply enjoying the game he loves."For me, right now I'm just enjoying where I'm at with my games and trying to make the most of it as we go along," Ames said, speaking to reporters at the Shaw Charity Classic. "The confidence is there, there's no doubt about it.Knowing where I'm at and how to fix things instantly when I'm not on the course, how I'm feeling a little bit more relaxed and enjoying it yeah I'm in that zone right now, and it's helpful," said Ames.

title: TEARFUL ENDING - Stroke proves difference as Lions fall short in state semifinals
author: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com
content:
TEARFUL ENDING - Stroke proves difference as Lions fall short in state semifinals

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com | Page: 32 | Section: Sports 
 
 994
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WHEATON - The official in Shana Corder knew it was the correct call.Corder, Queen Anne's County High's head field hockey coach, also knew that call - and the penalty stroke that followed - had the potential to be the deciding factor.It was.Hereford's Maddie Fuller snapped that stroke into the lower right corner of the cage with 2 minutes, 36 seconds remaining in the first quarter Wednesday night, as third-seeded Hereford defeated No. 2 seed Queen Anne's County, 1-0, in a Class 2A state semifinal at John F. Kennedy High School, ending the Lions' unbeaten season.Hereford (15-2) will face fourth-seeded and two-time defending state champion Glenelg (12-2) on Saturday at 5 p.m. for the 2A state title at Paint Branch High School in Burtonsville."It hit Ava's foot," said Corder of the ball that struck Queen Anne's Ava Fields in the circle late in the first quarter. "It was definitely the right call." Corder, who also officiates, said if a shot on goal hits a defender's foot - while the goalie is off to the side - and prevents a potential goal, a stroke can be called.Queen Anne's goalie Cassidy Alexander was off to one side of the cage, likely in an effort to spot the ball in the traffic in front of her.Hereford's shot just happened to hit Fields' foot, drawing the stroke.A senior defender, Fuller stepped up and sent a low drive into the right corner for what proved to be the game's lone goal. It was only the second goal allowed all year by Queen Anne's, which totaled 14 shutouts in a 15-1 season."I just hate losing the game on a stroke because both teams played so good," Corder said. "But that's field hockey, and it was the right call. And the girl who took the stroke, it was a great stroke. There was no way Cassidy was going to get it." The remainder of the game was a defensive stalemate, though Queen Anne's finished with six penalty corners to just one for the Bulls.A Hereford player received a card early in the second quarter and the Bulls had to play down a player. But the Lions could not muster any pressure on goal during that time. One of Queen Anne's best chances came with 3:22 left in the first half, when Abbie Denes drove a ball from the right of the circle that just missed connecting with Gabrielle Scully's stick at the far post.The Lions put another shot wide right with 2:15 left in the first half, and earned two corners in the final 45 seconds of the half, but could not put one past Hereford senior goalie Eliza Greenfield."We just could not get that one touch to go in," Corder said. "I think that was the best game my team's played all year.They definitely rose to the challenge. I'm super proud of them for that. But they weren't connecting with the other person's stick sometimes. You could see it. It would just get away, or it wasn't enough." Hereford's Caitlin Meeker and Queen Anne's Haley Cole each fired wide left early in the third quarter. Greenfield made a save off a Lions corner with 8 minutes left in the third. The Bulls pushed into the circle late in the period but could not beat Alexander.The fourth was basically a rerun of the first three periods, with only a few scoring chances sprinkled in the defensive domination."They played great field hockey tonight," Hereford head coach Caitlin Duvall said of her team, which will bid for its fourth state title under her direction Saturday. "They really communicated. Our goal is to play confidently with strong communication and they executed that."They are a strong program," Duvall said of Queen Anne's. "I knew it was going to be a 50-50 game. I knew it would be difficult to score on them. But they also played a superior game." Alexander made a save on a Bulls' corner with 9:30 left.Queen Anne's got its final corner with 8 minutes left, but couldn't get anything on the cage. One minute later, Greenfield made her final save of the contest."My defense has been outstanding all season long.And they were outstanding tonight," Corder said."Our type games have been one goal," added Corder, whose team won seven games by one-goal margins this season."And the one goal didn't go in our favor this time. But I'm super proud of the kids.Great year."VOLLEYBALL Q. ANNE's 3 KENT ISLAND 0CENTREVILLE - Kayce Titus had 26 kills and Bianca Baker delivered a team-high 10 kills Wednesday as the top-seeded Lions defeated the No. 2 seed Buccaneers, 25-20, 25-13, 25-20 to win the Class 2A East Region II championship.Queen Anne's (16-1) is seeded No. 1 for the 2A state tournament and will host eighth-seeded Lackey on Friday in a quarterfinal at 5 p.m.Titus also had six digs, two aces and two kills for the Lions, who have won 13 straight. Baillie Pinder finished with five kills, two blocks and two digs, and Caroline Taylor totaled 13 digs, six kills, two blocks and one ace.Autumn Huber added 11 digs and one ace, Jensen Nutley netted eight digs and one ace, Mackenzie Doyle had four kills and a block, and Kaisa Hickson contributed five digs and two aces.Kent Island finished the season 13-3.N. DORCHESTER 3 SNOW HILL 1SNOW HILL - Maggie Hubbard had 11 kills and Emily Freeman had six kills to go with five aces as second-seeded North Dorchester defeated No. 1 Snow Hill, 25-18, 25-17, 21-25, 25-23 Wednesday to win the Class 1A East Region II title.North Dorchester (9-8) is seeded sixth in the 1A state tournament and travels to No.3 Clear Spring on Saturday for a 2 p.m. quarterfinal.Brooke Outten finished with eight kills for North Dorchester.

title: Local brothers win big - Bobby Heim Jr. places in four Waterfowl calling contests
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Local brothers win big - Bobby Heim Jr. places in four Waterfowl calling contests

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 833
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Local brothers made a name for themselves at the World Waterfowl Calling Championships, Saturday evening, Nov. 11, in the Easton High School auditorium. The championship preliminaries and finals are featured events during the annual Waterfowl Festival, now in its 52nd year.Bobby Heim Jr. of Wittman and Bryan Heim of Stevensville won the World Championship Team Live Goose Calling competition.Their hearty bear hugs for each other and applause from their fellow competitors and audience of about 300 preceded the presentation of their prizes.The brothers each won $1,000, courtesy of Waterfowl Festival corporate partners, a Stoeger shotgun and a hand-carved decoy trophy from carver Charles Jobes.April Heim shed tears as she took snapshots of her sons onstage. "They're my boys," she said, weeping and smiling. "It's amazing.They've been drawing calls a long time." She and her husband Bobby Heim Sr. held onto their sons' decoy trophies.Bobby Heim placed within the top three positions in three other contests.He won second place in both the World Championship Goose and Live Duck Calling contests, second place with Domingo Sanchez in the Team Live Duck Calling contest, and third place in the World Live Goose Calling championship.The Team Live Goose Calling contest was swept by Eastern Shore contestants.In second place and winning $500 and a plaque each were Teddy Hoover of Preston and Seth Hampton of Denton. Third place winners Trevor Shannahan of Millington and Beau Maverly of Earleville each won $400 each and a plaque.Team Live Duck contest winners won similar prizes.Both adult and teenage callers were, indeed, world class contestants. Playing their calls as instruments, they mimicked the sounds of single waterfowl and flocks of geese and ducks.The calls are usually made of acrylic, the most popular material, as well as wood and polycarbonate. They range in price from $35 to $250, according to 2022 champion John Walls, who owns about 200 calls and has been hunting all kinds of game since he was a kid.Several vendors sold calls during the festival at the Sportsmans Pavilion across the street from the school.The premiere event was the World Championship Goose Calling contest, won for the second straight year by John Walls of Hockessin, Delaware. His $5,000 prize was accompanied by a Benelli shotgun, a Jobes goose decoy, a world championship ring and other prizes.Bobby Heim came only two points behind Walls.In third place was Austin Schelander of Monticello, Minnesota.Another standout was the winner of the two junior calling competitions. Alden Pugh, 16, of Berryville, Virginia, won the Junior World Championship Goose Calling contest for the third year in a row. He also won the Junior World Live Duck Championship for the second straight year.Each of the two contests awarded Pugh $300, and Jobes decoy trophies.The World Team Live Duck Calling Championship featured three teams that went to tie-breakers.With very narrow margins among the final results were Corey Niccum and Mike Benjamin in first place, Domingo Sanchez and Bobby Heim in second place and Ron Laun and Chandler Martin in third.In the World Live Goose Calling Championship, Chance Wadsworth of Prescott, Wisconsin, won first place, Trevor Shannahan of Millington won second and Bobby Heim won third.For the World Live Duck competition, Tyler Heaton of Norton Shore, Michigan, won first place; Bobby Heim placed second; and Mike Benjamin of Rochester, Minnesota won third.World Championship Duck and Live Goose championship winners won $2,000, Franchi and Benelli shotguns, a Jobes decoy trophy and other prizes.In the World Goose Calling competition Austin Schelander of Monticello, Minnesota, finished third behind Bobby Heim in second place and John Walls in first.Seven teams comprising five judges volunteered their time. "The Championship committee took a new approach for selecting judges, inviting those with degrees, past titles and years of experience around fowl," the program stated. Some of the judges competed in championships they didn't adjudicate.The judges sat in cubbies within a blind fronted by tall dried grass that masked them from the competitors and the audience. They listened to callers identified only by numbers, determining the one who sounded best in the field, not who could best operate the call.Teddy Hoover of Preston served as chairman of both the competition and the Sportsman Pavilion. He was also a competitor, winning fifth place with Lee Williams of Church Road, Virginia, in the World Team Live Goose contest.Founded in 1976, the trademarked World Championship Goose Calling Championship is the longest running goose calling championship in the United States.

title: Queen Anne's' title bid blocked - Eagles end Lions' season with sweep in semifinals
author: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com
content:
Queen Anne's' title bid blocked - Eagles end Lions' season with sweep in semifinals

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: William Haufe; bhaufe@chespub.com | Page: 24 | Section: Sports 
 
 1145
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GAITHERSBURG - Queen Anne's County High's volleyball team had regained its footing.Down one game, the Lions rebounded and were leading Centennial through the second game of Tuesday's Class 2A state semifinal at Watkins Mill High School. But the Eagles - despite having their top player briefly sidelined - rallied, scored the last three points of Game 2, and never trailed in Game 3 on the way to a 25-11, 25-22, 25-12 victory over top-seeded Queen Anne's.Fifth-seeded Centennial (13-4) advances to Saturday's 2A state championship at Harford Community College, where it will face sixthseeded Calvert at 4:30 p.m.Calvert earned its title shot with a 3-2 victory over No. 7 seed Williamsport in Tuesday's other semifinal."It's huge," Queen Anne's head coach Nevada Brice said of the Lions' run to the state semifinals that included 14 straight wins, a second straight Bayside Conference title, and a third consecutive Class 2A East Region II crown. "I talk about that North Caroline game (a 3-0 loss on Sept. 19). It was just a big change in our season.It was an eye-opener. That's when we decided we needed to be humble. It sent us in a good direction. They needed to work hard."But I'm so proud of these girls," continued Brice, whose team finished 17-2, went one step further than a year ago when it lost in the state quarterfinals, and is now 34-3 during her two years as head coach. "These girls are the first kids that I coached that are seniors. So they're my pride and joy." Joy Chen's four-point service run staked Centennial to a lead it never surrendered in Game 1. Queen Anne's never served back-toback points and watched the Eagles' lead steadily swell in a 14-point loss."The fast start helped us because I thought Friday (in the quarterfinals), Hereford's fast start, we had to fight through that," said Centennial's 24-year head coach Michael Bossom, who has guided the Eagles to eight state championships. "But I also felt we were capable of fighting back because we had already done it once."But it definitely puts the other team on the back foot, and they're not able to be as aggressive as they want to be because they don't want to make errors," Bossom added. "I kind of thought that set the tone because I thought in the first game they made more service errors, and then I thought in game three, when they were pushing a little bit, they made more service errors. And it's probably uncharacteristic of what they wanted to do." But the Lions bounced back in Game 2. Kills by Sydney Pinder (eight kills) and Bianca Baker (eight kills) helped build an early 4-1 lead. Centennial pulled even at 4-4, but Queen Anne's continued to nose back in front."I felt that (Queen Anne's) did a really nice job, 'cause Game 1 we got ahead," Bossom said. "They could have stopped and they didn't.In Game 1 they came through, they played hard. That's a good team. That's a good coach. That's a good program. Because they played hard and didn't give up. But Game 2, when they got out to that lead, I thought they did exactly what they should have done. They kind of let go Game 1 and started Game 2 strong. But we were doing a nice job of fighting back, pushing through." The Eagles moved to an 11-10 lead. Queen Anne's Caroline Taylor answered with a kill that created the game's fourth tie at 11-all."They started coming back," Brice said of her team. "They started finding that confidence in themselves again. We're fine if we drop a set or two. We're good with that. But it was huge. I'm glad they came back in that second game." Then Centennial senior outside hitter Mailinh Godschall, who is slated to play Libero at Duke University next year, rolled her ankle and was sidelined. Taylor promptly reeled off three consecutive service points - the Lions' longest run of the match - pushing Queen Anne's to a 14-11 lead."Mailinh goes down, they take advantage of that," Bossom said."They get three real quick points.I call timeout. Basically what I told my team was that this team isn't built around one person. 'You guys are all on this team for a reason.And you have to believe in each other. You just got to go out there and do what you do in practice.'" The Eagles pulled within 16-15 before Godshchall returned."I felt when Mailinh came back on the court our energy took a huge jump," Bossom said. "And I think they just kind of went ('She's back').And then the funny thing is we got the next three points and she didn't touch the ball." Centennial moved to a 22-20 lead before the Lions responded with back-to-back kills for the game's seventh tie at 22-all. But a long Queen Anne's serve, Godschall's gentle tap for a kill, and Amanda Xu's kill gave the Eagles the game's final three points for the 25-22 win."Our serves killed us," Brice said."We missed six serves in the second set and it was still, 22-25. We were dropping serves back to back.So it was like, 'Momentum. Lost momentum. Momentum. Lost momentum.'" Game 3 was back and forth early. Godschall put down one of her match-high 15 kills. Pinder answered with a kill. A Godschall kill and ace moved Centennial to a 3-1 lead. A kill from Baker pulled Queen Anne's within 3-2 before the Eagles started pulling away, as senior middle hitter Kaley MacLellan (10 kills) hammered kills to give Centennial leads of 5-2, 10-5 and 14-5."They started to focus on Mailinh and K-Mac is just going up there smacking," Bossom said of MacLellan. "The other thing is I think they got a little careful and it allowed us to pass a little better." A six-point service run by Christine Liu and MacLellan's threepoint burst extended the Eagles' lead to 19-6. A Pinder kill got the Lions within 20-11, but Queen Anne's wouldn't get any closer, as MacLellan delivered the match's final point with her final kill."Amazing," Brice said of Godschall and MacLellan. "That's who we basically planned everything around. I always teach my girls, appreciate the strong athletes. If it's a good hit, it's a great hit. We were trying to keep them out of system so they couldn't get the balls to them. But they're really good at being out of system too." Notes: Pinder had two blocks and Baker one. Kayce Titus finished with 19 assists, seven digs, a block and one ace for Queen Anne's. The Lions also got 11 digs and one kill from Jensen Nutley, two kills and a dig from Mackenzie Doyle, three kills, three digs and a block from Taylor, and 11 digs and two assists from Autumn Huber.

title: Redcoat Fisherman aims to boost carp fishing at Waterfowl
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Redcoat Fisherman aims to boost carp fishing at Waterfowl

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 569
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Since his childhood in the United Kingdom, the Redcoat Fisherman has always loved catching carp.On the gray and slightly rainy first full day of Waterfowl Festival activities, Simon, the Redcoat Fisherman, set up shop at Bay Street Ponds.Simon - who doesn't give out his last name when wearing his red coat - spent the early afternoon on Friday waiting for his lines to go. Nearby he had covered a folding table in different bait products and hooks."It's all about this," he said."Sitting on a bank, relaxing (and) enjoying the moment.Doing nothing but sitting there and waiting for lines to go." For Simon, a day where no carps are caught is no big deal."One of the places I sit all day, I caught nothing, but I watched bald eagles fly past me all day," he said, adding that the experience is truly about "resetting your batteries" and observing nature.When he moved to the United States, Simon learned that carp fishing was not as popular as it is in Europe."(Americans) think it's a junk fish," he said. "They go for bass. Bass is a big fish in the U.S." As the Redcoat Fisherman, Simon wants to see carp fishing become more popular in the United States. With all of the people across the (Atlantic) pond that love carp fishing, he thinks tourism would "go through the roof" if carp fishing in the U.S. were advertised more."There's potential," he said."There is severe potential." And that was a part of his mission at the Waterfowl Festival this year: to educate people on the value of carp fishing."It's teaching them and showing them examples of what we have," he said.Simon is a member of the American Carp Society, which was founded in 2002 to promote and educate people on carp fishing in the country, according to its website.He works alongside Amped Up Outdoors, which he said is a group that takes people out into nature to fish.A first-timer at the Waterfowl Festival, Simon said festival organizers reached out to him about joining the festival due to all the fishing he does at Skipton Creek.Until the festival ended on Sunday, Simon said he woulld be camping out in a white sprinter van. Carp fishing lasts longer than a day, he said."I will stay for the duration of nighttime and see what I can catch," he said.When he catches a carp, Simon takes a photo of it and releases it back into the water he caught it in."Catch, photo and release," he said.But there's one more step in that cycle. If the fish has any injuries, Simon said he tends to them."We even use a special material that is made solely for carp so that the hook doesn't cause infections," he said.From Texas to Vermont, Simon has fished all over the U.S. He said that wherever he travels, he always takes a rod with him."If I can put my rod in the water," he said. "I'm going to fish it." 
 
 Caption: MAGGIE TROVATO/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Simon, who goes by the Redcoat Fisherman, shows a handful of pineapple boilies, a corn product that is used as bait, at Bay Street Ponds in Easton during the Waterfowl Festival on Nov. 10. Simon said boilies come in various sizes.
 
MAGGIE TROVA TO/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Simon, the Redcoat Fisherman, at Bay Street Ponds in Easton during the Waterfowl Festival on Nov. 10. This is Simon's first year at the Waterfowl Festival

title: Ohtani first two-time unanimous MVP - Baseball
content:
Ohtani first two-time unanimous MVP - Baseball

 November 17, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 30 | Section: Sports 
 
 515
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NEW YORK - Sho-hei Ohtani, who has captivated baseball with his unprecedented combination of high-level hitting and premium pitching, became the first two-time unanimous Most Valuable Player when he won the American League honor on Thursday.Ohtani, a free agent after finishing his contract with the Los Angeles Angels, received all 30 first-place votes and 420 points in voting by the Baseball Writers' Association of America. He was a unanimous MVP in 2021 and finished second to the Yankees' Aaron Judge in voting last year.Atlanta's Ronald Acuña Jr. won the National League honor, also a unanimous pick. There have been 21 unanimous MVPs, and this year marked the first time since the awards began in 1931 that the winner in each league was unanimous.Corey Seager was second with 24 second--place votes and 264 points, and Texas teammate Marcus Semien was third with five second-place votes and 216 points. Balloting took place before the postseason, when the Rangers won their first World Series title.Ohtani led the AL with 44 homers and hit .304 with 96 RBIs, eight triples and 20 stolen bases in a season at the plate that ended Sept. 3 because of an oblique injury.Ohtani was 10-5 with a 3.14 ERA in 23 starts on the mound, striking out 167 and walking 55 in 132 innings before tearing the ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow on Aug. 23.Not even Babe Ruth starred at such lofty levels on the mound and at the plate in the same season. Ruth batted .300 with 11 homers and 61 RBIs in 1918 while going 13-7 with a 2.22 ERA for Boston, then hit .322 with 29 homers and 113 RBIs in 1919 while going 9-5 with a 2.97 ERA. He made just five mound appearances in his final 16 seasons.Ohtani averaged 96.8 mph with his four-seam fastball, 26th among qualified pitchers, and a 94.4 mph exit velocity off his bat, third among qualified batters behind Judge and Atlanta's Ronald Acuña Jr. Ohtani led the majors with a 10.0 Wins Above Replacement, according to Baseball Reference.A left-handed batter and right-handed pitcher, Ohtani had right elbow surgery on Sept. 19 and the team said he won't pitch again until 2025. He underwent Tommy John surgery in October 2018 and Ohtani's agent, Nez Balelo, did not specify details of the latest operation.Before the injury, it appeared Ohtani could gain the first $500 million contract in baseball history. The three-time AllStar has a .274 average, 171 homers, 437 RBIs and 86 steals in six major league seasons and is 38-19 with a 3.01 ERA in 86 starts with 608 strikeouts in 481 2/3 innings.Ohtani last spoke with reporters on Aug. 9, two weeks before he hurt the elbow while pitching against Cincinnati.Ohtani won AL Rookie of the Year in 2018 after leaving the Pacific League's Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters to sign with the Angels. He was voted the Pacific League's MVP in 2016.

 It's time for another thrilling NFLSunday, as the Baltimore Ravens head to the City of Angels for their Week 12 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFiStadium in Los Angeles, Sunday, Nov. 26, with the game broadcast live on NBC.It's been yet another MVP season for the Lamar Jackson, as the Pompano Beach, Florida, native and the Baltimore Ravens have led the AFC North all season long - including outscoring three different teams with a winning record by a combined 103-12 while holding teams to an impressive total of 13.8 points per game (as of Nov. 5).And, if the Ravens weren't scary enough for their opponents, 26-year-old Jackson has been world class straight out of the gates, having already thrown for over 2,000 passing yards and counting, while completing 70.5 per cent of his passes - the highest mark of his career.In his two encounters against the Chargers, Jackson holds a passer rating of 83.0 with 371 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions.The last time Baltimore clashed with Los Angeles, the Ravens put on a dominant performance, winning 34-6 and holding the Chargers to 208 total yards and one touchdown, never allowing quarterback Justin Herbert to find his groove, including an interception by then-Ravens safety DeShon Elliot.Overall, the Ravens are 8-6-0 against the Chargers and they'll look to improve that record this weekend with an explosive offence that's proven to be a handful for any opposing teams.

Simultaneously, commentators analyze the bidding and play. Sometimes, though, it is harder for the commentators to find the winning play, when looking at all 52 cards, than it is for the declarer, who can see only 26.Today's deal was played by the late Lou Bluhm during the final of a Vanderbilt teams.Two clubs was Drury, showing a maximum pass with spade support.The defenders began with two rounds of trumps. At this point, the commentators decided the contract had to finish down one, but Bluhm had seen the way home. After winning the second trick in the dummy, declarer cashed the heart ace and ruffed a heart in hand. Entering the dummy twice in diamonds, Bluhm ruffed two more hearts in his hand. So West ruffed. Now, though, he had to open up the club suit, giving a trick to South's king.Bluhm had gained one trump trick from the dummy reversal, ruffing those hearts in his hand, and one club trick from the endplay.©2023, UNITED FEATURE SYNDICATE DISTRIBUTED BY ANDREWS MCMEEL SYNDICATION FOR UFS

title: Historic Laurel Park Faces Shaky Future
author: Angelique Gingras; Capital News Service
content:
Historic Laurel Park Faces Shaky Future

 November 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Angelique Gingras; Capital News Service | Page: 12 | Section: News 
 
 1332
 Words 

 Read News Document

 LAUREL - Laurel Park's horse racing future hinges on a proposal to be made to the Maryland General Assembly next month that could alter Thoroughbred racing in the state as we know it.A determination will come from the Maryland Thoroughbred Racetrack Operating Authority, a commission established by Senate Bill 720 in the 2023 legislative session, to make recommendations on the redevelopment of Laurel Park and Pimlico racecourses - the two most prominent, historic, but aging, Thoroughbred racetracks in the state.Chairman Greg Cross, an experienced attorney with Venable LLP appointed to the racetrack operating authority in June, said the commission is tasked with assessing the conditions of the tracks and recommending a path forward for the industry.While the commission has not confirmed it, all signs point to a scenario that would end more than 100 years of racing in Laurel- whether it's turned into a training facility or closed as an equine center altogether."There has not been enough money to redevelop both tracks based upon what the legislature has authorized," Cross told Capital News Service."The Preakness is in Baltimore and it's going to stay in Baltimore, and so we have to put ourselves in a position to be a good host to the Preakness, and then we have to figure out what money we have left and what we can do with that money most efficiently."The state has authorized $375 million to renovate the race courses.Craig Fravel, executive vice chairman of 1/ST Racing and Gaming, a division of The Stronach Group that owns Laurel Park and Pimlico, told Capital News Service, "Ultimately Laurel would be transitioning away from both racing and training in all likelihood."Closing Laurel would end 112 years of racing history at the track, and change the course of a pastime that dates to pre-Revolutionary War days. The Maryland Jockey Club, which runs the state's Thoroughbred tracks, was founded in 1743, followed by the first official Thoroughbred horse race two years later.Baltimore's Pimlico Race Course - the second-oldest racetrack in the nation behind Saratoga Race Course in Saratoga Springs, New York - opened in 1870 and celebrated its 148th running of the Preakness Stakes in May. The Preakness is the state's premier horse race and the second leg of the most famous Thoroughbred racing series in the U.S. - the Triple Crown.Anne Arundel County's Laurel Park, home of the Maryland Million, debuted in 1911, followed by a number of other race courses over the years, including Bowie and Marlboro race tracks in 1914 and Rosecroft Raceway in 1949 - all which have since closed. Ocean Downs, a harness track, and Timonium racecourses still run seasonal races.But the hey-day for horse racing has long since passed.Pimlico and Laurel Park are both well overdue for renovation. Some facilities, including the clubhouse, backstretch and grandstands date back to the mid-20th century. In fact, Pimlico was forced to close a portion of its grandstand weeks before the Preakness in 2019 over concerns of its deterioration.The degeneration of the tracks - not to mention the decrease in revenue amid the pandemic and the rise of online sports betting - has led to declining participation, attendance and prestige."With the old, dilapidated, antiquated facilities, you don't attract some of the bigger and better outfits," said Tim Keefe, president of the Maryland Thoroughbred Horsemen's Association. "It's very important for the livelihood and longevity of the sport in Maryland to upgrade its facilities."And this isn't the first time that Maryland has considered consolidating its racing industry.According to a 1949 Associated Press article, former Maryland governor William Preston Lane Jr. withdrew his support of a bill to close Pimlico and move all racing days to Laurel, because there was overwhelming public support for keeping the then-79-year-old Baltimore facility running.Fast-forward 70 years to a near-identical circumstance, when in 2019, The Stronach Group considered moving the Preakness Stakes to the Anne Arundel County site because the conditions at Pimlico were too deteriorated to continue hosting the second leg of the Triple Crown.This, in turn, prompted the City of Baltimore to file a lawsuit against the owners, The Stronach Group and its affiliates, to obtain Pimlico through condemnation. The lawsuit was dropped in the subsequent months, and the owners reached an agreement to keep the Preakness in Baltimore.In 2020, the Maryland Stadium Authority was brought in to assess the planning, design and construction of the Laurel Park and Pimlico facilities.The Racing and Community Development Act of 2020 authorized the MSA to finance up to $375 million to redevelop both parks - a sum equal to the original cost of moving everything to Laurel the year before.It quickly became clear that conditions at both sites would require more than the estimates to rehabilitate, particularly with costs worsened by pandemic supply chain issues."We worked with the stakeholders for two and a half years, coming up with different plans that they wanted for the horse industry and Stronach," said Gary McGuigan, executive vice president of the Stadium Authority."We provided cost estimates for all those ideas and they all came in vastly over what the statutory limit is for the bonds."After two years without a shovel in the ground, new legislation was proposed in 2022. House Bill 897 required the Stadium Authority and the Maryland Economic Development Corporation to report to the Maryland General Assembly on the feasibility of renovating Laurel and Pimlico with the new cost estimates.That's what turned the tables back on Laurel."The cheapest scenario was $100 million over budget, and that was Pimlico redeveloped (to) be training and racing, and have Laurel just be a training facility," said McGuigan. "We can't do anything unless the state authorizes some more money."The economic development corporation's report pushed Laurel to the edge.Its Sept. 2022 feasibility report to the General Assembly rated components of the Laurel facility either "poor" or "bad," including the clubhouse and grandstand roofs, HVAC, plumbing and electrical systems.The corporation determined that "the structures at Laurel do not warrant additional investment, and demolition is the next logical step."The racetrack operating authority has been holding frequent meetings with the state's top racing affiliates to gather recommendations for its final report. At a Sept. 29 meeting, The Stronach Group and the Maryland Jockey Club called the redevelopment of Pimlico as the future home of Maryland racing a key consideration for the Authority."The idea of there being one racetrack in the state of Maryland is not something that is unique or unusual," said 1/ST's Fravel at the Sept. 29 meeting of the racetrack operating authority."Simply put, because it's so expensive to maintain these facilities and operate them, we need to find better and more efficient models."Despite the mounting criticism of Laurel, the support for shifting to Pimlico isn't universal."The idea that Laurel won't be a part of the big picture moving forward concerns me very much," said Keefe, of the Maryland Thoroughbred Horsemen's Association."But change is difficult for everyone and if the reality is that way, we have to move forward. I'm confident that in some respect we will be able to adjust."Outside Laurel, the panel is considering other ideas, including the renovation of the training center at the former Bowie Race Track or breaking ground on newer sites.The racetrack operating authority's report must be submitted to the General Assembly by Dec. 1. After the recommendation is made, it will be up to the General Assembly to lay out plans for its implementation."I'm confident with the abilities of this racing authority that (the plan) will move forward in some way, shape or form," said Keefe. "It wasn't going anywhere prior to the implementation of the Authority. I'm confident that it's because of the leadership with Greg Cross and the rest of the team that the governor has appointed to this authority that something will move forward." 
 
 Caption: JAY CANNON/CAPITAL NEWS SERVICE
 
The caption for this photo is here: Pimlico racetrack nearly closed in 2019, when, weeks before the Preakness Stakes, the deterioration of its grandstands made them unusable. (Jay Cannon/Capital News Service)

title: Athlete back in action with a new trike - Dantrail Hicks overcomes cerebral palsy to compete in Special Olympics
author: Tamara Forte; Special To The Star Democrat
content:
Athlete back in action with a new trike - Dantrail Hicks overcomes cerebral palsy to compete in Special Olympics

 November 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tamara Forte; Special To The Star Democrat | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1399
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - The right time. The right place. The right people.Sometimes all the details align even better than we could plan. Linda Buckle, a physical therapist at Advanced Orthopedics in Chestertown, was the right person, at the right place, at the right time. On July 5, 2023, Buckle met and treated her patient Dantrail Hicks, 42, for knee pain and swelling. Buckle quickly learned that Hicks has struggled with cerebral palsy his entire life.Cerebral palsy (cerebral palsy) is a group of disorders that affect a person's ability to move and maintain balance and posture. Cerebral means having to do with the brain. Palsy means weakness or problems with using the muscles.Cerebral palsy is caused by abnormal brain development or damage to the developing brain that affects a person's ability to control his muscles. Severe cerebral palsy (like Hick's) may use special equipment to be able to walk and might need lifelong care. cerebral palsy does not get worse over time, though the exact symptoms can change over a person's lifetime.Even with severe cerebral palsy, Hicks is a two-time Special Olympics bench press champion, a two-time gold medalist in the Maryland Special Olympics cycling championship, and a bronze medalist in the U.S. National Cycling Championship. Hicks has over 20 gold medals from 21 years of participating in the Special Olympics. But, a couple months ago, when Buckle and Hicks first met, he could lift no weight with his legs.Coincidentally, Hick's former Kent County High School coach Dan Zottarelli was a patient at the same clinic.During these sessions, Buckle learned how Zottarelli had mentored and trained Hicks from a shy and quiet high school freshman (who could not lift 45 pounds) to a confident high school senior (who benched 180-200 pounds) - more than his total body weight.Zottarelli proudly described Hicks as a "fine young man that is bubbly and funny." He noted Hicks had turned into a local hero at Kent County High School, a hero that the school, community, and even the nation cheered for, cheered on and was inspired by.During his recent physical therapy sessions, Hicks gravitated to the stationary bike. Buckle explained the clinic only has two stationary bikes. Hicks can only ride one of the clinic's bikes, as his muscle limitations require his feet to be strapped to the pedals in order to ride. Buckle laughed that Hicks "never wanted to get off the bike" during therapy sessions." She noted Hicks improvements, "his right leg is stronger than his left. He now lifts 10 pounds on the right and 8 pounds on the left. When we started, he couldn't lift any weight. So, the bicycling is helping him tremendously as he pushes himself on the bike to the point he is sweating." But there is always a line of people waiting at the clinic to use these stationary bikes to build and strengthen their bodies, she noted.During his physical therapy session, Hicks told Linda, "I gotta get a bike. I want to buy a bike. I am looking at a bike." Buckle soon learned Hicks did have a trike, or tricycle, that he loved to ride, but it was kept in a shed and hadn't been used for more than ten years.Back in high school, Zottarelli, surprisingly, too learned Hicks could ride a bike during a school training session. When seeing Hicks pedal a stationary bike at school at age 16, Zottarelli questioned why Hicks never told him he could ride. Hicks smiled and answered back, "You never asked me." Zottarelli saw how much Hicks loved the bike and knew that it was a good way to train and condition. So, Zottarelli invested his own money and bought Hicks a blue Miami Sun tricycle. This trike opened up many adventures for both Zottarelli and Hicks. In high school, Hicks used to ride this bike in the hallway.Hicks said, "It was good therapy for my legs." Upon qualifying and being invited to the 1999 United States National Cycling Championship in Fort Smith, Arkansas, Zottarelli and Hicks both flew to Arkansas and had the trike shipped too. To pay for this trip, Zottarelli held two yard sales and raised $1,800. That was Hick's first and only trip on a plane to date.With all race details in place, the trike was shipped to the race director at the U.S. National Cycling Championship, who built it again upon arrival. The race director remapped the track to exclude the hilly terrain with Hicks in mind. But Hick's trike started going too fast. The trike wobbled. Hick's feet were taped to the pedals. Zottarelli, who was running next to Hicks, went to catch Hicks and caught his own leg in the trike tire instead. This broke the specially made trike. Luckily, Hick's friendly nature encouraged other cyclists to help. He came in third place, using another rider's bike.Buckle hearing the trike stories during the multiple therapy visits each week, was curious. Buckle asked Hicks if they could go look at the trike one Saturday. Hicks said he didn't think she would really go. That Saturday came and both Hicks and Buckle drove together and found the trike."All the tires and tubes were shot.The brakes were shot. The handlebars were shot. It needed an overhaul from the mechanical standpoint," Buckle explained. She wanted to help but also would need some help.The blue trike took about six weeks to repair. Kelly Coleman, of Rock Hall, was instrumental in finalizing the straps so Hicks could manage them easily with his left hand.In 2015, Diana Laclaire, Kent County High School physical therapist, did the original pedal modification for the Olympic event. This time around, Buckle consulted with LaClaire regarding the addition of the Velcro straps for the pedals.Buckle explains this trike is just the first model or prototype, "The pedals are still a little difficult to manage but at this point, with a little assistance, he can get on the trike and get back to cycling. Kelly and I plan to refine the pedals this winter." "My friend, Daniel Ryan of Rock Hall, helped me pick up the trike, and he took over the entire job gratis, repairing and painting the bike red, as Hicks had requested. All of the other supplies for the trike restoration were covered by an anonymous donor (about $170)." In addition, Buckle's neighbors, Colleen and Andy Stapp, donated the fancy flashing rechargeable light for the front handle bars.On a recent Thursday, Hicks was reunited with his trike. Hicks explained when he saw his newly repaired bike, it was like when someone fixes up an old car. It was the same feeling and excitement. They rolled the bike right into the clinic to meet Hicks.When asked what keeps him going, Hicks said it's the therapy and exercise."The sports keep me going because I kept setting a whole bunch of state records. I was weighing 120 and benched 200," Hicks said. "No one ever broke that record before or yet. That was the best because it made me stronger." Added Buckle, "pedaling the bike and getting that exercise increases your endorphin levels and makes you happy. There's a certain degree about what exercise does for us." Now that Hicks is reunited with his trike again, will there be more races in the futureft"If I had the right kind of bike, the right coach, and the right sponsors, I probably would do races again," Hicks said. "I'd do it." With a huge smile, riding the newly repaired trike, Hicks shared he was given a red bike for Christmas when he was 5 years old, but he could never ride it because it didn't have straps for his feet - 37 years later, Hicks now gets to ride his red bike."It takes a village to make it to the finish line," Buckle said."Be positive," Hicks advised."With cerebral palsy my life is different.I see a lot of people who don't have cerebral palsy complain. And I am like you can get up, you don't have to get a walker to walk to the door. You want to complain? Man, I would do anything to trade places with that person cause I wanted to be a boxer so bad. I think about it all the time. But I know I can't do it.You don't know how good you got it though. I have good days and bad days. I try to stay positive."

title: Rivera tackling a familiar role - Will call defense for Commanders
content:
Rivera tackling a familiar role - Will call defense for Commanders

 ASHBURN, Va. - Twelve games and eight losses into a season that has slipped away from the Washington Commanders, Ron Rivera made the move he felt necessary to try to turn things around by firing defensive coordinator Jack Del Rio.Owner Josh Harris approved the move, which saved Rivera's job for now.Rivera is taking over the defensive play-calling duties - an adjustment for the veteran coach and his team just in time to host the AFC East-leading Miami Dolphins and their NFLbest offense.Rivera wants the defense, which ranks 29th of 32 teams and gave up 431 yards Thursday in a 45-10 loss at Dallas, to play faster.It's on him to make that happen."It's most certainly different and just takes a little bit to get used to," said Rivera, who last did this with Carolina in 2018 when he fired defensive coordinator Eric Washington."The biggest thing is just paying attention and watching the game tape and really just taking the notes from each game that we've had this year. I think it's just a matter of getting a sense and a feel for what our guys do best, and that will come as each game unfolds."In preparation for their game against the Dolphins, players practiced with helmets Wednesday - a departure from previous weeks - to get used to Rivera calling the plays. Already, the retired linebacker is making his voice heard."It's exciting seeing coach be hands-on and more involved with the defense," defensive tackle Jonathan Allen said. "I'm looking forward to seeing how we respond."After three full seasons and more than half of another with Del Rio in charge, defenders acknowledged it's weird not having him and defensive backs coach Brent Vieselmeyer on the practice field.But it's not surprising Rivera made the moves after the Commanders allowed 290-plus yards in 11 of 12 games and more than 30 points seven times."We could be as good as we want to be, but this league it's not about potential, it's about production," cornerback Kendall Fuller said."It's just about us going out there, executing and making the plays that we need to make to win football games."Fuller said it's incumbent on him and his teammates to make good on the plays Rivera calls. To read and react faster, the defense will be simplified from what Del Rio was running."When you're not thinking, you're playing fast," Allen said."We've got a lot of young guys on the back end. Have them thinking less and just playing faster, and that includes the linebackers and the D-line."Quarterback Sam Howell, while expressing disappointment in the firings of Del Rio and Vieselmeyer, does not expect the changes to affect much of his dealings with offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy.Howell and Bieniemy have worked together closely dating to offseason workouts."He learns more about me, and I learn more about him every single week as we kind of go through this thing," said Howell, who leads the league with 323 completions, 486 attempts, 3,339 passing yards and 55 times sacked and is tied with Buffalo's Josh Allen for the most interceptions with 13."(Bieniemy has) always asked for my feedback and input, and he's always respected my opinion as far as if it's something I do like, something I don't like. He's been very good about stuff like that. It's fun to play for a coach that values your opinion."

 LOS ANGELES - Joe Flacco took the first reps in practice for the Cleveland Browns on Wednesday, and it could happen again for their game against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday.Browns coach Kevin Stefanski said Flacco was the backup quarterback this week, which would put the Super Bowl 47 MVP in line to start if rookie Dorian Thompson-Robinson does not clear concussion protocol."No reason to make any decisions just yet," Stefanski said. "We'll see how it goes."Flacco signed with the Browns (7-4) on Nov. 20 after starter Deshaun Watson was ruled out for the season because of a right shoulder injury, joining Thompson-Robinson and P.J. Walker at the position.Thompson-Robinson was injured in a 29-12 loss to the Denver Broncos on Sunday, putting Flacco in line to play for the first time since starting for the New York Jets in the 2022 season finale. Flacco was 18 of 33 passing for 149 yards in the Jets' 11-6 loss to the Miami Dolphins.With the Browns spending the week in Los Angeles, including practicing at UCLA, Stefanski believes the format is conducive to preparing the 38-yearold Flacco in case he has to play."The nice part is we're all under one roof, so it's easy to meet extra on an off day if the guys are in the building and they want to swing by so that's the nice part," Stefanski said. "We're all together."This is Flacco's fourth NFL team, and Stefanski believes that previous experience is helping with the adjustment."Joe, as you guys know, has been in a bunch of different systems, been in a bunch of different buildings, so he knows how it works," Stefanski said. "He knows how different operations have different nuance, if you will, so he's getting up to speed with what we do.He's done a nice job."There might be more adjustments for Stefanski, offensive coordinator Alex Van Pelt and the Browns, who built a system for mobile passers in Watson, Thompson-Robinson and Walker.Flacco, who has thrown for 42,320 yards and 232 touchdowns with 147 interceptions in 183 games for Baltimore, Denver and the Jets, is not exactly known for his elusiveness."I'm sure we'll have a few more wrinkles in there," left guard Joel Bitonio said.Thompson-Robinson's status isn't the only question mark going into the game against the Rams (5-6).Defensive end Myles Garrett did not practice because of a shoulder injury, one of several players held out.Garrett left Denver with his arm in a sling, but Stefanski and teammates expressed optimism he would be able to play. He'll find a way."Others who did not participate included wide receiver Amari Cooper (ribs), running back Kareem Hunt (groin), right guard Wyatt Teller (calf) and cornerback Denzel Ward (shoulder).In spite of those absences, the Browns are currently in a playoff spot and are determined to hold it.

And coach grew up there.Had his dad got a job at Army, I'm sure he'd be on the right side of the rivalry."Monken, who spent five years as a Navy assistant, said he met Belichick when the Patriots coach stopped by in the offseason after one of the team's Super Bowl wins because he wanted to watch tape of the Army running game. And when you hear 'Belichick' and 'Gillette Stadium,' you think of winning," Navy defensive lineman Jacob Busic said.
