title: TIME TRIALS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
TIME TRIALS

 February 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1299
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Giuseppe Mellinger needed a late block.Tremaine Jackson needed an extra minute.
And Scottie Ford. Well, he needed more time than either one of them.
No matter the time frame, Jackson, Ford and Mellinger each finished with the same result Saturday night at Queen Anne's County High, winning their respective weight classes at the Class 2A-1A East Regional wrestling championships.
"He's been one of our elite wrestlers for three years now," Queen Anne's head coach David Stricker said of Jackson, who with his 5-3 overtime victory against Rising Sun's Xzavier Brown in the 126-pound final earned his 99th career win. "Tremaine, he's just so quick. And his power has really come along this year. When he gets in on a leg it's really hard to fend off."
Saturday's region final was the third time Jackson and Brown faced off this season. Brown pieced together an 8-3 decision at the Westminster Duals in late December, then earned a 3-1 overtime win when the two met in the 2A-1A East Regional Duals earlier this month. Their third encounter would also take longer than six minutes.
"They've been wrestling each other since youth, so they've known each other really well," Stricker said. "I'm not surprised it went that far."
A senior, Jackson (35-3) scored a first-period takedown, but Brown escaped with 44 seconds left in the period to make it 2-1 after one. Brown (35-8) rode Jackson through a scoreless second period, and hit a reversal 11 seconds into the third period for a 3-2 lead. Jackson then got an escape off a restart with 15 seconds left in the third to forge a 3-3 tie, sending the match into a 1-minute overtime.
"It's obviously been a bit harder because they've been training him, trying to study my style, his coaches," Jackson said. "They obviously know me very well, the good moves I do. So yeah, it definitely was a lot more difficult than the other times wrestling him."
Brown got in a single-leg shot in the overtime, but Jackson blocked, spun and earned the takedown for the 5-3 sudden victory.
"My last match at the high school, and what was going through my head was, I can't lose," said Jackson, whose second regional title came five days after winning his third Bayside Conference crown. "I feel great. I put in the work. I think I've got a good shot of getting in the state finals."
Ford also had a familiar opponent in his 138-pound final — Parkside junior Rocco Tully — who the Kent County sophomore decisioned 6-0 in the Bayside championship five days earlier.
"I knew it was going to be tougher," said Ford, who coupled two takedowns with a reversal for Monday's 6-0 victory. "Every time you wrestle somebody it feels like it gets tougher and tougher. They always learn from it. I was nervous. I would have much rather faced somebody else I hadn't seen before."
After a scoreless first period, Ford (37-1) hit a switch off bottom for a reversal with 35 seconds left in the second period for a 2-0 lead. Tully (35-9) scored a takedown with 44 seconds to go in the third and rode Ford the rest of the period, forcing overtime.
Neither wrestler scored in the 1-minute overtime. Starting on top, Ford rode Tully through the first 30-second sudden-victory period. Less than two seconds into the second 30-second period, Ford reversed Tully and rode out the remainder of the period on top for the 4-2 win.
"I knew I had a good switch on him because on Monday I had a nice switch," Ford said. "He knows how to throw legs, so he's really tough on top, but I knew I could get out. I just beat him off the whistle."
Something that did not surprise Kent County head coach Chris Yiannakis.
"He's been on that switch," Yiannakis said of Ford. "That's one of his number one escapes from bottom. Most people can't stop it. It's so fast. Rocco did stop it in the first couple of periods though. He just wore him down by the final (period) and he couldn't stop it."
The 175-pound final was yet another Bayside rematch, as Mellinger (36-5) clashed with Parkside's Canaan Mapp (24-8) for the third time this season.
"The first time we wrestled he actually was more aggressive," said Mellinger, who defeated Mapp via a 12-4 major decision during the dual-meet season. "He would actually tie up with me and stuff. So that allowed me to work my offense. The second time, at Baysides (a 7-2 Mellinger win), he would run around, he kept moving, but I got a few takedowns there.
"This time, because I think his coaches were telling him how to make some good adjustments, he wasn't tying up," Mellinger continued. "He was keeping me at a distance. He would try to work in some shots, I would try to work in mine. But we both got a good shot defense. And then when we're so far apart, it's hard to score points."
Mellinger got a double-leg takedown 54 seconds into the match, but Mapp escaped 11 seconds later, making it 2-1 heading into the second. Mapp escaped five seconds into he second period to tie the match.
It remained that way until 18 seconds into the third, when Mellinger, starting on bottom, escaped to take a 3-2 lead. Mellinger blocked a shot midway through the period before a neutral restart with 41 seconds left. Mellinger got in a shot, but Mapp countered with a shot with less than 20 seconds left. The Kent Island senior, who was named the Bayside Conference's defensive player of the year in football for 2023, could not be taken down though, hanging on for the 3-2 win.
"I started getting a little nervous at the end when I took a shot and then he re-shot and got in on my leg with like 15 seconds left," Mellinger said. "And I was able to defend that because if he had gotten that and I didn't get up in time, that would have been the match."
It was Mellinger's first regional title.
"It's nice to win, said Mellinger, whose younger sister Lilliana won the 120-pound title at Friday night's girls 2A-1A East Regional. "My sister and I, we're both Bayside champions. Now, we're both regional champions. Now, we're both competing for a state title. That's cool. It's a lot of fun."
Said Kent Island head coach Tommy Sitar of Mellinger, "He had another great tournament. He worked really well in his matches leading up to the final, and fortunately got the win in the final. It's hard to beat a wrestler three times in a season. It's a good feat."
Kent Island seniors Greg Couch (132) and Cody Sandefer (144) each took runner-up honors, and seniors Brandon Adler (157) and Nick Morey (190) each won their consolation final to place third.
The top four in each weight class advance to this year's state tournament, which begins Thursday at the Show Place Arena in Upper Marlboro and concludes Saturday.
Stephen Decatur and Rising Sun each advanced nine to states, while North Caroline finished with the most wrestlers from a North Bayside school, qualifying six and two alternates.
"We had a rough Monday at Baysides," North Caroline head coach Robin Eaton said. "I preached to them all week 'That wasn't the week to shine. 'Work harder and fix a few things and we could shine at regionals.' And that's what they did. They did everything we worked on; wrestled very smart, wrestled tough. Didn't make mistakes."
North Caroline freshman Caleb Melvin (120), junior Corey Bunce (165) and senior Dakota Kinsey (285) each wrestled-back to win their respective consolation finals, while sophomores Darly Ortega (106), Connor Frank (113), and Jacob Carpenter (126) placed fourth.
Kent County senior Brady Sutton decisioned Harford Vo Tech's Nikolai Chervak in the 144-pound consolation final, and Cambridge-South Dorchester sophomore Mark Jones placed fourth at 285.

title: Fighting alive and well even if it's diminished
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Fighting alive and well even if it's diminished

 February 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1220
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Minnesota's Marcus Foligno took a hit, delivered one of his own to Chicago's Jarred Tinordi, and the two big guys dropped the gloves. Outdoors in front of 82,000 people in the Meadowlands, it took even less for Matt Rempe and Matt Martin to spice up the Rangers-Islanders showdown with a fight.When Morgan Rielly cross-checked Ridly Greig for firing a slap shot into an empty net? Some pushing and shoving. Nothing more.
"How there wasn't a brawl there, I don't know how everyone didn't start fighting," wondered Todd Simpson, a 50-year-old retired player who piled up more than 1,300 penalty minutes in 580 NHL games. "That should've been a big fight."
All of these situations were over the past month alone, riveting reminders that fighting is alive and well in the NHL even if it is diminished in many ways. It has been 20 years since Simpson and his Ottawa teammates got into a fight fest at Philadelphia, a game that still holds the NHL record with an astounding 419 penalty minutes. Of 40 players who suited up, 23 got at least two minutes of penalty time. Many got far more.
Those kinds of massive clashes are long gone, faded like the cheap shots and blood in "Slap Shot." Like the beloved movie, however, fighting is warmly remembered, even desired, by many fans of the game and cheering on the brawls remains common. Those fans need not worry: Even in the NHL, which has fewer and fewer spots for goons these days, fighting is rare but certainly not gone, with a fight coming roughly every four or five games across the league.
Many see a permanent place for it in a sport that values standing up for teammates, even as they have watched some of the biggest fighters left shells of themselves by repeated blows to the head.
"It doesn't happen often, but you still have to have it," said Vancouver Canucks coach Rick Tocchet, whose 237 career fights rank 21st all-time. "When I played, you could really use as intimidation. You can still use it a little bit today but not as much. The staged fighting and all that stuff, that doesn't work anymore. But there is a time and place for it."
FIGHTING ON THE WANEThe NHL does not publicly list penalties by type, including fighting and other major infractions. According to HockeyFights.com, there have been 219 fights this season through Monday with 63 more projected before the playoffs begin for a total of 282, which would be a sharp drop from the 789 in 2003-04. That is a 200% decrease over 20 years and significantly down from 645 as recently as 2010-11.
Rule changes are part of the reason. The institution of the salary cap in 2005 made it more difficult for a team to pay a player whose skills were limited to throwing punches and protecting stars. In 2013, it became illegal to take a helmet off to fight and mandatory visors were grandfathered in.
"It's obviously evolved a lot where guys like myself back in the day no longer exist — one-dimensional fighters no longer exist," said Riley Cote, who fought 50 times in 156 games with Philadelphia from 2007-10 and countless other times in the minor leagues. "It's been a natural progression. ... I'm not sure at the NHL level they'll ever fully phase it out, but they're doing a pretty good job of trying."
No one expects a fighting ban, like the ejection and suspension policies that exist in college and internationally. NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman has said the fighting helps keep tensions from boiling over.
"Fighting, in the spontaneous sense, tends to act as a bit of a thermostat when things happen in the course of the game," Bettman said in 2013. Discussing a fight between Jarome Iginla and Vincent Lecavalier, Bettman said, "I'd rather them be punching each other than swinging sticks at each other."
WILL FIGHTING SURVIVE?A 2011 survey by the NHL Players' Association and CBC found that 98% of players at that time didn't support the total elimination of fighting. A vast majority of those players are now out of the league, replaced by a generation that has made hockey faster and more skilled than ever — but still willing to drop the gloves on occasion and wanting that option.
"It always needs to be in the game," said St. Louis Blues captain Brayden Schenn, who has fought twice this season but never more than four times a year as a professional. "You need guys to police it themselves, and if you're going to run around and make a big hit, you've got to know that sometimes you're going to have to deal with the consequences."
That is certainly the opinion of Steve Oleksy, who HockeyFights.com credits with 107 bouts at various levels, including the NHL. He is 38 and retired and, after at least a couple of concussions and other wear and tear, is sometimes irritated in noisy places. Long drives and playing recreational sports is hard on his hands, which delivered hundreds of punches over the years.
He believes fighting will be virtually extinct a decade from now.
"I think it declines exponentially, but I also think the definition of a fight has changed so much," Oleksy said. "The number of actual punches, actual fights — what we would deem a fight back in the day — I just don't think that's there, either. And I think with that comes the rise in incidents like the cross-checking incident, slashing, two-handers, things like that."
Oleksy and many others point to junior hockey and even younger levels of hockey banning or at least discouraging and not teaching fighting as a bellwether for where things are going: Fewer players knowing how to, or being willing to, fight.
FIGHTING'S LEGACYLike many sports, hockey is facing the fallout from decades of its players suffering concussions and other traumatic brain injuries when safety wasn't the top priority it is now.
Patrick Sharp, who fought a handful of times as a player and is now in the Flyers' front office, said he cringes when he sees a player's helmet come off taking a heavy punch or banging their head on the ice. It's what happened to George Parros during a fight in 2013 that left him unconscious after falling face first.
The deaths of old-school enforcers like Derek Boogaard and Bob Probert, who were posthumously found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, has changed some minds when it comes to glorifying fighting the way it used to be. Oleksy contends that heavyweights of that vintage are no longer in the game and the risk of serious injury is much less now.
Dan Gallant, who has run HockeyFights.com since 2016, understands the business aspects of the decline of fighting and believes it to be cyclical. Now, general managers are looking for the next Milan Lucic or Tom Wilson — the big guy who can play hockey first but also can drop the gloves.
"The types of players that teams are going out and looking for to create that championship team have just kind of evolved," Gallant said, confident fighting will never totally disappear. "Who knows what tomorrow might bring, but I do believe that the players that played the game before, being in the game now and the players that are currently here will make sure that fighting does stay in some form or fashion."

title: St. Paddy's Day runs set for March 16
author: Connie Connolly

St. Paddy's Day runs set for March 16

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News

 DENTON — Caroline County Recreation and Parks has announced the 16th annual St. Paddy's Day Race is set for Saturday, March 16.The day's events include the St. Paddy's Day 5K, 1-Mile Fun Run, and Lil' Leprechaun Dash.
"Start your salute to the Irish and your spring fitness conditioning on this certified fast and scenic course through Denton with a 5K and 1-Mile Fun Run," a department release stated. "Plenty of lucky surprises await on the course and at the finish."
The event benefits youth registration financial aid and scholarship fund for recreation programs produced by CCRP.
Registration begins at 8 a.m., and the race starts at 9 a.m. at the Fretterd Community Center, located at 107 South Fourth St. in Denton.
Pre-registration costs are $37 for the 5K and $22 for the 1-Mile Fun Run. Registration closes at 3 p.m. March 15. Shirts are not guaranteed for late registrations.
The Lil' Leprechaun Dash kicks off the festivities with a 100-meter dash down Fourth Street exclusively for youngsters ages 5 and younger. Special prizes will be given to all finishers.
Advance registration is required. Cost is $10, and the dash begins at 8:40 a.m., before the St. Patrick's Day event.
Participants can register anytime through the department's finish line production partner Seashore Striders at seashorestriders.com.

title: Harper settling in at first for Phillies
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Harper settling in at first for Phillies

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1090
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Bryce Harper is getting settled in as full-time first baseman for the Philadelphia Phillies.Harper hit a hard single in his first spring training at-bat Wednesday, but the two-time NL MVP also flashed some leather at first base in a 7-7 tie against Atlanta. Harper made a diving catch on Jarred Kelenic's grounder in the first inning, and started nifty 3-6-3 on a 105.3 mph grounder by Kelenic in the third.
"Both of them were real good," Phillies manager Rob Thomson said. "He looks very comfortable and he's improving every day."
Harper had Tommy John surgery in November 2022 and made his season debut last May 2 as a designated hitter. An outfielder the previous 11 seasons, his return to the field July 21 was at first base, where he started 36 times in the regular season and 13 in the playoffs.
"The sky's the limit for me because he's athletic," Thomson said. "He's calm, poised. A lot of a lot of good things can happen."
Former Phillies first baseman Rhys Hoskins tore his left ACL in a spring training game last March, and left in free agency after the season.
MUNCY HITBefore Japanese sensation Yoshinobu Yamamoto threw the first pitch in an impressive spring training debut for the Dodgers against World Series champion Texas, Los Angeles third baseman Max Muncy got hit by a pitch on his left hand in the top of the first inning.
Manager Dave Roberts said the ball hit Muncy on the knuckle of his ring finger and that the veteran was getting tests.
"I'm hopeful that it's not going to be too serious," Roberts said.
After getting hit by left-hander Cody Bradford, Muncy stayed in the game to play defense, and was replaced in the fourth inning by Austin Gauthier before his second at-bat. A mainstay in the middle of the Dodgers order the past six seasons, Muncy hit 36 homers and had 105 RBIs last year.
Yamamoto struck out three batters over two scoreless innings.
COUNSELL VS. BREWERSThere was a mix of cheers and boos when new Chicago Cubs manager Craig Counsell returned to his old spring training home for the first time.
The Cubs won 6-1 on the road Wednesday against the Milwaukee Brewers, the NL Central rival Counsell managed the past nine seasons.
"It's weird seeing him in those colors, but that's what reality is right now," said new Brewers manager Pat Murphy, who was on Counsell's staff the past eight years.
Brewers shortstop Willy Adames went across the field to hug Counsell before the game.
Budget-conscious Milwaukee won three NL Central titles and made five playoff appearances the past six years before Counsell's contract expired. The Cubs lured him away with a five-year contract worth more than $40 million that made him the highest-paid manager the majors.
SONNY OPENERSonny Gray will be the first Cardinals pitcher since Kyle Lohse in 2008 to make his debut for the Cardinals with a start on opening day.
"I don't take that lightly at all," said Gray, the veteran right-hander who signed a $75 million, three-year deal in November. "I appreciate the opportunity and what that shows."
Gray finished second in the AL Cy Young Award voting last season, when he was 8-8 with a 2.79 ERA in 32 starts for Minnesota. The Cardinals also added former All-Stars Kyle Gibson and Lance Lynn to their rotation in free agency.
St. Louis, coming off its first losing season since 2007, opens March 28 on the road against Shohei Ohtani and the Dodgers.
TOP PICK SKENES TO PITCH THURSDAYPittsburgh pitching prospect Paul Skenes, the top pick in last year's amateur draft, is to make his spring training debut on Thursday when the Pirates face Baltimore and Jackson Holliday, the No. 1 selection last summer.
The 21-year-old Skenes had a 5.40 ERA with 10 strikeouts and two walks in 6 2/3 innings in limited action in the minors after signing a record $9.2 million bonus to join Pittsburgh.
While the Pirates have a couple of open spots in their starting rotation, it's likely the hard-throwing Skenes will begin his first full season as a professional in the minors. He was 12-2 with a 1.69 ERA and 209 strikeouts in 122 2/3 innings last spring while playing for national champion LSU.
PEN PROBLEMThe Cleveland Guardians are shutting down reliever Trevor Stephan for three weeks with a deep bruise in his right elbow. Stephan, who appeared in 71 games last season, experienced soreness during a recent training session in Goodyear, Arizona. An MRI revealed the bruising.
Manager Stephen Vogt said Stephan has no structural or ligament issues.
The 28-year-old Stephan went 7-7 with a 4.06 ERA last season.
TJ AGAIN FOR THOMPSONNationals right-hander Mason Thompson will undergo Tommy John surgery for the second time.
Thompson first had the ligament replacement surgery when he was in high school. Now 26 and coming off 51 appearances for the Nationals last season, he felt a pop in his elbow at the start of spring training two weeks ago.
Manager Dave Martinez said Thompson will have the surgery on Friday.
GIANTS INJURIES
Giants right-hander Tristan Beck returned to San Francisco to see doctors after dealing with lingering soreness in his right hander.
"He's kind of been pitching through it a bit," San Francisco manager Bob Melvin said. "It just got to a point where we want to find out exactly what it is."
Beck made his big league debut last season by going 3-3 with a 3.92 ERA in 33 games for the Giants. While he started only three of those games, he is expected to be part of their rotation this year.
Meanwhile, Giants outfielder Mike Yastrzemski made his spring debut Wednesday going 0 for 2 with a walk in their 7-4 loss to Oakland. There are no restrictions at the plate even though he is still building up his throwing from a left shoulder issue that developed during offseason workouts.
SOME CLAIMS AND MOVES
— The Yankees claimed infielder Jahmai Jones off waivers from the Brewers. Infielder Jordan Groshans was designated for assignment to make room on New York's 40-man roster.
— Sam Hilliard is back with Colorado after being claimed the outfielder off waivers from Baltimore. The Rockies cleared a spot on their 40-man roster by putting right-hander Antonio Senzatela on the 60-day injured list.
Hilliard played 214 games with the Rockies from 2019-22 before getting traded to Atlanta. He played 40 games with the Braves last season before Baltimore claimed him off waivers in November.
— San Diego agreed to a minor league contract with 31-year-old outfielder Tim Locastro, who hit .232 with two homers and three RBIs and six stolen bases in 43 games and 67 plate appearances with the New York Mets last year.

title: Bucs ride post play, down NC
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bucs ride post play, down NC

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 691
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — There have been seasons when Kent Island High's girls basketball team has beaten opponents from long distance.That hasn't been the Bucs' most common thread to victory this season.
The one-two inside scoring punch of Sydney Riska and Makayla Kropfelder combined for 27 points, and Kent Island went on a 13-0 first-half scoring run Wednesday night to gain separation in an eventual 46-37 victory over North Caroline in a Class 2A East Region II quarterfinal.
The defending region champion, fourth-seeded Kent Island (18-3) advances to Friday's semifinal at top-seeded Wicomico (21-0). Second-seeded Queen Anne's (19-2) hosts No. 3 Parkside (18-3) in Friday's other semifinal.
"We used to be a three-point team and now we're a post team," Bucs head coach David Plumer said. "It's no secret. Everybody who watches film on us will know. But the post-play is getting better. Makayla and Sydney did great tonight. They can complement everybody else. We got the ball inside. We're a little bigger than them and we knew that."
North Caroline (14-7), which came in having won nine of its last 11, took a 6-4 lead a little over 3 minutes into the game, when Chloe Escoe (team-high 14 points) hit the second of her four 3-pointers. But Riska (game-high 17 points) scored on a put-back with 3:09 left in the first quarter to start the Buccaneers on a decisive 13-0 streak.
"We started off moving the ball early," North Caroline head coach A.J. Jackson said. "We had some good offensive possessions, but then we had a drought there where we got sort of undisciplined tonight, and that ended up hurting us later in the game."
The Bulldogs went 9 minutes without a field goal before Ashley Kercheval got behind the defense for a layup with 3:49 left in the first half, cutting Kent Island's lead to 20-8. Riska hit a pair of baskets during the run and Kropfelder (10 points) made a three-point play.
"We knew this was going to be a post-play game," said Riska, who finished with 13 rebounds for her 17th double-double of the season. "So just getting the ball down to me and Makayla, and then just getting the shots up. Obviously we didn't do well from the three-point line, but we did work well in the paint. The outside shots weren't falling for me but I worked inside to get it done."
As did Kropfelder.
"Just trying to make the best plays for my team," the sophomore center said. "If I'm not there, if there's too many defenders, pass it. I missed a couple opportunities but I just need to work on that personally."
Lacy Dauses hit a cutting Riska for a layup and a 23-10 halftime lead. Riska and Kropfelder then teamed to score all the points in a 6-0 burst to open the third quarter, expanding Kent Island's lead to 29-10 less than 3 minutes into the period.
But the Bulldogs outscored the Bucs, 14-4, over the remaining 4:52 of the third quarter to pull within 33-24 entering the fourth quarter.
Kent Island regained its double-digit lead with Lilli Dauses converting a pair of free throws and Kropfelder scoring off a Riska assist for a 37-24 cushion.
"Credit to their bigs," Jackson said. "Second-chance shots, they really battled down there. And the effort on defense, especially when we made a little run there in the fourth quarter. Like hustling, not giving up. That team is well coached. Credit to Plumer."
North Caroline again cut its deficit to under 10 with 5 minutes remaining when Escoe drilled another 3-pointer and Malayah Phillips scored on a layup to make it 37-29. But Kent Island twice worked the ball inside to Riska, who was fouled and hit four consecutive free throws to make it 41-29 midway through the final period.
The Bulldogs wouldn't get any closer than eight the remainder of the game, as their small runs were countered by the Bucs.
"It's always been a little bit of a dogfight," Kent Island guard Caroline Cavanaugh said. "We go in there, we get a lead, they come back. We just need to be a little more consistent with our defense and our offense. They played really well. We just played better this game."

title: RISE Flag Football to come to Cambridge in April
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
RISE Flag Football to come to Cambridge in April

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A youth flag football league is set to begin in Cambridge this spring.At a Dorchester County Council meeting on Feb. 20, the Council voted to allow the Cambridge Police Department, in partnership with the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention, Youth and Victim Services and local nonprofit ALL4LOVE, to use the J. Edward Walter Park for a RISE Flag Football league. RISE Flag Football is a national program.
This new league, for children in kindergarten through eighth grade, will use the park on Saturdays, starting April 27 and ending June 15.
The council voted in favor of allowing the use of the park on the condition that the program organizers adhere to a list of seven recommendations made by the county's insurance carrier, Local Government Insurance Trust.
At the meeting, interim County Manager Jeff Powell said the insurance trust shared liability concerns and recommendations regarding the flag football league's use of county property.
"I think one of the biggest (concerns) is that they want it in the daytime," Powell said about the insurance agency's recommendations. "No nighttime use."
Cambridge Police Capt. Antoine Patton said in an interview Wednesday that they will be able to do everything the county has requested.
In the interview, Patton said the police department hopes the RISE Flag Football league will address juvenile crime in Cambridge.
"We've had a lot of crime in our community," he said. "And a lot of our crime has been juveniles. We wanted to give them an alternative, something to do on Saturdays."
Patton said he thinks this program will give children an environment where they can learn life skills and have strong mentors. He sees this program as beneficial for the police department, as well.
"It's another tool that we can add to help us build strong relationships between the community and the police," he said.
Following conversation about the insurance trust's recommendations at the meeting Tuesday, Councilman Ricky Travers motioned to approve the use of the park for the flag football league on the condition that all the recommendations are met. The council voted unanimously in favor of this.
After the vote, both Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Councilman William Nichols thanked Patton for his work with youth in Cambridge, and in the county, overall.
"Capt. Patton, you are the definition of community policing," Pfeffer said. "You are involved so much in this community. ... So I thank you as well, sir, for all that you do."

title: ENDING ON A GREAT NOTE
author: Bill Haufe
content:
ENDING ON A GREAT NOTE

 February 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1261
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Gary Gould was admittedly a bit baffled as he kept watch on Beth Tfiloh School's boys basketball team heading toward the postseason."They lost a couple games the last week of the (regular) season," said Saints Peter and Paul High's head coach, whose team had lost three straight to the Warriors. "And then some of the games they won, they only won by like four or five points to teams that we were beating by double-digits. I was confused why other teams could play them so well and we couldn't. And then I thought about it and said, it had to be me. I was doing too much. I was trying to be too good in the x's and o's part, instead of just letting us play."
Gould let his team play Saturday night, made a halftime adjustment, then watched the Sabres pull away in the second half for a 68-58 victory over Beth Tfiloh in the Maryland Interscholastic Athletic Association C Conference championship game at UMBC's Chesapeake Employers Insurance Arena.
"It feels amazing," said senior forward K'den Spears, named player of the game after Sts. Peter & Paul won its first MIAA C title since 2016. "The only reason why we keep losing games is when we selfishly play. We really played as a group and really helped each other and built each other up."
Though a mid-season injury limited junior star Garett Hemingway's minutes, Sts. Peter & Paul had built a nice hot streak heading into the playoffs, having won nine of its last 10, including its last eight straight.
Beth Tfiloh defeated Sts. Peter & Paul in last year's conference championship, won a two-point nail-biter in Easton on Jan. 11, then rolled to a 72-45 victory at home Jan. 31, dealing the Sabres their most lopsided loss of the season, as well as the only blemish during their hot streak.
But Warriors head coach Ari Braun didn't necessarily put a lot of stock in his team's Jan. 31 romp.
"The first game this year was down to the wire at Saints Peter and Paul. Either team could have won it," Braun said of the Jan. 11 clash in which Hemingway scored 33 points. "The second time, I think that was (Hemingway's) first game back from his ankle and he was not the same player. They weren't all right yet, and we made shots and defended. Obviously we played an awesome game, and it looks worse than maybe it should have."
Then came Saturday night's title bout.
"I think the difference was we were more focused," Gould said. "We realized the game at Beth was something we knew wasn't going to happen again because we didn't shoot the ball well. Plus that second game, I did too much. I was trying to coach too much strategy wise and take away things and add stuff. I think I had my kids playing too slow.
"The kids knew that last year we didn't know what to expect, so we played with a little nerves," Gould said of the Sabres' 65-58 loss in the title game. "But this year we knew going in what to do. So the kids were just focused about getting it done, went out and just played. And we knew it was just our time."
Hemingway (game-high 19 points) canned a pair of 3-pointers early as the Sabres (16-8) carried a 27-24 lead into the locker room after a back-and-forth first half. And while he was guarded against over-coaching again, Gould searched for an edge during the first half.
"I was trying to figure out on the sideline what was happening; what were they doing that was working, and what we could take away to give us the advantage," Gould said.
Gould's key takeaway was switching from the man-to-man and 2-3 zone defenses the Sabres used in the first half to a 1-2-2 zone. The move proved critical, especially when it came to defending Warrior senior guard Michael Cohen, who scored a game-high 35-points in last year's title game.
"Their skip passing wasn't available to them," Gould said. "And then we kept number four, Michael Cohen, in front of us so he wasn't able to penetrate and do all the stuff he did to us last year. He was the guy who hurt us."
Consistently penetrating inside and drawing contact, Cohen went 19 of 28 from the line in last year's final, which included a 12-of-16 effort in the fourth quarter. In Saturday's rematch he finished with 17 points.
"Defense was big for us," Hemingway said. "We came into the game saying, if we can slow them down, hold Cohen. Slow him down, get in front of him, take charges. As long as we get the defense down the offense will just come."
Braun agreed Gould's defensive tweak was big.
"They did an unbelievable job with their defense, Braun said. "They started off in the man, which I didn't think it went great for them, but then they quickly pivoted to the zone. And they were very disciplined in staying back and clogging the paint and not really giving Michael as many opportunities to drive. Last year in the championship game, they were pressing and allowing us to get out in the open court, and that led to a lot of his free throws and baskets. But this year they did a great job of staying at home defensively."
That move produced steals and kick-started the Sabres' transition game. Senior point guard Brayden Smith scored eight of his 13 points in the third quarter, and Robbie Cunningham netted seven of his 11, as Sts. Peter & Paul outscored the Warriors 19-9 for a 46-33 lead heading into the fourth quarter.
Braun, who graduated a number of seniors from last season's title team, acknowledged two other significant factors. Elan Vogelstein, Beth Tfiloh's top rebounder and assist man, suffered a thigh injury in the second Sts. Peter & Paul game, and has been sidelined the remainder of the season.
"I don't know if that changes the outcome of the game, but obviously that would have helped us," Braun said.
And then there was Sts. Peter & Paul's job on the boards, especially the effort delivered by Spears.
"I think what really hurt us even more than the zone was their offensive rebounding," Braun said. "When we can get a stop and end it with a rebound we can then run. That's way different than them getting rebound after rebound and pounding us and then scoring. And then we're just playing against a settled defense. So I thought they just did an awesome job in terms of game plan and execution, just playing with a lot of effort on the court.
"And I think number zero, he was a beast on the glass and our guys really struggled with that," Braun said of Spears.
Spears was a force on the boards in the Sabres' semifinal victory over Cristo Rey. Against the Warriors, he was again tough on the glass, yanking down eight rebounds, and in the score column, finishing with 13 points.
"That's the best I've ever seen K'den play," Hemingway said.
Gould echoed that sentiment.
"He was more consistent and forceful in what he was doing," Gould said of Spears
Spears was also more confident.
"I just felt because this is the second time for us being there, and there was no point in us being nervous because it was the same team we played last year," Spears said.
Beth Tfiloh (25-8) outscored the Sabres, 25-22, in the fourth, but it couldn't rally enough.
"As a team I felt more together," Spears said. "This was our last game and I just wanted to end it off on a really great note."

title: Bailey's hot hand fuels Warriors
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bailey's hot hand fuels Warriors

 February 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 705
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Wicomico High's defensive plan had held Easton's Marshall Bailey without a field goal for almost three quarters Thursday night.Then in a bid to generate some offense, Indians head coach Butch Waller dropped his triangle-and-two scheme and went man to man. Bailey took advantage of the switch, connecting for 25 of his game-high 30 points over the final 11-plus minutes while leading Easton to a 69-56 victory over Wicomico in a Class 2A East Region II semifinal.
The second-seeded Warriors (15-6) travel to top-seeded Queen Anne's (17-4) on Tuesday for the 2A East Region II championship at 5 p.m. The Lions defeated fourth-seeded Parkside, 62-55, in last night's other semifinal.
"Second half they went man and he was hard to stop," Easton head coach Dionte Hynson said of Bailey. "He was hitting his jump shot, getting to the hole. He put us on his back in the second half."
With the Indians' triangle-and-two limiting Bailey and backcourt mate Ja'Kai Brooks, Easton worked the ball inside to Tymier Thomas (12 points) whose seven first-quarter points helped the Warriors take a 16-10 lead heading into the second quarter.
"They really couldn't get open," Hynson said of Bailey and Brooks in the first half. "Thankfully, Tymier was hitting. He kept us in the game in the first half."
Down 18-12, the Indians rallied to draw even at 18-all on Tyson Hayward's bucket with a little over 5 minutes remaining in the half. Brooks then hit a 3-pointer to break a 22-all tie with 2:06 left before intermission. Kyree Acree (12 points) sandwiched a 3-pointer and a layup around a Zymier Ramirez free throw to push the Warriors lead to 31-25 at halftime.
Waller stayed with his triangle-and-two zone until midway through the third when he opted to go man in hopes of kick-starting his offense.
"We ran a little triangle-and-two and we did an OK job, but we couldn't balance it by scoring," Waller said. "The defense was fine in the first half, even halfway through the third quarter. And then I just said, 'We've got to play them man to man, take our chances, pick the tempo up.' We couldn't do it.
"Same problem we've been plagued with all season long; can't score," Waller continued. "Shooting percentage tonight was 32.1. We've had that same problem, which is understandable with some new players. At this level, or any level really, you've got to be able to put the brown thing in the round thing."
Bailey began doing just that.
After consecutive baskets from Kahlil Batson, and a nice low-post bucket from Acree, Bailey made a three-point play with 3:13 left in the third quarter for a 40-29 Warrior lead. Wi-Hi's Tay'Shawn Swann (16 points) scored on a reverse layup. But Bailey answered with a 3-pointer and another three-point play, extending Easton's lead to 46-32 by the end of the third quarter.
"I just knew we had to lock in defensively because that first half we were only up by six and it was a sloppy game," Bailey said. "So once we locked in defensively — I think we held them to like seven points — everything offensively started clicking for us."
Thomas scored on a drive to maintain the Warriors' 14-point cushion at 48-34 early in the fourth quarter. Bailey then hit back-to-back 3-pointers, drove for a layup and buried a pull-up jumper for a commanding 58-41 lead with 5:13 remaining in the game.
"Excellent shooter," Waller said of Easton's sophomore guard. "One of the better shooters I've seen in years."
Bailey converted a Thomas dish for a layup, then assisted on Thomas and Acree baskets that gave Easton a 65-52 lead with just over two minutes remaining.
Takai Hugee led Wi-Hi with 18 points.
1A EAST REGION II PLAYOFFSCambridge-SD 84 Crisfield 32CAMBRIDGE — LaShaun Moody scored a game-high 30 points as the top-seeded Vikings rolled into the 1A East II final.
Koby Ennals had 15 points for the Vikings, who got 11 from Sterling Perkins and 10 from Semaj Pinder.
1A EAST REGION I PLAYOFFSCol. Richardson 75 Bohemia Manor 63AMERICAN CORNER — Dreden Lake led all scorers with 21 points and Jazir Dickerson and Makiah Batson each added 16 as the second-seeded Colonels advanced.
Manny Wallace finished with 15 points for Colonel Richardson.
Landon Horsey and Ayden Holderer scored 18 points apiece for Bohemia Manor.

title: QA's better half enough to top Rams
author: Bill Haufe
content:
QA's better half enough to top Rams

 March 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 846
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Freshmen Bea Holthaus, Laila Coles and Kariana Hickson have been huge in the Queen Anne's County High girls basketball team's return to the top of the North Bayside this season.Friday night, juniors Lucy Taylor and RJ Ensor showed how big they could be.
Taylor and Ensor combined for nine consecutive points during a 9-2 run to open the second half that staggered third-seeded Parkside while launching the Lions to a 47-31 victory in a Class 2A East Region II semifinal.
Second-seeded Queen Anne's (20-2) travels to Salisbury to face top-seed Wicomico (22-0) on Wednesday at 5 p.m. for the region title. The Indians are the only team to defeat the Lions this season, rolling to an 81-41 victory Feb. 8, and a 58-52 win in the Bayside Conference championship 12 days later.
"I've been trying to find my shot all year it feels like," said Taylor, who led Queen Anne's with 15 points. "But tonight, I don't know. I saw the freshmen, their first year being here (in the playoffs). And being one of the captains I felt like I needed to kind of do something. Kind of step up and keep the encouragement up. It was a really good team win tonight."
Queen Anne's looked like a team that was playing its first game in 10 days, as Jeliah Gardner scored six of her game-high 16 points in the first 4:28 to help the Rams (18-4) to a 10-2 lead.
"Slow start," Lions head coach Mike Kern said. "The first six points were off transition. Then their next couple baskets were backside so we switched to a 2-3."
Coles (11 points) sandwiched a 3-pointer and a layup around two Holthaus free throws to get Queen Anne's within 12-9 by the end of the first period.
Gardner's three-point play extended the Rams' lead to 15-9 with 2 minutes elapsed in the second quarter. But Ensor (eight points, six rebounds, four assists) scored on a drive. Coles snagged a rebound and went coast to coast for a layup before Jordan Taylor scored off an Ensor dish, tying the game at 15-15 with 2:50 remaining in the second quarter.
Gardner scored consecutive baskets to help move Parkside back to a 20-15 lead before Ensor hit a free throw with 5 seconds left to make it a four-point Lions' deficit at the half.
But Taylor and Ensor gave Queen Anne's a quick offensive jolt to start the third quarter. Taylor converted an Ensor pass for an inside bucket. Ensor splashed a 3-pointer. Taylor scored from in close for a 23-20 Lions lead.
Zion Oge scored the Rams' first basket of the second half with 4 minutes left in the third quarter. Taylor answered, taking a Coles feed and scoring inside. TaLayah Clark (nine points) scored, drawing Parkside within 25-24.
But the Rams wouldn't score again until 12 seconds remained in the third quarter, as the Lions dominated the defensive glass, allowing Parkside just one shot time after time.
"Total collapse," Parkside head coach Warren White said after the Rams were held to just six points in the third quarter and five in the fourth. "We've been telling these kids all year, 'You have to play through this mental stuff.
"And free throws killed us," said White, whose team was 3 of 15 from the foul line. "The whole game I don't think we made more than three free throws. That would have kept us in the game."
But Queen Anne's work on the defensive boards helped fuel a 16-6 third quarter and a 15-5 fourth period.
"Defensive rebounding," Kern said. "And that was what our mentality was: one shot and done. So we did better rebounding. We like to press but we kind of just sat back in a 2-3 zone and made it tough. And they shot a lot from the outside. We just got to get the rebound. I don't know how good they were from the three-point line but they weren't very good tonight."
Queen Anne's used a 7-0 run in the closing 2:21 of the third quarter to begin pulling away. Jordan hit a short jumper, Ensor converted a steal into a layup, and Coles sank a pair of free throws before a Taylor free throw capped a 15-4 third-quarter run, giving the Lions a 32-26 lead.
The Lions continued to widen their lead in the fourth, starting with Julia Rendulic, who came off the bench to drain a 3-pointer to start another 9-0 Queen Anne's run.
"Defensively we did well," Kern said. "I think in the second half when RJ hit that three got us going, got us playing with some momentum. Julia comes in and hits a three. Those are the kind of things that are big plays.
"Laila had a couple of good steals, and took it to the basket and got fouled," Kern continued. "And that combination was good. "K-5 (Hickson) was the leading scorer the last two big games we played and she had a little slow night, and so did Bea. But it was good to see Lucy and RJ step up, and Taylor Jordan came off the bench and got a couple big baskets."

title: Lions survive Easton rally for title
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Lions survive Easton rally for title

 March 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Jeff Hollis said he wasn't nervous, especially with seniors Vince Gilberto and Collin Woolford in the game."I always feel like with Vince and Collin on the court that somebody's going to make a winning play," said Hollis, Queen Anne's County High's boys head basketball coach.
Hollis was right. Somebody did make a winning play, and that somebody was freshman Jadereon Thompson.
Fouled with 1 second left, Thompson hit the first of two free throws Tuesday night to lift top-seeded Queen Anne's to a 66-65 victory over No. 2 seed Easton in the Class 2A East Region II championship.
The Lions (18-4), who have won six straight since a Jan. 30 loss at Easton, now wait for the Class 2A field to be reseeded, and will likely host a state quarterfinal either Friday or Saturday. Easton finishes the season 15-7.
"Really elated. It's been three years coming to this game and we've lost two of them," said Hollis, whose season was ended by Wicomico the past two years in the region final. "So to finally win one feels really good."
Down 32-31 at halftime, the Lions looked well on their way to victory as they outscored Easton, 22-7, in the third quarter to carry a 53-39 lead into the fourth.
But behind Marshall Bailey, who scored 17 of his game-high 27 points in the fourth quarter, Easton rallied as the sophomore guard scored on a drive with 4 seconds remaining to tie the game at 65-65.
On the ensuing inbounds pass, Gilberto threw a pass three-quarters of the court to Thompson, who drove straight to the basket and was fouled with 1 second left on the clock.
"I was either going to get the layup or get fouled," Thompson said.
During a timeout prior to his free-throw attempts, Thompson said all his teammates came up to him offering him encouragement.
"It felt great," Thompson said. "I had to knock 'em down to win the regional final."
Thompson hit the first, then watched the second attempt bounce and get rebounded by Gilberto to seal the win.
"He's really not a freshman," Hollis said of Thompson. "He's a freshman in age, but he's not a freshman. He's been building to this point. He's just an exceptional kid and an exceptional athlete."
Easton outscored the Lions 26-13 in the fourth quarter.
"I thought we were going to overtime," Warrior head coach Dionte Hynson said. "I'm proud of the kids. Helluva comeback. We had to dig deep. We had to play solid D. I'm not taking anything away from Queen Anne's but our kids played their butts off tonight."
Diontye Copper's 3-pointer with 6:27 left in the third quarter pulled Easton even with the Lions at 35-all. But Queen Anne's outscored the Warriors 18-4 over the final 5:39 of the quarter to build a 53-39 lead, with Woolford (12 points) scoring seven points in the run.
"We just couldn't score any points third quarter," Hynson said.
Bailey, who was 8 of 9 from the foul line, hit a pair of free throws to start Easton's fourth-quarter comeback, drained two 3-pointers and continuously attacked the rim, scoring or drawing contact.
"He's a great player," Hollis said of Bailey. "Hat's off to Easton. I thought their players and their coaching staff did a great job. They weathered the storm when we got up on 'em. They came back.
"But our kids made the final winning play," Hollis added. "We talk about it all the time. Things happen during a game. Who's going to be the man that makes the final winning play. We've had that a couple times this year."
Gilberto had 14 points for Queen Anne's, Nickai Gross and Hollace Branch each had 10, and Thompson finished with nine.
Rayan Haq had 10 for Easton and Kyree Acree eight.

title: Big spending doesn't guarantee success
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Big spending doesn't guarantee success

 March 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News 
 
 884
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NFL teams are set to dole out billions in free agent contracts in the coming weeks as teams around the league hope that bold moves in March will pay off with wins on the field once the season starts.But in a league with a sharp aging curve and specific systems that don't suit all players those dollars spent don't guarantee success.
According to the Spotrac website, NFL teams handed out more than $3.3 billion in contracts last offseason with nearly half of that money fully guaranteed at signing.
The biggest spenders were far from the biggest winners in the season as signing expensive free agents is typically not the best way to turn around a team.
The six biggest spenders last offseason all missed the postseason led by Denver committing more than $250 million in contracts only to miss the playoffs for the eighth straight season after going 8-9 in coach Sean Payton's first season.
Other big spenders such as New Orleans, Atlanta, Chicago, Las Vegas and Carolina also were back home when the playoffs started, while a team such as the Los Angeles Rams got into the postseason after spending only $10.2 million in free agency.
Green Bay, Baltimore and Dallas were among the other teams that spent less than $50 million in free agency last offseason and got into the playoffs.
Here's a look at some of the best signings from a year ago, as well as some big misses:
FREE AGENT BARGAINSQB Baker Mayfield, Tampa Bay: The Buccaneers viewed last season as a chance to re-set the roster after going all-in during Tom Brady's three-year run. Tampa Bay took on more than $80 million in dead money and went cheap at QB, signing Mayfield to a one-year, $4 million deal. Mayfield delivered with a career-high 28 TD passes to lead the Bucs to a division title and a playoff win. He earned about $2.85 million in incentives but was still a bargain.
DE Jadeveon Clowney, Baltimore: The Ravens became the latest team to give Clowney a one-year prove-it deal when they signed the 2014 No. 1 overall pick in August. Clowney earned just over $4 million for his one season with incentives after matching his career high with 9 1/2 sacks for the NFL's stingiest defense.
LB Drue Tranquill, Kansas City: The Chiefs added depth at linebacker when they made a low-profile move of signing Tranquill to a one-year, $3 million deal. He was a key part of a defense that helped carry Kansas City to a Super Bowl title with 4 1/2 sacks and 78 tackles in the regular season and 21 more tackles during the playoff run.
TE Dalton Schultz, Houston: The Texans were looking for a veteran pass catcher to help rookie QB C.J. Stroud and found one in Schultz. Houston signed him to a one-year, $6.25 million deal and got 59 catches for 635 yards and five TDs in the regular season and another TD in the playoffs from Schultz.
G Isaac Seumalo, Pittsburgh: The Steelers went into last offseason looking to bolster the offensive line and did a good job with the addition of Seumalo, who signed a three-year, $24 million deal. Seumalo allowed no sacks in the season and was the 10th-rated guard in the NFL, according to Pro Football Focus.
FREE AGENT BUSTSQB Jimmy Garoppolo, Las Vegas: The Raiders needed a replacement after moving on from Derek Carr and hoped that Garoppolo would be a good fit with his former OC Josh McDaniels as head coach in Las Vegas. But Garoppolo missed much of the offseason recovering from foot surgery after signing a three-year, $72.75 million contract. He struggled once he got on the field, throwing nine INTs in six starts before being benched. His suspension for performance-enhancing drugs will get the Raiders out of $11.25 million in guarantees this season
QB Derek Carr, New Orleans: The Saints' deal for Carr didn't work out a whole let better for New Orleans. Carr signed a $150 million, four-year deal with the hopes of leading the Saints to the playoffs in the NFL's weakest division. New Orleans couldn't take advantage as Carr got off to a shaky start to the season and narrowly missed the playoffs.
RT Mike McGlinchey, Denver: The Broncos gave the second-biggest deal in free agency when they signed him to a five-year, $87.5 million deal. But the same issues that led to San Francisco moving on from its 2018 first-round pick were still evident in Denver. McGlinchey struggled at times in pass protection with his 49 pressures allowed ranking sixth most among all tackles last season, according to PFF.
WR Allen Lazard, New York Jets: The Jets brought in one of Aaron Rodgers' receivers from Green Bay in hopes that the familiarity would lead to success in New York. But Rodgers lasted only one series and Lazard never lived up to the four-year, $44 million deal he signed. Lazard had just 23 catches for 311 yards and one TD with just four catches in the final nine games of the season.
WR JuJu Smith-Schuster, New England: The Patriots let Jakobi Meyers leave for Las Vegas in free agency and signed Smith-Schuster to a slightly cheaper deal instead. While Meyers had his third straight season with at least 800 yards, Smith-Schuster had just 29 catches for 260 yards and one TD after signing a three-year, $27 million deal.

title: Perryville outlasts Colonels in region final
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Perryville outlasts Colonels in region final

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PERRYVILLE — After 30 minutes of hard-fought play that featured multiple lead changes, Perryville High's boys basketball team found itself clinging to a three-point lead over Colonel Richardson with 1:45 remaining in Tuesday's Class 1A East Region I final.With a trip to the state tournament on the line, either team could have used a response from one of its players to cement a state berth. The player that answered the call was Perryville junior Devin Clore.
Clore knocked down back-to-back 3-pointers in a span of 40 seconds to extend the Panthers lead to nine with just over a minute remaining before Perryville held off a late Colonel charge to seal a 79-75 victory.
Winning the regional crown brings extra sentiment to this season's Perryville squad, as Clore and several teamates played under head coach Ron Kidd since they were as young as five years old.
"It feels amazing," Clore said. "We've all been playing since we were five or six and we've always had a dream to all come to a high school at one time and just hoop together and that's what we're doing."
After coaching many of his current players for over a decade, Perryville's head coach shared a similar sentiment for the meaning of capturing the region.
"I couldn't be more proud of a group of men in my entire life," Kidd said. "They worked hard every day and hats off to Colonel Richardson. They played us very hard, they were physical and my guys stood up and brought home the banner. I'm very proud of them."
Perryville built a 10-point lead by the end of the first quarter, before Colonel Richardson opened the second quarter on an 8-2 run to cut its deficit to four. Following an eight-point swing that grew the Perryville lead back to 12, Colonel ended the quarter on a 14-4 run, reducing its deficit to a bucket by the break.
After a back-and-forth third quarter saw six lead changes, Perryville went on a 13-2 run for a nine-point advantage by the opening minute of the fourth quarter. Despite Colonel Richardson coming back to cut Perryville's lead to as low as one in the final period, the Panthers used 20 fourth-quarter points from Clore, Sean Beard and Andrew Clark to hold their lead.
Clore led Perryville with 22 points, 18 coming from beyond the arc. Clark followed with 19 points, while Kyle Richards and Beard finished in double figures.
"You've got to stay calm under pressure in order to come out on top so I knew that and I just stuck to that," Beard said. "We've worked super hard all season so it's good to see the results from the work actually show."
Dreden Lake led Colonel Richardson with 23 points, followed by Jazir Dickerson and Makiah Batson, who each finished with 20 points. Colonel head coach Brad Plutschak though foul trouble and lack of defensive execution for a majority of the game led to his team coming up just short. With a young team however, Plutschak hopes the Colonels can use Tuesday's loss as a learning experience.
"We had a little foul trouble and we wanted to press, and we kind of weren't able to until later in the game when we wanted, and it was effective but we just came up a little bit short," Plutschak said. "It's tough but we've got a lot of young guys that will be back and I like their hustle and their effort and we'll just keep building on it."
Perryville will travel to Baltimore as the seven-seed after reseeding to face second-seed Edmondson-Westside in the Class 1A state quarterfinals on Friday. The Red Storm won last year's Class 1A state title. With the first goal of a regional title now behind them, Kidd has high confidence in his team as it moves on toward the state tournament.
"These guys can accomplish anything," Kidd said. "I wouldn't sell them short of any goal. They had this goal to hang a banner on the wall. We've got a regional final, who knows what's next."

title: STATE CHAMPS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
STATE CHAMPS

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1457
 Words 

 Read News Document

 David Stricker was trying to digest the past three days.Or maybe it was the past three years.
Some 16 hours earlier, Queen Anne's County High's girls wrestling team and coaching staff piled onto a podium at the Show Place Arena in Upper Marlboro in celebration of winning the first-ever team title at the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association's girls state wrestling tournament.
Seated at the end of a long table inside a school conference room early Sunday afternoon, Stricker was still wrestling to find the right words as he looked at the state championship trophy perched in front of him.
"As I told the girls, I had about three sentences of a speech prepared in my brain and I only got to about three, and then I started rambling," Stricker said with a smile. "It's just humbling. Even this morning, flipping through pictures and stuff, I still tear up just thinking about it."
It's only been three years since Stricker, Queen Anne's boys head wrestling coach, started the school's girls program.
That first team had only three girls but ended the season with then-freshman Ally Conley winning the 100-pound state title.
The program grew to 14 last season, and 22 this season, which started with a December bus ride to the Maverick Duals at Manchester Valley, during which Stricker and girls head coach John Waters joked about possibly winning a state title.
The Lions went 11-0 in dual-meet competition, which included defeating Winters Mill in the first dual meet in MPSSAA history where both teams filled all 14 weight classes.
They had three individual champions at the Bayside Conference tournament. Four days later, they crowned four champions at the Class 2A-1A East Region championships.
Then came the newly formatted three-day state tournament, which ended Saturday night with Conley earning a second-period pin in the 100-pound final for her second state title in three years.
"Yes, we ended up with that," Waters said Sunday, nodding toward the state championship trophy. "We earned that. But we wanted the girls and the entire team, coaches included, to enjoy the moment. We told them Thursday when we get there, 'Take pictures. Walk around the building. No matter what, us coaches will be there next year hopefully. But we're not going to bring the same team back. This team was special.'"
Queen Anne's had a wrestler in 12 of the 14 weight classes at states. Of those 12, only one, Morgan Morris, didn't win a match.
But Morris was symbolic of the hard work ethic Waters, Stricker and assistant Jimmy Swindell forever preached at practice.
Morris lost in a wrestle-off at 155 pounds with teammate Adelina Dickens prior to the conference championships. The sophomore could easily have opted to begin focusing on the upcoming softball season. Instead, Waters and Stricker asked if Morris would consider bumping up to 170 for regionals.
"We don't have anybody there," Waters said to Morris of the weight class, "and there's a good chance you might make states."
Though there were only three wrestlers in the 170 bracket at regionals, Morris chose to give it a shot, won a match, and placed second to qualify for states.
"She did one heckuva job," Waters said of Morris, who wrestled opponents that not only had 15 to 20 pounds on her, but had more experience. "She came across a couple of tough matches. The girls were just heavier."
Queen Anne's other 11 wrestlers won at least once.
Senior Julia Reburn, one of the originals on the inaugural 2021-22 team, earned a win at 140, as did sophomores Lilly Hammond (145), Dickens (155) and Maggie Rooney (220).
Juniors Ava Price (120) and Keira Corcoran (135) each went 2-2. Senior Delaney Gray (130), another 2022 original, went 3-2 and reached the consolation quarterfinals, as did sophomore Bree Conard, who went 2-2 at 115.
And while Conley went 4-0 en route to the title that capped a 21-5 season, no Lions wrestler won more over the tournament's three days than Kaylynn Bryant.
Bryant won her pigtail match at 190, lost 5-4 to two-time defending state champion Jabea Ewane of Winters Mill, then never lost again.
The junior pinned her first two consolation-bracket opponents, then gutted out a 5-4 victory in an ultimate tiebreaker. She earned another one-point decision in the quarterfinals, then pinned her next two opponents, notching a 4:33 fall in the consolation final.
"I knew she could get on the podium. But she just kept going," said Stricker of Bryant, who went 7-1 to finish a 24-5 season. "Actually her pin in the consolation quarterfinals is what kind of put us over the top team score wise."
Then there was Finley Patchett at 125.
"Finley and Kaylynn, they surpassed what they were supposed to do," Waters said. "Kaylynn we kind of figured she'd come back to get in that third- and fourth-(place) match.
"But Finley was a wild card because she's only wrestled for two months," Waters continued. "And she was probably in the hardest weight class from top to bottom. And she's one of the few freshmen in that weight class. A lot of the other girls were 11th graders with four or five years of wrestling experience."
Patchett (17-6) wrestled nothing but juniors the whole tournament. She won by fall in the first round before getting pinned in her second match. After winning her first two consolation bouts by decision, she lost by fall in the consolation semifinals, but bounced back with a pin to place fifth.
"Finley as a first-year wrestler just did amazing things," Stricker said. "At the beginning of the season she was in sort of a logjam with Bree and Ava. We were trying to figure out what weight class to get her to go to. As the season went on we kind of got everybody situated, and once she got more consistent mat time, I mean she just really kind of started to take off."
"She did extra practice at home," Stricker added. "Then what she did at the state tournament. … That's the biggest state tournament that there's ever been. There were 24 girls per weight class, which was even more than the boys (16 per weight class). The depth and the ability in the tournament, and then for her to go out and take fifth, and only lose to people who finished above her on the podium" — Hammond junior Clara Freeman (third, 21-13) and Montgomery Blair junior Joni Chuka (fourth, 24-7) — "was really impressive."
As has Queen Anne's rapid rise to the top.
"There's a joke in my house," Stricker said. "My wife says, 'My son can swim, but my daughters can wrestle.' So when I started this, my whole thought, at least at our school, was to take away the stigma of girls wrestling. It's not like this novelty thing, that one girl wrestler on the team."
Other schools around the state began building strong girls programs, most notably Manchester Valley, Francis Scott Key, Winters Mill, La Plata and Eastern Tech. Waters began tracking those "so-called big dogs" in tournaments and noticed a trend.
"I remember all the big-dog schools, they're just talking about these certain schools," Waters said. "I remember going to Dave and saying, 'There's a lot of good girls out there wrestling right now that these schools. ... they're not giving them any credit. These girls are going to come in and there's not going to be one team that dominates and wins like six state girls titles this year. It's going to be a lot of random schools with three or four good girls.'"
Waters was proven correct at states, with no school having more than one champion in the 14 weight classes.
Queen Anne's girls head coach also thought the way his team wrestled, it could challenge for a state title in the near future.
"We had four first-year wrestlers go to states," Waters said. "And we have some girls with only two years experience. So I'm thinking by Ally's senior year they should be able to push for the team title."
That time frame got pushed up last weekend, as the Lions amassed 119 points on the way to the title, outdistancing runner-up Oakland Mills (86), third-place Francis Scott Key (82) and fourth-place Stephen Decatur and Eastern Tech (80).
Fifteen of Queen Anne's combined 21 losses at the tournament came against wrestlers who placed in the top six.
"It's like they are on the forefront of the state of Maryland in the fastest growing sport in the nation," Stricker said. "They're doing more than I ever could have possibly imagined.
"I figured it would take us 10, 15 years to get to this point," Stricker said with another head nod toward the state trophy. "And I mean we led it from Thursday to Saturday the whole time. We were always in first."
Notes: Rondell Bryant, Frank Conley, Kyron Hutchins, Sean Blackwell, Kei Rickard and Cody Barbiche also helped coach this season.

title: Caps re-sign Sandin to 5-year deal
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Caps re-sign Sandin to 5-year deal

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Rasmus Sandin is sticking around with the Washington Capitals for a while after re-signing Wednesday on a five-year contract worth $23 million.Sandin will count $4.6 million against the salary cap through the 2028-29 NHL season as part of the new deal.
Set to be a restricted free agent this summer with the potential for arbitration, Sandin has rounded out his game since joining the Capitals a year ago from Toronto in a trade deadline deal that cost them a first-round draft pick. That price has proven to be worth it, as Sandin has averaged more than 21 minutes of ice time and has 20 points in 52 games this season.
"It all started really a year ago when I got here," Sandin told reporters after the team's practice in Arlington, Virginia. "It really felt like the organization really believed in me, and I love this organization and just living here. Very excited to get that extension."
The Swede, who turns 24 on Thursday, will now be part of Washington's blue line of the future along with franchise cornerstone John Carlson and young Slovak Martin Fehervary. Forward Aliaksei Protas also recently was extended through 2029, and only winger Tom Wilson — whose seven-year contract through 2031 begins next season — is signed for longer.
Re-signing Sandin comes on the heels of the Capitals trading Anthony Mantha to the Vegas Golden Knights for a 2024 second-round and a 2026 fourth-round pick. They also could make moves involving fellow pending free agents Joel Edmundson, Max Pacioretty and Nicolas Aube-Kubel and are receiving calls about valuable fourth-line center Nic Dowd.
"It can be a tough time," Edmundson said Tuesday. "It can wear you down if you keep thinking about what could happen, so we're just trying to keep things light at the rink and take everyone's mind off it. This comes around every year, it can be a stressful time for a lot of guys, but it's part of the business."
For his part, Aube-Kubel — who helped Colorado win it all in 2022 and famously dented the Stanley Cup by dropping it on the ice during the postgame celebration — said he doesn't think about trade possibilities.
"I think it just brings anxiety and stress, which I'm against," Aube-Kubel said. "Just try to stay as Zen as possible."
General manager Brian MacLellan has said he would like to add young players to the mix even while selling, similar to the trade he made with the Maple Leafs for Sandin. Getting high picks and flipping them could still happen before the deadline Friday.
"That would be ideal," MacLellan said last week. "That would be the type of thing we're looking to do, yes."

title: Yankees' Rodón gives up two HRs to Rays
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Yankees' Rodón gives up two HRs to Rays

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 980
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Carlos Rodón gave up two more homers over three-plus innings on Wednesday in the New York Yankees' 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays.AL batting champion Yandy Díaz homered on the game's first pitch, a 93 mph fastball. Richie Palocios had a two-run drive on Rodón's 60th and final offering at Tampa, Florida. Rodón allowed three runs and five hits
"He didn't have great life on his fastball today," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "I thought, really, in between the first and the last pitch I felt he pitched really well."
Rodon went 3-8 with a 6.85 ERA in 14 starts during an injury-filled 2023. He is in the second season of a $162 million, six-year contract.
"I just need to stay on the mound," Rodón said. "I'm pretty good when I'm healthy."
Rodón was coming off a simulated game last Friday in which he allowed four homers to Yankees' minor leaguers over three innings. He allowed one hit, a solo homer, in 2 1/3 innings against Toronto in his other spring training start on Feb. 25.
Yankees outfielder Alex Verdugo returned to the lineup and struck out in all three at-bats. He had been out with a bruised left leg after getting hit by a pitch last Saturday against Baltimore.
Reliever Tommy Kahnle, slowed by a shoulder injury, said "it's trending" that he won't be ready for opening day and may not start pitching in rehab games until the first week of the regular season.
OHTANI KEEPS HITTINGDodgers star Shohei Ohtani went 2 for 2 with a walk against the Chicago White Sox and is 7 of 12 with seven RBIs so far in Cactus League play.
The 29-year-old Ohtani is in his first season with the Dodgers since signing a record $700 million, 10-year contract. The two-way Japanese star had right elbow surgery in September that will keep him from pitching this year.
GIOLITO EXPLORING OPTIONS ON AILING ELBOWRed Sox pitcher Lucas Giolito will be headed to Alabama for a second opinion on his ailing right elbow.
Manager Alex Cora told reporters that Giolito will go to Birmingham on Monday to talk with Dr. Jeffrey R. Dugas as they explore treatment options, including surgery.
Giolito signed a $38.5 million, two-year deal with Boston. He made two starts in spring training, throwing two scoreless innings in his first outing before getting roughed up allowing four runs and three walks in 2 1/3 innings against Minnesota last Friday. Giolito then reported the discomfort in his elbow.
Giolito was the first overall pick by Washington in the 2012 amateur draft, agreed to a $2,925,000 signing bonus and made his professional debut that Aug. 14 in the Gulf Coast League. That was his only appearance before Tommy John surgery on Aug. 31, 2012, with Dr. Lewis Yocum.
The 29-year-old Giolito was an All-Star in 2019 and is 61-62 with a 4.43 ERA.
BELLINGER MAKES SPRING DEBUTChicago Cubs star Cody Bellinger made his spring training debut against the Los Angeles Angels, finishing with a walk in three plate appearances.
Bellinger finalized an $80 million, three-year deal on Feb. 27. He had a bounce-back season with the Cubs in 2023, batting .307 with 26 homers and 20 stolen bases.
ROSARIO TO NATS ON MINOR LEAGUE DEAL
Outfielder Eddie Rosario and the Washington Nationals have agreed to a minor league contract with a non-roster invitation to spring training, a person familiar with the deal told The Associated Press.
The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because Rosario's agreement had not been announced. The deal is pending the successful completion of a physical exam.
The 32-year-old Rosario is a left-handed hitter who has played nine seasons in the major leagues with the Minnesota Twins, Cleveland Indians and Atlanta Braves.
He started most of Atlanta's games in left field last season, hitting 21 homers with 74 RBIs while batting .255. But the Braves — who led the majors with 104 wins in 2023 — declined a $9 million option for him this season.
Rosario was a star of Atlanta's run to the 2021 World Series title. In the NL Championship Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers that year, he hit .560 (14 of 35) with three homers and nine RBIs to win MVP honors.
LOWE WORKING BACK TO '21 FORM
Rays infielder Brandon Lowe is healthy and working to put the previous two injury-marred seasons behind him.
After hitting 39 homers and driving in 99 runs in 2021, Lowe was limited to 65 games in 2022 and 109 last year due to back and knee injuries.
"Don't worry about results for a little while, and go out here and try to make sure to take your at-bats, get your timing down," Lowe said. "Try to put yourself in as many situations as you can to emulate the season and make sure that you're healthy."
Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said Lowe looks good and is motivated.
"I like the fact that he's able to do everything," Cash said. "He had to pull back on some of his routine, some of the amount of ground balls that he could take last year even before he got banged up because we were managing the workload on his back and then he fouled the ball off the knee and couldn't do anything."
CREWS HITS HR FOR NATS
Dylan Crews, last year's No. 2 overall pick for the Nationals, hit his first spring training homer against the Miami Marlins. He finished 2 for 3 and also had a double, two runs scored and two RBIs, lifting his batting average to .286.
The 22-year-old was a star in college at LSU, where he was teammates with No. 1 overall pick Paul Skenes, who was drafted by the Pittsburgh Pirates.
ADOLIS GARCÍA
Adolis García made his first 2024 appearance in a Cactus League game, going 1 for 3 with a solo home run down the left field line in the fourth inning. García, who had batted in camp games and Tuesday's "B" game against Kansas City, was the Rangers' designated hitter.
