title: Biggest free-agent deals may be re-signings
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Biggest free-agent deals may be re-signings

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1049
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Chris Jones won't have to wait so long to cash in this year.The Kansas City Chiefs' star defensive tackle will be among the headliners when free agency opens next week and he could eclipse Aaron Donald's three-year, $96 million deal that made Donald the league's highest-paid defensive tackle.
Teams can begin negotiating Monday and can sign players starting Wednesday.
Jones held out last year, missing the entire offseason plus the opener and a $1.1 million weekly paycheck, in a contract dispute that resulted in a restructure of the final year of his contract.
Although the Chiefs retained the right to franchise tag Jones in 2024, they decided to place that tag instead on cornerback L'Jarius Sneed at $19.8 million.
Call them priorities 1A and 1B for Chiefs GM Brett Veach, the architect of the NFL's latest dynasty with a trio of Lombardi Trophies since 2020.
"You'd like to ... pay all the guys and it's tough because the more you win, the more you've got to pay players, and obviously when you have this amount of success you're paying a lot of players a lot of money," Veach said.
"Hopefully, we'll be able to figure something out but every free agent is different, unique and crazy. But we do have one tag and ... our goal is to get both those players done and then work down the rest of our roster."
The 31 other teams looking to knock the Chiefs from their pedestal will begin plugging holes with veterans next week.
The team that made the most racket in free agency a year ago won't be noisy this year.
The Denver Broncos signed 14 veterans to contracts totaling a whopping $242,647,500, which was only slightly more than the $242,588,236 contract extension Russell Wilson signed less than a year earlier.
Now, the Broncos are moving on from Wilson, a separation that saddles them with a record $85 million in dead cap charges, crimping any designs on another spending spree even with the salary cap's historic spike.
"We can't do that every year," said Broncos general manager George Paton, who began the roster purge Thursday by releasing star safety Justin Simmons to save $14.5 million.
One truism about free agency is it's usually a whole lot less risky to re-sign one's own free agents than to acquire other teams' castoffs, misfits, pluggers or stars.
With that in mind, here's a free agent from every team that front offices want to keep from calling the moving trucks:
ARIZONA CARDINALSWR Marquise Brown has had a star-crossed stint in Arizona but he has flashed when he and Kyler Murray are healthy.
ATLANTA FALCONSEDGE Calais Campbell. He's valued more for his leadership at age 37, although he did post 6 1/2 sacks last season.
BALTIMORE RAVENSDL Justin Madubuike's 13 sacks and 33 QB hits led all defensive tackles. Baltimore put its $22.1 million franchise tag on him.
BUFFALO BILLSEDGE A.J. Epenesa is a consistent, improving player on a team whose purge of players this week cut deep into its core.
CAROLINA PANTHERSEDGE Brian Burns, a two-time Pro Bowl selection, received the franchise tag, which is worth $24 million.
CHICAGO BEARSCB Jaylon Johnson, a second-team All-Pro, received the franchise tag, which will pay him $19.8 million in 2024.
CINCINNATI BENGALSWR Tee Higgins received the franchise tag that will pay him just under $22 million next season.
CLEVELAND BROWNSJoe Flacco is the most valuable backup QB in the NFL and Deshaun Watson is recovering from shoulder surgery.
DALLAS COWBOYSLT Tyron Smith is 33 and often hurt, but he gave up one sack in '23 and remains the NFL's top pass-blocking tackle.
DENVER BRONCOSC Lloyd Cushenberry III is one of the NFL's best, but Luke Wattenberg or Alex Forsyth could step in if he bolts Denver.
DETROIT LIONSG Graham Glasgow had a resurgence in 2023 in his return to Detroit after a three-year stint in Denver.
GREEN BAY PACKERSKR-CB Keisean Nixon was an All-Pro kick returner in each of the last two seasons. No more one-year "prove it" deals.
HOUSTON TEXANSEDGE Jonathan Greenard collected 12½ sacks last season as the Texans returned to relevance.
INDIANAPOLIS COLTS
WR Michael Pittman is coming off his first 100-catch season and received the franchise tag worth $21.8 million in '24.
JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS
EDGE Josh Allen received the $24 million franchise tag after setting franchise record with 17½ sacks last season.
KANSAS CITY CHIEFS
DT Chris Jones and CB L'Jarius Sneed. Of course KC gets two mentions here. They're the team of the 2020s, after all.
LOS ANGELES RAMS
OG Kevin Dotson went from an afterthought in Pittsburgh to the NFL's best run-blocking guard in 2023.
LOS ANGELES CHARGERS
K Cameron Dicker has nailed 52 of 55 career FG attempts and absolutely crushed his Pro Bowl campaign video.
LAS VEGAS RAIDERS
C Andre James will get another big salary bump after seeing his pay jump from $505,000 in '19 to $6.5 million in '23.
MIAMI DOLPHINS
DT Christian Wilkins, a five-year pro, enjoyed a breakout 2023 season with a career-best nine sacks.
MINNESOTA VIKINGS
QB Kirk Cousins. Even at 36 in '24 and with a repaired Achilles, his exit would shake up the Vikings and the NFL QB market.
NEW ENGLAND PATRIOTS
Safety Kyle Dugger received the Patriots' transition tag, which will pay him $13.8 million in 2024.
NEW ORLEANS SAINTS
Jameis Winston provides a spark whenever he subs for starter Derek Carr, much like Flacco does with Watson out.
NEW YORK GIANTS
FS Xavier McKinney picked off three passes and didn't allow a single TD catch in 2023, solidifying his topflight status.
NEW YORK JETS
EDGE Bryce Huff was one of the few Jets who had a stellar 2023 with a career-high 10 sacks and a budding reputation.
PHILADELPHIA EAGLES
RB D'Andre Swift posted his first 1,000-yard season and made the Pro Bowl in '23 after three years in Detroit.
PITTSBURGH STEELERS
QB Mason Rudolph was terrific subbing for Kenny Pickett in '23 and could provide similar support for a new QB in '24.
SEATTLE SEAHAWKS
DT Leonard Williams is a 10th-year pro who has 43½ career sacks and averages 19.2 QB hits a year.
SAN FRANCISCO 49ERS
EDGE Chase Young, 2020's second overall pick, showed glimpses of greatness after his '23 trade from Washington.
TAMPA BAY BUCCANEERS
QB Baker Mayfield has finally arrived. He set career highs last year in accuracy (64.3%), yards (4,044) and TDs (28).
TENNESSEE TITANS
RB Derrick Henry, 30, was the NFL's second-leading rusher in '23 with 1,167 yards and 12 TDs, but seems set to leave.
WASHINGTON COMMANDERS
CB Kendall Fuller was the only bright spot on Washington's dreadful defense in '23 and should thrive under Dan Quinn.

title: Maple Leafs acquire Capitals' Edmundson
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Maple Leafs acquire Capitals' Edmundson

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 701
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With one sleep left before the NHL trade deadline, the Toronto Maple Leafs joined the party Thursday by bulking up on defense, while two Western Conference Stanley Cup contenders made more moves to improve in crucial areas.Colorado acquired a pair of versatile forwards from Central Division rivals, Brandon Duhaime from Minnesota and Yakov Trenin from Nashville, Edmonton got defenseman Troy Stecher from Arizona and Toronto received Joel Edmundson from Washington.
"Every team has a window in which they see success or a key moment of time for the organization — whether it's two years, five years, depending on expiring contracts who they have to renew," Avalanche coach Jared Bednar said. "There's lots of teams going all-in: teams that feel like they've got a chance to win, if they add certain things to their lineup, they're going to go all-in. Your goal is to win the Stanley Cup. We're not trying to be a mediocre team."
It shows. Colorado and Edmonton stayed active, after the Avalanche added center Casey Mittelstadt and defenseman Sean Walker in separate deals and the Oilers giving themselves serious depth down the middle by trading with Anaheim for Adam Henrique and Sam Carrick.
The Avalanche sent a 2026 third-round pick to the Wild for Duhaime and a 2025 third and defense prospect Jeremy Hanzel to the Predators for Trenin and the rights to unsigned draft pick Graham Sward. The Oilers sent a 2027 fourth-round pick to the Coyotes for Stecher, and the Leafs got Edmundson from the Capitals for a third-rounder this year and a 2025 fifth.
Toronto's trade for Edmundson started the action Thursday, adding some much needed toughness on the blue line. He's a left shot, which the Leafs have plenty of, but his playoff experience alone makes Edmundson a potentially important acquisition for a team dreaming of an extended run this spring.
The Capitals are retaining a quarter of Edmundson's salary after Montreal already has half from a trade last offseason and getting a third-rounder that originally belonged to the New York Islanders. Salary retention makes the him quite the bargain for the Leafs at a cap hit of $875,000, just above the league minimum.
Edmundson, 30, helped the St. Louis Blues win the Stanley Cup in 2019 and is a pending free agent. He has skated over 16 minutes a game this season with Washington.
Earlier in the week, Edmundson seemed content with the possibility of being traded to a contender, though his focus at the time was on helping the Capitals.
"Everyone wants to win," he said. "I want to win every year, so I think once you get that feeling once, you just want it to happen every year and when you see other teams win it, you just kind of get jealous and frustrated. So yeah, we all want to win it every year."
But it's not just the championship contenders getting in on the action. The Predators, who hold one of the two wild-card playoff spots in the West, acquired winger Anthony Beauvillier from Chicago for a 2024 fifth-round pick.
Nashville also claimed forward Jaret Anderson-Dolan off waivers from the Los Angeles Kings. Carolina could be making space for a big move, after the Hurricanes put goaltender Antti Raanta, defenseman Tony DeAngelo and forward Brendan Lemieux on waivers.
Still also likely to be moved before 3 p.m. EST on Friday are Pittsburgh's Jake Guentzel and Reilly Smith, New Jersey winger Tyler Toffoli, Washington center Nic Dowd and a couple of more Arizona pending free agents: defenseman Matthew Dumba and ex-Penguins forward Jason Zucker. The Devils are holding out Toffoli from their game Thursday night for trade-related reasons, and San Jose is doing the same with Alexander Barabanov and Anthony Duclair.
Seattle's Jordan Eberle, who's also on an expiring contract, could also be the next to go after the Kraken sent Alexander Wennberg to the New York Rangers on Wednesday.
"From a player standpoint, we just want to continue to win," Eberle said. "From a management standpoint, it's a little harder, right, because they're stuck between, do we have a chance, or do we want to get rid of some pieces? I can't really say anything on their behalf. I think I can only say as a player, we're just focusing on winning."

title: Taking the plunge for a good cause
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Taking the plunge for a good cause

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 325
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last year several law enforcement officers in Kent County formed a team named Kent County's Finest to participate in the 2024 Polar Plunge in support of Special Olympics Maryland (SOMD).Chestertown Police Chief Ron Dixon and Patrolman First Class Brandon McGinnis along with Corporal Scott Lockerman pledged to leap into the frigid waters of the Chesapeake Bay after soliciting donations for SOMD.
Feb. 2, along with K-9 Khari, the group braved the 38° degree water temperature, taking the plunge into the Bay at Sandy Point State Park with more than 1,000 other first responders and law enforcement officers from across the State.
The group then organized a chili cook-off competition held at Luisa's Cucina Italiana on Feb. 26; a fundraiser to support the team.
The event was open to the public, both as contestants and diners.
"We had five entries, one of whom travelled all the way from Georgetown, Delaware to compete," Dixon said.
In a very close vote, Lockerman won the title of "Best Chili in Chestertown".
"There was a good turnout and the crowd enjoyed some delicious chili," Dixon said.
In total, team Kent County's Finest raised $2,460 for Special Olympics Maryland in their first year of existence.
They will be launching t-shirt and hat sales later in the month of March, with proceeds going to SOMD.
Future events include supporting Special Olympics athletes competing in bocce ball at Washington College in May, hosting a Law Enforcement Torch Run in June, and welcoming the athletes back to Kent County in August for a kayaking event.
Dixon said, "Our goal for the rest of 2024 and the 2025 Plunge is to continue to spread the word about the fantastic athletes that participate in Special Olympics Maryland competitions and the great work done by SOMD. From a fundraising standpoint, we simply want to improve on what we have done in year one."
He invited everyone to like the Chestertown Police Department's Facebook page and stay updated on the upcoming events in support of Special Olympics Maryland.

title: QA's-Carver playoff cut short by altercation
author: Bill Haufe
content:
QA's-Carver playoff cut short by altercation

 March 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 516
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Friday night's Class 2A boys basketball state quarterfinal playoff between Carver Vo-Tech and host Queen Anne's County High was stopped with 6:57 remaining in the third quarter when an altercation broke out between the two teams that left one Queen Anne's player injured.In a press release late Friday night, the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff said, "it was actively investigating an assault that took place Friday on a Queen Anne's County High School basketball player at the game.
"We have obtained and are currently reviewing video surveillance footage as part of our ongoing efforts," the release stated. "No arrests have been made at this time as we continue to review evidence and fully investigate this incident."
Carver was winning 42-15 at halftime and extended that lead to 47-15, when Dorrian Sands hit a baseline jumper and a 3-pointer in the first minute.
Queen Anne's was approaching mid-court on its ensuing possession when a cross-court pass was intercepted by a Carver player, who drove quickly to the basket and was fouled from behind by Thompson. A Carver player confronted Thompson.
Video footage on Twitter showed players from both teams exchanging words near the Carver basket. Players and coaches from both benches came onto the court. The video then shows the altercation escalating when a Queen Anne's player is punched in the face. It is not clear from the video who struck the Queen Anne's player.
Members of the Queen Anne's County sheriff's department, Queen Anne's school administrators and staff, and both coaching staffs quickly separated players. The game's three officials conferred and decided to officially call the game.
"Our players, teams, community and school staff deserve a safe environment, we have zero tolerance for this type of behavior at our public events, and we can assure our community that this investigation will be thoroughly completed, and appropriate charges will be done at the conclusion," Queen Anne's Sheriff Gary Hofmann said in the press release.
Queen Anne's County athletic director Kwandrey Wilson and head basketball coach Jeff Hollis would not comment on the incident.
Carver advances to the semifinals where it will meet Middletown.
As of Saturday afternoon, it was not known if the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association would take any action on the incident or dole out any punishment.
Queen Anne's (18-4) took a 2-0 lead on a pair of Vince Gilberto free throws 1:23 into the game. The Bears (16-4) rattled off the next nine points before Collin Woolford hit a 3-pointer for the Lions midway through the first quarter.
Carver, which used a suffocating, in-your face pressure defense, stretched its lead to 16-5 when Sands (game-high 25 points) drained one of his five 3-pointers. Gilberto hit two free throws to get Queen Anne's within 16-7. But with 54.9 seconds left, Gilberto appeared to suffer an ankle injury while driving to the basket and was carried off the court. The senior guard did not return the rest of the game.
The Bears led 18-8 after one quarter, widened their lead to 32-14, then went on a 10-0 run to close the first half, taking a 42-15 lead into the locker room.

 CAMBRIDGE — The openings don't have to be big for LaShaun Moody."I just see the gap, I see the rim," Moody said. "I know if the gap is there I can get to the rim."
Moody got to the rim often Saturday afternoon, darting through slivers of space and around defenders during a dizzying 33-point performance that paced Cambridge-South Dorchester High's boys' basketball team to a 74-58 victory over CMIT-North in a Class 1A state quarterfinal.
The top-seeded Vikings (23-1) advance to the semifinals where they will meet No. 4 seed Fort Hill (19-3) at a site and date yet to be determined as of Saturday night.
"I think we're playing some of our best basketball we've played all season," Moody said. "I know coming into the game we started off hot, started off that with grit, and I know that's what got us this win."
Moody scored six points in an 11-0 Vikings run to open the game, as the Tigers (12-10) committed six turnovers before Micah Germain (team-high 13 points) scored near the midway point of the first quarter. Cambridge-SD center Koby Ennals (20 points) hammered down a dunk and added another inside bucket to cap the first quarter and give the Vikings an 18-6 lead.
"All year long that's all we preach is defense, defense, defense," Moody said. "So I know coming into the game that's one thing I don't have to worry about is defense. That's how we get our points most times for the games. That's what we look forward to every game."
Cambridge-SD needed less than three minutes to expand that lead to 26-6 as Ennals connected on one of his game-high four 3-pointers during an 8-0 spree to open the second quarter.
Amir Morton's 3-pointer and two free throws got CMIT-North within 26-11.
But Moody scored on a drive, buried a 3-pointer, and converted a pair of free throws. He then scored on yet another break-neck drive that started the Vikings on a 9-0 run to close the second quarter, giving Cambridge-SD a 44-16 halftime cushion.
"He's so hard," Vikings head coach Shawn Tucker said of defending Moody. "You can scout for him, but on tape it's not the same as you standing in front of him. He's going to that basket one way or another. He's a senior; battled-tested. I'm just so proud of him."
Tucker was also proud of his team's defense that hounded the Tigers into multiple turnovers through the first half and into the third quarter.
"The first three quarters we were locked in," Tucker said. "We were ready. And we were focused.
"Just be relaxed and play our game," Tucker said of his pregame speech to his team. "We've been playing defense all year and that's what we've been hanging our hat on. And why go away from that? We can score points. We just need to be able to stop them. And that's what we do."
Cambridge-SD widened its lead to 31 twice in the third quarter. Another Ennals three-ball made it 52-21 with just under five minutes left in the third. A Moody drive to the hole made it 54-23 with 4:09 left.
A drive and a three-point play from Germain pulled CMIT-North within 54-28 with 3:19 to go in the third. But Moody scored on a baseline drive as part of a three-point play, then tightroped along the baseline for another bucket that gave the Vikings a 58-28 lead with a little over two minutes remaining in the third.
CMIT-North closed the third quarter on a 13-5 run that got it within 21 at 63-42. And though the Vikings committed turnovers while continuing to push the pace in the fourth, and struggled from the foul line — 2 of 12 in the second half — their lead was too much for the Tigers, who wouldn't get any closer than 16 the rest of the game.
Notes: Anthony Hughes had eight points for Cambridge-SD. ... Antonio Waddy had 12 points for CMIT-North and Melvin Coutreyer came off the bench to add 10.

title: Henry leaves Titans for Jackson, Ravens
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Henry leaves Titans for Jackson, Ravens

 March 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 834
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Derrick Henry is leaving the Tennessee Titans to team up with MVP Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens with a two-year deal worth up to $20 million, a person with knowledge of the deal tells The Associated Press. Henry's deal follows several others for running backs during the NFL's two-day legal tampering period. The position has been devalued in recent years, but this year's run shows teams will go after running backs at the right price. At least a dozen running backs are switching teams along with at least 10 quarterbacks, including Kirk Cousins and Russell Wilson.Backfields are going to look a whole lot different in the NFL next season after a run on free agent quarterbacks and running backs during the league's two-day legal tampering period.
After QBs ruled Day 1, running backs continued to make strides in free agency Tuesday with four-time Pro Bowler Derrick Henry agreeing to a two-year deal with the Baltimore Ravens, a person with knowledge of the contract told The Associated Press.
Henry's jump from the Tennessee Titans, where he spent his first eight seasons, was among the biggest moves on the eve of the league's new year, which officially begins at 4 p.m. EDT Wednesday.
That's when free agents can sign contracts they've agreed to this week.
Henry's deal is worth up to $20 million and includes $9 million guaranteed. The two-time NFL rushing champ joins a Baltimore team that annually produces one of the league's leading ground games.
Running backs have struggled to earn big money in recent years — to the point where Henry organized a group chat among top players at the position last summer. This year's free agent class included Saquon Barkley, Josh Jacobs and Tony Pollard, all of whom found new homes during Monday's free agency frenzy.
Barkley, Jacobs and Pollard were the three running backs franchise tagged a year ago at $10.1 million, and none signed long-term deals with their teams by the July deadline. All three became free agents this year when their teams declined to tag them again, this time at $12 million.
Henry turned 30 in January. The four-time Pro Bowler led the NFL in 2023 with 280 rushing attempts and ranked second to Christian McCaffrey with 1,167 yards rushing. His 12 rushing TDs were fourth in the AFC.
Henry leaves Tennessee ranked second in franchise history with 9,502 rushing yards, trailing only Eddie George (10,009).
The Ravens finished with the NFL's best regular-season record in 2023 before losing to Kansas City in the AFC championship game. Now they add another proven offensive playmaker to work alongside quarterback Lamar Jackson, who is coming off his second MVP season.
Baltimore was also able to reach a long-term deal with defensive tackle Justin Madubuike after putting the franchise tag on him. But the Ravens lost inside linebacker Patrick Queen to rival Pittsburgh on Tuesday.
So far, 10 quarterbacks will be signing with new teams Wednesday: Kirk Cousins, Russell Wilson, Jacoby Brissett, Jameis Winston, Gardner Minshew, Tyrod Taylor, Drew Lock, Marcus Mariota, Mitchell Trubisky and Sam Darnold.
At least a dozen veteran running backs, led by Henry, Barkley, Jacobs and Pollard, are getting deals with new teams.
They're joined by Aaron Jones, D'Andre Swift, Austin Ekeler, Devin Singletary, Antonio Gibson, Zack Moss, Gus Edwards and Nyheim Hines, among others.
The Vikings added Jones, the former Green Bay running back and 2018 third overall draft pick Darnold as a temporary replacement at quarterback for Cousins, whose departure to Atlanta was the biggest move of free agency.
Also Tuesday, the Browns agreed to a one-year deal with Winston to back up Deshaun Watson that's worth up to $8.7 million, a person with knowledge of the negotiations told the AP.
Joe Flacco, who went 4-1 and helped the Browns reach the playoffs last season after Watson was sidelined by a shoulder injury, didn't receive a contract offer from the Browns, said his agent, Joe Linta.
Also, a person familiar with the deal told the AP that the Texans are acquiring running back Joe Mixon from the Bengals.
Mixon, who led Cincinnati with 1,034 yards rushing and nine TDs last season, will replace Singletary.
Cincinnati planned to release him after agreeing on a contract with running back Moss, who scored seven combined TDs in '23 for the Colts.
Mixon will join Dameon Pierce in the backfield for the AFC South champions.
Other notable moves Tuesday included edge rusher Danielle Hunter agreeing to a two-year, $49 million deal with the Texans; edge rusher Shaquil Barrett agreeing to a one-year, $9 million deal with Miami after five seasons in Tampa Bay; and former Saints defensive lineman Malcolm Roach agreeing to a two-year deal worth up to $8 million with Denver, according to people with knowledge of the deals. The Broncos allowed a league-worst 5 yards per carry last season.
The Broncos were the big spenders last year in free agency, signing 14 players to contracts worth nearly a quarter-billion dollars. But they have had to be much more judicious in their spending after their release of Wilson saddled them with a record $85 million in dead cap charges.

title: Late push seals Vikings' title shot
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Late push seals Vikings' title shot

 March 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 691
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SILVER SPRING — Anthony Hughes and Koby Ennals know basketball can be a game of runs.The two juniors were part of the run that mattered most Tuesday night.
A one-time 17-point lead reduced to three, Hughes and Ennals helped fuel a decisive 8-0 fourth-quarter burst that returned momentum back to Cambridge-South Dorchester High's boys basketball team en route to the Vikings earning a 60-53 victory over Fort Hill in a Class 1A state semifinal at Montgomery Blair High School.
Top-seeded Cambridge-SD (24-1) will bid for its first state title since 1996 Friday, when it faces No. 2 seed Edmondson-Westside (22-2) for the Class 1A championship at the University of Maryland's Xfinity Center. Edmondson defeated third-seeded Smithsburg, 79-59, in Tuesday's other 1A semifinal.
"We just got a believe attitude," Cambridge-SD head coach Shawn Tucker said. "We told them, 'If we just slow it down we'll be fine. We just got to be patient.'"
The Vikings went on an 11-1 run to open the game, and packaged a 13-2 scoring spree during the second quarter, when they outscored the Sentinels, 23-8, to carry a 37-20 lead into halftime.
"We turned it over way too much in the first half," Fort Hill head coach Thad Burner said. "I thought that their energy was a lot better than ours, particularly in the second quarter when they extended that lead."
Senior point guard LaShaun Moody (team-high 18 points) had a three-point play and a drive that helped Cambridge-SD build its early 11-1 lead. But Fort Hill (19-4) got 3-pointers from DeShaun Brown (team-high 18 points) and Jabril Daniels (10 points) in the final 3:16 of the first quarter to pull within 14-12 heading into the second quarter.
The Vikings led 16-14 when they pieced together a 9-0 run midway through the second quarter. Ennals (13 points), who scored his 1,000th-career point in the first quarter, converted a Moody dish for a bucket off the glass. Semaj Pinder (nine points) hit a turnaround jumper then scored on a drive. Ennals scored on a put-back before Thomas Wilson canned a 3-pointer for a 27-14 Vikings lead.
Brown hit another trey to end a three-plus minute Fort Hill scoring drought. But Moody hit a 3-pointer, Ennals made two free throws, and Darren Belizare scored on a follow before Moody splashed another trey at the buzzer for a 37-20 Vikings lead.
"We preach getting off to a fast start," Tucker said. "We knew Fort Hill was a second-half team and it was going to be a battle. So to get out on a team like that early is huge."
The Sentinels went on an 11-2 run to start the third quarter, getting within 39-31 with 4:36 to go in the period. Hughes stopped that momentum briefly when he converted a steal into a layup, putting the Vikings back up by 10. A pair of Sterling Perkins free throws moved Cambridge-SD to a 44-33 lead heading into the fourth quarter.
Fort Hill came out bombing in the fourth. Landon Sensabaugh hit back-to-back three-balls and Brown turned a steal into a layup, cutting Cambridge-SD's lead to 45-41 with 6:30 left. Tucker called time and watched Hughes score another big bucket inside to make it a six-point lead.
Jabril Daniels answered with another 3, shaving Fort Hill's deficit to three at 47-44 with 5:38 remaining.
But Cambridge-SD showed it too could respond.
"We just had to come back and be ourself," Hughes said. "It's win or go home."
Hughes scored on a put-back. Ennals converted a pair of free throws. Moody scored on a follow before Ennals snatched a rebound and raced coast-to-coast for a bucket that pushed Cambridge-SD's lead to 55-44 with under 4 minutes to play.
"We made some pretty good runs in the third and the fourth, but (number) two (Ennals) and five (Moody), they were pretty good," Burner said.
The Sentinels wouldn't get any closer than nine the rest of the way, as Moody scored on a drive and made three of four free throws in the final 1:24 to cement the victory and Cambridge-SD's first state final appearance since 1996.
"They're a team that's not going to give up," Ennals said of Fort Hill. "But we're a team that's not going to give up either."

title: Jets get Ravens' Moses
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Jets get Ravens' Moses

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 436
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The New York Jets are acquiring offensive tackle Morgan Moses from the Baltimore Ravens in a trade that includes draft picks for both teams, a person familiar with the deal told The Associated Press.The move Wednesday reunites Moses with the Jets after he spent the 2021 season with New York.
The Jets will also receive the Ravens' fourth-round pick (No. 134 overall) and New York will send its fourth-rounder (No. 112) and a sixth-rounder to Baltimore, the person told the AP on condition of anonymity because trades and free agent signings weren't official until the new league year began at 4 p.m. EDT Wednesday.
ESPN first reported the deal between the Jets and Ravens.
Later Wednesday, Baltimore announced it was releasing veteran linebacker Tyus Bowser, who missed all of last season because of knee problems. The Ravens also re-signed linebacker Malik Harrison.
The Jets re-signed punter and fan favorite Thomas Morstead to a two-year deal. New York kept two of its most consistent performers from last season, also bringing back kicker Greg Zuerlein after he agreed to terms on a two-year contract on Monday.
The Jets also released tight end C.J. Uzomah with a failed physical designation. He missed the final five games last season with an injured knee ligament.
The 33-year-old Moses helps bolster a revamped offensive line for New York, which struggled with consistency and production up front last season.
Moses is likely to take over as the starter at right tackle, joining center Joe Tippmann and guards Alijah Vera-Tucker and John Simpson — a former Ravens teammate who agreed to terms on a two-year deal with the Jets on Monday night.
New York currently holds the No. 10 overall pick in the draft next month and could target a left tackle. Mekhi Becton and Duane Brown are both scheduled to be free agents and are not expected to return.
Moses spent his first seven NFL seasons in Washington after being a third-round pick out of Virginia before he signed with the Jets as a free agent in 2021. He played in all 17 games that season, including 16 starts, but signed a three-year deal with Baltimore the following offseason.
Moses started 31 games during the past two seasons with the Ravens, helping block in front of Lamar Jackson.
Now, he'll be a major part of a unit that will try to protect Aaron Rodgers, who was lost for the season with a torn left Achilles tendon just four snaps into his debut. Rodgers is expected to be healthy in time for the start of training camp in July — and general manager Joe Douglas made improving the offensive line a priority this offseason.

title: C-SD locked in for last dance
author: Bill Haufe
content:
C-SD locked in for last dance

 March 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 964
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When Darnell Dantzler brought his Edmondson-Westside High boys basketball team together for its first practice Nov. 15, he established the same goal he's set the previous 17 seasons as head coach — winning a state title.That same day, Shawn Tucker, starting just his second season as Cambridge-South Dorchester's head coach, provided a string of goals for his team that included winning the North Bayside regular-season title, the Bayside Conference championship, the Class 1A East Region II crown and the state championship.
Tucker and the top-seeded Vikings (24-1) hope to complete that title string Saturday beginning at 1 p.m., when they face the No. 2 seed and defending state-champion Red Storm (22-2) for the Class 1A state championship at the University of Maryland's Xfinity Center.
"You had a lot of good pieces that needed to learn to play basketball together as a team really quickly," Tucker said, recalling his first impression of this season's team. "But there wasn't quite a team."
Tucker has quite a team on his hands now, one that won its first 13 games this season, lost its one and only game to Queen Anne's, then reeled off 11 consecutive wins to earn a shot at the school's first state title in basketball since 1996.
"It's going to be a really, really good challenge," Tucker said of Edmondson. "But I go back to us playing in the Bayside (Conference) championship versus a team like (Stephen) Decatur. It prepared us."
Cambridge-SD fell behind 8-0 to Decatur on Feb. 22, settled itself, then raced to its first outright conference championship since 1996.
The Vikings got off to blazing starts in their state quarterfinal and semifinals wins. The second of those came Tuesday against Fort Hill, when a one-time 17-point lead was whittled to just three with 5:38 remaining. But instead of calling timeout, Tucker let his team continuing playing, and watched as Anthony Hughes came up with two huge steals to spark a decisive 8-0 Vikings run.
"When that kid hit a three, I could have called a timeout," Tucker said of Jabril Daniels' trey that got the Sentinels within 47-44. "And I looked at them and I said, 'Nope.' I'm going to let them play through that because this is the only way they're going to learn this scenario. They know that's me. In that situation, I call a timeout and I don't have any faith in them. So by not calling that timeout, it showed them that I faith in them and they responded."
Now, the Vikings prepare for an Edmondson program that makes its sixth final appearance in Dantzler's 18 seasons at the helm, which include state championships in 2013, '14 and '23.
"First day of practice my goal always is to make it to the state championship, setting goals up as high as you can set 'em," Dantzler said during a phone interview Wednesday. "But sometime being realistic, you might not be as good. But the number one goal is to always win a state championship."
Danztler though wasn't sure the Red Storm would get the chance to defend their title this season.
"I'm really surprised," Dantzler said of reaching the state final. "We had a couple of people that graduated and transferred out. So going into the season I didn't think we were going to make it there. But through playing hard, I'm just happy and fortunate to make it there."
Adding even more meaning to this championship trip for Dantzler is the fact his son, Darnell Jr., is the Red Storm's starting point guard.
"It's been a dream come true," Coach Dantzler said. "Sometimes it's tough trying to draw the line as father and coach, but I wouldn't trade it for the world, just to have the experience of him being a part of my team, and me being part of his success for his high school career."
A 5-foot-9 junior, Dantzler Jr. has averaged 16.5 points and 11 assists a game this season. He is joined in the backcourt by senior Kyrie Sherrod (13.3 points per game). Then there is Edmondson's frontcourt that features 6-8 sophomore forward Chase Foster (19.8 ppg.; 11 rebounds per game) and 6-4 senior forward Josiah Brown (14.5 ppg., 11.5 rpg.).
"They've played hard all season," Coach Dantzler said. "Hopefully we can bring it home when we play."
That is also the hopes of a Cambridge-SD team that has hounded the opposition on defense this season and attacked the boards on both ends of the floor.
Leading the attack has been 5-9 senior point guard LaShaun Moody (25 ppg.) whose quickness has been a problem for opponents on both ends of the court. Moody may run the show, but has plenty of help. Koby Ennals, a 6-5 junior (19 ppg., 10 rpg), can slash to the rim or bury the 3-pointer. And there's the 6-2 Hughes (10 points), who has come up with huge rebounds, steals and buckets throughout the Vikings' run.
Complementing that trio has been a rotation that includes junior Darren Belizare and sophomores Semaj Pinder, Sterling Perkins (12 ppg) and Thomas Wilson, who have more than made their share of big plays throughout this season.
"I hear they're really good," Coach Dantzler said of Cambridge-SD.
Really good, and really locked in, a quality Tucker has praised during this postseason stretch.
"I wish people could be in the locker room for the pre-game speech," Tucker said. "When I say they are zeroed in, they are locked in. And I've never experienced a group of young men that get locked in so fast. Like one minute they can be joking and playing and when we say, 'All right, let's go,' they just locked in immediately. I thought that wasn't something possible, 'cause you know you can get caught turning that switch on and off. When they lock in, they're in. And that's the way we're going to have to be against Edmondson."

title: GOLDEN DELIVERY
author: Bill Haufe
content:
GOLDEN DELIVERY

 March 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 962
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Easton High head swim coach Tim Kroeger calls the 200-yard freestyle a hard race to swim."Everybody seems to have a love-hate relationship with that event because it's too short to be distance, and it's too long to be a sprint," Kroeger said. "It's one of those things you have to train for, you have to get a feel for. In a sense a lot of kids don't like swimming it because it's just hard. It's hard to find those kids who are really good at it."
In the 16 years the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association has held the state swimming championships, the Bayside Conference has had only four champions — all girls — win the 200-yard free, including three from Easton.
The Warriors added a fourth Feb. 24.
Maddie Weems showed why she was a heavy favorite in the event, as she outdistanced her closest competitor by over 4 seconds en route to winning the girls' 200 freestyle title during the Class 3A/2A/1A state championships at the University of Maryland's Eppley Recreation Center.
"Maddie always delivers the big swims when we she needs it," Kroeger said of his sophomore star who was the only Bayside swimmer to win a state title this year. "She's been very consistent.
"She's kind of branched out," Kroeger added. "Last year she was more of a freestyle sprinter for us, and this year she wanted to explore some of the other events. I mean she's good at all of the events, which is a good and bad thing for any swimmer really."
Weems was second in the 100 freestyle and third in the 50 free at last year's state meet.
She changed things up heading into this year's postseason, winning the 100 butterfly and 100 breaststroke at the conference championships in early February.
But when it came time for regionals and states, Weems opted for events she thought she could place in.
"I thought about doing the 100 fly and 100 breast, but then I really wanted to do freestyle," Weems said. "And I looked at where I would maybe place the best. I was like, I feel the best in the 200 free."
But.
"I've never liked the 200," Weems said smiling. "But I had been practicing it a lot, and I just felt the most comfortable in it. So I was like, I'll just try and give it my best."
Weems practiced a lot. She also swam a lot.
Because of poor weather conditions, the 3A/2A/1A East Regional championships were moved from Feb. 17 to Feb. 20 — four days before states. A member of the Talbot County YMCA team, Weems was also competing in the Maryland Club State Championships at St. Mary's College, which were sandwiched around the MPSSAA state meet.
Weems was admittedly tired and sore after swimming five events — including preliminaries — the Friday before the MPSSAA state meet. She didn't do well in the morning prelims of the 200 free, but rebounded that night, clocking a personal-record time of 1:54.17.
And though that effort potentially stoked Weems' confidence heading into Saturday's MPSSAA meet, it may have also added a bit more pressure to the favorite's shoulders.
"Everybody was telling me I was going to win," said Weems, who was seeded No. 1 by 6 seconds. "But I was like, 'I don't know.' I was nervous, but I felt confident. And even if it ended up being close I knew that I would be able to push through."
She did just that, reaching the first turn with a lead she never relinquished on the way to a first-place 1:54.53, giving Easton its third straight title in the 200 free. Kroeger's daughter, Molly, won the championship in 2022 (1:53.76) and last year, when she set a 3A/2A/1A record of 1:51.94. Weems' cousin, Tori Weems, won the event in 2017 (1:55.96).
The only other Bayside swimmer to win the 200 was Queen Anne's County's Kelsey Lessard (2:03.6) in 2010.
Weems was back in the pool for the 100 fly, and held the lead before getting passed over the final 25 yards, taking fourth in 1:00.58.
"My body just kind of gave out," Weems said.
Weems teamed with Katheryne Kelsey, Claire Morris and Isabella Westerfield to place sixth (1:59.42) 200 medley relay and fourth in the 400 freestyle relay (3:50.12), helping defending state champion Easton place sixth in the final girls standings — the highest finish by any Bayside team.
A senior, Westerfield posted fifth-place finishes in the 50 free (25.24) and 500 free (5:35.89).
Kent Island's girls finished seventh, led by freshmen Clare O'Keefe, who was second in the 50 free (24.82) and Kara Seymour, fourth in the 100 breaststroke (1:11.18), eighth in the 200 individual medley (2:24.88). Seymour and O'Keefe joined Marissa White and Maddie Parks to take fifth in the 200 free relay (1:45.29) and seventh in the 200 medley relay (1:59.86).
Queen Anne's sophomore Madalyn Clagett was fourth in the 100 free (55.50) and sixth in the 200 free (2:03.29). Kent County sophomore Mary Jane Joiner was ninth in the 200 free (2:06.74).
Kent County junior Henry Martinez delivered the top efforts of any Bayside swimmer on the boys side, finishing fourth in both the 50 free (22.32) and 100 free (49.71).
Easton again had the best finish of any Bayside boys team, placing 11th. Senior Brady Tipton was seventh in the 200 free (1:52.08), ninth in the 500 free (5:08.76), and teamed with Bryce Slaughter, Aiden Lavezzo and Alex Harding to take eighth in the 400 free relay (3:35.88) and ninth in the 200 free relay (1:37.31).
Kent Island's Jack Da Rosa, Reef Adams, Johnathan Mangold and Giovanni Aguirre were 10th in the 200 free relay (1:37.32). Mangold later joined Dylan McCormick, Jacob Reeder and Keefer Pullen to finish 10th in the 400 free relay.
Queen Anne's William Meyer, Quinlan Justice, Giles Stanton and Jacob Gardner were ninth in the 400 free relay (3:39.22).

title: Hard Knocks: Maryland's women of roller derby
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Hard Knocks: Maryland's women of roller derby

 March 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 503
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While they may not have all been childhood friends who grew up in close proximity to one another, the members of the 301 Derby Dames roller derby team that competed in their season opener on Saturday evening at the Charles County Fairgrounds have since been able to form a genuine common bond.The 301 Derby Dames defeated the DC Roller Derby 399-56 on March 9 in front of a packed facility of family and friends who lined the mat inside the pavilion. When many of the current members of the 301 Derby Dames initially joined the team 10 years ago, they practiced and played on the concrete floor of the building. It has since been covered with a softer, yet slicker mat.
"I love being able to come out here and play with these women," said Lauren (Creech) Hare, who was born and raised in Charles County and is a 2006 Lackey High graduate. "I first joined back in 2015, but then I took a few years off when I had some kids. Now that they're a little older, I came back and it's been a lot of fun."
On Saturday evening, Hare, whose roller derby moniker is "Vicious Creature" a play on her maiden name, was named the most valuable player of the 301 Derby Dames by members of the opposing DC Roller Derby. At the end of each bout, each team is asked to select the top blocker and top jammer of their respective foe from that evening's contest, and Creech was the choice as top jammer.
Kristi Zapfe, who goes by the simplistic "Zap" during the matches, was born and raised in Chicago and after her time in the Navy relocated to St. Mary's County. Initially while in the Navy, Zapfe had thoughts of playing rugby, but one of her fellow midshipman encouraged her to pursue the roller derby circuit and she has been part of the 301 Derby Dames for the past four years.
"I'm not entirely sure what brought me to St. Mary's County, but I'm glad that I did," Zapfe said. "I really enjoy being able to practice and play with these women. It gives us all a chance to grow together and bond together and participate in a sport that we love and where we can knock each other down."
Hal Metzler is the coach of the 301 Derby Dames and each week he enjoys having the women come together for practices and then roughly six or seven bouts each season. Like his players, Metzler is there on a voluntary basis and simply enjoys the camaraderie of practicing and playing together in front of their enthusiastic family and friends.
"For me, the fun is seeing how competitive the women can be while still having a fun time," Metlzer said. "At the end of the day, no one is getting paid. No one is going pro. It's just a good chance for them to have a good time doing something they love and having their family and friends here to cheer them on."

title: Vikings' title shot falls shy
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Vikings' title shot falls shy

 March 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1051
 Words 

 Read News Document

 COLLEGE PARK — Maybe the stage was too big. Or maybe the team from the big city was just too good.Either way, Cambridge-South Dorchester High wasn't going away.
Down 10 in the first quarter, the Vikings rallied to pull even with Edmondson-Westside of Baltimore with under a minute to play in the first half.
Maybe the defending state champions thought an early third-quarter flurry that pushed their lead to 11 was enough to wilt the team from the Eastern Shore. No such luck. Again Cambridge-SD battled back to tie with one quarter remaining.
Certainly the back-to-back 3-pointers that gave the Red Storm a nine-point cushion with less than three minutes left was enough to make their opponent concede. Still no dice, as Cambridge-SD twice cut that deficit to four in the final two minutes.
"They wouldn't quit," Edmondson head coach Darnell Dantzler said of the Vikings.
They wouldn't. But they wouldn't win either.
No. 2 seed Edmondson converted 5 of 6 free throws in the closing 33 seconds Saturday to finally seal a 69-65 victory over top-seeded Cambridge-SD in the Class 1A state boys' basketball championship at the University of Maryland's Xfinity Center.
"Unfortunately, we didn't come out on the right side of the clock and the game," said Cambridge-SD head coach Shawn Parker, whose team finished the season 25-3. "But man, you saw, they fought to the end. And that's what these guys have been doing all year; fighting 'til the end."
Bidding for its first state basketball title since 1996, Cambridge-SD fell behind 14-4 with less than a minute left in the first quarter, when Edmondson's Kyrie Sherrod hit a 3-pointer. Senior guard LaShaun Moody (team-high 17 points, 10 rebounds) scored a layup and a pair of free throws to get the Vikings within six before Xavier Davis (11 points) scored to beat the buzzer and give the Red Storm (26-2) a 17-8 lead after the first quarter.
Down eight, Cambridge-SD pieced together the first of its comebacks. Semaj Pinder (11 points) and Sterling Perkins drained back-to-back 3-pointers before Kobe Ennals (12 points) scored a lay-in to forge a 23-23 tie with 51 seconds left in the first half.
But Chase Foster, Edmondson's talented 6-foot-10 sophomore center who finished with 18 points, 13 rebounds and five blocked shots, hit a pair of free throws before Sherrod drilled a 3-pointer just before the halftime buzzer for a 28-23 Red Storm lead.
Edmondson looked on the verge of taking control in the opening 2:33 of the third quarter, as Ennals picked up his third foul while the Red Storm were in the midst of a 10-4 run that gave them a 38-27 lead with 5:27 to go in the third.
But trailing 39-31, Cambridge-SD again began whittling away its deficit. Moody made a three-point play, then scored on a put-back to make it a three-point game. Darnell Dantzler Jr.'s jumper with 2:07 to go in the third gave the Red Storm a 45-38 lead.
But Darren Belizaire (10 points) hit a trey. Moody made yet another three-point play. Belizaire converted one of two free throws, before Moody zipped one of his five assists to Anthony Hughes for a layup just before the buzzer, tying the game at 47-all entering the fourth.
"Unfortunately, you don't want to get down that big 'cause it takes a lot of energy to come back," Tucker said. "But one word that sticks out to my head is resilient. We're resilient. No matter what, we're going to fight until the end and that's what we did."
Foster's follow nudged the Red Storm back in front at 49-47. Ennals answered with a jumper to create the game's fourth and final tie.
It remained close. But Josiah Brown (13 points) hit two free throws and a 3-pointer before Sherrod nailed a 3 for a 60-51 Edmondson lead with 2:20 remaining.
Pinder's 3-pointer and Hughes' layup off a steal pulled Cambridge-SD within 60-56 with 1:57 left.
"They played hard," Coach Dantzler said. "Even when we went up a couple points they came down and hit a couple big shots."
Dantzler Jr. scored on a drive, extending Edmondson's lead to 62-56. Ennals hit a free throw. Brown scored inside to make it 64-57 Red Storm. But Pinder drilled a 3-pointer with 52 seconds left, getting the Vikings within four again at 64-60.
Brown made one of two free throws with 33.4 seconds left for a five-point edge. Pinder fouled out when he was called for a charge. Ennals tipped the ensuing inbounds pass, but the Vikings could not come up with the ball. A quick foul by Moody sent Foster to the foul line, where he made both free throws for a 67-60 lead with 19.9 left.
Belizaire connected for a 3-pointer with 10.6 seconds left, drawing Cambridge-SD within 67-63. But Dantzler Jr. hit a pair of free throws with 9 seconds to go for a 69-63 advantage.
"It says that we wanted it," Moody said when asked about the Vikings' unwillingness to fold. "We came up a little short but it definitely says that we wanted it."
Tucker agreed.
"When that buzzer went off we just fell a little short," Tucker said. "We competed. We showed everybody in the state of Maryland that we can compete."
It was Edmondson's fourth state championship under Dantzler, and the second time the Red Storm have won consecutive titles, matching the 2013 and '14 teams. But it was the first time Edmondson has won the Baltimore city title and state championship in the same year.
"It just speaks volumes about these kids," said Dantzler, who has coached Edmondson for 18 seasons. "They went undefeated in Baltimore city, they won the city championship, and then to come in and win the state championship. Who could ask for anything more when it comes to these kids? This is the best record I had overall to be 26-2. It's a remarkable season that these guys had."
Dantzler had similar praise for Cambridge-SD.
"I told all of them when we were shaking hands that they played well," Dantzler said. "And I told the coach I know this is only his first year down here, and he's only a second-year coach, but they did a remarkable job."
Notes: Cambridge-SD outrebounded Edmondson, 37-33. … The Red Storm had 17 turnovers to Cambridge-SD's 16. … Edmondson finished 12 of 17 from the foul line, while the Vikings were 9 of 16. … Edmondson made nine 3-pointers to Cambridge-SD's eight.

title: Sabres' first game may be toughest of season
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Sabres' first game may be toughest of season

 March 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Saints Peter and Paul High's girls lacrosse team may not play a tougher opponent this season."I knew this was going to be a great matchup," Sabres head coach Alison Beyer said of Friday's season-opening clash with St. Mary's. "It was just an exciting game to watch. This is how lacrosse should be, and that's what I told them at halftime. I said, 'Just play lacrosse. Play like you know how to play.' And that's what they did."
Sts. Peter & Paul shaved a five-goal deficit to one midway through the third quarter, but couldn't get any closer, as the Saints scored seven of the game's last eight goals on the way to a 16-9 victory on a cloudy afternoon.
"This will be our toughest game of the season," Beyer said. "I got to see how I know they can play. I saw some real good things."
Among those good things was sophomore goalie Kylie Kroniser, who made five big saves to keep the Sabres within striking distance until late.
"Kylie (Kroniser) played a heckuva game," Beyer said. "She was on fire. I'm loving Kylie this year. It could have been way worse than it was. She made some real difficult saves, at real key moments too. That was crucial."
Sophomore Caroline Ewing (three goals) scored twice and classmate Avery McCall (three goals) once to give Sts. Peter & Paul and early 3-2 lead. But Sydney DeMaio (two goals), Kendall Kemezis and Anna Ervin (two goals) each scored in a 2-minute, 21-second span to give St. Mary's a 5-3 lead after one quarter,
Ervin scored her second goal 39 seconds into the second quarter, but Sabres senior Morgan Quade countered. Circling from behind the net, Quade took a stick check to the head before slipping a shot past St. Mary's goalie Addy Drain to get Sts. Peter & Paul back within two at 6-4.
But St. Mary's steadily passed the ball around the perimeter before working a weave in front of Kroniser that produced goals from Chloe Wiese (hat trick), Ellie Spurge and Jayci Frederick for a 9-4 advantage heading into the break.
"St. Mary's knew how to work us," said Beyer, who watched nine different Saints score, including six with multiple goals. "And they're just good. They knew exactly what angle to get through our defense, and they were killing us on the slide."
Sts. Peter & Paul rallied though in the third quarter.
Ewing bounced a free-position opportunity into the net 1:15 into the third. Freshman Emery Zimmerman tallied on another free-position chance with just under 9 minutes left in the period. McCall capitalized on another free-position shot with an overhand shot, drawing the Sabres within 9-7. Quade then took possession behind the left post, was knocked off her feet, but on the way down slid a shot into the net to make it 9-8 with 5:31 to go in the third.
"I love that I have so many contributors," Beyer said. "We have such a young team this year. And again, like every year, I can put my girls on offense or defense. And I can move them around and switch them back and forth. And no matter, I have contributors at every angle."
St. Mary's also appears to have a slew of contributors heading into the season, and showed that quality the remainder of the game. Marin Hodor (two goals) and Frederick (two goals) scored 10 seconds apart to give the Saints an 11-8 lead entering the fourth quarter.
McCall scored 38 seconds into the fourth to get the Sabres within two. But St. Mary's got two goals from Wiese and one apiece from Hodor, Grace Mitchell (two) and Maggie Marohl over the final 10:32 to pull away.
"It just happened our very first game was against St. Mary's and this was the best game of the season." Beyer said.

title: Scheffler has a big game buty not a big head
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Scheffler has a big game buty not a big head

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 879
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PONTE VEDRA BEACH, Fla. — Scottie Scheffler would rank near the bottom if the popular "strokes gained" statistic of golf had a category for celebrations. And he would be the first to concede that.Just two weeks ago — right before he earned $8.5 million for winning two big trophies in a span of 10 days and erased any questions whether he deserved to be ranked No. 1 in the world — Scheffler spoke about how quickly he can forget the past, win or lose.
"I don't celebrate accomplishments that well. I don't feel like I dwell on failures that much either," Scheffler said. "If you ask my wife, she would say I need to celebrate more. She's definitely right."
Then he won the Arnold Palmer Invitational and the celebration was on — cheeseburgers in the Bay Hill clubhouse with his family, followed by a two-hour drive to the TPC Sawgrass.
Woo-hoo!
The day after Scheffler became the only player in 50 editions of The Players Championship to win back to back, he was texting swing coach Randy Smith about their practice schedule.
Scheffler is a big man in golf with a big game. What he lacks is a big head.
"Given the things that have gone on the last year or so, and watching him, he is definitely grounded — more than what you can dream of," Smith said. "And he has created a lot of things that could keep him from being grounded.
"He knows you're not bigger than anything else because of anything you do."
The money?
His latest victory pushed him over $50 million for his PGA Tour earnings in just five years, one spot ahead of Jon Rahm on the career money list. Rahm had a four-year head start.
The ranking?
He has been at No. 1 since last May, and his gap over everyone else is the largest since Dustin Johnson seven years ago. Barring injury, Scheffler has a chance to become the first player since Tiger Woods in 2009 to hold the No. 1 ranking for an entire calendar year.
The platform?
Scheffler doesn't go out of his way to share his opinions. Insightful answers start with a good question, though he showed last week he is not afraid to speak his mind. He was asked whether fans were disillusioned by the splintering between the PGA Tour and LIV Golf.
"If the fans are upset, then look at the guys that left," he said. "We had a tour, we were all together, and the people that left are no longer here. At the end of the day, that's where all the splintering comes from. As far as our tour goes, we're doing our best to create the best product for the fans."
And then there's the attention, the least of his worries because Scheffler doesn't spend much time on social media.
He also takes precautions not to listen or read about himself, whether it's his nine worldwide wins in the last 25 months, his two PGA Tour awards as player or the year or the putting struggles that kept him from winning even more.
"When it comes to reading things about yourself, let's say I remember all the good things. Then I walk around with a big head thinking, 'This is how great I am.' That's not good, either," Scheffler said in an interview before he went on his most recent run.
"If I read the bad stuff, that's all I'm going to remember is the bad stuff. 'Scottie can't putt. He hadn't won in a year. Is he the best player in the world?' It's a losing game."
Mostly what keeps him grounded are the people around him. His mother has been a chief operating officer for law firms in New York and Dallas, and his father stayed at home with Scheffler and his three sisters.
His wife, Meredith, is pregnant with their first child, due around the end of April. She's the one who told Scheffler on Sunday morning of the 2022 Masters, when he had a three-shot lead and woke up with tears and self-doubt, "Who are you to say that you are not ready?"
He wound up winning his first major, building such a big lead he mindlessly four-putted on the final hole and still won by two. More tears.
"Crying for me is not an abnormal thing," he said with a laugh.
That much was clear when he was at TPC Sawgrass a few weeks ago to promote The Players, reliving the winning moment on the 18th green. His voice choked up just mentioning his family.
"I always get emotional when I talk about Meredith for some reason," he said.
That was the point Scheffler drove home Sunday evening, as he moved the gold trophy on the table to be able to make eye contact with whomever was asking a question.
"At the end of the day, it all goes back to the support system I have at home," he said. "I have a great wife, and if I started taking my trophies and putting them all over the house and walking in all big-time, I think she would smack me on the side of the head and tell me to get over myself pretty quickly.
"Winning golf tournaments doesn't give me any brownie points at home," he said, stifling a laugh. "So I just try and do my best."
It seems to be working.

title: NEW HEIGHTS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
NEW HEIGHTS

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 804
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As March Madness is set to tip off, three of the most recognizable names in college basketball are in the women's tournament: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers.Clark drew record crowds and ratings all season long. Reese has LSU in contention for a second straight national championship. Bueckers is finally healthy and doing things on the court for UConn reminiscent of her freshman season when she was the AP Player of the Year.
Throw in a few stellar freshmen like JuJu Watkins and Hannah Hidalgo and the game is reaching heights it's never seen.
"One thousand percent we've seen a shift in just the perception of women's college basketball in general," USC coach Lindsay Gottlieb said. "It doesn't have to be at the detriment of men's college basketball. The increased coverage and star power these players have; they are legitimate, popcorn-worthy type of players."
For countless seasons, the buzz around the NCAA tournaments have often been on the men's game. The one-and-done stars, the juggernaut blueblood programs, the buzzer beaters and athleticism all getting more attention. The women's game has pretty much all of that too, and the ratings and attendance this season suggest casual fans are fully engaged with a game that boasts star power and an increasingly high level of play.
It helps that the women's players stick around for three, four or even five years without the chance to leave early for the pros so fans get to know them and watch them grow. Three years ago, Clark said she thought women's players should be allowed to turn pro after their freshman year, like the men can.
Instead, she stuck around and had a record-setting year that grabbed the nation's attention.
"It's really, really evident that there's stars out there in this game," UConn coach Geno Auriemma said. "Whereas before I think they were there, but nobody wanted to acknowledge it and appreciate it as much. ... They're just really good. Everybody is going around telling everybody how good they are. They're all visible."
ESPN said it just saw the most watched women's college basketball regular season in more than 15 years, with viewership up 37% on its platforms from last season. That doesn't really even include the Clark effect as Iowa's star wasn't on the network much this season. Iowa's ratings on Fox Sports were the highest in a generation.
ESPN plans to show all of Iowa's games, including a few on ABC, as far as the No. 1 seed advances in the tourney.
"It's not just UConn and Tennessee on TV," Auriemma said. "Those kids are on TV a lot. They're in the limelight a lot. They know how to handle it because they're used to it now."
Clark, who broke the NCAA all-time scoring record this season, has helped six different networks reach all-time viewership marks for women's basketball over the past year, starting with last season's NCAA championship game that drew nearly 10 million viewers.
"I kind of get to be in the spotlight and I get to change people's viewpoint of how they see women's basketball," Clark said before the season. "The amount of people that have come up to me and said, 'I've never watched women's basketball before before you and your team ... .' Some people could take that as a negative. But to me that's a positive. We're finally getting them to turn on the TV and watch it, but not only watch it once. They're coming back for more."
People aren't just watching, they are also coming to games too. All five of the power conferences had huge crowds for their tournaments. The SEC and Big Ten had their best attendance ever. The Pac-12, ACC and Big 12 weren't far behind.
"The big names continue to put up big numbers and people are watching and the media is paying attention," Bueckers said. "The tournament will be great and will continue the rise of women's basketball."
Fans who pack the arenas are also sticking around afterward, hoping to get a coveted autograph. The importance of the moment isn't lost on the game's stars. Clark, Reese, Bueckers, Watkins and many others spend time postgame signing and taking pictures with not only young girls, but boys, too.
"There were 400 people in the stands before she got here and now we're selling out," Gottlieb said of Watkins. "We've got NBA players who want to see her, WNBA players, musicians and actors too. Regular fans also, it's a diversified crowd. Little boys and girls who ask me if I know JuJu. Could they meet Juju? Grown men you run into in downtown LA."
Even when Clark leaves for the WNBA after the NCAA Tournament, the future of women's basketball is still strong with Bueckers, Watkins, Hidalgo and many other up-and-coming players.
"It's going to get even better. So many kids coming out of high school are just unbelievably good," Auriemma said.

ESCR schedules Learn-to-Row clinics for May

 March 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 369
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Eastern Shore Community Rowers, an adult rowing program, has scheduled free information sessions for April 20 and May 4, from 8:30-9:30 a.m., at Evergreen 770 Port Street.This is a chance for interested rowers to meet the ESCR coaches and team members, learn about the boats, and how rowing is the most fun exercise on the Shore.
"There is nothing else like it," said Doug Webb, a new member who recently began rowing. "It has changed my life."
ESCR members learn to row a variety of boats, from eight-person boats to single-sculling boats.
ESCR has scheduled two week-long Learn-to-Row clinics, May 13-18 and May 20-23. The clinics are Monday through Thursday from 5:30-7:30 p.m., and Saturdays, from 8:30-10:30 a.m. The cost is $400 for the week-long, three-coach lessons of which 50% can be applied to membership for those who wish to join the club.
ESCR is dedicated to teaching the community to row while offering more access to area rivers. The club welcomes everyone and offers scholarships.
Beginners are encouraged to join the Learn-To-Row clinics, or to take private lessons from one of ESCR's accredited coaches to acquire the skills needed for practices.
"The only criteria," Board Safety Officer and registered nurse, Terry Gleim said, "are that you be able to swim and that you are strong enough to properly hold an oar and help lift the boats."
If swimming is an obstacle, ESCR will assist in helping you learn.
All scheduled workouts are accompanied by a chase boat for safety and coaching.
The rowing season runs from March through December, with early morning workouts Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and later morning rows on Tuesday and Thursday. Saturday rows are at 7:30 a.m. for all members. Evening rows are available for more experienced scullers during the summer.
"ESCR is open to anyone over 18 interested in having fun, getting healthy, and appreciating our beautiful waters," said Chloe Tong, the executive director. "The health of our rivers, as well as personal health, is an intrinsic part of our conversation."
As a non-profit, Eastern Shore Community Rowers raises money through private donations, grants, and membership dues needed to fund additional boats and necessary equipment for next year's season.
For more information visit www.ESCRowers.org, or email head coach Chloe Allen: Director@escrowers.org
