title: O'Connor, Easton top Kent Island
author: Bill Haufe
content:
O'Connor, Easton top Kent Island

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 669
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Kent Island High head football coach Zach Davis has seen enough of Mikey O'Connor."I'm glad he graduates," Davis said of Easton High's senior quarterback. "He basically beat us by himself. I told him before the game, I thought he was a great player. And he showed it tonight."
O'Connor ran for two touchdowns and threw for two, including a 43-yard connection to Diontaye Copper with 2 minutes, 15 seconds remaining Friday night, as the third-seeded Warriors defeated the No. 2 seed Buccaneers, 28-21, in a Class 2A East Region second-round playoff at Andy Schipul Stadium.
After going 1-9 a year ago, Easton is 8-3 and now awaits for the state tournament to be re-seeded for next weekend's state quarterfinals.
"We didn't score the whole second half," said O'Connor, whose 3-yard touchdown run with 1:17 left in the first half helped Easton to a 21-14 halftime lead. "They were really stopping us and we were just thinking, 'First down. Next first down.' So we were taking it one play at a time. And when you do that, you put a bunch of good plays together, and you bust one, that really turned the tide."
After a scoreless third quarter, Kent Island (7-4) tied the game 4 seconds into the fourth quarter on quarterback Gavan Henry's 1-yard sneak. Spencer Chappell's point-after kick tied the game at 21-all.
Easton's ensuing possession ended with a fourth-down incompletion. Kent Island punted the next time it had the ball.
The Warriors took possession at their 20-yard line with 6:17 remaining. On third-and-11, O'Connor hit Colin Mooney for an 11-yard pick-up and a first down. Five consecutive O'Connor runs set up a third-and-five at the Bucs' 43. O'Connor hit Copper on an out route, then watched his receiver cut toward the middle of the field and outrun everyone into the end zone for a 27-21 lead. Dominic Stanco drilled his fourth straight point after for a 28-21 Easton lead.
"You try to stop him running the football and he throws on you," Davis said of O'Connor.
Kent Island got the ball back on its 37 with 2:15 left. As the Bucs lined up on first down, Easton called time to make a defensive adjustment. On the next play, Copper intercepted Henry, giving the Warriors the ball at the Kent Island 49 with 2:09 left.
"Luckily for us we were able to make one more big play than Kent Island tonight, on both sides of the ball," Easton head coach Matt Griffith said. "Big drive. Drove down and scored with like 2:15 left. And then get a huge pick. Call a timeout to see the formation, made a quick adjustment on our coverage, and, man, played it perfect."
O'Connor picked up two first downs to kill the remaining 2:09, cementing the victory.
"They came through when they needed to and that was at the most important time," O'Connor said of his offensive line. "When we got those first downs, it was all them. Like I didn't get touched literally until I had the first down."
Easton took a 7-0 lead, when O'Connor busted loose around right end for a 41-yard touchdown just over 2 minutes into the game. Stanco added the PAT.
Kent Island fumbled on its first play of the game, giving Easton the ball on the Bucs 45. The Warriors drove to the Bucs' 13, setting up Stanco's 30-yard field goal attempt that drifted wide right.
Henry's 1-yard sneak and Chappell's extra-point tied the game at 7-7 with 32 seconds left in the first quarter.
The Warriors moved back ahead with 8:50 to go in the second quarter, when O'Connor hit Mooney with a 23-yard touchdown pass in the left, front corner of end zone for a 14-7 lead.
The Bucs again pulled even, as Nate Green was sprung for an 11-yard touchdown run with 2:26 to go before halftime.
Easton responded. Dustin Blue broke free on a 50-yard run on his first carry. O'Connor carried for 12 yards and then raced around left end and squeezed down the sideline for the go-ahead touchdown and a 21-14 halftime lead.

title: Queen Anne's ready for its final shot
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Queen Anne's ready for its final shot

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 697
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Usually by mid-November, Mike Kern has stuffed and stored all soccer balls away in nylon bags and is rolling basketballs off the rack, preparing Queen Anne's County High's girls basketball team for the upcoming season.The Lions indeed had their first practice Friday night, but their longtime head coach may have seemed a bit distracted. You see, Kern and the Queen Anne's girls soccer team still have one game left, and it's kind of a big deal.
"From Day 1 we thought we had a chance to go far," said Kern, who leads second-seeded Queen Anne's (13-3-1) against No. 5 seed C. Milton Wright (12-4) at noon Saturday in the Class 2A state championship at Loyola University's Ridley Athletic Complex. "If we stayed healthy I thought we had a really good chance. And now we're at the point. We have one game left, and I do feel it's a game that we have a shot. We just have to make sure we come in and play with confidence.
Confidence.
The Lions began gaining that in early September, when they lost in the last minute of double overtime against Stephen Decatur.
"At the end of the game, at that moment, we thought we were the better team," Kern said. "I told them, 'We can learn from this loss.' And I think we did."
Queen Anne's turned around and lost to Chesapeake in the annual Lions Cup tourney. The margin of defeat again was one goal. But another dose of confidence had been earned.
"We played them even," Kern said of Chesapeake, which lost in last weekend's Class 3A state semifinals. "That got us confidence."
So did two losses to perennial Bayside Conference power James M. Bennett, which blanked the Lions 3-0 during the regular season, then got a late second-half goal to pull out a 3-2 victory in the conference championship.
"Both Bennett games were well played and we kind of kept going," Kern said.
And the Lions have kept right on going, reaching their first state final since 2003.
Kern's biggest concern is to not 'let the moment get too big for us."
Queen Anne's has passed its last three big-moment tests.
It defeated longtime nemesis Kent Island, 2-0, for the 2A East Region II title. It outlasted Wilde Lake in the quarterfinals via penalty kicks. Then came last Saturday's victory over Century, when Shannon Rath, Morgan Scott, Kara Ringold and Taylor Napier each converted their PKs and keeper Bea Holthaus stopped two of the four penalty kicks she faced for a 1-0 victory in the state semifinals.
Now, the Lions face an opponent Kern thinks looks a lot like his team.
"They are very similar to us," Kern said. "They possess well between the 18s. And they're defensive."
The Mustangs are led by senior midfielder Delainey Proctor, an all-state first-team selection. Kern has also been impressed by sophomore forward Lily Budelis and junior defender Mackenzi Milich, who is part of a defense that has not allowed a goal in its last three postseason games, which included a 1-0 shutout of top-seeded Sparrows Point last Saturday.
The Lions' defense has also been outstanding. Holthaus (11 shutouts) has posted shutouts in the last three games and has benefitted greatly from the unit in front of her that includes Rath (seven goals, team-high 12 assists), Hayden Legg, Finley Patchett, Kathryn Baer and Abigail Robinson.
"Against Century, all five of those girls played a phenomenal game," Kern said. "We just got to keep the ball in front of them. Anything far out we know Bea can make the save. We just can't let them get behind us and have these one-on-one opportunities.
"We support each other well," Kern continued. "When one does get beat there's always someone there to recover. They do a good job stepping to the ball, pressuring the other team's attackers."
Offensively, Queen Anne's will look to build from the midfield with Ringold (13 goals), Napier (9 goals) and Olivia Ryan (11 goals), along with forward and leading goal-scorer Madi Horney (20 goals, 7 assists).
"It's a little strange because we have a really good basketball team this year," Kern said. "And I'm excited for basketball. But at the same time I'm trying to hold off that excitement for basketball until we see how we do Saturday."

title: STATE CHAMPS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
STATE CHAMPS

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1085
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE — Mike Kern's belief never wavered.From the beginning of the season, Queen Anne's County High's girls head soccer coach said his team could compete for a state title. Kern said it after wins. He seemed more emphatic after losses. He continued saying it one narrow postseason victory after another.
"We just have to put the ball in the back of the net," Kern said.
Kara Ringold did that twice early Saturday afternoon as Queen Anne's shut out C. Milton Wright, 2-0, to win the Class 2A state championship at Loyola University's Ridley Athletic Complex.
It was the first state title in the history of Queen Anne's girls soccer program, and the first by a Bayside Conference school since the Maryland Public Secondary School Athletic Association began holding the girls state championship in 1989.
"At the beginning of the season our goal was to get to a state championship," said Kern, who has been the Lions head coach for 24 years. "To win it, this is like a bonus. We knew we had the team."
Whether it was early-game jitters or the strong winds that whipped across the field, neither team mounted much offense through the first 12 minutes. C. Milton Wright (12-5), which was playing into the wind during the first half, had two early chances, the first coming on a corner kick 5 minutes in that produced no shot. Then with 28:30 left in the half, Emma Jankowiak broke in alone only to have Queen Anne's Finley Patchett angle in to take the ball away.
"I think the first half, playing into the wind, that was really difficult," Mustangs head coach Andrew Harrell said. "It was probably the toughest conditions we've played with all season. We've played with a little bit of drizzle, we've played with cold, we played with hot. But the wind is something we've never played with. And it's definitely a game-changer, especially in the first half. Playing into the wind, it's like you're playing against an extra person."
Queen Anne's (14-3-1) ended the scoreless duel more than 14 minutes later.
Shannon Rath struck a beautiful ball on a direct kick toward the center of the goal that C.M. Wright's Nani Milich headed. The ball drifted toward the right post. Mustangs goalie Alix Bramble moved to her left in an attempt to knock the ball away. But Queen Anne's Morgan Scott headed the ball back across the crease to an ummarked Ringold, who got her right foot on the ball for a tap-in and a 1-0 lead with 14 minutes, 47 seconds left in the first half.
"Shannon hit a great ball and then Morgan got a head on it and I just hit it right in," Ringold said.
The Lions, who won their state quarterfinal and semifinal on penalty kicks, scored in regulation for the first time since their 2-0 victory over Kent Island on Oct. 29 in the Class 2A East Region II final.
"I think it gave us all a lot of comfort because we have been trying to get that goal in regulation," Queen Anne's senior midfielder Olivia Ryan said. "And we ended up getting another one. But we wanted to at least get one. So it gave us a lot of comfort and we all could relax a little bit, but still have the momentum to keep going."
The fifth-seeded Mustangs got a corner kick with 51 seconds left in the first half, and then back-to-back corners in the opening 4 minutes of the second half, but put nothing on Lions sophomore keeper Bea Holthaus, who notched her 12th shutout of the season.
"Our goalie saved our butt a lot of times this season," Ryan said of Holthaus, who after giving up a goal in the regional semifinals posted four straight shutouts to end the season.
Having a stellar defense also helped.
"A lot of us have played together since we were very little so we kind of know each other's habits," senior center back Shannon Rath said. "That definitely helps a lot. Our communication is what gets us through. We are constantly talking, tracking down runners. That's just the only way we know how to do it."
Ten minutes after the Mustangs' second corner of the half, Queen Anne's put together another score.
Mia Barnette came down left wing and touched the ball to Taylor Napier, who pushed toward the middle of the field and dished to Ringold. With two defenders in front of her, and a third closing in from the left, Ringold settled the ball then quickly drove a left-footed shot inside the right post for a 2-0 lead with 26:05 left in the game.
"We were just on an attack and then we had really good passing on the left side, and Taylor (Napier) played me a great ball and I just took a touch around the defender and hoped for the best, and it went in," Ringold said. "it was just one of the best moments of my life.
"Kara was in the right place at the right time that first goal," Kerr said. "But that second goal, she earned that goal. There was a lot of things that led up to it. But when she got the ball she had to do a couple things there to get a good shot off and put it far post, low."
C.M. Wright got a shot off from outside the box that Holthaus caught in the midsection with 13:39 left, then sent a corner kick through the box and out of bounds with 6:37 left. The Mustangs didn't build a serious scoring threat the rest of the game.
"I think when you get to this stage, you watch enough game film to come up with a game plan for the other team," Harrell said. "But what you can't game plan for is the work ethic and the hard work and that kind of stuff. And I think Queen Anne's brought a ton of intensity and a lot of hard work today. They beat us to balls for the majority of the game. That was one of our halftime talks; we got to do better getting to the ball first."
It was Queen Anne's first state finals appearance since 2003, when it lost 2-0 to Loch Raven.
"I felt like last year we had the team," Kern said. "We did get some injuries at the end of the year and things didn't go our way. But we had a good core of the group back and thought this was going to be the year for us. Everything just kind of fell into place for us."

title: 2-week firearms hunting season for deer opens Nov. 30
author: MARYLAND DEPARTMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES
content:
2-week firearms hunting season for deer opens Nov. 30

 November 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARYLAND DEPARTMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES | Section: State News 
 
 552
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland's two-week firearms hunting season for sika and white-tailed deer opens Saturday, Nov. 30, and runs through Saturday, Dec. 14.The two-week season includes Sunday hunting in all but three counties, affording hunters more weekend opportunities to hunt and contribute to managing Maryland's deer population.
"The two-week firearms season remains one of Maryland's most popular hunts," Maryland Department of Natural Resources Wildlife and Heritage Service Director Karina Stonesifer said. "The season occurs when temperatures are often cooler and provides hunters the opportunity to spend time with friends and family enjoying the outdoors. For thousands of Marylanders, venison provides high protein meals with a low carbon footprint. And the firearms season is also essential for managing the state's abundant deer population."
Bag limits and antlerless season dates for the firearm season, along with other deer hunting seasons and regulations, are available in the 2024-2025 Maryland Guide to Hunting and Trapping.
Hunters are reminded that if they intend to pursue sika deer, they must purchase a sika hunting stamp. Sika stamps may be purchased online through DNR's online licensing website, at a licensing agent, or by calling DNR Licensing and Registration Services at 866-344-8889.
Hunters are also reminded that an antler-point restriction remains in effect. Deer hunters may harvest one antlered white-tailed deer within the yearly bag limit that does not meet the requirement of having at least three points on one antler. Any additional antlered deer taken within the established bag limit must meet the minimum point restriction. Licensed junior hunters and apprentice license holders, 16 years of age or younger, are exempt from this restriction.
Hunters should also be aware that the Chronic Wasting Disease Management Area expanded earlier this year and now includes all of Allegany, Baltimore, Carroll, Frederick, Montgomery, and Washington counties. Hunters are reminded they cannot transport whole carcasses or certain parts of deer harvested from within the management area to locations outside of its boundaries unless meeting certain exceptions. Research suggests chronic wasting disease is not naturally transmitted to humans. However, as a general safety precaution it is recommended that hunters avoid consuming the meat of sick animals as well as the brain, lymph nodes or spinal column of any deer – all of which are normally removed during the butchering process.
During firearms season, Maryland requires deer hunters and their companions to wear daylight fluorescent orange or daylight fluorescent pink in one of the following manners: a cap of solid fluorescent daylight orange or pink, a vest or jacket containing back and front panels of at least 250 square inches of fluorescent daylight orange or pink, or an outer garment of camouflage daylight fluorescent orange or pink worn above the waist and containing at least 50 percent daylight fluorescent color.
Hunters should carefully inspect all tree stands and always wear a full-body safety harness while in the stand and while climbing in or out. The department strongly recommends using a sliding knot, commonly known as a prusik knot, attached to a line that is secured above the stand that allows the hunter to be safely tethered to the tree as soon as they leave the ground.
Hunters are encouraged to help others by donating deer taken in Maryland. A state tax credit offers hunters an incentive for donated deer. Other local or state programs are also available, so hunters should check with their deer processor.

title: Chesapeake passes early eye test
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Chesapeake passes early eye test

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 792
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — Chesapeake College men's head basketball coach Andrew Sachs knew his team was going to lose at some point this season.The Skipjacks did that for only the first time this young season on Tuesday night, 92-88, in overtime to visiting Montgomery College.
But Chesapeake has also won — all four of its games prior to Tuesday — and Sachs has liked what he's seen.
"They like being around each other," said Sachs, now in his fifth season at Wye Mills. "There's no selfishness, which again at this level, you get that at times.
"And look how many guys are averaging double figures (in scoring) for us," continued Sachs, who has four after five games. "That's always a telltale sign. It should be four, almost six. That's what you want. All my good teams at every level that I've been at, we've always had four or five guys averaging in double figures. Always."
Leading that foursome is freshman point guard La'Shaun Moody (19.2 points per game), who helped lead Cambridge-South Dorchester High to the Class 1A state final last season. He is followed by sophomore backcourt mates Brandon Hooks (14.8 ppg.) and Eli Credle (12.2 ppg.), and sophomore forward Willie Jones (15.0), who is yanking down an average of nine rebounds a contest.
Not far behind them are sophomore guard Ashton Pratt (9.3) and freshman guard Brayden Smith (8.0), who helped Saints Peter and Paul win the Maryland Interscholastic Athletic Association C Conference championship earlier this year.
"Winning helps everybody," Sachs said as his team was wrapping up practice Friday morning. "And I think another thing is they see themselves getting better. That's a big thing. Because if they didn't see that, then you would hear grumbling. But they can see themselves getting better."
And the Skipjacks have the potential to get even better as soon as sophomore forwards Shaft Clark and DaQuan Johnson get on the court. Chesapeake's frontcourt is currently a rotation of the 6-foot-5 Jones, 6-4 Josh Rivers, who returns from last season, and freshmen Kionne Lang (6-6) and Narayan Thomas (6-5).
"I still think we have a big learning curve," Sachs said. "But we've really played some pretty good teams."
Chesapeake opened with an 83-66 victory over Fayetteville Technical Community College (N.C.) before a road win at Louisburg Community College (N.C.). The Skipjacks drained a school single-game record 21 3-pointers in a 41-point rout of Pennsylvania Highlands, then defeated defending Region XIX champion Raritan Valley (N.J.).
"I feel like the starting five we have right now is pretty good all around," said Credle, a member of the 2022-23 Chesapeake team that reached the national tournament, but sat out all last year due to a knee injury. "We have three really good wings. We have Brandon that can shoot the ball really well off the catch. Josh can shoot it well. And we have Willie that can shoot the ball probably the best on our team right now. And we have Kionne, and he's getting better ever day. We just have to keep on building."
Sachs thinks he already has a better-built backcourt than last season, when the Skipjacks finished 14-17. A transfer, Hooks has a quick release and has started strong, and Credle has returned after red-shirting last season.
"A really good player," Sachs said of Credle. "Handles the basketball. Runs the team. We had no point guard last year. And to have two really good ones this year makes a world of difference."
That other point guard is the mercurial Moody, who's "been way more than anyone has asked for," Sachs said. "He's been the energy guy for us. Good on-ball defender. Makes plays. Got a lot of grit. It's been a great start to his career."
Moody led Cambridge-SD to a 25-3 record, its first Bayside Conference championship since 1996 last season, as well as a berth in the Class 1A state final, where the Vikings lost to Edmondson-Westside. And it doesn't appear he's lost an ounce of the intensity he played with throughout his high school career.
"There's some things he needs to learn and he's had a few rough spots," Sachs said of Moody. "But In terms of consistency, no one matches his energy. And everybody gets better when he's on the floor. And that's what a point guard does. Number one job of a point guard is to make the other four guys on the floor better. And both of those guys do that. We did not have that last year."
Depth in the backcourt is provided by sophomores Da'Mir Camper and Joshua DeJesus, and freshman Xavier Buchanan.
"I love the group of kids we have," Sachs said. "They all love each other. They love basketball. Basketball's important to them. Winning's important. I think we can be pretty good. We're just going to try to keep getting better."

title: Blueford, Vikings rise up to get past stubborn Colonels
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Blueford, Vikings rise up to get past stubborn Colonels

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 533
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Colonel Richardson High head football coach James Jackson didn't think Cambridge-South Dorchester was 23 points better than his team in the fourth week of the season.The Colonels certainly proved that last Friday night, as they battled the top-seeded and undefeated Vikings down to the wire in a Class 1A East Region second-round playoff. But with 1 minute, 15 seconds remaining, senior wide receiver Antonio Blueford made a leaping grab in the back of the end zone on Anthony Hughes' pass for the winning touchdown, lifting Cambridge-SD to a 14-7 victory.
The top-seeded Vikings (10-0) will host three-time defending Class 1A state champion Fort Hill (4-7) on Friday at 6:30 p.m. in a 1A state quarterfinal. The Sentinels, who forfeited five victories this season for using an ineligible player, outscored their two regional opponents by a combined 103-20.
"Even though our season ended, the way we played, and Cambridge was the number one undefeated team (in the 1A East Region), I couldn't be more proud of our guys the way they stepped up," said Jackson, whose team lost 23-0 to the Vikings during the regular season. "We showed we shouldn't have lost that game by 23 points. We should have been in that game, but we didn't play to our potential. So when we play to our potential I feel like we can play with anybody."
Cambridge-SD took a 7-0 lead in the first quarter when Hughes' broke up the middle for a touchdown run and Collin Bair tacked on the extra point.
Colonel (6-5) answered in the second quarter, when Ja'Zir Dickerson (18 carries, 82 yards) ran off right tackle for a touchdown run inside run 10-yard line. Morgan Demir added the extra point.
An interception by Colonel's Jay Wilkins kept the game tied at 7-7.
It remained that way until late in the fourth quarter, when Cambridge-SD drove inside Colonel's 5-yard line. The Vikings were backed up after getting tagged with an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty. But Hughes then dropped back and arced a pass that Blueford jumped and came down with despite good coverage.
"It was just a great ball," Blueford said. "I just went up and got it and the game was on the line. I knew it was going to be a good pass. I just had to come down with it."
It was the lowest point total of the season for the Vikings.
"We had opportunities," Cambridge-SD head coach Rob Burnham said. "Right before the half we got a short field and got inside the 5 and then ended up kicking a field goal off the left upright and missing it. Then early in fourth quarter we got inside the 20 and threw an interception.
"They played well and tackled well and took some things away that they gave us last game," Burnham added of Colonel. "We took some things away that we gave them last game. They played better offensively than they did the first time. A win's a win and we'll take it."
T.J. Wenger had 14 tackles for Colonel, Chatydrick Pickrom had 13, Collin Brewer nine, and Chris Rockwell eight.
"I thought our defense held up," Jackson said. "Even on the last play we were in perfect position. On that play Blueford just made a great catch."

title: Easton playing with familiar tag
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton playing with familiar tag

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 736
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Underdog.Easton High's football team started the season with that tag when it was ranked 10th in a preseason poll.
The Warriors steadily shedded that label through a 6-3 regular season, won two Class 2A East Regional playoffs, and are one of three Bayside Conference teams still playing along with defending 2A state champion Stephen Decatur and undefeated Cambridge-South Dorchester, the No. 1 seed in Class 1A.
Now, as it heads into Friday's Class 2A state quarterfinal at second-seeded Milford Mill (9-1) at 6:30 p.m., No. 7 seed Easton (8-3) returns to its familiar role.
"We know we're the underdog," Warrior head coach Matt Griffith said. "And we love it. And while we're happy with a lot of things we've done this year, we're not done. We have a lot of work still to do.
"Yes, we're playing a very good football team," Griffith said of the Millers, who won the 2A state title two years ago then lost in last year's state semifinals to eventual state champ Decatur. "Yes, they're very athletic. Yes, they're big. Yes, they're fast. We're focused on not who's the toughest, but who can be the toughest the longest. We need to be able to take their punches early and be able to respond. And if we can do that I like our chances, if we can keep it close at the end of the game."
If the Warriors are to keep it close, they will have to limit a Millers team that scored 32 or more points in eight of their nine victories this season.
Leading the way is junior quarterback Owen Newberns, who has completed 88 of 140 passes for 1,586 yards, 18 touchdowns and just four interceptions. Easton's secondary figures to be challenged by receivers Romero Ison (33 receptions, 534 yards, five touchdowns) and Derrell Pierson (23-497-6). Then there's running back Damon Ferguson, who has carried 72 times for 975 yards and 12 touchdowns.
"Each team is different because they have a different formula for winning," Milford Mill head coach Reggie White said. "It's really cool to coach these different types of teams. One year you may have a running team. One year you may have a passing team. One year you might have a ferocious defense.
"So this year's team, we've got some guys who are very, very athletic," White continued. "We've got some guys who can break a game open. It's the little nuances that you try to lean on during the game to help you win."
The Millers also have the biggest offensive line the Warriors have faced all year,
"Their center is like 6-(foot)-6, 320," Griffith said. "They run tight zone and outside zone really, really well. They got a really fast running back. Their quarterback is super athletic and he can throw the deep ball to receivers who are really athletic."
Easton has a really athletic quarterback of its own in senior Mikey O'Connor, who has completed 123 of 228 passes for 1,908 yards, 21 touchdowns and 14 interceptions, and also run for 1,247 yards and 18 touchdowns on 186 carries.
"The first thing has to start with the signal-caller, their quarterback," White said when asked his biggest concerns with Easton. "He's a lefty. He's different. He has it. And I know about the O-line. They might be young, but they'll fight you."
That young front will look to open avenues for not only O'Connor, but junior running back Dustin Blue, who has carried 107 times for 632 yards and seven touchdowns.
The Warriors also have a fleet of receivers, which include Chase Raab (24 receptions, 519 yards, 8 touchdowns) and Diontaye Copper (21-382-6), who had the winning touchdown catch in last Friday's 28-21 second-round win over Kent Island. O'Connor's other targets are Colin Mooney (32-452-5), Carter Mooney (16-304-1) and Zach Barnhart (10-115-1).
"They're very athletic on defense," Griffith said of Milford Mill. "They're overly aggressive at times, which we're hoping we can take advantage of, and try to be a little patient in how we do things. Try to make them uncomfortable. No one's really made them uncomfortable this year except Loyola-(Blakefield), who beat them."
The Warriors, who have won four of their last five, also have to continue protecting the football. They have committed just one turnover in their last two games.
White also noted keeping mistakes to a minimum.
"I think our biggest obstacle is when we look in the mirror; it's ourselves sometimes," White said. "We're just trying to eliminate mental errors and play a whole game."

title: Vikings face Fort Hill in quarterfinals instead of title bout
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Vikings face Fort Hill in quarterfinals instead of title bout

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 798
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With the exception of a few injuries, and the assorted turnovers and penalties that leave coaches muttering, the season has gone pretty much as planned for Cambridge-South Dorchester High's football team."We had talked all season," first-year Vikings' head coach Rob Burnham said, "about doing the things we're supposed to do, and being successful, and work hard, and improve day after day. Get through the season undefeated. Get the number one overall seed in the (Class) 1A, and then we won't play the Sentinels until we go to Annapolis. Obviously, things changed on that."
Cambridge-SD did go undefeated during the regular season and earned the No. 1 overall seed when the state playoffs were reseeded last week.
As for meeting three-time defending 1A state champion Fort Hill in a potential state-title showdown in Annapolis? Well, that changed when the Sentinels forfeited five regular-season games for using an ineligible player. Fort Hill remained eligible for the postseason though, romped to a pair of regional victories, and come into Friday's 6:30 p.m. state quarterfinal at Cambridge-SD (10-0) as the No. 8 seed at 4-7.
"I met with our guys and said, 'Obviously the circumstances have changed and what we worked hard for isn't necessarily going to be given to us,'" Burnham said. "'We still have to go out and take it. So in order to get what we want we have to beat them. We just have to do it two weeks earlier than we had planned on.'"
A Cambridge-SD assistant last year, Burnham and Fort Hill head coach Zack Alkire agreed this is not the same Sentinels team that routed the Vikings, 38-20, in last year's state semifinals in Cumberland.
"We have a much better shot to run the ball on them this year than last year," Burnham said. "I've coached for 26 years and that was the best high school team I've seen regardless of classification in three different states. They were really good."
But that team that went on to win a third straight state title while extending its winning streak to 21 games, graduated 20 players, and is not as senior heavy this year.
"We play 10 sophomores throughout the course of a game and they've done really well for us," Alkire said. "There's been some growing pains. But the seniors have shown good leadership and gotten those guys to get us to where we are today."
One thing hasn't changed though with the Sentinels.
"Still the same ground-and-pound style of offense," Alkire said. "We try to spread you out when we can, but it's mostly going to be under center, ground and pound."
Leading that rushing attack is senior running back Jabril Daniels, who has toted the ball 156 times for 1,664 yards and 26 touchdowns this season. Braelyn Younger (43-485-9) is also a threat. And though senior quarterback Nash Cassell, who has completed 13 of 27 passes for 276 yards and six touchdowns, isn't a huge running threat, Alkire said he "does a great job of getting the ball where it needs to be."
That offense faces one of the Bayside Conference's quickest defenses.
"They're very aggressive defensively; try to cause problems in your backfield," Alkire said of Cambridge-SD.
But Burnham knows the unit he's called the backbone of his team since August, faces perhaps its biggest test of the season.
"Fort Hill football is Fort Hill football," Burnham said. "They play physical. They play fast. They do multiple things offensively. They run the ball consistently with multiple backs. We have to contain their run, limit their explosive plays on defense."
Cambridge-SD also possesses big-play talent, with senior quarterback Anthony Hughes and senior running back Sterling Perkins Jr., who has gained over a 1,000 yards this season.
"Offensively, we need to protect the football and then be opportunistic and make plays when we can," Burnham said.
Though the Sentinels have usually been at home during the past three postseasons, Alkire said his team has adapted to playing on the road after the ineligibility ruling.
"Just a matter of getting the kids in the mindset to be able to go on the road and endure some of the longer road trips, and experience some of the things that opposing teams have had to experience against us," Alkire said. "It's been a transition but the kids have accepted it and they moved on."
And though its date with Fort Hill has come two weeks earlier than expected, Burnham thinks the Vikings are ready.
"I think our kids are excited about an opportunity to prove ourself on a big stage against a quality opponent," Burnham said. "In order to get where we want to be we have to beat them. To coin the phrase, 'To be the man you've got to beat the man.' They've been the man the last three years and we want to take it. So we have to win. That's how it is."

title: Sentinels end Vikings' unbeaten run
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Sentinels end Vikings' unbeaten run

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 709
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — It was a great run.And for one half, it looked like top-seeded Cambridge-South Dorchester High's football team might extend that run, as it carried momentum and a six-point lead into the locker room.
But Fort Hill shut down the Vikings in the second half en route to a 30-12 come-from-behind victory Friday night in a Class 1A state quarterfinal played in a steady, wind-driven rain.
"Kids worked really hard. Coaches worked really hard," said Cambridge-SD head coach Rob Burnham, whose team finished the season 10-1. "Didn't end the way we wanted it to end. It hurts. It really does."
Eighth-seeded Fort Hill (5-7) took a 6-0 lead with just under 8 minutes left in the first quarter, when Jabril Daniels broke loose down the visitors' sideline for a 54-yard touchdown run. Jacob Bone's point-after kick was no good.
The Sentinels carried that 6-0 lead into the second quarter. But Cambridge-SD recovered a second Fort Hill fumble at the Vikings 46. Cambridge-SD quarterback Anthony Hughes hit Majestic Jones for a 20-yard gain to the Sentinels' 31. Six plays later, Hughes found Ka'Marii Stanley for an 8-yard touchdown pass. Fort Hill blocked Collin Bair's point-after attempt, leaving the score tied at 6-all with 4:44 remaining in the first half.
The three-time defending state champions lost a third fumble on their next possession that Hughes returned to the Fort Hill 15. The Sentinels defense stiffened. But on fourth-and-four, Hughes hit Antonio Blueford for a 9-yard touchdown pass and a 12-6 lead. Fort Hill was called for pass interference on the two-point attempt. Hughes tried running the two-point conversion in, but was stopped short.
"We had opportunities in the first half and we capitalized," Burnham said.
Despite being held to its lowest first-half point total in these playoffs, Fort Hill didn't panic.
"We weren't playing our style of football," Fort Hill head coach Zack Alkire said. "Lot of guys were down, probably feeling a bit sorry for themselves and we just tried to remind them that we're only down six points. It only takes one play to get going. And we got that one play early and we didn't stop from there."
Cambridge-SD took the second-half kickoff and gained a first down on an 18-yard carry by Sterling Perkins Jr. The Vikings went backwards from there, a low snap from center resulted in a 7-yard sack of Hughes on third down. The Vikings attempted to salvage a second low snap from center on the ensuing punt, but turned the ball over on downs, giving Fort Hill possession at the Cambridge-SD 16.
Daniels worked his way through the left side before reaching the ball across the goal for a 15-yard touchdown run. Bone kicked the extra point to give the Sentinels a 13-12 led with 9:24 to go in the third quarter.
A short kickoff return and an 8-yard sack of Hughes forced another Vikings' punt, giving Fort Hill another short field at the 35. The Sentinels moved 34 yards before Daniels scored on a 1-yard run on fourth-and-goal. Daniels' two-point run extended Fort Hill's lead to 21-12 with 2:13 left in the third quarter.
"Jabril's a tough player," Alkire said. "Jabril, he's all heart, he's all emotion. He was trying to put too much on his shoulders (in the first half). He was able to control himself a little better in the second half. Can't say enough great things about him. He's the leader of our team for sure."
Fort Hill widened its lead to 28-12 with 8:25 remaining when Braelyn Younger caught a 9-yard touchdown pass from Nash Cassell with 8:25 left.
On the ensuing kickoff, Cambridge-SD's Willie Jackson slipped at the 1-yard line. On the next play, Fort Hill's Noah House shot through the line and tackled Hughes for a safety and a 30-12 lead.
"Defense was great," Alkire said. "Defense was really good all night long. We gave up two cheap ones, but for the most part I thought we did a nice job all night long on defense."
Fort Hill killed almost 5 minutes of clock before turning the ball over on downs to the Vikings with 3:05 left. Hughes hit Perkins for a gain down to the Fort Hill 30. But the Vikings were flagged for an ineligible man downfield.
"We didn't make plays when we needed to," Burnham said. "They did."

title: EASTON TURNS IT AROUND
author: Bill Haufe
content:
EASTON TURNS IT AROUND

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 876
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It certainly wasn't the ending it was looking for.It was raining sideways and blowing hard, which neutralized the passing game really for both teams.
The opponent, Milford Mill, was big, talented, and two years removed from a state championship.
And the last thing Easton High's football team wanted to do was give the Millers extra opportunities via turnovers. But the seventh-seeded Warriors committed four turnovers during last Friday night's season-ending 42-7 loss to second-seeded Milford Mill in a Class 2A state quarterfinal.
"If we could have thrown the ball like we normally do, I think it's a little different," Easton head coach Matt Griffith said of a game that at one point was 13-7 in the first half. "I still think they beat us, but I think it's probably 42-21, 35-21, something like that.
"They're good," Griffith added of the Millers (10-1), who advance to Friday's semifinals, where they will host No. 3 seed Huntingtown (9-2). "They've got some good players."
But in a season that started with Easton being ranked 10th in one preseason poll, the Warriors showed they too had some good players.
"We had a tremendous year," said Griffith, whose team was one of only three Bayside Conference teams still playing last Friday along with defending Class 2A state champion Stephen Decatur and Cambridge-South Dorchester, the overall No. 1 seed in Class 1A whose undefeated season also ended in the rain and wind.
There have been other Easton teams that posted better records.
But over the past 40 years, no Warriors team had ever won two playoff games in the same season. Perhaps more impressive is no Easton team over that same time frame enjoyed a greater turnaround from one season to the next.
The Warriors lost starting quarterback Mikey O'Connor in Week 2 of the 2023 season and struggled to a 1-8 finish. O'Connor returned this season and helped Easton to an 8-4 record. The closest any previous Warrior team came to that seven-win improvement was in 1979, when Easton finished 9-1 after a 3-7 slate the previous year.
"We had a good year," said Griffith, who finished with his highest win total in his 10 years as Easton's head coach, and earned his 50th career win with the Warriors' 28-21 victory over Kent Island in the second round of the 2A East Regional playoffs. "The kids bought into the process in the offseason, which I think made a big difference, including Mikey. Mikey put on 15, 20 pounds and I think that was the difference in him being able to do what he did this year versus not being able to finish the (previous) year."
Though Easton's senior quarterback completed just 4 of his 14 attempts for 30 yards and an interception Friday, he rushed for 189 yards and a touchdown on a career-high 33 carries. O'Connor finished the season 127 for 242 through the air for 1,938 yards, 21 touchdowns and 15 interceptions. He also led the team in rushing, carrying 219 times for 1,436 yards and 19 touchdowns.
There were plenty of other parts to Easton's success this year.
A fleet of receivers that included Chase Raab, Diontaye Copper, Zach Barnhart and brothers Colin and Carter Mooney took turns making big catches and plays week after week. There was also the emergence of junior running back Dustin Blue, who became a brute force inside and out, totaling 652 yards and seven touchdowns.
Then there was an offensive line, that lost four starters from 2023 for various reasons. But together with sole returner Tymiere Thomas at right tackle, center TJ Truxon, guards Jack Chappell and freshman Brady Gilliece, and left tackle Xavier Stowers steadily developed and improved.
"Jack Chappell stepped up and started at right guard," Griffith said. "He gives you everything he has every play. TJ Truxon played center and did a good job for us this year. We had an outstanding freshman in Brady Gilliece at left guard, who I think is going to be one helluva player over the next couple years. And then we had sophomore left tackle in Xavier Stowers. And every so often we'd mix in Jaden Prestwood to give some guys some breaks. But those five pretty much played iron man football on the offensive line all year long."
Senior place-kicker Dominic Stanco also proved to a consistent weapon.
"He got better as the season went on and had a strong leg," Griffith said of Stanco. "It's a shame this is the only year he played football and he's a senior."
Not to be overshadowed was a defense that despite giving up its share of big plays, showed grit and delivered plenty of big stops and came up with timely takeaways. Jordan Horsey and Kyree Acree led the Warriors in tackles under the guidance of new defensive coordinator Al Waters. Thomas again proved an interior anchor up front, while Prestwood developed into a problem for opponents with his ability to play tackle, end and linebacker.
"Everything we tried to get out of them I think we got," Griffith said. "They gave it to us. They should be proud of their accomplishments for sure. And hopefully this is a part about setting a standard moving forward of what we're trying to do. But I think we got all the juice out of this squeeze, and maybe even a little bit of pulp."

title: Seahawks on record pace
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Seahawks on record pace

 November 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 867
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Stephen Decatur High made history last year when it became the first Bayside Conference school to win a state football championship in 26 years.Not quite one year later, the Seahawks are making yet another historic bid. But don't expect head coach Jake Coleman to get overly excited just yet.
"I don't think being on the cusp of history means a whole lot," Coleman said. "It just means you ain't done it. It's kind of like when people say, 'You've got potential.'"
The top-seeded Seahawks (12-0) can put themselves in position to challenge for a second straight state title match Friday, when they host No. 4 seed Westlake (10-2) in a Class 2A state semifinal at 6:30 p.m. in Berlin.
A win would also give defending-champion Decatur at chance to challenge for a second consecutive title, something that hasn't been done since Coleman slipped on his helmet and fastened his chin strap for Cambridge-South Dorchester in 1995 and '96.
Coleman thought his team had the chance to contend for a second straight state title this season, despite the graduation of his son and starting quarterback Brycen Coleman, and fellow standouts Gavin Solito and Careen Bolden. Decatur's head coach also knew Brycen's successor behind center, junior Johnny Hobgood, needed support from this year's senior cast.
"Last year on the offensive side you had an extra special player obviously with Brycen," said Coleman, whose son now plays flex tight end at Vanderbilt. "And he had some guys around him that he was able to lift up and show them the way."
So before this season began, Coach Coleman told seniors and Division I commits Davin Chandler (Vanderbilt), Trybe Wise (Georgetown) and Ethan Bradshaw (Army), as well as his offensive line, it was their turn to provide support.
"I told them, 'Johnny's got really, really big shoes to fill,"' Jake Coleman said. "'So I don't want to hear that the ball was not perfect. I don't want to hear any excuses. We got to play like guys with experience and we got to start playing like Division I athletes, too.' And they really have. And they've given Johnny the pocket that's clean. He's thrown balls and they've made plays. And really it's been exactly what I knew was possible for this group."
Hobgood has been outstanding, completing 107 of 157 passes for 1,824 yards, 30 touchdowns and just two interceptions. He's also run for four touchdowns.
"Johnny Hobgood is playing as well offensively as any player in Bayside history," Coleman said. "And the thing you won't see within those stats is he's played probably 90 percent of the games this year only playing two quarters, because we've been running the clock on people."
Hobgood injured his leg during the Seahawks' 2A East Regional first-round victory over North Caroline. He sat out Decatur's 19-14 second-round win over Wicomico, but returned for last Friday's 37-0 state-quarterfinal rout of Walkersville, completing 8 of 13 for 93 yards and four touchdowns.
"Johnny throws the ball on time," Coleman said. "He's accurate. He can make plays with his legs when he needs to. But Johnny is that pro-style quarterback, where he throws on time and he's accurate, and he goes through his reads and his process."
Then there's that supporting cast.
Chandler has 29 receptions for 676 yards and eight touchdowns. Wise has snagged 28 passes for 512 yards and a team-high 10 TDs. Evan Copeland has 24 catches for 323 yards and seven touchdowns. And Zakhari Baker has totaled 26 grabs for 420 yards and seven touchdowns.
"Zakhari Baker, he starts the season off with a kickoff return for a touchdown and I don't think he's slowed down since," Coleman said. "He has just made explosive play after explosive play all season long. We have other good wide receivers, but Zahkari Baker has just been amazing this year."
Coleman said the same thing of running back Vernon DeShields, who's carried 97 times for 803 yards and 10 touchdowns.
Decatur also had a big hole to fill at inside linebacker with Solito's graduation. But that was the lone loss on a defense that returned its other 10 starters, and put together a string of five straight shutouts this year. Filling Solito's void have been linebackers Peyton Travers and Kyle Mumford.
That group prepares for its toughest test of the season in Westlake, which is led by senior running back Devin Cox (180 carries, 1,554 yards, 29 touchdowns) and junior quarterback William Drakeford Jr. (103 of 164, 1,169 yards, 14 touchdowns, 4 interceptions).
"Super fast," Coleman said of the Wolverines, who have shut out six of their last eight opponents. "They are probably the fastest defense that we have seen.
"Offensively, they're a power football team," Coleman added. "They got a really good running in (Cox), and he's tough to tackle. They've got an athletic dual threat quarterback. They've got weapons on the outside. It's exactly who you expect to see out a 10-2 semifinal team. They're definitely a team that has the ability to win it."
So does Decatur.
"This is right where I thought we'd be, is being contender," Coleman said. "Last year we were young. Now, we have experience. They're senior laden and they've been through the fire. Now, we just want to get ourselves back to Annapolis (site of the state title game)."

title: KEEPING UP WITH THE JONESES
author: Bill Haufe
content:
KEEPING UP WITH THE JONESES

 November 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The biggest question at the Jones family Thanksgiving this year wasn't who was going to get to the dinner table first.No, the bigger question was who was going to cross the finish line first at the annual Easton 5K Turkey Trot?
"I wanted to beat him," said a smiling Judi Spinks of her big brother Bill Jones, a former collegiate All-American in the 5,000 and 10,000 meters who made the drive down from New Freedom, Pennsylvania.
"She's still in really good shape so I thought if I could run with my sister, who's an Olympic Trials athlete, I can be in pretty good shape," Jones said of Spinks, who competed in the steeplechase at the U.S. Olympic track and field trials this past summer and came up from Quantico, Virginia.
Jill and Paul Jones' kids probably had plenty to chew on at the family dinner in St. Michaels later Thursday, especially after Bill won the overall competition and Judi took the women's title while placing third overall on a wet and dreary morning.
Though over 750 registered to run in the annual holiday event that starts and finishes at the Easton Family YMCA, 458 left the starting line in the cold and rain and 439 finished.
As the pack left the YMCA parking lot, spilled onto Peachblossom Road, and turned into a steady, narrow string pushing down the Easton Bypass, Jones, Easton High graduate Nathaniel Andrews, and Spinks began gradually distancing themselves from the field.
"I just went out how I felt," said Bill Jones, who along with his sister, has made the Turkey Trot part of their yearly running schedule. "I just like to have fun at these races, and I'm trying to get back in shape."
Jones was an All-American at Division III Franciscan (Ohio) University, where he competed in cross country and track, and twice qualified for nationals. Ten years of battling injury problems slowed Jones' running career, but now at 35 he is trying to regain his stride.
"I'm just trying to come out, run as fast as I can, and try and get in shape," said Jones, who clocked a winning time of 17 minutes, 6.47 seconds. "And just have some fun with everybody here. We had some good camaraderie out there after we turned onto the main road. My sister was running with us."
So was Andrews, who finished second overall in 17:19.09, and Spinks, who incorporated the Turkey Trot as part of a workout.
"After I finished I went back out and did two more miles and some strides; part of a broken-out, tempo run," said the 27-year-old Spinks, who finished in 17:29.59. "I was trying to exert the least amount of energy possible to beat my brother. But he went too fast and I didn't want to go lactic; like lactic acid. But he did a great job. He beat me fair and square today.
"I'm just thankful I have someone in the family now that can challenge me at the Turkey Trot," added Spinks, who ran for the University of Nebraska. "He's just getting back into running. I think it brought on the intensity. I hit the paces I was supposed to hit. I'm happy. I got my workout in before Thanksgiving dinner."
Drew Bobesink of Alexadria, Virginia was fourth in 18:15.45, and recent Easton High grad Colin Smith was fifth (18:44.38).
Others in the field ran for fun, with friends, or perhaps in hopes of reaching a certain time. Some ran just to see if they could finish. Some ran with dogs. Others ran in costume. Some were young and some were not-so young. And yet despite the raw conditions, several in the Trot paused for family photos and group shots after collecting their breath, and shared hugs and laughs before heading for drier, warmer confines.
"Feels great," Jones said of his victory. "I just wanted to see what would happen if I pushed as fast as I could today. I love the rain. It makes it exciting. There's a thrill to it. It makes it fun."

title: Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 2164
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It wasn't a prediction.It was just something Mike Kern believed.
"If we can get out of the region, I think we have a good shot at states," Kern said of Queen Anne's County High's girls soccer team.
That was at the outset of the season. The Lions did get out of the region, then went on to become the first Bayside Conference school ever to win a girls state soccer championship.
Now, as the girls basketball season approaches tip-off, Kern again strongly believes if Queen Anne's can get out of its region, it has a chance to do well at the state level.
"We're very multi-dimensional," Kern said. "All of our guards can penetrate and shoot. And then our post players are very dangerous inside. They move well. They're very athletic. So I think the sky's the limit for them. The biggest thing is play as a team. We learned that in soccer. If we play as a team and aren't selfish, and do the little things, I think we can do really well."
Getting out of the Class 2A East Region II could prove more difficult than in soccer. Kent Island still has Sydney Riska and Lacey Dauses. Wicomico returns the bulk of the team that handed the Lions their only three losses last season, including bouts for the Bayside Conference and 2A East Region II championships. And Parkside has improved.
But this Queen Anne's team is different.
Not only does Kern return the majority of a team that went 20-3 and won the North Bayside championship, he welcomes two additions who have the potential to be impact players in juniors Damya Henry, a transfer from Cambridge-South Dorchester, and Cheyanne Hollis — daughter of Queen Anne's boys head coach Jeff Hollis — who has been sidelined by injury the past two seasons.
"With our core coming back, plus those additions, I think we stand a good chance of challenging them this year," Kern said of Wicomico. "Damya gives us that defensive pressure. She reads well. Anticipates well. And she's quick. So she definitely helps on the defensive end.
"And Chayenne, she's a true post player; and that will free up Bea (Holthaus) and Lucy (Taylor) a little bit having her in there," Kern continued.
Then there's the core group. Seniors RJ Ensor and Lucy Taylor return along with sophomores Laila Coles, Kariana Hickson, and Holthaus, the 2023 North Bayside Player of the Year.
"The thing about our team right now, I feel like we can score so many different ways," Kern said. "We have pretty good shooters. We can get the ball inside. We can drive. We're a very multi-dimensional team. And Bea herself is very multi-dimensional. She can play outside, go inside. She can drive.
"I'm not worried about us being able to score this year," Kern added. "My biggest focus so far is making sure we play good defense. One of the things that we've done well over the years is we've been a really good defensive team. And I feel like we have so much energy on the offense, that we kind of rest on the defense. And we can't do that with good teams. So we have to play up-tempo defense the entire game."
Kent Island remains Queen Anne's biggest challenger, though Cambridge-SD, with the senior core of Le'Asia Todd, Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin have the potential to give Queen Anne's a battle.
Here's a look at this season's teams.
CAMBRIDGE-SD
Head Coach: Shamya Johnson.
Who's Where: Le'Asia Todd (Sr., C); Destiny Johnson (Sr., G); Tejanae Ballin (Sr., PG); AzEyera Johnson (Sr., F); Skyla Ali (So., F); Jade Ballin (So., F); JaNaya Stanley (Jr., G); Tonyia Brooks (Sr., G); Aamiyah Wilcox (Sr., C); Neveah Adams (Fr., G); Montiasha Jackson (So., G); Amari Winters (Fr., F/C); Kennedy Bourne (So., F); Kamryn Bourne (So., F); D'Asia Mack (So., G).
Outlook: Todd can reach 1,000 career points in Thursday's opener against Crisfield, and together with Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin makes the Vikings a favorite in 1A East Region II.
And though Coach Johnson thinks Cambridge-SD can again reach the 1A state quarterfinals, one of her biggest challenges is keeping her team's intensity and discipline up from start to finish.
"That was the conversation we had tonight,' Coach Johnson said Tuesday in a phone interview. "'You all got it. You've got the pieces. But you all don't have the discipline. And that's the difference.'"
Johnson also knows her team needs to play great transition defense and create points off turnovers if it hopes to challenge Queen Anne's and Kent Island.
COL. RICHARDSON
Head Coach: Tom Corsey.
Who's Where: Jaz Jackson (Jr., G); Monae Ross (Sr., C); Selina Austriville (So., F); Tybria Williams (Sr., G); Ella Downie (So., F); Angelina Algre (Fr., C).
Outlook: Corsey thinks the 6-foot-5 Algre can develop into an inside force.
"She's a work in progress," Corsey said. "She's a presence. She's learning, but I'm going to get her there."
This is one of the younger teams Corsey's coached, but the goal is another 10-win season with eyes on upsetting a 2A school.
EASTON
Head Coach: Lesley Staehli.
Who's Where: Sam Murphy (Sr., G); Serenity Velez (Jr., G); Maia Bailey (Fr., G); Ki'Mauri Lewis (So., G); Jordyn Wilson-Colbert (So., F/C); Myles Booker (Sr., F/C); Dakota Dietrich (Sr., G); Addison Knox (So., G/F); Stella Kabler (Jr., G); Taylor Bowen (Fr., F/C); Addison Chandler (Sr., G/F).
Outlook: The Warriors are an interesting mix.
Velez returns as one of the team's top scorers, and Murphy has transferred from Saints Peter and Paul.
"She is one of the scrappiest people I have ever played against the last four years that I've been coaching defense wise," Staehli said of Murphy. "Now it's awesome to have her with us because she barely comes out."
Bailey, daughter of Marty Bailey, who has come over from the boys team to be an assistant, could be one of the Bayside's top newcomers. And then there is a list of talent that includes Knox, Kabler and Bowen, who helped the Warriors reach the state field hockey semifinals this past season, and Chandler, a force on the Easton soccer team.
"We're going to be fast," Staehli said. "Everybody has talent. I think we're going to shock a lot of people this year with the fact (they're) not expecting a lot of athletic people to come back into the program with us having no jayvee last year. There's certain teams we'll struggle with, but I think we're going to be pretty good."
KENT COUNTY
Head Coach: Tyray Johnson.
Who's Where: Kate Cannon (Sr., C); Talicia Wright (So., PG); Jane Cleary (So., F); Love Jackson (Jr., SF); Kaliyah Smith (Sr., SF); Ariyana Green (So., SF); Saniyah Jones (So., C); Tameeia Savage (Jr., SF); Juliette Camilli (Jr., SG); Sanorra Parker (Fr., SG); Abigael Lachance (Sr., SF); Emerence Boutaud (Jr., PF).
Outlook: Johnson begins his fourth season with the biggest roster he's ever had at Kent with 12. Though still young, experience was gained last year, especially with Wright, who returns at point guard.
"We turned the ball over a lot last year," Johnson said. "She (Wright) stepped up toward the end of the season. So a lot of the mistakes she made early on we won't really have them this year. So it's going to be less turnovers for us."
Speed and defense will be critical if the undersized Trojans are to improve on last season's five-win mark.
KENT ISLAND
Head Coach: Dave Plumer.
Who's Where: Sydney Riska (Sr., F); Lacey Dauses (Jr., G); Abigail Staton (Sr., PG); Ellie Burnside (Sr., G); Machaela Thomas (So., C); Avery Eaton (Sr., G)
Outlook: Lilli Dauses graduated and Makayla Kropfelder transferred to Broadneck. But don't expect the Bucs to fall far from the top.
The smooth-playing Riska was a double-double machine last season, and Lacey Dauses gained confidence with her ability to attack the rim and draw contact. Add Thomas, a 6-foot-2 center, who could create problems for opponents, and Burnside, the first player off the bench from last season.
"I think Lacey had grown as a player and in size," Plumer said. "Obviously Sydney had a big year last year, and now adding another 6-2 center to play along side of her is going to benefit her as well. Who are you going to guard? Machaela's got great footwork. She just needs playing time to get better.
"I think we got to run," Plumer continued. "I mean we're guard heavy. We do have a big player inside but I think we're going to be a running team. We just got to play. There's talent there. It's going to take them a month or two to get them up to speed. But they can play."
NORTH CAROLINE
Head Coach: AJ Jackson.
Who's Where: Taryn Brandt (Sr., G); Jasiyah Henry (Sr., G); Emma Keating (Sr., F); Ashley Kercheval (Sr., F); Megan Rogers (Sr., G); Kaitlyn Thompson (Sr., C); Sarah Brown (Sr., G); MyKira Allen (Jr., F); Yariah Dowell (Jr., G); Irma Sanchez (Jr., G); Nevaeh Irby (So., G).
Outlook: The Bulldogs lost the majority of their scoring from last season with the graduation of Precious Phillips, Chloe Escoe, Ashleigh Lawry and first-team all-North Bayside pick Selaya Garrison.
Jackson will lean heavily on Henry, a four-year varsity starter, for scoring, along with Keating and Dowell.
"Getting back to the fundamentals," Jackson said Caroline's key to success. "Rebounding, boxing out, good passes. The basics. So far I've loved what I've seen in preseason. The girls are buying in. There are some things we need to improve on, but the girls are working hard."
NORTH DORCHESTER
Head Coach: Dontele Pinder.
Who's Where: Remedy Wongus (So., G/F); Areinya Taylor (Sr., G); Ziya Patton (Sr., F); Diamond Newbill (Fr., G); Sammir Holland (Fr., G); Destiny Wongus (Fr., G).
Outlook: An assistant at Colonel Richardson the past eight seasons, Pinder begins his first head coaching job with plenty of optimism.
"I feel like we have a great core group," Pinder said. "We're kind of in the middle of the transition, where we have some of our key seniors that are leading, but we have a good group of freshmen that I feel like are going to be productive in the beginning. I'm excited and I think they're excited about the change. Hopefully we can make some noise here in the North."
QUEEN ANNE'S
Head Coach: Mike Kern.
Who's Where: Damya Henry (Jr., G); Cheyanne Hollis (Jr., F/C); Bea Holthaus (So., F); Laila Coles (So., G); Kariana Hickson (So., G); Taylor Jordan (So., G); RJ Ensor (Sr., G); Lucy Taylor (Sr., C); Sydney Pinder (Jr., F); Keilah Reed (Jr., G); Abby Robinson (So., G); Dillon Simpler (So., G); Lex Kern (So., G).
Outlook: With practically everyone back from last season, as well as the additions of Hollis and Henry, it's not surprising Kern thinks the potential is there to do well at the state level, if Queen Anne's can advance out of the region.
"We've never had a team that can all shoot," Kern said. "We've had teams where we had one true shooter and that's it. We might have a kid who could drive. We had Kendall Moxey (Queen Anne's career leading scorer) who could play the post. But we've never had a solid (team) that can shoot from so many different area's of the court."
That's a combination that could have the Lions driving deep into another postseason.
ST. MICHAELS
Head Coach: Jonathan Matthews.
Who's Where: Jordyn Beckett (So., F/C); Hanna Corkran (So., F/C); Aleah George (So., F); Rebeca Martinez (Jr., G); Evelyn Mautz (Fr., G); Kayla Montoya (So. SG); Olivia Patrick (Jr., G/F); Alayna Porter (Fr., G); Maddisyn Roe (Jr., G); Bella Simmons (Fr., G); Kendall Rosenberger (So., C); Tess Weller (Jr., PG); Shayla Frink (Jr., C); Kaelyn Hicks (Fr., G/F); Maleia Loffland (Fr., G).
Outlook: Another former Colonel Richardson assistant, Matthews begins his first head coaching job hoping to build on what former head coach Mark Potter started.
"Mark gave us a good start from last year for the ninth graders that are 10th graders this year," Matthews said. "We're still working on some of our developmental things, but I think in the long run we'll be all right. I have high hopes for them."
SAINTS PETER & PAUL
Head Coach: Katie Murphy.
Who's Where: Avery McCall (Jr., F/C); Annie Albright (Jr., G); Lucy Rankin (Jr., G/F); Hazel Spurry (Jr., G); Emma Hainey (So., G); Kaylin Palmer (So., F/C); Bridget Gilman (So., G); Tara Foley (So., G/F); Ryleigh Briddell (So., C/F); Veronica Pool (So., G); Natalee Lyons (Fr., G); Caroline Jallade (Fr., C/F).
Outlook: While the Sabres and Delmarva Christian have met for the Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference title the last three seasons, Murphy thinks this season could be more wide open with Worcester Prep, Gunston and Salisbury School pushing to improve.
"Everyone is a threat," Murphy said.
Murphy admits it's been somewhat hard to gauge her team's potential because she hasn't had her full lineup for games or practices.
And though the losses of Morgan Quade (graduation) and Sam Murphy (transfer) will hurt, the Sabres have a solid core with McCall, Albright, Rankin, Hainey and the continuing emergence of Palmer and Gilman.
"We finally have everybody back and we're working on a few things to find out who those (starting) five are," Murphy said. "They want to learn. They want to get better. Working together as a team is where we are right now."

title: Decatur bids for second straight state title in rematch with Huntingtown
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Decatur bids for second straight state title in rematch with Huntingtown

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 994
 Words 

 Read News Document

 His team was undefeated and still wearing the tag of defending state champion.And though Stephen Decatur High trailed 14-0 at halftime in last Friday's Class 2A state semifinal, Seahawks head coach Jake Coleman said he felt no stress.
"I was pretty calm. Having to win a game when your son's a senior and it's the state championship, that was pressure," said Coleman, whose son Brycen quarterbacked Decatur to last year's 2A state crown.
"We came out very determined," Coleman said of last Friday's semifinal against Westlake. "I told them, 'Hey, we just got to get that first score.'"
But then the Wolverines widened their advantage to 20-0 with 3 minutes, 34 seconds left in the third quarter.
"I just told the guys, 'Keep fighting. Keep coaching,'" Coleman said. "Yeah, we were at the precipice of breaking, but we didn't. And we kept saying, 'Hey, get one score and then get one stop.' And as soon as we got the score, it was like, you could feel something changing on the field. Our guys were like, 'Oh, OK. We're still good.'"
The Seahawks proved to be real good, reeling off the game's final 27 points for a 27-20 overtime victory that launched them into Saturday's Class 2A state title game against Huntingtown (10-2) at 3:30 p.m. at Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium in Annapolis.
A win Saturday would make Decatur (13-0) only the fourth football team in Bayside history to win back-to-back state titles, joining James M. Bennett (1982-83), Kent County (1989-90) and Cambridge-South Dorchester (1995-96).
"So now we have the challenge," Coleman said of the rematch with Huntingtown, which Decatur defeated 21-13 in last year's title game. "I told my seniors that are returning state champions, I was like, 'Hey. Are you satisfied? You got your ring. We got other guys that don't have a ring. I know they're going to be ready and they want it. And in practice this week, in the game, I don't know when, but you've got to answer that bell. Is this something you want?
"'You want to go back-to-back?'" Coleman continued. "'Because I can tell you this, Huntingtown has been thinking about you just like you were thinking about Milford Mill (which eliminated Decatur in the 2022 state semifinals, then lost to the Seahawks in last year's semis), and how you were waiting for the opportunity to go and beat them. Everything they've done has been for this moment. So they got the edge and now you've got to answer that question. Do you want it more than they want it? Do you want to go back-to- back?' We'll find out Saturday."
Of course, it wasn't looking like there would be a rematch with Westlake holding a 20-0 lead deep into last Friday's third quarter. That's when Coleman got into his defense.
"I told them, 'No excuses, man,'" Coleman said. "'This offense has been making it easy for us all year. It's our time to step up.' When we got the (first) score, we said, 'Hey, let's get 'em three-and-out. And if we get three-and-out, I promise you that offense is going to score.' And they did. We went three-and-out, and boom. We go right down field like we have done on many teams this season."
Decatur's comeback began when junior quarterback Johnny Hobgood connected with Zakhari Baker for a 38-yard touchdown pass with 34 seconds left in the third, and Blake Wallace booted the extra point, pulling the Seahawks within 20-7.
The defending champs pared their deficit to 20-14 with 6:15 left in the game on Nate Tapley's 2-yard touchdown run and Wallace's PAT.
"Once we got it to 20-14, I could just tell our guys were so determined," Coleman said. "I saw Johnny Hobgood transform. He goes from the first half really struggling, and then I saw him all of a sudden start to get that look. Everything just slowed down. Our offensive line starting handling them a little bit better."
Davin Chandler caught a 10-yard touchdown pass from Hobgood with 1:03 left, but Wallace missed the extra point, leaving the game knotted at 20-all and forcing overtime.
Westlake opted to go on defense first. Hobgood scored on an 8-yard run and Wallace converted the PAT to make it 27-20 before Decatur's defense stopped the Wolverines on their OT possession.
Now, comes Saturday's rematch.
"They're a premier program," Coleman said of the Huntingtown. "They're running the ball a little bit more than last year. Last year they were a little bit more balanced run to pass. This year a little bit heavier in the run in the games that we've seen. They certainly can pass unquestionably, and they are great on defense."
The Hurricanes' ground game is led by senior Landon Cawley (101 carries, 670 yards, 13 touchdowns) and juniors Gabriel Copeland (93-666-8) and Brody Whittington (53-542-5). Senior quarterback Dominic Hickman has completed 63 of 116 passes for 920 yards, six touchdowns and six interceptions.
Senior defensive end Evan Powell, a West Virginia University commit, is part of a defensive unit that will look to contain the Seahawks' run and passing game.
Hobgood has connected on 120 of his 190 attempts this season for 1,973 yards, 32 touchdowns and just two interceptions. His receiving fleet includes Chandler (36 receptions, 762 yards, 9 touchdowns), who Wednesday signed with Vanderbilt, and Trybe Wise (29-521-10), who signed with Georgetown. The Canes also have Baker (28-457-8) to contend with, and a running attack led by Vernon DeShields (106 carries, 855 yards, 10 touchdowns).
"You look across the board, all the teams that are playing in the state championship, all of them can run the ball," Coleman said. "All of them have good defenses. All of them have quarterbacks that most of the time are dual-threat kids. And they got playmakers. They are good in all three phases and they're well coached. And Huntingtown is no different.
"And I know that they are hungry," added Coleman of the Hurricanes, who are making their fourth state championship appearance. "(They) haven't been able to win one yet. It's going to be a great challenge."
