title: Decatur rallies for second straight state title
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Decatur rallies for second straight state title

 December 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1039
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — One minute. Three plays.That's all it took.
That's all Stephen Decatur High's football team needed Saturday to score the game-winning touchdown for a 13-12 victory over Huntingtown that earned the Seahawks a second straight Class 2A state championship, and completed a second consecutive 14-0 season at Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium.
"To come back on a team like that is unbelievable," Seahawks head coach Jake Coleman said after beating the Hurricanes for a second straight year in the title game.
Especially considering after two strong game-opening drives — one ending with a touchdown for a 7-0 first-quarter lead, the second ending with a missed field goal — the Seahawks' high-octane offense was virtually silenced by Huntingtown.
"All the teams in the state championship games have great defenses year in and year out," Coleman said. "Because you can't get there without having a really tough defense. And Huntingtown's good. They made us struggle."
Those struggles came after Decatur took the opening kickoff and crafted a 12-play, 68-yard scoring march that ended with Nathan Tapley stretching across the goal line for a 2-yard touchdown run and Blake Wallace booming the extra point for a seven-point lead with 5:55 left in the first quarter.
The Seahawks were on the verge of widening that lead on their next possession, when a high snap from center on third-and-goal at the Huntingtown 1-yard line resulted in a 14-yard loss, setting up Wallace's 32-yard field goal attempt that sailed wide left. While those two plays, penalties, and a rare Johnny Hobgood interception hurt the Seahawks, the Hurricanes held the defending state champions to just 30 yards and two first downs on 20 plays over Decatur's next five possessions.
Huntingtown (10-3) trimmed its deficit, cobbling together an 18-play, 80-yard march that ended with Landon Cawley's 2-yard touchdown run with 7:05 left in the third quarter. But the Hurricanes couldn't pull even, as Decatur's Sully Auker delivered one of the season's biggest plays, blocking Max Hall's point-after attempt, keeping the Seahawks in front at 7-6.
Huntingtown then took the lead, when quarterback Dominic Hickman (13 carries, 108 yards) found room on the right side, and didn't stop until he had raced 57 yards for a touchdown and a 12-7 lead with 3:02 left in the game. Again Decatur came up big on the conversion attempt, stuffing Cawley (28 carries, 127 yards) one yard short on the two-point try.
Decatur's Davin Chandler returned the ensuing kickoff 22 yards, setting the Seahawks up at their own 39 with 2:58 left.
Eight days earlier, Decatur faced an even greater deficit when it trailed Westlake 20-0 with 3:34 left in the third quarter of the state semifinal before rallying for a 27-20 overtime victory.
Now, once again, Decatur's shot at history was in jeopardy.
Saturday, Decatur had less than 3 minutes to achieve what only three other Bayside Conference schools — James M. Bennett (1982-83), Kent County (1989-90) and Cambridge-South Dorchester (1995-96) — had done in winning back-to-back state titles. Perhaps more impressive, the Seahawks were less than 3 minutes away from becoming just the second Bayside program to win back-to-back state championships while going undefeated, joining John Usiltion's Bennett teams that went a combined 24-0 on the way to the '82 and '83 titles.
But this was different.
This a smaller window of time that was closing by the second.
And this was a defense that had proved much stingier than anything the Seahawks had faced before, holding Decatur to its lowest point total in two seasons — not counting the 1-0 season-opening forfeit over Queen Anne's in 2023.
But none of that seemed to matter to Decatur. There was no panic on the Seahawks' sideline from players or coaches. Instead, the offense calmly returned to the field led by the ever efficient Hobgood, who completed 17 of 21 passes for 233 yards in the game, and sounded more like a veteran signal-caller than a first-year starter at quarterback.
"Take what they give us," Hobgood said in the postgame press conference. "If it's short, take it."
He did just that, finding Vernon Deshields for a modest 5-yard pickup on first down that moved Decatur to their 44.
"If it's there deep, take that too," Hobgood said.
He did that, connecting with Trybe Wise for a pivotal 32-yard gain to the Hurricanes 24 on the next play.
"We had to be patient," Coleman said of the final drive. "We wanted to be patient with our game plan. They were a very good team and they were coached up very well. But we were trying to set guys up and that's what (offensive coordinator) Russell (Croteau) did on that last drive; went to some plays that we knew and had a probability of being some long gains."
The last of those high-probability calls came on the next play, when Hobgood looked left and tossed a 24-yard rainbow into Zakhari Baker's hands for a touchdown and a 13-12 Decatur lead with 1:58 left in the game.
"I had a feeling I was going to be open," said Baker, who got behind his defender to haul in the game-winning score. "I told Johnny, 'Trust me. I got you.' I just went up and got it."
Coleman wasn't surprised.
"When Johnny threw the ball I thought there's only one guy on the team that can go get that one," Coleman said of Baker.
Hobgood's two-point pass attempt fell incomplete.
Trent DePompa returned the ensuing kickoff 13 yards to the Hurricanes' 26. A 12-yard pass from Hickman to Trevor Robbins pushed Huntingtown to its 44. Auker sacked Hickman for a 4-yard loss. After two incompletions, Decatur was flagged for defensive holding on fourth down, setting up a fourth-and-four from the Seahawks' 35. But Hickman's final pass fell incomplete, sealing Decatur's victory.
"It was 100 percent about repeating," Coleman, who played on Cambridge-SD's back-to-back state title teams, said of his team's objective from the beginning of the season. "Make no mistake about it.
"My son told me, 'Hey Dad. You ain't won one without me,'" Coleman said of son Brycen, who quarterbacked the Seahawks to last year's title. "And I was like, 'OK.' And I whispered that into a couple of guys' ears. And I also told them at the beginning of the year, 'It's your time. You're the superstars now.' And they played like it. Two-time state champion. 28-0. What else can you say?"

title: Wicomico defeats Easton
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Wicomico defeats Easton

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 577
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Jason Biringer has no illusion of flipping Easton High's wrestling program around overnight."It's growing pains," said Biringer, who has returned as the Warriors head coach after three seasons away from the program. "We set small goals for each of these guys. Hey, sometimes it might be just, get through the first period for those super raw new guys. After that we just keep building a little more. Make it through your first match. Get your first win. Get another win. Small steps."
Biringer saw some of his green roster take some small steps Wednesday night during a 58-24 loss to Wicomico, which won four of the five varsity matches wrestled to go along with six forfeit wins.
"We know we have to work," said Biringer, whose roster of 30 has only six wrestlers with more experience than just this season. "And we know there's a lot to do, and a lot of ways to get better. But I'm happy with the effort they are putting in. Like I said, it's a lot to ask."
Wicomico had an 18-6 lead via three forfeits through the first four weight classes, then extended that cushion to 24-6, when Deion Finney pinned AJ Matulay in 1 minute, 4 seconds at 132 pounds.
Easton (0-2) picked up its lone win not by way of forfeit at 138, when Shawn Arnold fell into a 3-0 first-period hole, scored a late escape, then pinned Ethan Brewington at 2:39, pulling the Warriors within 24-12.
"Shawn is a scrappy kid," Biringer said. "We've been working with him. He's got a high octane motor. Getting him to be settle down and be more controlled out there, that's our focus. But he has a ton of potential. He's a second-year kid. Bright future for him if he keeps working hard."
The Indians won the other three matches that were wrestled, the tightest being at 144, where Corey Richardson decisioned Easton's Adonis Schmitt, 7-2. Wi-Hi's Adelson Theajeon pinned Anthony Melendez in 2:45 at 175, and Keven Mondestin got a 21-second fall over Matthew Brunner at 285.
"Those guys who wrestled, we're asking a lot of those kids," Biringer said. "Wi-Hi also has experience. They have a good program. (Head coach) Nate Stone's been there for many years now and always has a solid group."
Wicomico's Terry Scott (106), Tavenon Outlaw (120), Davidson Fortunel (126), Rowan Okerblom (157), Cameron Wawrzenak (165) and Jamier Johnson (215) each won by forfeit.
"We've got a core of guys that have several years of experience, but they are all kind of lumped down in like in the lower weights," Stone said. "But we have a bunch of guys we think are going to do really well. Overall I thought our conditioning was pretty good for it being this early (in the season). And we didn't look super sloppy. So fundamentally we did OK."
Easton's other wins came via forfeit from Estaben Velasquez (113), Matthew Bravo (150) and Wahaab Popal (190).
"We're focused on each individual's production," said Biringer, who was also encouraged by his girls winning three of five matches, and his boys winning three of the seven junior-varsity bouts. "Lot of youth. Almost exclusively sophomores and freshmen, and then a few juniors and two seniors.
"And the kids have had a good attitude," Biringer added. "They're trying. They want to learn the moves. They want to get better. It takes showing up and putting in that work every day. It's a sport of experience and you have to have the long view."

 Brad Plutschak was offering a quick overview of the Bayside Conference boys basketball landscape early Thursday afternoon, then narrowed the conversation toward the North division."I'm not sure there's a whole lot of teams that are going to pull away," Colonel Richardson High's head coach said. "Well, maybe (defending South Bayside champion Stephen) Decatur. And then up here it's a crapshoot. I have no idea. I think it could be a wild North this year."
Plutschak then checked himself after being reminded of Cambridge-South Dorchester.
"Oh, yeah," Plutschak said of the Vikings, who reached the Class 1A state final last season. "I guess Cambridge and Decatur would be the early-season favorites. I mean Cambridge is just putting a lot of points up."
Through three games, Cambridge-SD is already averaging 87.6 points a game and allowing the opposition 41. To say the Vikings are eager for another shot at a state title may be the season's biggest understatement.
"I took a bigger break than they did," Cambridge-SD head coach Shawn Tucker said of a team, whose 25-3 record included winning the North Bayside regular-season title, the Bayside Conference crown and a 1A regional championship before losing 69-65 to Edmondson-Westside in the 1A state final in College Park. "Those guys got back in the gym early and they've been in the gym since honestly last season. They've been in the gym every day. We want to do more than just get there, and obviously we had to do more in the offseason."
The lone impact player graduated from last season is mercurial guard Shaun Moody, the North Bayside player of the year now at Chesapeake College. Just about everyone else has returned, including a core group that features seniors Koby Ennals and Anthony Hughes, and juniors Sterling Perkins Jr. and Semaj Pinder.
"Our same four goals still apply," Tucker said. "Win the Bayside North, win the Bayside championship, win the region championship, and bring home the states. That's our goal."
A goal that figures to be within reach considering Tucker thinks despite Moody's loss, this team's overall defense may be better than last season.
"The guys push each other and I feel our defense is better," Tucker said. Once we get in better shape — our football guys who are transitioning into basketball — one of our strengths now is we can really guard the ball."
Plutschak may be correct in regard to the rest of the North, when considering Colonel defeated Queen Anne's, and St. Michaels notched its first victory over North Caroline since 2008.
Senior Garett Hemingway and Saints Peter & Paul will challenge for a second straight Maryland Interscholastic Athletic Association C Conference championship, with Sabres head coach Gary Gould — like C-SD's Tucker — thinking this team has the potential to be better than a year ago.
Here's a look at this season's teams:
CAMBRIDGE-SD
Head Coach: Shawn Tucker.
Who's Where: Koby Ennals (Sr., G/F); Anthony Hughes (Sr., G); Semaj Pinder (Jr., G); Sterling Perkins Jr. (Jr., G); K'Marion Hall (So., F); Jaden Harris (Sr., F); Darren Belizaire (Sr., F); Thomas Wilson (Jr., G); Ka'Lel Johnson (Sr., G); William Jackson (Sr., G); Telorian Williams (Fr., C); Ta'Brion Watts (Sr., F).
Outlook: Tucker enters his third season at the helm with a group that looks to be the class of the North.
"The offense will come," Tucker said. "Offense is always the second to come. We're guarding exceptionally well. We're still turning the ball over, which is not to my liking, but once we cut that in half, we're going to be a really, really good team."
COL. RICHARDSON
Head Coach: Brad Plutschak.
Who's Where: Mikiah Batson (Jr., G); Shaun Allen (So., PG); Ja'Zir Dickerson (So., G); David Thomas (Jr., G); Robbie Cunningham (Jr., G); Tarron Hammond (Sr., G/F); Jakai Jones (Jr., F); Bradley Thomas (Jr., G/F); Jacklin Novembre (Jr., F/C); Max Zapata (Jr., G); Cavin Wilcox (Jr., G/F); Damein Murray (Sr., F).
Outlook: The Colonels are off to a 3-0 start — entering Friday's game at Mardela — and already snared a big, early win with their 71-55 victory over Queen Anne's.
"We've got a little bit more team speed and we're sharing the ball well," said Plutschak, whose looks to have one of the North's deeper backcourts. "We've got to continue to get better offensively and defensively, keep hitting the open man. Just keep it simple."
EASTON
Head Coach: Dionte Hynson.
Who's Where: Conner Hensley (Sr., F); Mikey O'Connor (Sr., F); Zymier Ramirez (Jr., F); Tymiere Thomas (Jr., F); Diontaye Copper (Jr., G); Landon Finney (Jr., G); Da'Shawn Johnson (Jr., G); Darrell Lee (Sr., F); Zyan Finney (Sr., G); Jamari Copper (Jr., G); Tahjmere Murray (Sr., G); Lamont Simms (Sr., F).
Outlook: Marshall Bailey, the Warriors' leading scorer from last season, transferred to Westtown School in West Chester, Pennsylvania.
So where does the offense come from now?
"Everybody has to be prepared to shoot the ball," Hynson said. "Everybody has to look to score. The main thing is we have to play defense, try and get up and down the floor."
Hensley, Johnson, Ramirez and Thomas each scored in double figures during Thursday's win over North Dorchester, but Hynson knows his team must do a better job of protecting the basketball.
"As long as we compete we'll be fine," Hynson said.
NORTH CAROLINE
Head Coach: BJ Miller.
Who's Where: Quinneil Gross (So., G); Nehemiah Miller (So., G); Jarvis Thomas Jr. (Sr., G); Tyson Weber (Sr., G); Sam Holland (Sr., F); Darrell Jackson (Jr., F); Ryan Shanks (Sr., F); Verquan Warner (Sr., C); Tyler Gutierrez (Jr., G).
Outlook: The Bulldogs are still reeling from two senior starters deciding to quit right the season tipped off.
"We're going to have to win ugly," Miller said. "We're going to have to do all the little things right, and play with intensity and poise. And that's difficult when you're playing hard-nosed, man-to-man and physical play, also to realize you have to keep your emotions in check. Once we master the three e's (energy, effort and execution) we'll be fine. But we have to master the three e's. Our energy and effort is there. We've got to execute."
NORTH DORCHESTER
Head Coach: Robert Smith Jr.
Who's Where: Alvin Hutton (Sr., G); Victor Merritt (Sr., F); Kaden Andrews (Sr., F); Tajere Pritchett (Jr., G); Tyrone Smith (Jr., G); Eddie Savage (Sr., F); TJ McCoy (Jr., G); Jazeon Cephas (So., G); Christian Chase (Jr., F); Dayshaujn Pinkett (Sr., F).
Outlook: The Eagles struggled last season, but Coach Smith saw an encouraging sign during Thursday's loss at Easton. Though North Dorchester fell into an early hole, it rallied to close within two points late in the second quarter before watching the Warriors pull away in the second half.
"We got to limit our turnovers and play for four quarters," Smith said. "We're not a team that can play catch-up. Both games going into the half we were right there. At big moments we had some lapses on defense. But we are fighting and we're not giving up. It's just continuing to stay positive. We're in the games. We just got to stay in it for four quarters."
QUEEN ANNE'S
Head Coach: Jeff Hollis.
Who's Where: Ja'Dereon Thompson (So., G); Chance Hegedus (So., G); Amari Baynard (Jr., F); Jimmy Holthaus (Sr., F); Ahijah Hutchins (Jr., G); Brice Gordon (Jr., G); Ayden Hicks (Jr., G); John Connelly (Sr., F); Jameson Kendall (Jr., G); James Rath (Jr., G); Mika Hutchins (Sr., C); DeRodney Smith (Jr., G).
Outlook: Baynard is the lone returning starter from a year ago, and was part of the team that handed Cambridge-SD its lone division loss last year.
"That's the goal," Hollis said. "I know they're going to be good again this year. One of our goals is to beat Cambridge."
For that to happen, Hollis said he's going to need scoring by committee. Hegedus had a big game in the season-opening win against Parkside. Holthaus, the lone returning senior starter, can fill the net. Hollis is also hoping Ahijah Hutchins, a transfer from North Carolina, can team with Thompson and develop into one of the division's top backcourt tandems.
ST. MICHAELS
Head Coach: Kentrell "Boo" Rickets.
Who's Where: Johnny Mautz (Jr., G); Luca Dew (Jr., F); Wyatt Barone (Jr., F/C); Zavion Goldsborough (Jr., G/F); Brody McDaniel (Jr., PG); Chris Davis (Sr., PG); Aiden Quigley (Sr., G/F); Connor Wheeler (Jr., G); Jack Brennan (Sr., G/F); Ethan Wells (Sr., G).
Outlook: Despite the graduation of leading scorer Nakhi Miller, Rickets said the Saints are still creating a new identity.
The Saints had six wins last season, and if they are to improve on that they will need their returning junior class to step up, led by Mautz.
"We're finding our new identity with a couple of key pieces still missing," Rickets said. "But I think we're changing our identity, and I think we're a more athletic team this year. We're trusting the process and building a more hard-nosed, consistent team that needs to look to win every game, no matter who the opponent is."
STS. PETER & PAUL
Head Coach: Gary Gould.
Who's Where: Garett Hemingway (Sr., G); JJ Rardin (Jr., G); Porter Bishop (Jr., C); Hank Wolters (Jr., F); Andrew Steinhardt (So., G); Rob Mangold (So., F); Peter Mangold (So., G); Jamir Demby (Fr., G); Bradan Lindsey (So., F); Niko Nicoloupoulis (So., G); Victor Kleppinger (Sr., C).
Outlook: The Sabres are off to a 2-3 start, which included a 65-60 victory over Easton on Wednesday behind Hemingway's 32 points. Gould isn't ready to say this team is better than last season's conference champion, but he thinks the potential is there.
"I think we have some different weapons, and we have some young, energetic kids," Gould said. "Our sophomore class actually went to the championship game in the jayvee division last year. They understand the commitment and what we want.
"I don't want to say this year's team is better than last year's team," Gould added. "But we have different pieces that make me more comfortable."

title: Queen Anne's shuts down Warriors
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Queen Anne's shuts down Warriors

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 636
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — While his offense may be the most dynamic he's had in years as Queen Anne's County High's girls head basketball coach, defense has been Mike Kern's greater focus early this season.The Lions gave Easton a heavy dose of both Tuesday night.
Damiya Henry scored 16 points, Karianna Hickson had 14, and Queen Anne's, after yielding 10 first-quarter points, only allowed 10 over the final three quarters on the way to a 52-20 victory over the Warriors.
The Lions improved to 5-0 overall, 3-0 North Bayside, setting up Thursday's early division clash with Cambridge-South Dorchester (4-0, 2-0) in Centreville.
"I'm looking for good defense," said Kern, whose team trailed 10-9 after the first quarter. "We gave up 10 points in the first quarter and then I think we gave up 10 the rest of the game. I think it's one of those things we've got to play good defense. We can't give up easy baskets. We've got to move more, contest every shot."
Ki'Mauri Lewis scored on a drive to give Easton (1-3, 1-1) an early 2-0 lead. Queen Anne's moved to a 5-2 lead, but Serenity Velez buried a 3-pointer and Lewis scored from the baseline for a 7-5 Warriors lead with 3:51 left in the first quarter.
A pair of Hickson free throws and a Laila Coles layup off a backdoor cut nudged the Lions back in front at 9-7 with 2 minutes left in the first. But freshman Maia Bailey connected on a 3 that gave Easton a 10-9 lead heading into the second quarter.
"I thought Easton did a great job driving," Kern said. "We've got to cut the drive off. We've got to slide our feet and get in position.
"They're very athletic," Kern added of Easton. "They pressured us, played us in a man, and it took us a little while to figure it out. And then on the defensive end they were probably a little quicker than we anticipated. We made a couple of adjustments, and I think once we settled down we started playing better."
The Lions did just that while taking control of the game in the second quarter. Hickson scored 12 straight points, which included a pair of 3-pointers, Cheyanne Hollis scored on a putback, and Coles hit a free throw for a 15-0 run that gave Queen Anne's a 24-10 lead.
"Hickson came out big in the first half," Kern said.
Velez hit a basket with 7.3 seconds left in the half for Easton's only points of the quarter.
"Excellent first quarter," Easton head coach Lesley Staehli said of her team. "Then we stopped moving on offense and we got a little lazy on defense. I think that hurt us. We went into halftime with high spirits. Just being within arm's length of them is a positive for us with how good they are. They move the ball well. They cut well."
Queen Anne's maintained its 12-point cushion at 26-14 with 4:24 left in the third quarter.
Then Henry, who played at Easton two years ago and was at Cambridge-SD last season before transferring to Queen Anne's, scored eight consecutive points that extended the Lions lead to 36-14 with 1:10 remaining in the third quarter.
"Henry showed off tonight for sure," Staehli said with a smile of her former player. "Totally miss that kid. Definitely would have done us some good to have her this year. And she went out in two quarters and led the team."
Easton ended a 6-minute scoring drought when Velez canned a 3-pointer with 40 seconds left in the third quarter, making it 36-17 Lions.
Defending North Bayside-champions Queen Anne's then reeled off the first 14 points of the fourth quarter to widen its lead to 50-17 with just under 3 minutes left.
Velez and Bailey each had eight points to lead Easton.
Queen Anne's Bea Holthaus had nine points, 16 rebounds and blocked three shots.

title: Colonel tops Easton, evens slate
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Colonel tops Easton, evens slate

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 AMERICAN CORNER — Easton High's wrestling team is rebuilding this season.Colonel Richardson?
Colonels head coach Bryan Hall winces at the idea of a rebuild, preferring to say, "We're filling in."
Colonel filled in quite nicely Wednesday night, scoring the first takedown in eight of the 10 matches wrestled en route to a 58-24 victory over Easton.
"It hurts 'cause we thought last year we had eight sophomore starters, three freshmen starters, and only one senior," Hall said. "But we've lost four of our starters from last year. One transferred to North Caroline. One is injured. Two decided not to come out. We lost some guys we were going to be counting on as part of our season, so we're filling in."
One of those filling in for Colonel, 120-pounder Elisee Pierre-Louis, won by injury default. Pierre-Louis was taking Otto Perez to the mat, when the Easton freshman injured his arm while trying to brace his fall. Perez was taken by ambulance to have the injury treated.
"That was a momentum punch in the gut for the guys," Easton head coach Jason Biringer said of losing Perez.
Easton (0-3) had built an early 12-0 lead on Skye Matthews' forfeit win at 106, and Esteban Velasquez' 1:59 pinfall over Brody Omohundro at 113.
The injury default cut Easton's lead in half, but Colonel (2-2) won the next three matches. Jayquan Wilkins crafted a 17-2 technical fall over John Seymour at 126, pulling Colonel within 12-11. Zy Nichols (132) and Evan Alexander (138) each won by forfeit, pushing the Colonels' lead to 23-12.
The Warriors stopped that streak when Adonis Schmidt pinned Trynton Parks in 59 seconds of the 144-pound match, drawing the visitors within 23-18.
But Colonel Richardson won six of the final seven matches, scoring bonus points in five of the bouts.
Anthony Alexander (150) started Colonel's roll, pinning Matthew Bravo just as the first-period buzzer sounded. Gary Koeneman (157) followed, working a 19-4 technical fall over Vlad Oslam. Colonel's Ethan Thomas then got turned to his back, yet rolled through on the way to a 2:47 pinfall over Darren Foxwell at 165, stretching the Colonel lead to 40-18.
"They wrestled amazing," Hall said of his team. "We've been shocked by Ethan Thomas. He's a freshman, just started wrestling last year in a middle school club. He's wrestling up a weight class and has been huge.
"Other guys we expected to win, won," Hall continued. "Other guys we're expecting to go out there and wrestle hard, are. It's been a good season so far."
Tony Melendez got Easton back in the win column with a 1:07 fall over freshman Brox Meissner at 175. But the Colonels closed the match, with Richard Taylor (190) pinning Wahaab Popal in 2:15, Wilson Clough (215) winning by forfeit, and Chatydrick Pickrom (285) pinning Matthew Brunner in 2:45.
Still, Biringer was encouraged by what he saw.
"We are seeing some better habits," Biringer said. "We're also seeing some self-destructive moves, where it's, 'Don't make up your own moves. Do the moves you're taught.' Usually when something bad was happening they were trying something that wasn't a fundamental move. So it's beginner's mistakes, but at the same time a lot more effort, and progress is being made."
Colonel's girls earned 39-22 victory in what was Easton's first girls dual meet. Each team won two of the four matches wrestled.
Colonel's Luna Infante-Reyes (115) pinned Leah Gonzalez-Reyes in 3:38, and Estelle Lima (190) earned a 7-0 decision over Khadija Popal.
Easton's wins came from Shiza Gondal (135), who pinned Lizzy Hesson, and Thanh Mai Pham (140), who earned a 10-2 major decision over Aiyanna Groce.

title: Vikings' Hughes adds to big year
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Vikings' Hughes adds to big year

 December 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 608
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — It's already been quite a school year for Cambridge-South Dorchester High's Anthony Hughes.As a first-year starting quarterback, Hughes led the Vikings' football team to an undefeated regular season while earning the Bayside Conference Player of the Year.
The senior earned yet another milestone Thursday night, scoring 10 points to reach 1,000 for his career during Cambridge-SD's 73-62 victory over Queen Anne's County.
"It felt great because all my teammates encouraged me to get it," said Hughes, who scored on a tip-in with under 3 minutes remaining for his 1,000th-career point. "They knew I wanted it. I felt like they wanted to get it more than I wanted it myself to get it."
It may have been the toughest 10 points Hughes has scored during his basketball career.
"Kind of felt like I wanted it more than I thought," Hughes admitted. "I was putting too much pressure on myself."
Hughes scored on a 3-pointer with 4 minutes, 38 seconds remaining in the first quarter, but wouldn't score the remainder of the first half. It didn't matter though, as Cambridge-SD (5-0 overall, 3-0 North Bayside) went on a 16-4 tear to close the first half for a 37-24 halftime lead.
Semaj Pinder (17 points) had seven points in the run, starting it with a 3-pointer. Thomas Wilson Jr. (18 points) netted five points, including a 3-pointer during the closing blitz, and Koby Ennals (game-high 20 points) added four points, including a dunk.
"We got back to ourselves," Vikings head coach Shawn Tucker said. "Defense first. That's our motto. And Thomas Wilson Jr. stepped up and hit some big-time shots and that ballooned the lead for us. We were just playing CSD basketball the right way."
A lay-in from Jimmy Holthaus (team-high 19 points) and an Amari Baynard 3-pointer pulled Queen Anne's (4-2, 2-2) within 37-29 in the opening 46 seconds of the second half.
But Wilson buried a trey, scored a layup, hit another 3, and converted a pair of free throws, widening the Vikings' lead to 47-33. Hughes then scored a bucket and made 1 of 2 from the foul line to make it 50-35 with 2:42 left in the third quarter.
The Vikings extended their lead to as much as 60-41 at the end of the third quarter.
But as Cambridge-SD was focusing on trying to get Hughes his milestone on his home floor, its offense began to sputter some, allowing the Lions to slowly close their deficit, as a Chance Hegedus bucket and two Ayden Hicks free throws capped a 14-5 run that drew Queen Anne's within 65-55 with 3:41 left.
But Ennals scored on a drive before Hughes reached his milestone with a tip-in, bumping the Vikings' lead back to 69-55.
"This is a milestone," Tucker said. "We know who we are. We didn't want it (the opportunity for Hughes to score his 1,000th point at home) to slip. We missed some free throws at the end, but those are some things we can correct. The most important thing was for him to have his night, and we were going to do everything in our power for him to get it tonight. And most importantly, we got the W."
But not before Queen Anne's made things a bit more interesting, trimming its deficit to 70-63 on Holthaus' layup with 17.7 seconds left. The Lions would get no closer though, as their three-game win streak was ended.
"I told them, 'We won the second half,'" said Queen Anne's head coach Jeff Hollis, who got 16 points from Baynard and 14 from Hegedus. "We just can't have a second quarter like we did. They outscored 23-8 in the second quarter and that was just too much to come back from."

title: RFK Stadium deal in jeopardy with revised budget bill
author: Staff Writer
content:
RFK Stadium deal in jeopardy with revised budget bill

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Sports 
 
 443
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — A provision to transfer the land that is the site of the old RFK Stadium from the federal government to the District of Columbia is no longer included in Congress' slimmed-down, short-term spending bill that lawmakers are racing to pass before a government shutdown.The removal Thursday of that part of the bill is a loss for the NFL's Washington Commanders, who were hoping to have the land available as an option to build a new stadium. Controlling owner Josh Harris and Commissioner Roger Goodell lobbied on Capitol Hill in favor of its inclusion earlier this month.
The revised bill came after President-elect Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk criticized and rejected the initial package, which included the RFK Stadium land remaining in control of the city for 99 years.
A team spokesperson had no comment when reached by email. Messages left for the offices of the league and Rep. James Comer, R.-Ky., who initially introduced the legislation, were not immediately returned.
District of Columbia Mayor Muriel Bowser addressed the situation at an event commemorating the start of an $800 million downtown arena renovation for the NBA's Wizards and NHL's Capitals earlier in the day. She tried to refute incorrect reports amplified by Musk on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter, about the cost of the RFK Stadium provision, and pleaded her case for why the land transfer was good for the city after bipartisan negotiation.
"We've done all we're supposed to do, and this is the vehicle that has been identified — and agreed to by Democrats and Republicans," Bowser said. "Have you been to RFK? Anybody? (It is) 177 acres surrounded by asphalt and a stadium that hasn't been used in 10 years that is a blight on the nation's capital. Now, I agree with the president-elect on this point: We want to make our nation's capital the most beautiful capital in the world, so we have to move and free RFK."
The Commanders are considering places in the district, Maryland and Virginia to build a stadium in the coming years. Their lease at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland, runs through 2027, and Harris called 2030 a "reasonable target" for a new one.
The team played at RFK Stadium 2 miles (3.22 kilometers) east of the Capitol from 1961-96 before moving to Maryland. Harris and several co-owners, including Mitch Rales and Mark Ein, grew up as Washington football fans during that era, which included the glory days of three Super Bowl championships from 1982-91.
It was not immediately clear how ownership would pivot and what would become of an agreement with Maryland about what to do with the old site if the team moves elsewhere.

title: Chestertown martial arts master promotes students to black belt
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Chestertown martial arts master promotes students to black belt

 December 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 438
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — On Saturday, Dec. 15, owner and Master Instructor for Eastern Shore Tang Soo Do, Mark Pagano promoted Ian Stotts to fourth degree black belt/master. Recognition was also given to Master Bob Campbell at Eastern Shore Karate and Fitness in Easton that Pagano co-owns with Campbell.Pagano had high praise for Stotts, who has overcome many challenges to make it to Sa Dan (fourth degree black belt) to earn the title of Master. Pagano said of the 600 people who has walked through his doors, only 41 of those make it to that degree.
Pagano noted, "Ian has faced many challenges over the years. He has Asperger's [on the Autism spectrum], but has an incredibly inquisitive mind that always searches for the deeper meaning behind everything which makes him a rather ideal martial arts student."
Stotts underwent 14 years of training, Pagano added.
"He has competed in many tournaments over the years, performing very well in State, National and World competitions, as well as regional/smaller tournaments."
Additionally, Pagano remarked, Stotts has grown into a competent, and technically demanding instructor, often teaching the weekends when Pagano is out of town on business for his Master, Grandmaster Chun Sik Kim.
On Saturday, Dec. 22, also achieving black belt, two young women were promoted to Cho Dan: Faith Frase and Azumi Espejo, joining Stott.
Pagano said Frase began in June 2019. Initially it was just to learn self-defense before heading off to college, he said.
"COVID forced me to learn how to teach over Zoom in order to remain a viable business. Faith took advantage of this and continued her training with me while away at The Culinary Arts School in New York. She trained hard and is a very dedicated student," Pagano said.
Pagano pointed out that after five years, at just age 23, she is finally breaking the Black Belt barrier. She has also become an Assistant Instructor, aspiring to be a fully certified instructor one day, Pagano said.
Espejo immigrated here from the Philippines in July 2021, Pagano said.
"She began training with me that August, with an already established background in Tae Kwon Do and Shotokan karate. She has been an incredibly dedicated student that takes her training very seriously, becoming a fierce tournament competitor, rarely placing less than 1st or 2nd in any division (Sparring, Forms, Breaking, Weapons) for her age/rank."
At only 17 and a senior at The Christian Academy, she is planning to attend Chesapeake College and is in Pagano's Leadership Program.
"She genuinely wants to help everyone she meets," Pagano said, proud of her achievements.
For more information, visit Eastern Shore Tang Soo Do/Phoenix Martial Arts at 903 Washington Ave. #3 in Chestertown or easternshoretangsoodo.com.

title: Former hoops player pens book on European experience
author: Staff Writer
content:
Former hoops player pens book on European experience

 December 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 790
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Bobby Kinzer recently released his book "The Other Side of the Hoop," which offers a unique perspective on the European professional basketball experience.The Bowie resident learned the game of basketball in Northwest Washington, D.C.
He grew six inches one summer to 6-feet, 5-inches and started to develop an all-around game. Since he modeled his game on his basketball heroes, he became a prolific point guard for his size.
He received a basketball scholarship to Penn State University but when legendary coach John Bach left to coach the Golden State Warriors, Kinzer transferred to Texas A&I University and in his first year, was selected to the All Lone Star Conference Team.
He played five years in Great Britain, Two years in England and three years in Scotland.
Currently, he is the President of the Literacy Institute for Financial Enrichment that teaches financial literacy and education to youth, young adults, adults and senior citizens across America. He is a member of the Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity, Inc. and a Certified Financial Education Instructor.
He is also a recipient of the Nancy K Rector Award, the national award for community service.
"I've heard many stories of guys that went overseas to play professionally, but my curiosity has grown over the years as I've tried to imagine all the complexities that come with that experience," former Washington Bullet Phil Chenier said of the book. "This book will help players better understand the European Professional Basketball Experience should they decide to take the journey. It will also serve as a guide for non-basketball people to learn how to cope with life's everyday challenges."
He also appeared in the 2019 television movie "Making it Rain: A Scottish Basketball Story" starring former NBA players Vince Carter and Pau Gasol, former NBA coach Mike D'Antoni and tennis player Andy Murray.
The 224-page "The Other Side of the Hoop" is available for $19.95 at www.bobbykinzer.com.
How long have you been writing, and how did you get started?
This is my first book. I have been writing it for approximately two years. I got started by writing chronologically the events in my European basketball experience.
What inspires you to write?
Stories I read from other authors. About life's unpredictable events.
What kind of writing process do you use?
I pick a theme or topic. I only focus on non-fiction writing, mostly personal development and self-education.
How did you publish your book?
I published my book through Dorrance Publishing because of their extensive history and stellar service.
Who are some of your favorite authors and why?
Dennis Kimbro. Florence Scovel Shinn. Michael A. Singer. Willie Jolley. Mainly because of their unique insight and love for humanity and helping people. Also, easy to read and to discern.
What are you working on now?
A book titled "How To Keep From Getting Got! The consumer's guide to overcoming sellers, marketers, and scammers"
What do you want readers to know about you?
I am very insightful. I truly care about educating people and enhancing their awareness to better their lives.
Please include a brief description of the book
"The Other Side of the Hoop" offers a unique perspective on the European professional basketball experience. The book touches on cultural assimilation and the challenges of adjusting to life overseas. In a time when themes of diversity, cultural understanding, and global mobility resonate with many audiences, this story can appeal to a wide audience, not just sports fans. Exploring the unique cultural experiences faced by athletes abroad makes the narrative relevant to modern discussions on identity and adaptation. The book isn't just about basketball but about the universal lessons of stardom, fortune, temptation, and personal growth. These themes transcend the sports world, offering valuable takeaways about resilience, life's unpredictability, and the pursuit of dreams.
Please include an excerpt from the book
Nineteen-eighty, there I was sitting in a warehouse in Hali- fax, England where the movie "Aliens" was filmed. I have my own personal actor's chair. Every player's dream! Everyone's pampering me like a major movie superstar.
Fame and Fortune! All my life, I have wished and worked for this moment. Finally, a little old boy from 14th & Webster Street in Washington, D.C., is starring in a major television commercial for Rowntree's Fruit Pastilles that will be broadcast on national television in England, Scotland, Ireland, and Wales for the next eight years, two to three times a day right after school.
My professional basketball career is getting ready to take off. Like a man smoking a cigarette at a gas station, I'm about to BLOW UP!
No one else in British professional basketball has ever had a chance as significant as this. This is the break of a lifetime. One that would open so many doors to the entertainment and celebrity world. I always wanted to become a professional basketball star player for all the main reasons of obtaining fame, fortune, and self-realization.

title: Running backs rival receivers in 1,000-yard
author: Staff Writer
content:
Running backs rival receivers in 1,000-yard

 December 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Sports 
 
 688
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Led by free-agent bargains Saquon Barkley and Derrick Henry, the number of big-play running backs is rivaling the number of high-production wide receivers for a change.With two weeks remaining in the season, there are 11 players who have reached the 1,000-yard milestone in both rushing and receiving, a far cry from the pattern in recent seasons.
The last time there were as many 1,000-yard rushers as receivers in an entire season came in 2010 when there were 17 of each. While that might not happen this season, with more pass catchers nearing the mark than runners, it does figure to be far closer than it has been the last decade when there were more than twice as many receivers (233) hitting the mark than runners (110).
The running renaissance is being led by Barkley and Henry, who have elevated their teams with their big-play ability after signing deals that are far smaller than the ones that go to top wideouts.
The Eagles' Barkley leads the NFL in rushing with 1,838 yards and could become the ninth player in NFL history to reach 2,000 yards in a season. He still has an outside shot at breaking Eric Dickerson's single-season record of 2,105 in a 16-game season in 1984. Barkley needs 268 yards to break that in a 17-game season.
Barkley has been a big-play threat all season, including a 68-yard TD run on Sunday against Washington. He's the first player in NFL history with at least four TD runs of 65 yards or more in the same season.
The Ravens' Henry has 1,636 yards rushing, making this the first season since 2012 with multiple backs topping the 1,600-yard mark. Henry became the fifth player to top 1,500 yards at least four times in a career and is one shy of Barry Sanders' record of five. Dickerson, Walter Payton and Edgerrin James also did it four times.
RARE ROOKIESWashington's Jayden Daniels and Las Vegas' Brock Bowers are on the verge of some record-setting rookie seasons.
Daniels threw five touchdown passes to lead the Commanders to a 36-33 comeback win over Philadelphia that snapped Washington's 98-game losing streak in games the team trailed by at least 13 points in the fourth quarter.
Daniels threw for 258 yards and ran for 81 more, joining 2015 MVP Cam Newton as the only players NFL history with at least 250 yards passing, 75 yards rushing and five TD passes in a game.
Daniels has 737 yards rushing this season and needs just 79 more to break the record of 815 that Robert Griffin III set for Washington in 2012. Daniels is already just the second rookie QB to win 10 starts and produce at least 4,000 yards rushing and passing, joining Andrew Luck, who did it in 2012 for Indianapolis.
Bowers had 11 catches for 99 yards for the Raiders on Sunday to tie Anquan Boldin for the third-most catches in a season by a rookie with 101. Bowers needs five more catches in the final two weeks to break Puka Nacua's record set last season for the Rams. Malik Nabers of the New York Giants also could do it; he has 97 catches this season.
Bowers' 1,067 yards receiving are 9 shy of matching the rookie record for tight ends set by Hall of Famer Mike Ditka in 1961 for Chicago.
JUST FOR KICKSIn a record-setting season for long kicks, no one has done it quite at the level of Dallas' Brandon Aubrey.
Aubrey has made an NFL-record 14 field goals from at least 50 yards, one more than Houston's Ka'imi Fairbairn has made.
Those two account for 27 of the record 173 field goals of at least 50 yards, beating the record of 158 set just last season. There already have been twice as many field goals from at least 50 yards this season as there were as recently as 2019, when there were just 84.
Aubrey made two kicks from 58 yards, one from 53 and another from 49 this past week, to set another record. His 36 made field goals have combined for 1,636 yards for the most yards on made field goals in any season, topping Justin Tucker's 1,601 in 2016 for Baltimore.

title: LeBron James: 'The details of winning matter to him'
author: Staff Writer
content:
LeBron James: 'The details of winning matter to him'

 January 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Sports 
 
 388
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "It's always a blast. The competitive spirit, the history, his greatness, it allows me to just appreciate all that we've been through, all the battles back and forth and the fact that in 2024, we're still doing it. Somehow the games are pretty electric, kind of a must-see-TV-type situation. And I love it." — Golden State's Stephen Curry, on facing James."What LeBron is doing, it could happen again. I just don't see it. … LeBron is deadly serious about taking care of his body. Most people wouldn't do what LeBron does off the floor, and that's why they don't last. LeBron has decided to do it all, and that's why he lasts. But it's amazing to watch." — Milwaukee Bucks coach Doc Rivers.
"The details of winning matter to him. I just wish that I could have had all of our young players watch him in the team meetings, every locker room and film session. Every franchise is saying the same thing: 'You need to communicate. You need to be present in these sessions.' And LeBron is not fatigued at all in terms of preparation and being involved and all of that, noticing things on film and being an active participant in that. And you want young players to see that." — Miami Heat coach Erik Spoelstra.
"I think in the case of LeBron, there's a mental aspect of it as well. I think all of us know that, in addition to keeping in tip-top shape physically, he works a lot on his mind. And that ability, over having played that many years in the league, to stay motivated, to maintain a level of concentration, maintain a level of motivation ... he's amazing to watch." — NBA Commissioner Adam Silver.
"It's a blessing, for sure. It's definitely a blessing to be able to have fans." — James, when asked what it's like to be cheered in road arenas.
"He knows what he's talking about. He pays attention. He supports the game. He doesn't just talk about it. He really shows up and supports. I think that's the coolest thing; one of the greatest players of all time really helping support and grow women's basketball. That's exactly what we need. He's somebody I've always idolized." — WNBA rookie of the year Caitlin Clark, earlier this year at the NCAA women's Final Four.

title: Queen Anne's, Cambridge-SD girls sweep two at annual showcase
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Queen Anne's, Cambridge-SD girls sweep two at annual showcase

 January 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 648
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Mike Kern knew his Queen Anne's County High girls basketball team was going to be good heading into this season.The Lions' longtime head coach got a better idea of his team's potential over the holiday break, as Queen Anne's pulled out a pair of overtime victories at the annual Governor's Challenge tournament.
"I learned that we can close out a game," said Kern, whose Lions improved to 8-0 with victories over Carter G. Woodson of Virginia (50-46) and Bethesda-Chevy Chase (40-39) to win their bracket at the University of Maryland Eastern Shore in Princess Anne.
Queen Anne's held a seven-point lead on Woodson heading into the third quarter, but the Cavaliers pressed the Lions and rallied to take the lead. The defending Bayside Conference-champions forged overtime down the stretch largely behind Laila Coles' free-throw shooting before going on a 10-4 run in OT to earn the win.
Coles finished with a team-high 19 points and sophomore Bea Holthaus netted 16.
Queen Anne's also had to rally late to force overtime against B-CC, which reach the Maryland Class 4A state championship game last year.
With RJ Ensor and Coles in foul trouble, the Lions trailed by six in the fourth quarter. But with less than 6 seconds remaining, Coles drove to the rim and threw up an off-balanced shot that rolled around the rim and dropped with 2 seconds left in regulation, sending the Lions into yet another extra session.
The Barons hit a quick 3-pointer in OT, then traded foul shots with Queen Anne's. B-CC held a three-point lead with under 20 seconds remaining, when Holthaus (19 points, 12 blocked shots, eight rebounds) scored off a give-and-go with Ensor. Damiya Henry then stole the inbounds pass and dished to Holthaus, who scored with 6 seconds remaining, nudging the Lions in front at 40-39. The Barons drove down for one final shot, only to have Holthaus reject the attempt.
"We were down in both games and were able to come back, with foul trouble, and hit big shots," said Kern, who watched Coles finish with 11 points and Henry score eight.
"It was great," Kern said of being tested during the holiday break. "At this time of year, Bea played pretty much both games without coming out. And then Laila played the majority of the games. To be able to play that many minutes that that group did was good."
Cambridge-South Dorchester, which lost to Queen Anne's on Dec. 19 in its final game before the break, rebounded nicely with a pair of wins, routing Delmarva Christian, 48-32, before earning a 40-38 victory over Dover.
"It really motivated them to understand that if they put their best foot forward they can compete with anybody," Vikings head coach Shamya Johnson said after her team raised its record to 6-1. "And we needed that redemption, especially against some Delaware teams, because a lot of times we hear on the Bayside, Delaware teams are much stronger. That win over Dover was real big because they reminded us of a Queen Anne's or a Kent Island."
Cambridge-SD senior Le'Asia Todd had 19 points and 15 rebounds in the victory over Delmarva Christian, while Destiny Johnson finished with 12 points.
The Vikings showed their coach they could find a way to win as they edged Dover despite late turnover troubles.
"It was almost very humbling, 'cause we definitely could have lost," coach Johnson said. "We turned the ball over like three times in the last minute. We just struggled closing that game."
Todd put together her sixth double-double of the season, scoring 17 points and hauling down 21 rebounds. Tejanae Ballin had 11 points, six rebounds and four assists, and Destiny Johnson had 10 points.
North Caroline split its two games, with Ashley Kercheval scoring 17 points in a 33-26 victory over Woodbridge (Del.) on Dec. 26. Kercheval scored a team-high 14 points on Dec. 30, but it wasn't enough, as the Bulldogs fell 41-21 to Delmar (Del.).

title: C-SD earns split; Colonel rebounds with two wins
author: Bill Haufe
content:
C-SD earns split; Colonel rebounds with two wins

 January 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 669
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The agenda remains the same for Cambridge-South Dorchester High's boys basketball team — win every title in its path.Last season, the Vikings' goal-filled docket including winning the division, conference, regional and state championships. Cambridge-SD went three for four, missing out on only a Class 1A state crown, as it lost to Edmondson-Westside in the final.
Vikings third-year head coach Shawn Tucker said that loss has served as a motivating force since his team walked off the floor in College Park last season. Tucker's team may have gained an added pinch of motivation last week with its 71-61 loss to Seaford (Delaware) during the annual Governor's Challenge tournament at the Wicomico County Civic Center in Salisbury.
"I think it was an awesome opportunity for our guys to face a little bit of adversity just like we did last year against Queen Anne's," said Tucker, whose team was undefeated before losing to the Lions in Cambridge late in the regular season, then didn't lose again until the state final. "I think it kind of brings us back and we eat a little bit of humble pie. And now we'll move forward."
Cambridge-SD opened the tournament with a 72-49 victory over Laurel (Delaware), with senior forward Koby Ennals scoring 20 points followed by Semaj Pinder (19) and Sterling Perkins Jr. (13).
Then the Vikings lost to the Bluejays.
"It was the last game of the tournament," Tucker said. "We couldn't really impose our will. Hats off to coach Vincent (Evans) and Seaford. He had his kids prepared, and they were ready for the challenge."
As he paced the sideline, Tucker watched Pinder score 19 points, Ennals 17 and Perkins 12, and learned where his team needs work.
"One, we got to get in better shape playing on that big court," Tucker said. "And we just have to rise to the challenge of competition because on any night, any team can beat any team."
Tucker also walked away with more positives than negatives.
"We were able to see the type of guards we're going to face across the bridge," Tucker said in reference to the Vikings' bid for another deep postseason run. "The two guards (Seaford) had were just scrappy and relentless. That's a great opportunity to play against a couple of guards, and a big (man) that has some length and some size and some athleticism that we're going to see when we go across the bridge. I think it was a great opportunity, and it was on a big stage. You've got everybody there from every town looking at you. You have to show up."
Cambridge-SD (5-0 overall, 3-0 North Bayside — holiday games do not count toward a team's overall record when it comes to determining playoff seeding) is scheduled to return to action Monday in a battle for first place in the North Bayside at Kent Island (4-1, 4-0).
While Cambridge-SD, Queen Anne's and Easton each went 1-1 in last week's Governor's Challenge, Colonel Richardson won both its games.
"I think it's just good to keep playing," Colonels' head coach Brad Plutschak said. "My first year we didn't get in a Christmas holiday tournament. It's tough when they just shut it down. Even though you practice, there's something good about playing real games."
Colonel defeated Polytech, 64-51, behind the 18-point performances of Makiah Batson and Ja'Zir Dickerson.
The Colonels then built a commanding 41-14 halftime lead en route to 69-56 victory over Sussex Tech (Delaware). Robbie Cunningham led Colonel with 19 points, followed by Batson (18), Dickerson (15) and LeShaun Allen (11).
"We got to continue playing, and we also got to kind of get away from the two losses we had before the break," Plutschak said losing to Mardela and Kent Island. "So it was good to get a couple wins and build some momentum. And it's always good to play somebody different and see different styles."
Zymier Ramirez had 25 points and 15 rebounds in Easton's 56-50 victory over Winston Churchill. The Warriors lost to Smyrna (Del.) in its other game.
Queen Anne's defeated Walkersville, 63-53, and lost to Appoquinimink of Delaware, 55-46.

title: Bucs' early season has Sitar optimistic
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bucs' early season has Sitar optimistic

 January 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 711
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Though the high school wrestling season has yet to reach its midway point, Kent Island may have already battled through the toughest part of its schedule.After defeating Colonel Richardson in its dual-meet opener, the Bucs lost to three-time defending Class 1A state dual-meet champion South Carroll, 64-15, but fell by 11 points to Broadneck, the 4A state runner-up a year ago.
Head coach Tommy Sitar's crew then went 5-4 at the South River Duals, notching victories over Arundel and Archbishop Curley, losing a close loss to Montgomery Blair, and battling Middletown and Chopticon.
Then came last weekend's annual War on the Shore, which attracted 43 teams, including teams from Delaware, Pennsylvania and Virginia, and Bayside Conference rivals Stephen Decatur — which is bidding for a sixth consecutive state dual-meet title this year — and Parkside.
Kent Island wasn't in title contention last weekend, but Sitar left the annual showcase encouraged.
"We just wrestled War on the Shore and saw the best competition we're going to see this year," Sitar said. "We're in a good position."
Boosting Sitar's optimism is the fact that it wasn't too many seasons ago he was forfeiting the first five weight classes, and still winning. Now, as he prepares for this weekend's Iron Horse Duals at C. Milton Wright — weather permitting — the Bucs' head coach thinks he has potentially one of the best groups he's ever had.
"We're youngish I would say," Sitar said. "But I told them this past weekend, it's one of the better lineups I feel like we can put out there since I've been coaching. Maybe that's just my optimism, but I truly felt that way.
"We don't have many, if any holes in our lineup," Sitar said. "It's nice to have all those weight classes filled with people who want to work hard and want the spots. We've got backups that want spots and our practice room is just awesome to be a part of right now."
The Bucs are off to a 3-2 start in dual-meet competition — not counting the South River Duals — but early season tournaments have always have been beneficial for multiple reasons.
"It definitely gives them a lot of mat experience, and can expose some of the things as coaches we need to work on going forward," Sitar said.
And while Kent Island's "youngish" lineup has the potential to keep the Bucs near the top of the conference standings over the next few seasons, Sitar said his team's focus is on this year.
"You try to stay in the present," Sitar said. "But I mean being young is a great thing because obviously you would think that only bodes better for the future and next year. But we're worried about this year. We're trying to get as better as we can get this season and hopefully see some good results at the end."
While Kent Island and Queen Anne's — which has competed in the Kent Holiday Tournament and Westminster Duals, and now readies for the Battle of the Bridge tourney at Bohemia Manor — prepare for their third tournaments of the season this weekend, North Caroline heads to its second, joining Queen Anne's at Bo Manor.
"One of the things we do is an individual round-robin (the Andy Perez tournament in Cambridge), then we do an individual-bracket (tournament), which is what this one is," said North Caroline head coach Robin Eaton, whose team is off to a 5-1 start and placed third in the Perez tourney. "And then we do a team one (the Tomahawk Duals at Havre de Grace later this month).
"This one here, I put my best guys in it and they see what they can do," continued Eaton of a tournament that will have teams from Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Virginia. "We'll go out there and let it all hang out; try to win three before you lose two."
Like Sitar, Eaton is filling every weight class, and has at least one backup at every weight, including five or six at 165.
"I've got 44 on the roster and I have 40 showing up every day for practice," Eaton said. "It's a good team atmosphere."
Easton is slated to host its annual New Year's Brawl tournament, beginning at 4:30 p.m. Friday. Four rounds are slated for Friday, with wrestling resuming Saturday at 9:30 a.m.

title: Woman running Boston Marathon to honor terminally ill dad
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Woman running Boston Marathon to honor terminally ill dad

 January 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1191
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RISING SUN — Emma Cease loves running really, really far."Long distance runners, we love pain," the 23-year-old Rising Sun resident joked, before shifting into her real reason. "Long-distance running is about pushing yourself past the point of where you think you would break, and that's what I love about it."
Cease realizes that only long-distance runners can fully appreciate such a seemingly agonizing personal-challenge commitment to run many miles per outing.
But on April 21, when Cease runs the Boston Marathon, she will have this extra-special motivation to complete the 26.2-mile course: Her 53-year-old father, David Cease, who has been diagnosed with terminal esophageal cancer.
"My dad has always been my biggest supporter when it comes to sports, and the Boston Marathon is the biggest marathon in the world," Cease said. "I am running the Boston Marathon in honor of my father, and I want him to see me cross that finish line."
Cease will be running the long-distance race as a member of the Boston Marathon Cam Neely Cance Foundation team, which falls under one of three classifications of the 30,000 runners that participate.
As such, Cease must raise $12,000 for cancer research by late March to be eligible to run the famous marathon. To that end, Cease is kindly asking people to make donations at https://www.givengain.com/. As of Monday, early $5,000 had already been raised.
Cease applied for the Boston Marathon Cam Neely Cancer Foundation team in honor of her dad's ongoing fight with the disease and to show her appreciation for him.
"My dad means the absolute world to me. I owe so much of who I am today to the love and unwavering support he's always shown me," Cease wrote on that social media site.
(Although she is running the Boston Marathon in honor of her dad, Cease made sure to note that her mom, Lori, and her 19-year-old sister, Sophia, also give her tremendous support.)
Cease is a 2019 graduate of Rising Sun High School, where she played on the girls soccer team as a freshman before switching to the cross-country squad.
She credits her dad for preparing her for organized sports.
"From as early as I can remember, we bonded over time spent in the backyard, with him encouraging me to try any sport we could get our hands on. Our evenings after dinner were spent outside, with him challenging me to hit whiffle balls over the neighbor's fence line, learning how to throw a football with a spiral, or using cardboard boxes as street hockey goals in the driveway," Cease recalled.
When she entered the third grade, Cease transitioned from backyard games to a travel soccer team. And for the next seven years, Cease competed in organized soccer leagues, buoyed by the cheering of her biggest fan.
"He rarely missed a practice or game, his presence on the sideline being a given, regardless of how far the drive," she said of her dad.
She found her niche as a soccer player. "I was a defensive mid, so basically all I did was run," Cease explained.
Soccer and other fall-sports players were encouraged to participate on the Rising Sun High School track-and-field teams. Fall sports coaches viewed the springtime activity of track-and-field as off-season conditioning for their players.
Cease was drawn to cross-country and soon felt conflicted.
"When I ran track my freshman year of high school, I quickly realized that running was something far more special than a means to stay in shape for soccer. I felt like I had found my calling. I decided to run cross country the following season, expecting my dad to be disappointed after all of the years we had invested in playing soccer. Instead, he embraced my newfound passion, rearranging his work schedule to be at every meet in time for the starting gun to go off," Cease remembered.
As a high school runner, she typically competed in 5K (3.2 miles) races. In her junior year, though, Cease ran a half-marathon (13.1 miles) during the Baltimore Running Festival.
Cease's passion for long-distance running continued to grow during her three years at Washington College, from which she graduated in May 2022 with a Bachelor of Science degree in environmental science. Cease now works for Washington College in Chestertown as an Experiential Learning Program manager.
The college did not have a track team or cross-country squad, so Cease ran on her own. But she never felt alone in her endeavors.
"Even after I graduated high school and began training individually for half-marathon runs and trail races, he still showed up whenever he could. To this day, I can count on one hand how many races he wasn't at the finish line. For those he missed, his number was the first one I called to give a full race recap to," Cease outlined.
She and her dad also have bonded over the years by watching televised broadcasts of NCAA cross country championships, the Olympics and other major running races. Calling it her "personal favorite," the Boston Marathon is on that list.
It had been Cease's dream to run the Boston Marathon "one day far in the future," according to her. When her dad was diagnosed with terminal cancer in late 2023, however, Cease expedited her plans to make that dream a reality.
"I've talked about this dream with my dad countless times, never imagining the possibility that he wouldn't be there to cheer me on. That was until his diagnosis flipped our world upside down," she explained.
Applying to run for the Cam Neely Foundation's 2025 Boston Marathon team was a "no-brainer," she said. The charity provides resources and support to cancer patients and their families, helping them navigate the emotional, financial, and physical challenges of treatment while fostering a sense of community and hope during difficult times.
"The truth is that tomorrow isn't guaranteed. If there's anything that my family has learned over the past year's rollercoaster ride of emotions, medical bills, and my dad's ongoing treatment, it's that every moment counts. I decided that I wanted to do something to show my dad how much I love him, thank him for his unwavering support of me, and give him something to look forward to when reality feels so heavy," Cease emphasized.
She has been training for the Boston Marathon for the past few months, waking every weekday morning between 4:30 and 5 to take practice runs that typically range from eight to 10 miles. On weekends, Cease runs 12 to 18 miles per outing.
Cease knows for a fact that she can run 26.2 miles. In June, Cease ran her first and only marathon during an event held at the Fair Hill State Natural Resources Management Area, completing a course marked by long stretches of elevation in three hours and 55 minutes.
People training for a marathon usually don't run 26.2 miles during an outing. They typically will stop their practices runs at 18 miles or so, essentially to conserve energy and to preserve their bodies for the big race.
"There is a saying that, in a marathon, you run the first 20 miles with your head and the last six miles with your heart," Cease said.
Because she is dedicating her 2025 Boston Marathon run to her dad, Cease should have plenty of heart to go the distance.

title: Bucs surge past Vikings, stay unbeaten
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bucs surge past Vikings, stay unbeaten

 January 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 605
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — It could have been rust from playing only one game since before Christmas.Maybe it was nerves.
Then again, it could have been both.
Kent Island High girls head basketball coach David Plumer didn't really care what it was, he was just glad his team's shots finally started falling when it needed them most. The Buccaneers used a strong third-quarter finish, then went on a decisive run over the first 5-plus minutes of the fourth Tuesday night en route to pulling away for a 52-40 victory over Cambridge-South Dorchester.
"We had really good shots all game long," Plumer said. "We just weren't making shots. I don't know if that's the rust, the nerves. But we just didn't make shots pretty much through the first half."
The Vikings (5-2 overall, 3-2 North Bayside) did make shots in the first half, especially senior Le'Asia Todd, who scored 11 of her game-high 21 points in the first-quarter.
"As frustrated as I was that we lost, that girl did stuff tonight that I have been begging and dying to see her do," Cambridge-SD head coach Shamya Johnson said of Todd. "She played so well. I was proud of her. But that early foul trouble just killed her."
The Vikings carried a 19-15 lead into the second quarter. But back-to-back baskets from sophomore Machaela Thomas (team-high 17 points) and another inside score from Sydney Riska (11 points) pushed Kent Island (7-0, 6-0) to a 21-19 lead with 4:28 left in the second quarter.
Todd converted one of two free throws, scored on a coast-to-coast layup, then slid inside for another bucket to move the Vikings back in front at 24-21 with a little over a minute remaining before half. Riska hit a free throw, cutting the Cambridge-SD lead to 24-22 at the break.
The Vikings maintained their slim lead through most of the third quarter, with Destiny Johnson making one of two from the line for a 29-27 lead with 2:36 to go in the period.
But Lacey Dauses' 3-pointer with 1:49 left gave Kent Island a 30-29 lead, and more importantly sent up a signal that Buccaneer shots were starting to fall.
Todd picked up her fourth personal foul 14 seconds later and took a seat on the bench, watching as Thomas scored on a follow to give Kent Island a 32-29 lead after three quarters.
The Bucs then delivered what proved to be the knockout blow in the opening 2 minutes of the fourth quarter. Amani Black hit a 3-pointer. Thomas scored on a putback before Dauses drained another trey for a 40-31 lead, prompting a Vikings timeout.
"That was the shift of the game right there," Coach Johnson said. "We just couldn't recover."
Tejanae Ballin's baseline drive and Destiny Johnson's free throw were Cambridge-SD's only points over the first 4:48 of the third. Though Todd returned with 6:41 left, she could only watch Thomas score consecutive buckets while trying to avoid fouling out. Abigail Staton drilled Kent Island's third 3-pointer of the final period to cap a 16-5 run that gave the Bucs a 48-34 lead with 2:32 left.
"Midway through the third quarter a couple of shots went down and I think that gave them some confidence," Plumer said. "Once the shots started going in we were able to run the offense. I think that's when we got on the runs. And it didn't help them that Le'Asia Todd got in foul trouble. With her out of the game, we could just pound it inside."
Thomas had 31 points in the Bucs' 49-31 victory over Easton on Monday.
Kent Island now prepares to host Queen Anne's (8-0, 6-0) on Thursday in a battle for first place in the North Bayside.

title: Eagles pull out a happy ending
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Eagles pull out a happy ending

 January 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — This was setting up like so many other past unhappy endings for North Dorchester High's boys basketball team.The Eagles had held the lead for the bulk of the first half, only to falter when the opposition rallied to take the lead after halftime.
St. Michaels was pretty much following that script Monday night, erasing a first-half deficit on the way to building a modest six-point lead heading into the fourth quarter. But North Dorchester pieced together a comeback of its own, outscoring the Saints 15-6 in the final period for a 50-49 victory that ended its three-game slide.
"We're lucky to get out of here with a win," said Eagles head coach Robert Smith Jr., his team now 2-3 overall, 1-3 North Bayside. "There was a time where we would of settled in and been like, 'Oh, this is over.' But they didn't stop fighting. They never quit, and good things will come if they keep playing like that."
St. Michaels (2-4, 2-3) — which dressed only seven players after eight were suspended for leaving the bench during an altercation with Kent County on Dec. 19 — trailed 15-9 after the first quarter, then outscored North Dorchester, 34-22, over the next two quarters to carry a 43-37 lead into the fourth.
But the Saints went cold from the floor over the final 8 minutes while the Eagles steadily chipped away at their deficit.
Victor Merrit began the rally when he made one of two free-throw attempts, then scored on a layup, drawing the visitors within three. Tahjere Pritchett (eight points) tied the game at 43-all with 5 minutes, 46 seconds remaining. North Dorchester, which converted just 7 of 24 attempts from the foul line, had chance to take the lead less than 30 seconds later, but Merrit missed a pair of free throws.
St. Michaels regained the lead at 45-43, when Johnny Mautz (game-high 20 points) scored on a drive with 5:09 remaining.
The Eagles answered, with Jazeon Cephas hitting a jumper with 4:30 to go, and Pritchett scoring a layup 20 seconds later for a 47-45 lead.
Both teams missed a pair of foul shots before North Dorchester's Alvin Hutton (team-high 18 points) made the second of two attempts with 2:49 left, nudging the Eagles' lead to 48-45.
Mautz scored on a follow 14 seconds later, was fouled, but couldn't complete the three-point play. Hutton, who buried five first-half 3-pointers, grabbed the ball and raced coast to coast for a layup before getting fouled. Hutton missed the free throw, but had provided what proved to be the game-winning bucket with 2:25 remaining for a 50-47 Eagles lead.
"Nothing is easy in the Bayside," Smith said. "It was one of them games where it could have gone either way. We were back and forth, back and forth. But I give our guys credit because they fought."
The drama wasn't quite over though.
Mautz made a left-handed shot with 1:35 remaining to pull St. Michaels within 50-49. Pritchett was fouled on a 3-point attempt, but could not lengthen North Dorchester's lead from the foul line
St. Michaels had chances over the final minute, with Connor Wheeler (eight points) watching a shot spin around and off the rim, and Mautz missing on a pair of putback attempts.
"It came down to a couple of possessions late in the game going back and forth," Saints head coach Kentrell "Boo" Ricketts said. "I thought we got a real good look at the basket at the end when we were down one. It just happened to not go in.
"We missed a lot of shots that usually go down for us," Ricketts added. "Some times I think we were taking quick shots and forcing the issue. I keep telling my guys, 'Some times we're beating ourselves. It's not necessarily these teams beating us.' But hat's off to North Dorchester for finishing out. They hit a lot of key shots. They had the one kid (Hutton who) shot the ball very well."
