title: Daniels to McLaurin connection has blossomed
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Daniels to McLaurin connection has blossomed

 January 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 796
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ASHBURN, Va. — When the Washington Commanders had to have it — fourth down, trailing in the fourth quarter of a playoff game — Jayden Daniels found Terry McLaurin in the end zone for a touchdown.That moment marked the pinnacle of the rapport between the dynamic rookie quarterback and dependable sixth-year wide receiver that has been developing since offseason workouts.
Daniels has connected with McLaurin 77 times for 1,033 yards and 13 TDs, and that relationship blossoming on and off the field is a big reason the Commanders are in the postseason and advanced to the divisional round to face NFC-leading Detroit on Saturday night.
"They have built through the year, there's no doubt," offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury said Wednesday. "The first couple of games, the ball wasn't coming to him as much as we would have liked, and we've had our ups and downs. ... Those two guys are just going to get better and better as they go. They're two very conscientious players that are team-first guys and work really hard at it."
Daniels and McLaurin are the first Washington QB-WR duo to be selected to the Pro Bowl since Mark Rypien and Gary Clark in 1991. That was also the franchise's most recent Super Bowl season.
This one started with very different, much lower expectations. The Commanders were expected to win six or seven games and start the climb toward being a contender.
Instead, they went 12-5 with the NFL's fifth-highest scoring offense and beat Tampa Bay to set up another road challenge against the Lions, when McLaurin said he needs to "be ready to make plays for Jayden." He has since September.
"Come game day, you don't really think about it," Daniels said. "You just put the ball in the vicinity for Terry to go make a play, and nine times out of 10 he makes them."
What Daniels called "continuous growth" for him and McLaurin has not been progress in a straight line, even beyond the early season bumps in the road Kingsbury pointed out. Daniels has thrown the ball McLaurin's direction as many as 10 times in a game down to as few as twice.
Even through those times, there was never tension between teammates at those positions that can often fester in football. Nothing beyond two athletes at the top of their sport wanting to maximize their performances.
"We're extremely competitive people," McLaurin said. "We really put a lot of time and effort into our craft. Good is not good enough, and you're not just happy being here. I think that is what we have in common. Even the great plays we've had, we've still focused on the plays that we missed and the ways that we could continue to get better."
On the field, coach Dan Quinn has consistently lauded Daniels' poise beyond his 24 years of age and limited professional experience — something evidenced by the Commanders winning their past five games in a row all on the final play from scrimmage. He also credited McLaurin for the offense's immense success down the field for the receiver's ability to read deep throws and get under the ball at the perfect time.
"Obviously you have to have speed, but tracking a deep ball is one of the most difficult things," Quinn said. "He's got a knack on a deep ball of tracking it that not everybody has because to get some of the plays that he has to get behind people."
That has not gone unnoticed among Lions coaches, and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn compared McLaurin to Detroit All-Pro wideout Amon-Ra St. Brown for his all-around willingness to compete on every catch.
"He does a really good job on 50-50 balls, which you wouldn't think that he would because of his stature, but he does a really good job of that," said Glenn, who was a standout cornerback as a player. "He will block, he'll go across the middle, he'll take hits, he'll get back up, get back to the huddle, so he's a gamer. He's a gamer, so it doesn't surprise me the success he's having."
Off the field, Daniels has learned from "the ultimate pro" McLaurin's film study and workout routines and said the two have bonded over their faith and had conversations about life that have helped them bond quickly.
McLaurin, after Washington cycled through 10 different quarterbacks in his first five seasons said he's "fortunate to play with a young player who's coming into the league and been so ready right off the bat where a lot of our communication and conversations are more next level." The play has shown the results of that.
"He makes my job a lot easier when I just know I have to put myself in position to be open," McLaurin said. "He's going to put the ball right where it needs to be."

title: Fast-starting Lions roll past Bucs
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Fast-starting Lions roll past Bucs

 January 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 594
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — They played pretty much even for three quarters.Unfortunately for Kent Island High's girls basketball team, it never recovered from the first one.
Kariana Hickson scored 10 of her game-high 14 points during an 18-2 first-quarter blitz Thursday that launched Queen Anne's County to a 49-28 victory over the Buccaneers and into sole possession of first place in the North Bayside Division.
"First quarter," said Kent Island head coach David Plumer, whose team avoided being shut out in the opening period when Sydney Riska (team-high 11 points) kissed a shot off the glass with 4 seconds remaining. "We spot a team 18 points and lost by (21). You simply can't do that. Coming in here it's always a tough place to play, and they're the top team. They're good."
The Lions (9-0 overall, 7-0 North Bayside) were very good in the first quarter, especially on defense, as their full-court press forced the Bucs (7-1, 6-1) into multiple turnovers, triggering an 18-2 onslaught that was led by Hickson, who buried a pair of 3-pointers to help fuel the offense.
"Our pressure was really good," said Queen Anne's head coach Mike Kern of a press that was anchored by sophomore standout Bea Holthaus. "We were able to put pressure on them full-court, knowing if it went behind us Bea's there. That's kind of how the first quarter went. And they struggled getting the ball over (half court)."
Despite catching an inadvertent elbow in the eye with 1 minute, 32 seconds remaining in the first quarter, Holthaus had one of her finest all-around efforts of the season, finishing with 13 points, six assists and five rebounds. But Holthaus may have hurt Kent Island most with her outstanding anticipation on defense, as she totaled eight steals and seven blocked shots.
"Bea, she was obviously the player on the court I thought," Kern said. "We know if they get behind the front four Bea's going to block it or intercept the pass. And that's what she did tonight. Even in our halfcourt defense, we get beat on the dribble, Bea's there, and she'll alter the shot or block it. She's a great one to have back there.
After sitting out the final 1:32 of the opening quarter, Holthaus returned at the start of the second quarter. She blocked a shot and fired an outlet pass that Hickson converted into a layup. Less than 30 seconds, Holthaus made a steal and went coast-to-coast for a layup. A little over a minute later, she turned yet another steal into a layup, helping Queen Anne's take a 28-10 lead into the locker room.
"Bea's a player," Plumer said. "Bea's a great player."
The Buccaneers settled after the opening 8 minutes, and played the Lions almost even, though the hosts outscored their county rival 10-8 in the second quarter, and 12-7 in the third, with Riska accounting for all seven of the visitors' points. Kent Island outscored the Lions 11-9 in the fourth.
"When we settled down, we played pretty much even basketball," Plumer said. "But you spot 'em 18, it's hard to come back from.
"We know to go anywhere we're going to have to go through them," Plumer said, referencing the Class 2A East Region postseason play. "As much as we want to win the game, this isn't the one that's going to define our season. And the girls know that."
Despite not having starting point guard Laila Coles, Queen Anne's finished with three double-figure scorers, with Damiya Henry scoring 11 to join Hickson and Holthaus.
"This team has the potential to go really, really far," Kern said. "It's a special group."

title: 'I feel so lucky': 71-year-old fencer competes at international championships in Dubai
author: Staff Writer
content:
'I feel so lucky': 71-year-old fencer competes at international championships in Dubai

 January 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Seniors 
 
 959
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When 71-year-old Lotte Bowie of Still Pond stepped onto the fencing strip in Dubai this October, she faced off against elite competitors from Poland, Kazakhstan, and Finland in front of an international crowd. The third-ranked fencer in her age group would go on to secure sixth place in the International Fencing Federation Championships for the Veteran 70-plus class, adding another achievement to her impressive competitive career.While she engaged them with her weapon of choice, she had to counter their attacks, while drowning out the crowd cheering her opponent in a language unknown to her.
As Bowie blocked out all the noise, like she does in every confrontation, she had a conversation with herself, gripping the handle of her sword.
Bowie used distance, avoiding the flashing blade from striking any part of her body, whether foot, hand, chest or head.
When the conflict was over, Bowie, currently ranked third in the world, had won sixth place in the 2024 International Fencing Federation Championships for Veteran class (70s-plus). She was ultimately defeated by a Polish woman who used an attack-first strategy, but she was encouraged with her performance.
"You always learn in this sport," Bowie remarked.
The USA team she travelled with fared better, winning silver, being bested by a tough Russian team with a skilled team leader.
They secured a silver medal in Vet Team Women's Epee to end their record-breaking tournament on a high note. "The team's final tally of 26 medals is the most ever won by any country in a single Vet Worlds, surpassing their own previous record of 24 medals set last year," stated usafencing.org.
Bowie reflected on that intense and rarified experience.
The championship was seven days of individual and team competition with 736 fencers in their 50s, 60s and 70s-plus from 58 countries. In all, 855 fencers participated.
Bowie was one of 37 competitors, in the Veteran's Women's class for the epee — a sharp-pointed dueling sword, designed for thrusting.
Despite traveling the farthest she had ever gone in her eight years of fencing, Bowie felt comforted by her teammates, encouraged by her coaches.
"I feel so lucky. My friends in the other age groups were cheering me on," Bowie remarked.
She felt proud to represent the United States.
"The veteran fencers we have seen this week in Dubai have been an inspiration to the entire world of fencing", said FIE Vice President Abdelmoneim Elhamy El Husseiny. "They represent passion, athleticism and a love for fencing as a lifelong sport."
Not just the fact Bowie travelled to Dubai, but her multiple accomplishments in the sport, highlights her rigorous work ethic.
Training is tough. A typical week consist of swimming, weight lifting three days a week, squats to strengthen thighs and leg flexibility as well as yoga for limberness and mental dexterity.
When she is not competing in regional and local championships, she is at Modern Duelists Fencing Academy, Elkton, Maryland, four days a week, practicing foot work and open bouting, (like sparring).
"You have to put in the work — it takes sacrifice," she said.
Putting on her Italian-made suit, especially made for competitions, electronically hooking up to the line, and donning the mask can only take you so far.
Learning the footwork and working on cardio can take you a little further. However physical is only a part of the equation, she said. It takes mental toughness in order to be successful.
Bowie said each opponent is different. There is an intellectual and psychological battle, she noted.
"During those moments you score a point, it feels like you wins a battle with herself."
That toughness is evident even in a loss.
Bowie said there were times she was defeated on a Saturday, then had to find it in herself to enter a competition on Sunday, summoning the psychological strength to keep going.
This kind of dedication takes much of her time, which she juggles with a career in marketing and brand design.
"I have to pay for my fencing somehow, " Bowie said.
Fencing is a niche sport, and so her travel was not covered when she went to the January North Cup in Kansas City earlier this year. Bowie was in the heart of the winter storm; ice, and snow shut down the airport for days, delaying her trip back.
But it was well worth it.
"It was the most expensive gold medal I ever got," Bowie laughed.
During that blistery, wintry weekend, she toppled all her opponents and faced off in the finals with someone she could never beat. Displaying a can-do attitude, she defeated all her rivals, 10-3, 10-7, 10-4 and 10-3, winning the entire event.
She received a gold medal and a video interview, expressing thankfulness for the sport she has grown to love.
That affectation began through her son, George, who always wanted to fence, and finally got the chance to when he went to University of Pennsylvania. From that, Bowie grew to love it, as her son who ranked in a major competition in 2017.
"It's mentally challenging in an invigorating way. If you're older it helps use your mind strategy to employ physical moves."
She also participates in international events in Central and South America (the PanAms) and in Toronto (the CanAms). For the former she earned bronze two years in a row for Vet 60 and over.
And last year, she won bronze in the national championships in Daytona, employing a strike-first method.
Her swordplay skills has her world-hopping.
"Fencing has changed my life in a dynamic way," Bowie said. "It gave me a path to a mental, physical and spiritual journey, filled with interesting travel. I am so blessed to do it."
Bowie urged people in the community to try it too. If it's not too late for her, it's not for you, she commented.
And don't argue with her either, she's trained with a sword.
See more of Bowie's accomplishments at usafencing.org., and for more information about her Dubai competition, see:https://www.usafencing.org/news/2024/october/17/vet-worlds-2024-day-7.

title: Bucs surpass expectations, beat Bulldogs
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bucs surpass expectations, beat Bulldogs

 January 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 674
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Tommy Sitar tries to keep the word out of his vocabulary."I don't want to use that word, surprised, because I preach to them that I know they always have more in them," Kent Island High's head wrestling coach said of his team.
Sitar's preferable word of choice is "surpassed", which is exactly what the Buccaneers did to their coach's projections Wednesday night while logging seven pinfalls during an impressive 49-25 victory over North Caroline in a clash of North Bayside rivals.
"Like the way I projected some things, we surpassed those projections," Sitar said, his team now 5-2 overall, 5-0 Bayside Conference. "It was great. It was a good night."
Sitar had just one concern with his team's latest dual-meet win.
"I told them it sets a bad precedent because we've practiced like three times in the past three weeks," said a smiling Sitar, whose Bucs, like most teams, have had only limited mat time since last week's snow — which canceled school throughout the Bayside — came right after the Christmas holiday break.
Still, the Buccaneers were dominant against a Bulldogs team that had only lost once in dual-meet competition prior to Wednesday.
North Caroline (5-2, 4-1) took a 3-0 lead, when Caleb Melvin got a third-period takedown then blocked a late shot to earn a 4-2 decision over Silas Brobst at 138 pounds in the night's first bout.
Kent Island reeled off the next five straight wins, with only one going the full three periods. That came at 144, where Gavin Taylor pieced together a 15-5 major decision over Anthony Shepherd for a 4-3 lead the Bucs steadily widened.
Mason Guy (150) followed with a pinfall over Michael Dyke in 3:37. Roy Scott (157) yielded a first-period takedown, but then pinned Gabriel Glother in 3:15. Marcus Tate (165) earned a 1-minute fall over Joseph Brown, and Brian Potter (175) pinned Quinten Doyle in 2:23 for a 28-3 Kent Island lead.
"I knew it would be close, that it could come down to the wire," North Caroline head coach Robin Eaton said of his match projection. "It could be right up to criteria of first points scored. But we just didn't show up tonight. This is the worst we've wrestled all year. I don't know what else to say."
North Caroline cut into its deficit slightly at 28-15, with Corey Bunce getting a forfeit at 190 and Arif Mohammadi pinning Zach Bunce in 42 seconds at 215.
But Kent Island won four more in succession, including three by fall, starting with Greg Coffey's 50-second pin of DeMarcus Forsythe at 285.
"My projections tonight. … I'll use Greg Coffey for example," Sitar said. "I projected him to get a pin. But the way he went out there, and it was just like, 'I'm getting a pin. There's no doubt in my mind that this is what's happening.' And Mason Guy had a matchup with their Michael Dyke and he earned a pin."
Kent Island continued stretching its advantage.
Shane Bunce (106) pinned Samuel Heimbach in 28 seconds. Gavin Lindner (113) decisioned Darly Ortega, 5-0, before Robert Martinez (120) delivered his team's seventh and final fall with a pin of Jayden Robinson in 1:58.
"I've done a bunch with trying to make sure their mindset is right; they're only worried about their effort, attitude and energy," Sitar said. "And it looked like it paid off tonight."
North Caroline made the score more respectable with wins in the final two weight classes, Connor Frank (126) pinning Tyler Stokes with 2 seconds left in the first period, and Jacob Carpenter putting together a 20-8 major over Finn McGrath at 132.
"The things we were successful at, we would stop doing them," Eaton said. "One guy who takes a guy down three times at will and then never takes another shot and ends up pinned. Those are things that frustrate you. It's not like he couldn't do it. He just stopped doing it. We just didn't have the mental toughness tonight."
The match was North Caroline's first since defeating Northeast of Anne Arundel on Dec. 19, whereas Kent Island defeated Wicomico on Monday.

title: Bucs stay close, Vikes stay unbeaten
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bucs stay close, Vikes stay unbeaten

 January 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 724
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — The combination was new territory for Cambridge-South Dorchester High's boys basketball team.The unbeaten Vikings were in their tightest game against a North Bayside opponent this season, were away from home, and minus one of their top scorers.
And their head coach Shawn Tucker did not care.
"I know you can score," Tucker shouted as his players transitioned into their defensive end midway through the third quarter. "Play defense. Don't put your heads down. No one feels sorry for you."
One night after being humbled by county rival Queen Anne's, Kent Island certainly didn't feel sorry for Cambridge-SD, as it played the defending Bayside Conference champions even through the first half.
The Buccaneers even took a brief lead early in the third quarter Friday night, only to have the Vikings answer with a 22-7 tear over the final 6 minutes of the period en route to a 65-59 victory.
"Kudos to (Kent Island head) coach (Frank Kratovil)," Tucker said after his team — which defeated its first five North opponents by an average of 34.4 points — won by its narrowest margin against a division team this season. "Coach K has those guys always prepared and I respect him immensely. Those guys competed.
"And even though we were short tonight with (injured forward) Semaj Pinder being on the bench, I saw something in our guys that I haven't seen in a long time," Tucker continued. "And that's the will to jell together and fight until the end."
Despite Cambridge-SD's Koby Ennals scoring 21 of his season-high 30 points in the first half, Kent Island (5-3 overall, 5-2 North Bayside) scored the final six points of the second quarter to forge a 29-29 halftime tie. Gavan Henry then buried a 3-pointer 19 seconds into the third quarter to give the Buccaneers a 32-29 lead.
But Ka'Marion Hall (11 points) sparked a 22-7 Vikings' run over the remaining 6 minutes of the third, that included Sterling Perkins Jr. splashing a pair of 3-pointers and Thomas Wilson connecting on a third.
"We have periods of time when we execute our offenses and defenses, and don't run helter-skelter," Kratovil said. "We play well. When we allow the excitement of the game to take over we get careless, we make mistakes, take bad shots. And that allows teams to take advantage of it. So most of their points probably came off of turnovers or bad shots that we took."
Scooter Wright's layup and a drive from Kam Green (team-high 23 points) pulled the Bucs within 51-42 by the end of the third period.
Kent Island's Max Hershkowitz (18 points) converted three of four foul shots early in the fourth quarter, trimming Cambridge-SD's lead to 53-47 with over 6 minutes left in the game. But Ennals responded with his third three-point play of the game to extend the Vikings' lead to 59-50 with just over 5 minutes to play.
"The team needed this type of win because it showed us everybody can put something into the team," Ennals said. "I feel great right now. But we've got a lot more we can work on."
With Pinder sidelined, Ennals felt the need to shoulder more of the scoring load, and netted 11 of the Vikings' 16 first-quarter points.
"Number two was obviously difficult to stop," Kratovil said of Ennals. "He had a great game. He's a great player."
Tucker agreed.
"Kobe is amazing," Tucker said. "This kid has come so far. And college coaches need to take interest in this kid because this kid is going work hard. He's a D-A-W-G. He's a dawg."
Henry drilled his second 3-pointer with 5:12 left, shaving the Vikings lead to 56-50. But the Bucs lost sight of Hall, who got free for a layup, was fouled, and converted the foul shot for Cambridge-SD's fourth three-point play of the game and a 59-50 cushion.
Cambridge-SD finished 6 for 6 from the foul line, with Ennals going 5 for 5.
Kent Island twice cut its deficit to six in the closing 2 minutes, but could get no closer.
"We just had to slow down on offense," Tucker said of his team's third-quarter run. "The shots are there. We're just rushing it a little bit because we're pressing. I told them, 'One basket at a time. Come down, get a stop. Come down score, come down get a stop. Come down and get three stops and watch this game flip. And that's what it did."

Local girl to compete in national bowling championships

 The Eastern Shore has some really cool athletes — add 11-year-old Abigail Ticknor from Millington to that list.This year she will become the first Kent County resident to ever compete at the USBC Junior Gold Championships, an annual tournament for the top male and female youth bowlers in the United States.
At Milford Bowling Lanes on Sept. 22, Ticknor qualified for the national championship event, finishing third place in a co-ed field of a dozen U12 boys and girls in the first Delaware-sanctioned Junior Gold Qualifier of the season.
"She will take to the lanes at Ashwaubenon Bowling Alley in Green Bay, Wisconsin, on July 14," her father Phil Ticknor said, competing in the U12 Girls division. Bowling center assignments for the tournament, which will be held at eight different venues across northeast Wisconsin, were announced on Jan. 7, when registration opened.
The event begins with three days of practice, followed by an opening ceremony. Four qualifying rounds of four games each take place over the next four days with the highest finishing bowlers moving on to the final rounds on the 18th and 19th. Ticknor will bowl two of her qualifying rounds at Ashwaubenon Bowling Alley and the other two at Dale's Weston Lanes in Weston, Wisconsin.
The Junior Gold Championships have been held annually since 1998, other than in 2020 when the event was cancelled due to the Covid pandemic.
Ticknor will prepare by training with the Varsity Division of the Doverama Dragons Youth League in Dover.
"While she has been bowling in leagues since the age of 4 (beginning with bumpers), this was her first year pursuing a spot in the Junior Gold Championships," Phil said. "So far she's earned nearly $1,000 in college scholarship money via her achievements in youth bowling."
Naturally, Ticknor acknowledged she is nervous about the national competition. However, she will not be alone on the trip. She has a friend who qualified and will be going along with her.
And she has plenty of time to hone her skills, partaking in tournaments to ready herself. Like for example, over the weekend she competed at the Delaware USBC Singles and Doubles Tournament where she averaged 141 in singles and doubles, keeping consistent.
Her father is proud of all her accomplishments, recalling back when she bowled in pee wee league, always a hard right-handed thrower, who appreciates the independence of the sport of bowling.

title: Bulldogs rebound, win Tomahawk Duals title
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bulldogs rebound, win Tomahawk Duals title

 January 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 North Caroline High head wrestling coach Robin Eaton thought last Wednesday's showdown with Kent Island would be close, and possibly decided by criteria."I told the guys the day before, '36-36 is what I got,'" Eaton said. "'So it's up to one of you to make the difference.' And we didn't make no difference."
The Buccaneers registered seven pinfalls on the way to a convincing 49-25 victory over the Bulldogs, leaving Eaton to wonder what happened to the team he saw wrestle so well in December.
"That's the worst we've wrestled all year," Eaton said afterward.
It didn't take long for Caroline to shake off that effort, as it went a perfect 7-0 over Friday and Saturday to win the title at the annual Tomahawk Duals tournament at Havre de Grace High.
"Proud of the effort. And the effort of never quitting on their teammates," Eaton said. "Very excited. Just happy for the guys."
Two of the guys, Corey Bunce (190 pounds) and Connor Frank (120), went 7-0. Three others, Jacob Carpenter (126), Caleb Melvin (132) and Michael Dyke (150), each compiled 6-1 marks.
"We just went back to old-school, hard-drill, constant-movement practice," Eaton said of the Thursday practice that followed the Kent Island loss. "Spin drills. Sprawl drills. Hip heists. A lot of constant drilling of basic moves. That's what we did Thursday."
The Bulldogs went 4-0 on Friday, starting with a 40-39 victory over Sparrows Point — ranked 35th in the state — which was decided on tiebreaker E, with Caroline having five pins to the Pointers' four. Victories over Magruder (39-5) and Towson (58-15) followed before another narrow triumph over Perry Hall (41-40).
North Caroline routed Loch Raven 71-12 to begin Saturday's competition, defeated North Harford 52-28 in the semifinals, before capping its perfect run with a 47-25 victory over Havre de Grace in the championship match.
"We went after shots," said Eaton, comparing his team's weekend performance to Wednesday's. "We got on top. We did grinding. We were hitting moves. And there was sheer determination on some of the guys at some time. There was no quit.
"We used the minimize-maximize (approach), which is only minimize and let the other team get three at best if the guy's better than you," Eaton added. "And if you're better, you get the six. So minimize with three, maximize with earning six. And a lot of them did that. Like they didn't get turned. They didn't get pinned. I had guys save one point by getting tech fall(ed), fighting from their back instead of getting pinned. Proud of the effort."

title: Col. Richardson pitching standout Regulski signs with Demon Deacons
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Col. Richardson pitching standout Regulski signs with Demon Deacons

 January 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 763
 Words 

 Read News Document

 AMERICAN CORNER — Jordan Regulski had seen plenty of pitches from the college ranks.But none of them compared to the early deliveries from Wake Forest University.
"Recruitment from them was different," said Regulski, the senior baseball standout from Colonel Richardson High. "The pitching coach (Corey Muscara) gave me homework the first three calls, just to see how I thought; see my mental muscles, see what I had to offer. And it wasn't about baseball; wasn't about pitching.
"Then we started to speak baseball and stuff," Regulski continued. "For every other school, it was more the flash and the fancy equipment and the facilities. With them it was different."
So different that Regulski signed his national letter of intent with Wake Forest last Friday afternoon as family, friends, coaches and administrators crowded inside Colonel Richardson's media center.
"Now that it's officially on paper, I would say it's relief, not only for me, but my mom," Regulski said. "She's big in me getting my education."
Regulski, who has a 4.0 grade-point average, plans to major in math economics for actuaries, which combines math, economics and statistics, and minor in statistics.
"I've always been a numbers nerd," Regulski said smiling. "Love my math. I'm one of the guys who gets excited at solving problems in class. Big numbers guy."
After two years at North Dorchester, Regulski transferred to Colonel Richardson, where he put up big numbers last season while helping the Colonels win the North Bayside championship. The 6-foot-3, 175-pound right-hander went 6-0 with a 1.29 earned-run average, striking out 69 and walking 21. Opponents had an on-base percentage of .128 against Regulski, who allowed eight earned runs and 19 hits over 43 1/3 innings.
The North Bayside Player of the Year, who played shortstop when he wasn't on the mound, finished with a .324 batting average, .516 on-base percentage, drove in 24 runs, and was caught stealing only once in 35 attempts.
"He's worked really hard," longtime Colonel assistant coach Neil Lambert said. "When you look at the success that's earned today, when you're sleeping at 5 o'clock in the morning, he and other guys are working. You've got to have talent, but you've got to have drive."
Regulski estimated between 30 to 35 schools contacted him on August 1, 2023 — Day 1 of the recruiting period.
"I was hearing the same stuff," said Regulski, who estimated between 55 to 60 schools overall reached out to him over the entire recruiting process. "It was hard to decipher."
That field began to thin as the 2023-24 school year progressed. Then in February of last year, Regulski was clocked at 94 mph during his first bullpen and schools began circling back, including Southeastern Conference heavyweights LSU, Vanderbilt and Alabama.
"I wanted to go south so that was perfect for me," Regulski said.
And Wake Forest soon proved to have the right combination Regulski was looking for.
"The background of pitchers they've produced out of Wake Forest was big for me," Regulski said of a program that had six players selected in last year's amateur draft, including right-handed pitcher Chase Burns — the second overall pick of the first round by the Cincinnati Reds — and left-hander Will Gervase, taken by the Los Angeles Angels in the 16th round.
"When I first started watching them they were in the College World Series," added Regulski of the Demon Deacons, who lost to eventual national champion LSU in the 2023 CWS but were eliminated early in regional play last year. "So I knew they had the potential to go to Omaha (site of the College World Series) and taking it all. They've been there."
Regulski admitted having family not far from the Winston-Salem, North Carolina campus was another contributing factor.
"My aunt is right down the road," Regulski said. "I know a lot of people that get homesick and I won't have that. I talked to schools like Miami and Alabama, and out there I'm on my own. She's right down the street (in Durham). So it's perfect."
Regulski's arsenal includes a two- and four-seam fastball, a changeup, and a slurve (combination slider-curveball). He touched 95-96 mph with the Richmond Braves scout team over the summer, but said control has become a priority.
"One of my goals this year is to have a five-to-one strikeout-to-walk ratio," Regulski said. "Big focus for me this year is control. I've talked to the pitching coach at Wake and he said, I'll always throw hard. It was something that I was born with, I'm a talented kid. If I can get control under way he thinks I'll take off. So that's a big thing for me and we'll see how it goes."

title: Still Pond's 71-year-old fencing champion takes sixth place at World Championships
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Still Pond's 71-year-old fencing champion takes sixth place at World Championships

 January 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 951
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STILL POND — When 71-year-old Lotte Bowie of Still Pond stepped onto the fencing strip in Dubai this October, she faced off against elite competitors from Poland, Kazakhstan and Finland in front of an international crowd.The third-ranked fencer in her age group would go on to secure sixth place in the International Fencing Federation Championships for the veteran 70-plus class, adding another achievement to her impressive competitive career.
While she engaged them with her weapon of choice, she had to counter their attacks, while drowning out the crowd cheering her opponent in a language unknown to her.
As Bowie blocked out all the noise, like she does in every confrontation, she had a conversation with herself, gripping the handle of her sword.
Bowie used distance, avoiding the flashing blade from striking any part of her body, whether foot, hand, chest or head.
When the conflict was over, Bowie, currently ranked third in the world, had won sixth place in the 2024 International Fencing Federation Championships for veteran class (70s-plus). She was ultimately defeated by a Polish woman who used an attack-first strategy, but she was encouraged with her performance.
"You always learn in this sport," Bowie remarked.
The USA team she traveled with fared better, winning silver, being bested by a tough Russian team with a skilled team leader.
They secured a silver medal in Vet Team Women's Epee to end their record-breaking tournament on a high note.
"The team's final tally of 26 medals is the most ever won by any country in a single Vet Worlds, surpassing their own previous record of 24 medals set last year," stated usafencing.org.
Bowie reflected on that intense and rarified experience.
The championship was seven days of individual and team competition with 736 fencers in their 50s, 60s and 70s-plus from 58 countries. In all, 855 fencers participated.
Bowie was one of 37 competitors, in the Veteran's Women's class for the epee — a sharp-pointed dueling sword, designed for thrusting.
Despite traveling the farthest she had ever gone in her eight years of fencing, Bowie felt comforted by her teammates, encouraged by her coaches.
"I feel so lucky. My friends in the other age groups were cheering me on," Bowie remarked.
She felt proud to represent the United States.
"The veteran fencers we have seen this week in Dubai have been an inspiration to the entire world of fencing", said FIE Vice President Abdelmoneim Elhamy El Husseiny. "They represent passion, athleticism and a love for fencing as a lifelong sport."
Not just the fact Bowie travelled to Dubai, but her multiple accomplishments in the sport, highlights her rigorous work ethic.
Training is tough. A typical week consist of swimming, weight lifting three days a week, squats to strengthen thighs and leg flexibility as well as yoga for limberness and mental dexterity.
When she is not competing in regional and local championships, she is at Modern Duelists Fencing Academy, Elkton, Maryland, four days a week, practicing foot work and open bouting, (like sparring).
"You have to put in the work — it takes sacrifice," she said.
Putting on her Italian-made suit, especially made for competitions, electronically hooking up to the line, and donning the mask can only take you so far.
Learning the footwork and working on cardio can take you a little further. However physical is only a part of the equation, she said. It takes mental toughness in order to be successful.
Bowie said each opponent is different. There is an intellectual and psychological battle, she noted.
"During those moments you score a point, it feels like you wins a battle with herself."
That toughness is evident even in a loss.
Bowie said there were times she was defeated on a Saturday, then had to find it in herself to enter a competition on Sunday, summoning the psychological strength to keep going.
This kind of dedication takes much of her time, which she juggles with a career in marketing and brand design.
"I have to pay for my fencing somehow, " Bowie said.
Fencing is a niche sport, and so her travel was not covered when she went to the January North Cup in Kansas City earlier this year. Bowie was in the heart of the winter storm; ice, and snow shut down the airport for days, delaying her trip back.
But it was well worth it.
"It was the most expensive gold medal I ever got," Bowie laughed.
During that blistery, wintry weekend, she toppled all her opponents and faced off in the finals with someone she could never beat. Displaying a can-do attitude, she defeated all her rivals, 10-3, 10-7, 10-4 and 10-3, winning the entire event.
She received a gold medal and a video interview, expressing thankfulness for the sport she has grown to love.
That affectation began through her son, George, who always wanted to fence, and finally got the chance to when he went to University of Pennsylvania. From that, Bowie grew to love it, as her son who ranked in a major competition in 2017.
"It's mentally challenging in an invigorating way. If you're older it helps use your mind strategy to employ physical moves."
She also participates in international events in Central and South America (the PanAms) and in Toronto (the CanAms). For the former she earned bronze two years in a row for Vet 60 and over.
And last year, she won bronze in the national championships in Daytona, employing a strike-first method.
Her swordplay skills has her world-hopping.
"Fencing has changed my life in a dynamic way," Bowie said. "It gave me a path to a mental, physical and spiritual journey, filled with interesting travel. I am so blessed to do it."
Bowie urged people in the community to try it too. If it's not too late for her, it's not for you, she commented.
And don't argue with her either, she's trained with a sword.
See more of Bowie's accomplishments at usafencing.org.

title: Saints' rally falls shy against Colonels
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Saints' rally falls shy against Colonels

 January 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 648
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Stevie Mister knows what he's talking about."I told them once we got to the top of our lineup the game would change, it would flip a little bit," St. Michaels High's second-year head wrestling coach said to his team. "And it did."
The Saints were staring at 23-point deficit after eight matches Wednesday night against Colonel Richardson. That's when the dual-meet reached the lower weights and St. Michaels strung together four consecutive victories, whittling its deficit to just two points.
But Zyarron Nichols' second-period pinfall clinched the match, and Evan Alexander's technical fall one bout later provided some extra padding as the Colonels held on for a 46-33 victory.
"We wrestled tough," Colonel Richardson head coach Bryan Hall said after his team improved to 4-3. "Zy picked up Jay(Quan Wilkins). I know Jay was upset because he is one of our top guys. He wasn't feeling well. He just couldn't finish that kid off before it caught up to him. But Zy picked it up. And we knew we had Evan in the hole at the end. So we had a feeling it was going to come down to that last match."
Hall may have thought his team was going to jump on the Saints (2-4) early, as both Gary Koeneman (144 pounds) and Ethan Thomas (150) scored quick takedowns in their respective matches. But Jacob Jenkins caught Koeneman in a reverse cradle for a fall in 1 minutes, 32 seconds. St. Michaels' Sylis Showacre followed his teammate's lead, erasing a 6-2 deficit with another reverse cradle and fall in 2:42 over Thomas, staking the Saints to a 12-0 lead.
"They caught us early," Hall said.
But Colonel Richardson took control of the match by winning the next six straight bouts, starting with Anthony Alexander's 1:35 pinfall over Wyatt Currie at 157 that cut St. Michaels' lead in half at 12-6. Carleans Jean-Baptiste (165) followed with a 19-3 technical fall over Lane Cappa, drawing the Colonels within 12-11.
Colonel took the lead when Brox Meissner defeated Sherwin Mendez by injury default early in the 175-pound match. Richard Taylor (190) extended the lead, pinning Oliver Cummings in 3:34. The Colonels closed the upper weight classes, with Wilson Clough earning a 41-second fall over Blake Carter at 215, and Chatydrick Pickrom picking up a forfeit at 285, stretching the visitors' lead to 35-12 with six matches remaining.
The Saints then showed their strength at the lower weights, though Andrew Sanchez earned a forfeit at 106.
St. Michaels picked up nine more points at 112 — Hudson Jones piecing together a 17-2 technical fall over Brody Omohundro — at Willie Coale earning a 14-1 major decision over Elisee Pierre-Louis at 120.
But Omohundro and Pierre-Louis' ability to avoid pinfalls prevented St. Michaels from cutting into that gap further.
"Couple of kids in the middle there, Elisse, Brody not getting pinned, just giving up the decisions kind of put us back ahead of the curve there," Hall said. "So it gave us a chance with Evan coming up to know that we could get a pin there (in the last match) and we could win."
Wilkins built an 8-1 lead on St. Michaels' Ben Murphy in the first period of the 126-pound match. But Murphy hit a five-point move before pinning Wilkins in 3:12 to pull St. Michaels within 35-33.
Nichols (132) then turned a 4-4 first-period tie into a 17-8 lead before pinning Erlin Romero in 4:27 fall before Alexander rolled to a 19-4 tech fall over Manny Henry in the 138-pound finale.
"We hung in there," Mister said. "We don't have any holes (at the top). Some things didn't work out our way, but it's just how it goes."
"Some tweaks need to be made," said Mister, whose team, like all Bayside teams, haven't had much practice time since coming off the holiday break due to snow. "But we're a young team and I think we're doing pretty good so far."

title: Sabres extend win streak to four
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Sabres extend win streak to four

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 583
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Garett Hemingway can carry Saints Peter and Paul High's boys basketball team when needed.He didn't have to Thursday night.
On a night he admitted wasn't his best, Hemingway still scored a team-high 22 points, including eight in the fourth quarter, as the Sabres extended their winning streak to four with a 64-51 victory over Delmarva Christian.
"We're playing good team ball," Sts. Peter & Paul head coach Gary Gould said after his team improved to 10-8 overall for the season. "That's what I keep preaching. When he's not having a Garett game we need everyone else to have their game. And tonight they (Delmarva Christian) tried to play a box-and-one on him, and I'll take my four guys against any four guys any day."
Hemingway scored eight points in the first quarter, connecting on his only 3-pointer, and slamming down a dunk to give the Sabres a 14-12 lead at the end of the first quarter.
The Royals (8-3), who are in first place in the Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference, kept it a two-point difference in the early minutes of the second quarter. But Porter Bishop scored inside and Peter Mangold canned a 3-pointer to start Sts. Peter & Paul on a 17-8 run to close the second quarter.
Daniel Liles (22 points) hit a 3-pointer to pull Delmarva Christian within 23-19 with 3:45 remaining in the first half. But JJ Rarden (14 points) sandwiched two 3-pointers and a put-back around a Hemingway drive to widen the Sabres lead to 33-23 with 1:30 left before the break.
"Everyone has accepted their roles," Gould said. "Everyone plays to their maximum capability when they touch the floor, and it's been easy to switch and sub and interchange. And everything's been wonderful so far."
Hemingway scored inside and on a drive to close the Sabres' first-half scoring, helping the home team to a 37-24 halftime advantage.
Based on its consistency, Gould thinks this team may be better than the Sabres team that won the Maryland Interscholastic Athletic Association C Conference championship last year.
"Right now any five I put in the game I feel very confident in," Gould said. "And I can go five and five if I need to. I feel we're deeper with more skill and more concept (than last year)."
The Royals kept Hemingway off the scoresheet in the third quarter while shaving their deficit to nine at 48-39 heading into the fourth quarter. But Delmarva Christian wouldn't get any closer than seven in the fourth quarter.
"We try to take away their first options," Gould said. "And when we do that we wear teams down, and eventually we get to where we want to be. But we are disciplined when it comes to having a game plan. We understand what other teams' best strengths are and we go from there."
Peter Mangold hit his second trey of the game and Hemingway scored on a drive with 7 minutes to play to give Sts. Peter and Paul a 53-41 lead. Daniel Liles' 3-pointer got the Royals within 54-47 with 3 minutes left.
But Hemingway hit a free throw, scored on a put-back, and scored on a spinning baseline drive to push the Sabres lead to 59-49 with 1:18 remaining. Two Jamir Demby free throws and a Hemingway foul shot bumped the lead to 62-49 with under a minute to play.
"Everyone stepped up," Gould said. "He (Hemingway) still had 22. He had eight in the fourth quarter. That's when you want him. You want the points in the fourth. That worked out well."

title: Despite low numbers, Spies likes where Warriors are heading into final stretch
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Despite low numbers, Spies likes where Warriors are heading into final stretch

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 685
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Her team numbers are down.And like any other Bayside Conference sport this winter, trying to get a regular practice or meet schedule has been near impossible because of the snow that blanketed the area following the holiday break.
Despite those struggles, Easton High first-year head swim coach Katie Spies likes where her team is heading into the final week of the regular season and next Saturday's Bayside Conference championships.
"I think they are right where they should be," Spies said Friday, one day after her girls lost to Kent Island, 50-44 — the Warriors' first loss of the season. "I think we're going to have a week of practice and stay focused and stay strong. We're not tapering for Baysides or anything like that. But I have high hopes."
Those hopes may have been heightened on Tuesday, after Easton's girls defeated Saints Peter and Paul, 69-22, at the Easton Family YMCA, running their record to 5-0.
Spies' spirits received another boost Thursday. Though the Warriors lost, Spies noted Easton — including her the two swimmers on her boys team — registered season-best times in 17 of their 26 combined swims.
That was not enough to defeat a Kent Island team that appears positioned for another Bayside title run. Against Easton, Clare O'Keefe won the 50-yard freestyle (26.17 seconds) the 100 butterfly (1:05.96), and teamed with Kara Seymour, Alexia Grossman and Maddie Parks to win the 200 free relay in 1:49.55. The Bucs also got individual wins from Seymour (100 breaststroke, 1:11.05), Parks (100 backstroke, 1:06.12) and Jordan Sarier (500 free, 6:12.14).
Leading Easton was Maddie Weems, the defending Class 3A/2A/1A state champion in the 200 freestyle. Weems won the 200 free (2:04.89) and the 100 free (55.58), teamed with Katheryn Kelsey, Madelyn Finch and KC Sauter on the first-place 200 medley relay (1:58.76), then joined Finch, Sauter and Claire Morris to win the 400 free relay (4:04.53).
Finch won the 200 individual medley in 2:25.50.
Kent Island easily won the boys' competition, 74-8. Keefer Pullen (50 free, 24.73; 500 free, 5:41.91) and Jacob Reeder (100 free, 54.92; 100 back, 1:05.19) each posted two individual victories, and Stefan Schifanelli (200 IM, 2:45.85) and Henry MacMillan (100 breaststroke, 1:19.21) each picked up a win. The Bucs swept the relays.
Easton's only swimmer, Aiden Wroe-Street won both the 200 free (2:04.57) and the 100 fly (1:01.70).
Against Sts. Peter & Paul, Weems (200 IM, 2:25.89; 100 fly, 1:07.51) and Finch (200 free, 2:14.92; 100 back, 1:10.84)) each notched a pair of individual wins, joined Kelsey and Morris on the winning 200 medley relay, and together with Paige Bodle and Kelsey won the 400 free relay. Morris, Bodle, Sauter and Gabriella Streaker won the 200 free relay.
Also notching individual wins were Bodle (100 free, 1:05.57), Sauter (500 free, 6:28.06) and Morris (100 breaststroke, 1:19.94).
"After they beat (Stephen) Decatur I came up with 'We're small but mighty," Spies said of her team, which consists of 11 girls and just two boys. "That's what they are. They're rocking it even though we don't have the numbers. They have heart, they have the (work) ethic, and the hard work to make it happen."
Wroe-Street won the 50 free (25.91) and the 500 free (6:00.705) against the Sabres, and Mason Quicke was first in the 100 free (1:21.54).
Sts. Peter & Paul first-year head coach Kristina Henry can sympathize with Spies. Henry has no one on the boys team, and a girls team of seven which includes Emily Rosswork, who prevented a Warrior sweep on Tuesday, when she won the 50 freestyle.
"I think they're doing well. I'm very proud of them," Henry said. "They're at the meets and practice when they can be. They take it very seriously.
"We'll find something we like; something they're good at, and then something maybe outside of what they normally do," Henry said when it comes to what events her girls compete in. "And they are always willing. They never say, no. If I say, 'Let's put you in an IM, OK, they do it.'"
The Sabres have two more regular-season meets before competing in the Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference championships on Feb. 7 at Delmarva Christian.

title: Referees weather the storm throughout the year
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Referees weather the storm throughout the year

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 1645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 At virtually every level of every sport, game officials, referees and umpires often hear the brunt of complaints from coaches and fans. While many have maintained a genuine thick-skinned approach of tuning out the vociferous chatter, other longtime officials have opted to hang up their stripes and whistles in recent years, a move that has organizers concerned.Whether the games are played indoors or outside, game officials, referees and umpires are genuinely a necessary part of any contest. Without them, rules could not be objectively enforced and games could venture into absolute chaos. Local officials for recreation leagues, high school and college are paid a modest per diem for their services, but they often arrive having already worked a full day at their full-time jobs, and occasionally the combination of the commute and the chatter can be daunting.
In fact, from a peak of 210 active officials in 2015, the roster of available referees in the Maryland Basketball Officials Association has fallen by about a quarter at the outset of the current winter season. The main reason for the diminishing number of officials has been the interactions of the fans, according to people interviewed for this story. Although that is hardly the only factor; for instance, MBOA refs get $89 per game, whereas IAABO 12 and IAABO 134 officials in other parts of the state get $110 per game.
Charles County resident Kenneth "Larry" Johnson was a basketball official for over 30 years before transitioning to become the primary evaluator of basketball referees. During this long tenure as a ref, Johnson gradually got accustomed to a lot of the chatter from coaches and fans, but he has clearly noticed an increase in the verbal abuse a lot of them endure.
"After running up and down the floor for 30 years and dealing with a war injury that I suffered in Vietnam, I decided I had enough running," said Johnson, noting that he still has shrapnel left in his left knee from combat. "When I was an official, I knew there was a lot of noise from the crowd, but not like today. A lot of the fans have become really vocal and now it's tougher to keep refs. The ones that leave tell me their No. 1 reason is the fans."
'It's a tough job'Dave Cross, the current MBOA board president, works his full-time job nine to 10 hours each day then referees basketball games in the region two nights each week. He noted that several factors have played a key role in the decreased number of basketball officials over the last decade.
Cross, along with fellow referee Chris Miller, also teach the officiating class which typically has 20 to 22 new recruits each session. The class for basketball referees is offered each summer two nights per week for nine weeks.
"I think we had a really good number of available officials until COVID hit [in 2020]," Cross said. "COVID really changed everything. At one time we had over 200 officials, but now we're down around 160. When you have a lot of basketball games on Friday nights in SMAC, you need almost every available official to cover the games."
In addition to COVID prompting a number of officials to leave and not return, Cross said the fan interaction has also played a role in keeping veteran refs and attracting new ones. Cross also acknowledged the pay scale for local games is not on par with neighboring jurisdictions, which can put SMAC games in the hands of less experienced refs.
"At one time, you had to work junior varsity games for five years before you could start working varsity games," Cross said. "But now, with the shortage of available refs, we have guys working J.V. games for two years and then varsity games. It's tough to really know the rules and adapt to the speed of the game in that short of a time frame."
Like Cross, Miller also works a full-time job each day as a letter carrier for the U.S. Postal Service and then, two nights each week, departs the post office and heads to officiate a game. Miller has been an active basketball referee for nearly 20 years and he and Cross have steadfast recommendations for their new student referees.
"First thing, you have to know the rules," Miller said. "We try to make sure the new refs study to rule book and know the rules and understand the game. Not every coach or player is going to agree with every call that you make. But if a coach has a question about a call, you have to explain the rule first. There are also a lot of judgment calls you have to make, but you have to have thick skin when you start hearing it from the fans."
Thomas Stone High School boys basketball coach Dale Lamberth noted that he rarely will argue with a referee over a call but will occasionally ask for an explanation. Over the years, Lamberth has maintained a composed dignity while interacting with the referees and would like to see fellow coaches, players and spectators approach them with the same respect.
"It's a tough job," Lamberth said. "I know I could not do it. We understand they're getting paid and everyone expects a certain level from them. But by the same token they're not full-time officials. They have jobs just like everyone else. I might ask a ref for an explanation from time to time, but I don't believe in showing up the refs. I've only gotten one technical foul called on me in over 30 years of coaching."
Likewise, North Point boys basketball coach Jimmy Ball is quick to admit that while he may not agree with every call the officials make over the course of a game, he understands they provide a necessary role. Like Lamberth, Ball also admits that despite his vast knowledge of the game of basketball and general understanding of the rules, he could not function as a referee.
"Being a game official is not easy," Ball said. "You have to make split-second calls and a lot of them are judgment calls, so you're not always going to agree with them. But I know I could not be a ref. There's just constant noise, especially from the fans, and inside a gym the refs are definitely going to hear it. But I never berate an official — there's really no benefit to doing that."
During the football season, Brad Hewick is perhaps the most recognizable figure on the field while donning the proverbial white hat, signifying that he is in charge of the six-man officiating crew working that game.
Hewick, who will turn 62 later this month and is often referred to as "Pappy" by his peers and football coaches, said he generally hears more fan chatter at volleyball matches than at football games.
"When I'm on the football field, I'm so far from the crowd I can barely hear anything," Hewick said. "Most of the refs working a game usually only hear from the players and the coaches. The crowd noise is typically not an issue. But at volleyball matches, when I'm up in the chair [as the main officiant] and the crowd is right behind me, I can hear a lot. But it's like anything else, you have to block it out and just focus on calling the game."
Hewick also serves as an umpire during the spring and summer, working high school, American Legion and Charles & St. Mary's County Baseball League games during the dog days of summer. As the home plate umpire in those games, Hewick is quick to establish the strike zone early and maintain it throughout the contest.
"Anyone that has ever watched me work a game from behind home plate knows that I'm a low ball umpire," Hewick said. "I'm going to call strikes down in the zone. That's the way I'm going to call it in the first inning and I'm going to stay with it through the last inning. Batters and coaches might chirp at me early, but once they realize the zone that I've established they'll back off as long as I remain consistent and call it the same way for both teams."
Time to trainWhile the number of available officials has been declining in recent years, especially since COVID when several entire seasons were nixed altogether, fans are reminded at each game that officials are needed and classes for each sport are available to enable them to become accredited and approved and paid for their work. But those announcements rarely elicit an immediate response from spectators to sign up.
"They make the announcement [for new officials] at every game," Johnson said. "But you hardly ever see anyone leave their seats and go sign up. I think if a lot of people took the test of basic rules they would fail it. From talking to refs who have left, the No. 1 reason is the fans. We have a lot of really good refs in Southern Maryland, but it is getting tougher and tougher to keep them and then get new refs to replace them."
Former referees and current referees as well as coaches all insist that consistency is the primary aspect of officiating a game. Calls made in the first quarter or first inning should be consistent throughout the game, all the way through the last whistle or last pitch. Perhaps the greatest compliment to any officiating crew is that they had little to no impact on the outcome and no one noticed them.
"It's the same for any sport," Cross said. "If you didn't notice the officials, they must have done a good job. Basketball is the toughest game to officiate because there are so many judgment calls, like blocking or charging or possessions decided by which player touched the ball last before it went out of bounds. But those calls tend to even out over the course of the game."

title: More coverage needed of women's sports
author: Staff Writer
content:
More coverage needed of women's sports

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I am writing to express my concern regarding the lack of equality in your sports coverage, particularly the glaring disparity in reporting on women's sports compared to men's. While women's sports continue to grow in popularity and participation at all levels, this trend is not reflected in your publication.Week after week, I see articles — both locally written and sourced from the AP wire — and photos heavily focused on men's teams, while coverage of women's teams is minimal or nonexistent. Recently, the online edition featured seven local sports stories, but only one highlighted a women's team. Similarly, in the college section, seven stories were published, yet just one focused on college softball.
This imbalance is especially frustrating as the No. 8 Maryland women's basketball team prepares to face No. 1 UCLA this Sunday — a high-stakes game that wasn't even mentioned in the Jan. 24 print edition. Of the six stories featured on the front page of the Sports section, only two referenced the efforts of local girls' teams.
In Friday's "pro" section, no women's sports were featured, despite the recent launch of new pro women's basketball and ice hockey leagues. The "youth" sports section listed seven stories with only one about girl's teams.
This imbalance sends a disheartening message to female athletes, coaches, and fans — that their efforts and achievements are not as valuable or newsworthy. In reality, nothing could be further from the truth.
Consider the rising viewership of women's college and professional basketball, the growing support for the U.S. Women's National Soccer Team, and the increasing attendance at local high school girls' games. These trends clearly demonstrate a strong demand and appreciation for women's sports. Ignoring this interest not only undervalues the athletes but also deprives your readers of the opportunity to celebrate their achievements. Women make up over half of the population, and your sports coverage should reflect this reality.
Fair and balanced reporting would enrich your publication and inspire a broader audience. Highlighting women's sports with the same depth and frequency as men's would reflect the values of equity and inclusion that so many in our community hold dear. Feature stories on standout athletes, detailed game recaps and equal space for photos are simple but impactful steps that could make a world of difference.
As a trusted source of information for the community, The Star Democrat has the power to influence perceptions and shape conversations. By prioritizing equal coverage, you can play a vital role in promoting gender equity in sports and fostering pride in all of our local athletes. Thank you for considering this important issue. I hope to see The Star Democrat take meaningful steps toward more inclusive sports coverage.

title: Sabres ride fast start to win
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Sabres ride fast start to win

 January 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 876
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — It may have been the most complete 8 minutes of basketball Saints Peter and Paul High's girls have played this season."It was the most amazing first quarter ever," Sabres head coach Katie Murphy said.
Avery McCall splashed three of her four 3-pointers in the opening 8 minutes, and Lucy Rankin scored six of her 10 points in the first quarter Tuesday, as the Sabres registered their third victory in four games with a 45-25 victory over Salisbury School.
"If we play every game like we played the first quarter. … I mean, I would just have to sit there and not do anything," Murphy said with a smile as Sts. Peter & Paul improved to 6-8 overall, 5-2 in the Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference.
The Sabres' two conference losses this season have been by a grand total of three points. Should it continue to play the way it did in the first quarter, Sts. Peter and Paul could challenge for its second ESIAC title in three years.
The left-handed McCall drained a pair of feathery 3-pointers and sliced through the lane for layup, and Rankin calmly buried three open set shots during an 18-0 blitz over the game's first 5:37.
The Dragons (3-8, 1-5) got on the board with 2:53 left in the first, when Allie Collins (15 points) converted a steal into a layup. McCall answered with her third 3. Collins connected for a trey before a Kaylin Palmer foul shot and Rankin's layup gave the Sabres a 24-5 lead after one.
"Confidence and staying cool and collected," said McCall, who finished with a game-high 21 points and 10 rebounds to go with five assists and five steals. "When we just play, we don't think, we have games like these, and the games that we've won. The first Delmarva (Christian) game [a 33-31 Sabres' win] we didn't think. We just played basketball and it worked."
Sts. Peter & Paul barely missed a shot in the first quarter, consistently worked the ball around the perimeter and rotated it back around until it found an open player, and limited Salisbury's possessions to just one shot for the bulk of the first quarter.
"That's the biggest thing," Murphy said in regard to trying to have her players not overthink situations. "I just want them to go out there and play basketball. The more thought you put into it you start getting afraid, you miss a few shots.
"I never tell anybody not to shoot," Murphy continued. "I just tell them to keep shooting. They're eventually going to go in. You're going to get more comfortable shooting. Like if you're nervous at first it's going to be a little rigid. But as you continue on, keep shooting. It's going to be relaxed and it's going to continue to fall for them."
It seemed everything McCall put up in the first quarter fell through.
"We lost some key outside players," McCall said of the graduated Morgan Quade. "So I have to be able to take the shots that they won't take occasionally."
Rankin and Kaylin Palmer hit consecutive layups before Rankin and McCall connected again from the outside to give the Sabres a 32-10 halftime lead.
"Avery's experience has given her the opportunity to obviously play anywhere," Murphy said. "And she has a really good shot, and she has the distance to be able to do that. Lucy is another one who can really shoot with confidence. Everyone else, we're a young team. They need to build up to that. I think a lot of that has to do with some confidence and we just keep working on the skill work so they feel more confident."
Sts. Peter & Paul limited the Dragons to just two third-quarter points while modestly stretching its lead to 38-12 entering the fourth quarter. Salisbury outscored the Sabres 13-7 in the fourth.
"On our win against Gunston I think five or six players all scored," McCall said of last Friday's 51-18 victory over the Herons. "Now, everyone is contributing. More people are putting up buckets every game."
The Sabres had six of their 10 players score Tuesday, including Emma Hainey, who had eight.
"I think everyone is starting to come together," Murphy said. "And that's the biggest thing."

title: Kent Island sweeps Baysides
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Kent Island sweeps Baysides

 February 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1187
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Corey Coulbourn was already nervous.Kent Island High's head swim coach knew the battle for the girls title at Saturday's Bayside Conference swim championships was going to be close, with Easton having won five events, her Buccaneers four, and Stephen Decatur two.
With swimmers, coaches and parents congregated inside the Dorchester County Family YMCA's gymnasium, meet director and Queen Anne's County head coach Kelley Moore step onto a folding chair, announced Decatur as the girls runner-up, then, unaware she was adding a splash of suspense, stepped out of the gym to retrieve the trophies for first and second place.
"Easton's girls. That's definitely who I was nervous about," Coulbourn said.
Five anxious minutes later, Moore was back on her chair announcing Kent Island's girls had finished first, and that the boys had won by an even narrower margin, making the Buccaneers the first program to sweep both titles in back-to-back seasons in the seven-year history of the championships.
"When Kelley went straight to announcing second place without telling us who was in third, I was a little bit nervous," Coulbourn confessed. "We had some DQs that were making me nervous. But I'm super excited and super proud, and I'm hoping we can ride this going into regionals in a couple weeks."
Clare O'Keefe set a new conference record in the 50-yard freestyle, and also swam a leg on the Bucs' record-setting 200 medley relay, as Kent Island's girls totaled 387 points, edging Decatur by six points and Easton by 24.
Keefer Pullen won the 100 backstroke, was part of the winning 200 medley relay, and later watched his teammates win the 200 freestyle relay, lifting the Bucs to the boys crown by a seven-point margin over Queen Anne's.
"One of our outstanding sophomore boys was out," Coulbourn said of Jacob Reeder. "I was really impressed with the rest of the boys, how they rallied and made up for that loss."
Among those stepping up were junior Reef Adams, who filled Reeder's spot on the 400 free relay, joining Jack Da Rosa, Ethan Rudolfi and Pullen for a second-place time of 3 minutes, 43.59 seconds. Coulbourn also praised senior captain Dylan McCormick, who anchored the winning 200 medley relay team (1:51.24) of Pullen, Ethan Yonts and Da Rosa.
"Reef did a fantastic job of stepping up in his not favorite event, the 4 by 100 (freestyle) relay," Coulbourn said. "I was really impressed to see him swim one of his best times in that all year. And then Dylan McCormick, stepped up in the medley relay. We rearranged a little bit so Jack Da Rosa took the butterfly leg that Jacob was supposed to swim, and then Dylan did a season-best time 50 free split for that."
McCormick and Adams also helped the Bucs win the 200 freestyle relay (1:38.63), teaming with AJ Harmse and Da Rosa.
Pullen delivered Kent Island's lone individual victory, going under a minute for the first time this season to win the 100 backstroke in 59.90, and was second in the 100 butterfly (59.28).
"That was awesome," Coulbourn said of Pullen's backstroke.
Kent Island needed every one of those efforts to hold off a Queen Anne's team that won a meet-high five individual events, three of those coming from freshmen.
"We've had a phenomenal season," said Moore, whose team is undefeated in dual-meet competition heading into Thursday's makeup against Kent Island. "We gained some strong freshman this year and they stepped up and did a great job today."
Leading that freshman cast was Levi Corcoran, who won the 200 individual medley (2:14.38) then romped to victory in the 500 freestyle (5:03.72), winning by 45 seconds. Classmate Connor Evans was first to touch the wall in the 200 free (1:57.22). Still another freshman, Tre Moore, the coach's son, joined Corcoran, Evans and sophomore Will Meyer to win the 400 free relay in 3:42.19. Meyer boosted the Lions' point total with a pair of individual wins, out-dueling Pullen to win the 100 fly (58.72) for the second consecutive year before clocking a first-place 1:06.94 in the 100 breaststroke.
Then there was Kent County's Henry Martinez, the conference's fastest man in the pool for the second straight year. The senior won the 50 freestyle in a meet-record 22.47, then came back to post another new conference mark, winning the 100 free in 49.48.
"He's dedicated and really come a long ways since his freshman year," Kent County head coach Grayson Wise said of Martinez. "I'm speechless when it comes to talking about him. He's a great kid in and out of the pool."
Kent's Island's O'Keefe was also part of two record-setting performances. The sophomore helped get Kent Island's girls off to a hot start, joining Maddie Parks, Kara Seymour and Alexia Grossman to win the 200 medley relay in a conference-record 1:56.82, taking one full second off the previous mark.
Two events later, O'Keefe was back in the pool setting a meet record in the 50 free (25.08), finishing 3 seconds ahead of her closest competitor. She then turned around in the first event after the meet's short break, to take first the 100 fly (1:02.98).
"She's set some awesome goals for herself and is willing to do what it takes to reach them," Coulbourn said of O'Keefe. "One of her goals was to set that Bayside record. She's a powerhouse, so we're very lucky to have her on the team."
Kent Island's other individual victory came from Maddie Parks, who rolled to victory in the 100 backstroke (1:04.77), winning by a 4-second margin.
Easton head coach Katie Spies had reason to think the Warriors had a shot at their third title in the meet's short history after Maddie Weems and Maddy Finch each won a pair of individual races, then joined Claire Morris and KC Sauter to win the 400 free relay.
Finch won the 200 IM in 2:19.95 and later won the 100 breaststroke (1:09.66), edging Seymour, who was second in 1:10.28.
"Maddy Finch has been working very hard on her breaststroke," Spies said. "We've really been thinking about the dynamics of her stroke and reaching out, and she has been thinking about that lot during her swims. And she did that. And so that then pulled off that win, 'cause she's staying long in her stroke and not keeping it quite as short."
The defending Class 3A/2A/1A state champion in the 200 freestyle, Weems cruised to victory in the event with a 2:00.98, finishing 11 seconds ahead of runner-up Mary Jane Joiner of Kent County. Weems was also dominant in the 100 free, winning by more than 3 seconds with a 55.23.
"She's a powerhouse in whatever she's put in," Spies said of Weems. "But when she sets her mind to do something, she does it. Even though she didn't quite hit her mark in the 100 free in terms of what she wanted it to be, she did it in the 100-free relay (split). She sets goals for herself and she makes it happen."
Sauter swam the third leg of the 400 free relay, and rallied to put the Warriors in front to stay, as her, Morris and Finch — who had both just finished swimming the breaststroke — and Weems won in a season-best 4:02.14.
