title: Willis caps career with a trail of gold
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Willis caps career with a trail of gold

 May 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1113
 Words 

 Read News Document

 He's fast, smart, athletic, fast, competitive, graceful, tactical and … oh yeah, really fast.Tori Willis Jr. is also consistent.
"His comment whenever you ask, 'How are you doing; how are you feeling?' (is) We got this,'" Cambridge-South Dorchester High co-head outdoor track and field coach Dr. Lois Narr said of Willis. "'We got this. Don't worry about it.'"
Well, Willis got three more gold medals to add to his school-record collection Saturday at the Class 1A state championships, winning two individual titles — coming within 0.01 seconds of a third — and running a leg on the winning 4x100-meter relay while helping the Vikings to a third-place finish in the boys competition at the Prince George's Sports and Learning Complex in Landover.
The defending 1A boys state champion, Cambridge-SD totaled 81 points to place third behind first-place Liberty (87) and runner-up Friendly (82).
Leading the charge was Willis, who just missed striking gold in the boys first event, the 110-high hurdles, clocking a personal-record 14.44 seconds to finish a fraction behind Western Tech's Ojigwe Olua (14.43).
"I was mad because I lost obviously, but I was happy with my time," said Willis, who noted that near miss gave him added motivation for the rest of the meet.
Willis was back in the blocks a little over 10 minutes later for the 100-meter final, and this time no one finished in front of C-SD's senior standout, as he blazed across the finish line in a season-best 10.74 seconds, edging Central's Cameron Jefferson (10.82) and Kent County's Rah'zir Wilson (10.94).
"My start was great," Willis said. "I knew I won from like the first 20 meters, and I was just making sure I held it."
Willis made history the next time he stepped on the track, running away from the field to win the 300 intermediate hurdles in a new 1A-record 36.99 seconds — more than a full second ahead of Friendly's Fahad Kamarah, who edged Cambridge-SD's Antonio Blueford for second despite both hitting the finish line in 38.09.
Willis' time was the third fastest in state meet history, leaving him behind only Potomac's Dondre Nichols (36.26 in 2012) and Northwestern's James Graham (36.51 in 1999).
Willis, who had set the 1A state record last season, also became only the second athlete from a Bayside Conference school to win the 300 hurdles three consecutive years, matching a feat set by Kent Island's Jack Hutchison, who won three straight 2A titles from 2004-06.
"Not a possibility," Willis said when asked if there was a chance he would not win the 300 hurdles. "That's the one thing I was like, 'It's guaranteed. I'm making sure.' My 300 hurdles has always been my bread and butter, and to be able to run that fast at the state meet was amazing."
Willis earned his third gold medal of the day, running the second leg on the Vikings' 4x100 relay. Antonio Blueford handed the baton to Willis, who moved Cambridge-SD into the lead. Willis made a clean exchange with Tekai Drummond, who maintained that lead before handing off to William Jackson. Central's anchor closed the gap over the final 20 meters and thought he had won as he crossed the finish line. But Jackson dipped his shoulders across the line before falling, giving Cambridge-SD the win in 43.33. Central was later disqualified.
"He played a big role in just the set up of everything so the kids could win the relay that they won," Narr said of Willis. "He knew where the other teams were going to put their faster guys. And he would use that to help determine the lineup, and where he thought he should be in the relay."
Willis, who finished his high school career with a school-record seven state titles — five outdoors, two indoors — teamed with Blueford, Drummond and Jackson on Day 1 of the meet Thursday to place second in the 4x200 relay (1:29.94) and capped his Day 2 in the 4x400 relay, joining Zy'Meir Wilson, Christen Dockins and Drummond for a fifth-place 3:27.47.
"He really elevated his game with his leadership and his support of his team, and his encouragement of them," Narr said of Willis, who plans to continue his track career at Delaware State University. "He did everything he could do."
In addition to running the 4x100 and 4x200 relays, Blueford provided big points with his third place in the 300 hurdles, and his fourth-place efforts in the 110 hurdles (15.16) and long jump (20-8½). The senior was 10th in the triple jump (41-6½).
After his anchor leg in the 4x100 relay, Jackson returned to the pole vault, where he finished third, clearing the bar at 13 feet. Jakuez Snead also earned a bronze, with a personal-record 48-9 in the shot put.
Cambridge-SD senior Enazajah Young won her fifth state title, but her first gold outdoors, winning the girls 100 meter hurdles in 14.22. Young was fourth in the long jump (17-2¼) and teamed with Le'Asia Todd, Al'Janae Jackson and Te'Janae Ballin to place third in the 4x100 relay (50.76) and sixth in the 4x200 relay (1:48.88).
"She does her best to lead," Narr said of Young.
Todd closed her track and field career with a strong performance. In addition to the two relays, the senior earned runner-up honors in the high jump (4-10) and long jump (17-5½), a placed fourth in the triple jump (34-8).
One year after taking second in the long jump, Colonel Richardson senior Ayden Downie earned runner-up honors in the triple jump, soaring to a personal-record 45-10¾.
"He worked all throughout the year to get better," Colonel head coach James Jackson said. "Every year he wanted to improve and set his goal to be a state champion in either long jump or (triple) jump."
The North Bayside's top performers in the 2A meet, were Kent Island's Jack Morey — third in the pole vault at 14 feet — and Queen Anne's County's Ja'Dereon Thompson, who was third in the long jump (21-5¾).
Queen Anne's senior Ben Marks, who was bidding for his first state title outdoors, ran despite being sick and finished fourth in the 1,600 (4:23.08) and fifth in the 800 (1:57.51).
2A Notables: Kent Island's Giovanni Aguirre was fourth in the boys 400 (49.51) and Nora Koch was fourth in the girls pole vault (8-6). … Queen Anne's Makenna Fellows was fourth in the girls shot put (35-7); Kent Island's Lacey Dauses was sixth in the 800 (2:23.23); and North Caroline's Jayah Taylor was sixth in the discus (101-9).
1A Notables: North Dorchester's Remedy Wongus was fourth in the shot put (35-5½) and Kent County's Ke'yare Hawkins was fourth in the discus (103-8). … Kent County's RJ Peterson was third in the boys triple jump (43-5¼) and Rah'zir Wilson placed third in the high jump at 6 foot.

title: Ravens flock to Mid-Shore elementary schools
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Ravens flock to Mid-Shore elementary schools

 May 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 337
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Baltimore Ravens Cheerleaders and band surprised students at Choptank Elementary School as part as their Eastern Shore Takeover Thursday. The visit aimed to get students energized for the summer.Although it doesn't take a lot to get students excited for the summer, the Ravens managed to get hundreds of elementary schoolers to cheer just as loud as fans at M&T Bank Stadium in the fall.
"I think it's always fun to spread Raven cheer and always make sure the Ravens are doing their part in the community," said Yajaira Rivas, senior marketing coordinator for the Ravens.
"These are events we can't make too often because we're located in the city of Baltimore, but knowing that our fans are of (all) ages everywhere spread through Maryland, it is our duty to make sure that we're spreading Ravens pride at all times," she said.
At 12:15 p.m., multiple Ravens cheerleaders and band members entered the gym giving students high fives and playing music. The Ravens' feathered mascot, Poe, ran around and gave children hugs, urging the crowd to get loud.
As cheerleaders flew through the air, students cheered. Although some students didn't enjoy the loud noises, all students and staff members loved when Principal Gaven Parker was called on to answer trivia questions about the Ravens and guess cheerleader ages.
Parker appreciated the Ravens for reaching out to Choptank Elementary and hoped the team would return soon.
"It's a nice little atmosphere boost here to finish the school year," Parker said. "The kids just finished MCAP testing... it's nice to have something on a Thursday afternoon where we can all have fun... We hope we can continue doing this in years in the future.
The Ravens also visited Easton Elementary School on Thursday morning.
"All 1300 Easton Elementary students and the entire staff were treated to a Ravens Pep Rally Experience, right in their bus loop! It was an entertaining and engaging assembly featuring the Ravens Cheerleaders, Poe the mascot, and the Ravens Marching Band," Talbot County Public Schools said in a press release.

title: Rockwell, Weller net Saints' first state title
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Rockwell, Weller net Saints' first state title

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1212
 Words 

 Read News Document

 One of the first entries St. Michaels High senior Lexi Rockwell made in her personal journal for 2025 was a New Year's resolution — win a state title.Some may have considered that a bit of a reach. After all, the Saints had never won a state tennis championship of any sort in program history.
A reach? Maybe to some.
Far-fetched? Not really, considering St. Michaels made school history just a year ago, when it advanced a pair of doubles teams into the Class 1A state finals for the first time. Rockwell and Lila Jones were part of that historic breakthrough, as they reached the girls doubles final.
With Jones choosing not to play this spring, Rockwell's options for states were narrowed to singles or mixed doubles. Rockwell had gone undefeated at No. 1 singles this year, and for that reason Saints head coach Jordan Miller allowed the senior star to make her own decision. That didn't mean Miller was going to withhold his opinion.
"I said, 'Look. If you want to give it a run (in singles), it's your senior year, I understand,'" Miller said. "'However, if you want to win a state championship, play with Tom (Weller).'"
Rockwell heeded her coach's advice, teaming with Weller to become St. Michaels' first state tennis champions last Saturday, when they earned a 6-1, 6-2 victory over Marissa Greg and Aiden Pirolozzi of Mountain Ridge in the 1A mixed doubles final at the Wilde Lake Tennis Club in Columbia.
Rockwell and Weller's title run also helped St. Michaels to a runner-up finish in the 1A team competition — another program best — as the Saints (11 points) finished just two points behind first-place Liberty and one point ahead of third-place Boonsboro.
"It's been a really good season," said Miller, whose boys team won its first North Bayside championship before the boys and girls combined to win a fourth straight 1A East Region I title.
"Going into the last day the worst we could do was third," Miller said of the state tournament. "Going into the last match, the best we could have done was first. We had opportunities. Liberty had more players there. They deserved it."
But the Saints gave it a run.
The boys doubles team of Sean Kline and Miles Fox lost to Liberty in the semifinals, but bounced back Saturday to defeat Southern Garrett's Ben Nazelrod and Shane Sisler, 6-1, 6-2 in the consolation final.
Tess Weller, Tom's younger sister, also reached the semifinals, where she lost to eventual state singles champion Atlee Hilliard of Smithsburg, 6-1, 6-2, before finishing fourth.
But there was no stopping Tom Weller and Rockwell, even though the pair had never played mixed doubles prior to this year's regionals.
"I've seen Tom playing tennis since middle school," Miller said. "And Lexi kind of stumbled out in ninth grade. But we knew what we had from the beginning, that (they're) definitely going to be some special players.
"You never expect anything," Miller added. "Obviously as a coach, you just kind of hope they stick with it and continue to improve. So we just provided opportunities for them to improve every year and they did. And it just seemed that every obstacle that got in their way they got right past."
Miller removed the only potential obstacle before the postseason began, telling Weller he would not be playing singles in hopes of getting another crack at Boonsboro's Hunter Liao, who defeated Weller in last year's quarterfinals.
"I told him absolutely not," Miller said.
Liao defeated Kent County's Sebastian Cousineau, 6-0, 6-0 in the 1A boys singles final Saturday, becoming the first four-time boys singles state champion in the history of the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association tournament.
"Coach had a plan for like trying to get as many teams to win at states as possible," Weller said. "And part of that plan was me not playing boys singles. I was happy playing with Lexi."
And Rockwell was happy to be paired with Weller.
"I knew with mixed doubles I could rely on Tom," Rockwell said. "He was a very reliable partner. That's why I chose mixed doubles."
Miller scouted the field prior to Friday's competition and thought his team's toughest challenge would be in the quarterfinals against Clear Spring's Kaisy Custer and Brady Emst. It proved to be just that, as Rockwell and Weller crafted a 6-4, 6-3 victory for their closest match of the tourney.
"We felt like if we could get through that one unscathed that we would have a pretty nice road to the finals," Miller said. "And then we just have to see where we are at that point."
Rockwell and Weller were familiar with their semifinal opponent, having seen Snow Hill's Jay Hardy and Cash Von Marsh during the regular season, and moved into the finals with a 6-2, 6-2 win.
Afterwards, Miller scouted the other semifinal, while Rockwell took notes in her journal, as Greg and Pirolozzi outlasted Liberty's Aubrey Anderson and Jason Murphy, 7-6 (4), 7-6 (8) to reach the final.
"She showed them to me that morning," Miller said of Rockwell's notes. "Just mentioned some of their weaknesses, and it certainly held true when we played."
Rockwell was back on the exact same court she had played on last year when she and Jones lost in the girls doubles final. But Mountain Ridge held serve just once in the opening set while Weller ratcheted his service game to another level during a 6-1 win.
"He went from a very low serve percentage on first serves, and in the final match, I'm not exaggerating, probably 70 percent," Miller said of Weller.
Rockwell and Weller were also playing smart, driving shots to Greg's backhand while trying to keep the ball away from Pirolozzi at the net.
"We had advantages over both players," Miller said. "If we could keep the rallies going to the baseline, and I felt like any baseline rally we would win, and that would give our net player time to step in and do something at net. Tom put away a lot of balls. Lexi got a few as well. It all started from the baseline."
But Rockwell and Weller began struggling to make returns in the second set. Pirolozzi started hitting big serves and big ground strokes, helping Mountain Ridge to a 2-1 lead.
"I got them on the changeover and basically was like, 'What are we doing?'" Miller said. "'Everything I just told you not do do we're doing right now. Just do everything that has worked up until this point.'"
Rockwell and Weller settled and won the next five straight games for the set, the match, the title and a piece of history.
"I always thought I'd hopefully make it to states a few times," Weller said. "But I didn't think I'd actually win."
Rockwell may have had similar thoughts early in her high school career, but said Miller's coaching and setting high goals and achieving them was vital.
"He helped us every year from freshmen," Rockwell said of Miller. "I knew I wanted to make an impression on the school. At least and we were able to bring home a state title, and team state finalist title. And history is made."
North Dorchester's sister combination of Maddie and Jules Tobat made a bid to give the Eagles their first state tennis crown, reaching the girls 1A doubles final, before falling 7-5, 6-1 to South Carroll's Audrey Lillycrop and Iryna Kovalenko.

title: Broncos, Dobbins reach 1-year deal
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Broncos, Dobbins reach 1-year deal

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News 
 
 327
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — The Denver Broncos beefed up their offensive backfield on Tuesday, agreeing with free agent running back J.K. Dobbins on a one-year deal worth up to $5.25 million.A 2020 second-round pick by Baltimore, Dobbins has an extensive injury history, including an ACL tear in 2021 and a torn Achilles tendon in 2023, but he's been productive when healthy.
He gained a career-best 905 yards on 195 carries and tied his career high with nine rushing touchdowns last year with the Los Angeles Chargers despite missing four games with a sprained knee.
Word broke of Dobbins' acquisition just as the first day of the Broncos' mandatory minicamp was wrapping up, and coach Sean Payton was coy when asked about, saying, "I'm not going to answer to any reports. I think we're close."
When Dobbins visited the team last week, Payton said: "It's just another opportunity to possibly bring in another good football player to help us win."
If healthy, Dobbins figures to be one of the primary ballcarriers along with rookie R.J. Harvey, a second-round draft pick out of Central Florida. Other running backs on the roster include second-year pros Blake Watson and Audric Estime, third-year player Jaleel McLaughlin and fourth-year pro Tyler Badie.
A lot will be expected of Dobbins on third down after the Broncos lost their best pass protector in their backfield when Javonte Williams left for Dallas in free agency.
One of Dobbins' best games last season was at Denver in mid-October, when he rushed 25 times for 96 yards and a touchdown in the Chargers' 23-16 win.
"Yeah, he's a good back, especially when healthy," Broncos safety Brandon Jones said. "We kind of go back a little bit to high school and college, so I'm very familiar with him as a person and his game on the field. Yeah, he's a baller. He was one of the running backs that had the better rushing games against us last year.
"So, I'm super excited for him to be here."

title: Spurry's big night pace Talbot in opener
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Spurry's big night pace Talbot in opener

 June 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nathan Spurry was in a closer's role this spring for St. Michaels High's baseball team.Tuesday night he showed he's a pretty fair starter as well.
Spurry hurled a complete game and drove in Nico Nicolopoulos with the winning run in the bottom of the sixth inning, lifting Talbot Post 70 to a 4-3 victory over four-time defending Eastern Shore North Division American Legion champion Caroline Post 29 at Warrior Field.
"Just came out here trying to throw strikes; trying to produce ground balls, get outs," Spurry said.
Mixing a cutter with fastballs, Spurry allowed only two runners to reach base over the first three innings — one on an error, the other on a fielder's choice in the second inning.
Down 3-0, Caroline (0-1-1) scratched across a pair of runs in the fourth. Austin Frank drilled a leadoff double to center field. Colton Maans walked and was lifted for courtesy runner Wes Thomas. Eric Deck (2 for 3) singled to center, scoring Frank. Gavin Whitby (2 for 3) singled to load the bases before Johnny Radcliff grounded out, scoring Thomas to make it 3-2
But Spurry ended the threat there, getting a strikeout before catcher Nicolopolous alertly grabbed a ball that was chopped in front of the plate and tagged Caleb Cole for an inning-ending, unassisted putout.
Caroline rallied to pull even in the top of the sixth on Whitby's one-out RBI single. Again, Spurry escaped any further damage, retiring two of the next three batters to keep it at 3-3 heading into the home half of the sixth.
"Threw strikes," Talbot manager Albert Pritchett said of Spurry, who finished with four strikeouts and two walks. "Got ahead of every batter, mixed it up. Very impressive."
Talbot (1-0) took a 1-0 lead in the home first. Frank issued back-to-back walks to Gavin Murphy and Couper Barletta. Two batters later, Pearson Greenwood laced a double to right field, plating Murphy. Frank squelched the rally there, getting Ethan Royer to pop out and Jesus Crespo on a comebacker to the mound.
Post 70 pushed its lead to 2-0 in the second. Brennen Griffin (2 for 2) hit a leadoff single and Nathan Merchant walked. Spurry then hit an 0-2 offering into left-center field for a double that scored Griffin. Again Frank extinguished a potential big rally, striking out the next three straight batters.
Talbot made it 3-0 in the third, as Tim McGuckin worked a leadoff walk, stole second, advanced to third on Greenwood's groundout to first, and scored when Crespo singled sharply to left field.
Caroline pulled even in the sixth before Talbot moved back in front in the home sixth. Nicolopoulos worked a leadoff walk against Post 29 reliever Chase Hitchens then stole second. Hitchens came off the mound to catch Brody McDaniel's bunt attempt for the first out. Nicolopoulos advanced to third on an errant pickoff attempt. Spurry then grounded out deep in the hole at shortstop, allowing Nicolopolous to score what proved to be the winning run.
"Knocked in the winning run for himself," Pritchett said of Spurry. "Nice game.
"First game, little rusty," said Pritchett, who was without Cullen Murphy, Josh Dressler and Anthony Massaro Tuesday. "Some of the guys haven't played since high school (season ended). We could have had a few more runs, but I think the hitting will come around."

title: QACHS wins inaugural Maryland High School Skeet Team Championship
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QACHS wins inaugural Maryland High School Skeet Team Championship

 June 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Sports 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SUDLERSVILLE — Queen Anne's County High School Clay Target Team came away with the victory against skeeters from Kent Island High School Clay Target Team and the Easton High School Clay Shooting Team during the inaugural Maryland State High School Skeet Championship at Sudlersville Skeet Club June 7.Queen Anne's County High School brought home the championship with a team total of 460, followed by Easton High School with a score of 439.
Shooting skeet throughout the morning, the three high schools also competed in a "War on the Shore" Trap Tournament for bragging rights in the afternoon, and students earned individual honors in their respective divisions.
Despite a morning downpour, "the kids persevered and conquered the weather adversities to finish up in the sunshine," Queen Anne's County High School Clay Target Team Head Coach Nathan Powell said.
"We are ecstatic with the performance of our student athletes, and the great competition from Easton and Kent Island. All of these student athletes are amazing young adults. The growth and expansion of our league continues across the Mid-Shore, and we look forward to competing with even more teams next year," he said.
Kent Island High School was the first public high school in the state of Maryland to establish a skeet team. With Easton and Queen Anne's recently established clubs, there were finally enough for a tournament, Kent Island Clay Target Team Head Coach Sean Connolly said.
Student athletes couldn't be more excited to pit their skills against local schools, he said.
A non-traditional sport that focuses on hand eye coordination, clay target shooting is an inclusive, unique and growing outlet for kids who might not otherwise compete in sports, he said.
Coming in second overall for the championship was Easton High School, which also won first place in their conference during the Maryland State High School Clay Target League earlier this year, notable as the club is only in its first year, according to Head Coach Joe Cap.
"The fact that we've come this far is pretty exceptional," he said, "Practice makes perfect, and the students put in a lot of hard work and a lot of hours. It's very exciting and a long time coming."
The sport has seen support and sponsorship from the local community, and the team also does a lot to pay that forward, according to Cap, including visiting county government departments, the sheriff's office, and the Waterfowl Festival.
Seeking to expand youth shooting sports across Maryland, the skeet coaches are happy to help schools seeking to establish their own clubs.
"We have done a lot to grow this sport in a short time, and we aren't done yet. Whoever has interest, we'll help them out," Connolly said.
"The more teams and the more kids we have, the better for everybody," Cap said.

title: Man completes Eagleman after non-Hodgkins lymphoma
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Man completes Eagleman after non-Hodgkins lymphoma

 June 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 389
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — For Craig Casterella, mind over matter is more of a lifestyle than a saying. This was especially true on Sunday, when Casterella finished the Ironman 70.3 Eagleman in six and a half hours.The triathlon, held in Cambridge, consisted of a 1.2-mile swim, a 56-mile bike ride and a 13.1-mile run.
"I cried at the end. I was ecstatic. I couldn't hold my emotions in, and it truly just goes to show that with determination, consistency and resilience, you can do so much in any facet of life," Casterella said.
The 31-year-old was inspired to train for the Eagleman in 2024 after a yearlong battle with non-Hodgkins lymphoma, a blood cancer most commonly found in older adults. Casterella said only 22,000 people a year get diagnosed with the disease, so it's important to create and spread awareness.
When Casterella was diagnosed in October of 2023, his perspective on life changed.
"Your life flashes before you. You start thinking about your past, you start thinking about your present and then about your future," he said. "And when younger people get diagnosed with a serious illness that is life or death, your future becomes so important, and you think about what you can accomplish and what you can possibly do before ending up in a coffin or six feet under. You start thinking about those things."
While going through chemotherapy, Casterella found a community on social media.
"Social media was my outlet to find others who were going through disease and illness, but also attacking life while going through disease and illness," he said. Online, Casterella fostered relationships with people who he now considers mentors.
Since going into remission, he uses social media to inspire others to "attack life," even when facing adversity.
Casterella said endurance sports are like going through a disease or illness. He had to endure a lot of things he didn't want to while going through treatment, but he saw it as a way to challenge himself mentally and physically, just like the triathlon.
"For me, coming out of this weekend, realizing that truly anything we set our minds to, dedicate, commit to, you can do anything. Don't just dream it. The things you wish you could do, just set goals will do it. I promise, it's never too late to start," he said.
Casterella plans on racing in another Eagleman in the near future.

title: Kent Island's Green, Henry, Woolley earn top honors
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Kent Island's Green, Henry, Woolley earn top honors

 June 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1261
 Words 

 Read News Document

 His approach was basic."I look at it pretty simply," Kent Island High boys head lacrosse coach Bobby Woolley said. "I can either send my seniors off in tears or send them off elated."
For the third time in four years, a group of Kent Island seniors walked off the field elated after earning the title of state champion.
"Anytime you put hardware on the shelf it's incredibly rewarding," Woolley said of the Bucs' 13-12 victory over Stephen Decatur on May 20 in the Class 2A state final at Stevenson University in Owings Mills. "Nothing beats the feeling of putting them in a position to be so happy to kind of cap off their career as a Buccaneer."
Woolley admitted this 17-1 championship season, which had a vibe of family and sacrifice from start to finish, carried an added dimension for him, having been around this senior class since they were kids.
"It added a little extra joy just because I've seen these guys grow up from little kids to early, budding young men," Woolley said. "To see that they could go out with three out of four as a graduating class was pretty special."
Wedged in that graduating class were midfielder Keegan Green, named the North Bayside Offensive Player of the Year by division coaches, and Gavan Henry, selected the North's Defensive Player of the Year.
"Gavan matured into a senior leader, which was kind of the hope for him," Woolley said. "Really led by example through his actions on the field. Settled into a role that wasn't just, take away the ball at all costs, but fit into the position that we needed. And stats piled up for him, but with a disciplined approach."
Henry, who is headed to Merrimack (Massachusetts) College to play, scooped 53 ground balls, forced 12 turnovers, picked up two assists, and scored six goals, including the game-winner against Decatur in the regular-season clash between the two schools.
But his biggest impact may have been helping freshman goalie Quinn Burns settle in between the pipes.
"No way I could measure that," Woolley said of Henry's helping build up Burns through the season. "He was instrumental in Quinn's confidence. A voice of reason, when like any freshman doubts himself, and continued to pour belief into the young guy. By the time the end of the season hit it was valuable."
While Henry was a steady anchor on the defensive end, Green helped fill the huge void created on the offensive end with the graduation of Tucker Claxton, the 2024 North Offensive Player of the Year.
"Last year, everybody will tell you, it was the Tucker Claxton show," Woolley said. "We had to lean so heavily on him being the guy. We still knew that there was room for us to have a guy, but an unselfish, do-whatever-he-could-to-help-supplement the offense (guy). So he (Green) was more of a sparkplug to the rest, which made him just critically important to the overall success of that offense."
Green was the Bucs' second leading goal scorer with 38, doled out 11 assists, had 49 points — third best on the team — and collected 14 ground balls.
"He was everything we longed for in a three-year process," Woolley said of Green, who is headed to Frostburg to play. "To watch it come to fruition. … He just grew into a big body that could attack the goal downfield, but still had the finesse of an attackman from his younger years. So he was a real nice threat, left-handed, right-handed, that put a lot of points on the board for us."
Selected North Coach of the Year by his peers, Woolley said this season wasn't about seeking redemption after falling shy of a three-peat last year in the state semifinals.
"I would say the idea was to pick up where we left off, knowing we had a great group of senior leadership intact that we could really pour into," said Woolley, whose team's lone loss was against Decatur in the Bayside championship. "Fortunately, we had those guys a bunch of years. We knew them as little guys growing up. And we knew the future for this year was so promising with the return of Eric Hofmann coming back from his ACL tear.
"It was a matter of trying to start the season as fast as we could, taking a little bit less of an approach to installation and more of a, let's get up the pace as fast as possible so we can really find our stride heading into May, versus letting May kind of build, build, build," Woolley said. "I think we were excited at our potential earlier than past years."
Here's a look at this year's all-North Bayside teams:
First Team
Attack
Mark Rees, Sr., Kent Island: Led the Bucs in assists with 35 and scored 17 goals for 52 points, which ranked second on the team. He also picked up 30 ground balls.
Brian Rees, Jr., Kent Island: Mark's younger brother, Brian netted a North Bayside-high 43 goals and 54 points. He dished out 11 assists and snagged 29 ground balls.
Jamison Kendall, Jr., Queen Anne's: Scored his 100th career goal in the Lions' playoff loss to Kent Island. Led Queen Anne's with 32 goals and 43 points. Finished with 11 assists and 19 ground balls.
Campbell Taliaferro, Sr., Easton: With the graduation of their three leading scorers from 2024, Taliaferro stepped in to become one of the Warriors' top scoring threats, totaling 13 goals and 16 assists (29 points) to go with 39 ground balls and seven caused turnovers.
Midfield
Aidan Henry, Sr., Kent Island: Bound for St. Mary's College, Henry was yet another scoring option for the Bucs and finished with 25 goals, 13 assists (38 points) and 22 ground balls.
Jackson Shiley, Jr., Queen Anne's: Passed out a team-high 19 assists to go with 16 goals (35 points) and 31 ground balls.
Long Stick Midfielder
Eric Hofmann, Sr., Kent Island: After missing 2024 with an injury, Hofmann returned as a stabilizing force in the Bucs' title run, scooping 61 ground balls and scoring seven goals. Headed to Harford Community College.
Short Stick Defensive Midfielder

Faceoff Specialist

title: Little League Home Run Derby gives players chance to participate nationally
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Little League Home Run Derby gives players chance to participate nationally

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 293
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Friday, Denton Little League hosted the Little League Home Run Derby to give players a chance to participate in the T-Mobile Little League Home Run Derby at the Little League World Series.Youth leagues around the nation host a qualifier for the event in hopes of one of their players being selected to participate in the regional qualifier, then the national event.
"It's a lot of fun for the kids from our league to come out, and we actually have kids from around the Mid-Shore in other leagues, and so obviously it just gives them the opportunity potentially be a part of something bigger with the the T-Mobile Home Run Derby," said Kyle Bringman, president of Denton Little League.
After the derby, the league officials sends the scores to T-Mobile, who selects who well be sent to the state or regional qualifier round.
While no players from Denton have been selected to participate in the national home run derby in the past, Bringman says the players enjoy the event and the possibility.
"It's awesome," Bringman said. "The kids have a blast with it. Everybody in our league is all together. The players all know each other. They all know who can come out and can hit home runs. So, it's fun to to watch them cheer each other on and compete against each other."
While the season has ended for the little leaguers, all-star tournaments are right around the corner.
The all-star tournaments gives players a chance to make a bid to participate in the Little League World Series, if the teams can win the tournament, state games and regional championships.
"We've got a lot of talent amongst our three teams at the younger age group, so it's going to be pretty neat to see," Bringman said.

title: Easton police join athletes in carrying the torch for Special Olympics
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton police join athletes in carrying the torch for Special Olympics

 June 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 321
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Special Olympics Maryland athletes joined with police officers on Tuesday to carry the torch through Easton.Beginning on Dover Street, a group of around 100 athletes, families, law enforcement officers and community members participated in Talbot County's leg of the Law Enforcement Torch Run, an annual tradition to raise money for the Special Olympics. They brought along the Special Olympics torch, called the Flame of Hope, as they traversed the downtown streets of Easton.
Officers from the Easton Police Department and Talbot County Sheriff's Office, as well as local officials such as Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Talbot County Council member Dave Stepp, participated in the event. Some local organizations stood outside to cheer on the athletes, including employees from the Town of Easton offices and Rauch Inc.
Walking down Harrison Street, athlete Hannah McNiece beamed with joy alongside Easton officer Cordero Proctor, as the two each placed a hand on the torch and led the entourage of athletes to the finish line at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department.
Some officers and athletes took a running route through town and caught up with the walkers toward the finish.
Jill Garvey, management assistant for the Easton Police Department, helps organize the torch run. She said it means a lot when the athletes interact with law enforcement and build relationships with the officers.
Other counties across the state participate in the torch tradition. Also on Tuesday, Queen Anne's County police officers joined with Kent Island High School students for the Law Enforcement Torch Run.
"This event is about more than a run, it's about promoting inclusion, dignity, and respect for every athlete," said Queen Anne's Sheriff Gary Hofmann in a press release. "We're honored to be part of this tradition and proud to stand alongside our partners and students in support of such a meaningful cause."
The Summer Games for Special Olympics Maryland athletes is set to take place this weekend at Towson University from Friday to Sunday.

title: Former Raven Mosley retires
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Former Raven Mosley retires

 June 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 823
 Words 

 Read News Document

 C.J. Mosley is ready to tackle life beyond playing football.A five-time Pro Bowl selection during an 11-year NFL career with the New York Jets and Baltimore Ravens, Mosley announced Thursday, his 33rd birthday, that he's retiring.
Mosley was released by the Jets in March after playing in just four games last season because of a toe injury and later a herniated disk in his neck.
A popular playmaker and leader during his career, Mosley made his announcement with a 2-minute, 10-second video post on his Instagram page titled "Once upon a time ..." that included highlights of his playing career.
"Today, it is time to wake up from my childhood dream and share it with the next generation," Mosley said. "I spent my whole life and career building my legacy. Now it's time to start a new chapter with new dreams. It won't be easy, but I'm here to tell you every sacrifice is worth it.
"When you wake up, what will your legacy look like?"
Mosley, the 17th overall pick by Baltimore in the 2014 draft out of Alabama, had nearly 1,100 tackles with 12 sacks, 12 interceptions, 10 forced fumbles, nine fumble recoveries and three touchdowns.
He played five standout seasons with the Ravens before signing a five-year, $85 million contract with the Jets in 2019 and was the heartbeat of New York's defense during his tenure as one of the NFL's top tacklers.
Both the Jets and Ravens posted congratulatory messages for Mosley on social media.
"Captain! Thankful for the memories we couldn't have asked for a better leader!" former Jets teammate and current Broncos defensive end John Franklin-Myers commented on Mosley's post.
"Half-Man Half-Amazing congrats on a great career bro," former Ravens teammate and current Baltimore assistant special teams coach Anthony Levine wrote.
Mosley, who is from Theodore, Alabama, was rated as one of the top high school linebackers in the country before heading to Tuscaloosa to play for Nick Saban and the Crimson Tide after getting offers from several top football programs.
He made a quick impact in college, earning Freshman All-American honors, and helped Alabama win consecutive BCS national championships during the 2011 and 2012 seasons. Mosley also was selected the SEC defensive player of the year and won the Butkus Award in 2013 as college football's top linebacker.
Mosley became the first Ravens player voted to the Pro Bowl as a rookie. He made the Pro Bowl three more times before leaving for New York and signing what was then the largest free agent deal for an inside linebacker.
Mosley had an impressive debut with the Jets with five tackles and returned an interception by Josh Allen for a touchdown against the Bills, but he injured his groin in the third quarter and played in just one more game that season.
He opted out in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic but returned the following season and reestablished himself as a consistent playmaker who routinely was among the NFL leaders in tackles while playing in all but one game during the next three years. Mosley, who made his final Pro Bowl in 2022, was voted a team captain during each season he played in New York.
Mosley also was praised by then-coach Robert Saleh and defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich in 2021 when the linebacker remade his body by slimming down from 250 pounds to 231 to be more mobile in New York's faster sideline-to-sideline defense.
He was limited to just four games last season by his toe and neck injuries, but said in January he didn't anticipate not playing again.
"My main goal is just to really get back to 100% so I can work out and run and do everything I need to, then just take it from there," Mosley said. "I mean, I don't have any thoughts about retiring or anything. So my main focus is just to make sure I'm 100% on the field and off the field."
Jamien Sherwood, who replaced Mosley last season when the veteran was injured, led the Jets in tackles and was re-signed to a three-year, $45 million contract in the offseason — signaling an end to Mosley's time in New York.
"C.J. was the epitome of a class act as a teammate, player and leader for the last six seasons," Jets owner Woody Johnson said in a statement when Mosley was released.
Sherwood said last week during the Jets' minicamp that he stays in close contact with Mosley, who lives near his former teammate.
"We always get our hair done together," Sherwood said with a smile. "So whenever the hair lady comes to town, we get our hair done. I actually just texted him just to check up on him because, again, without him, this process for me would not be possible.
"From the day I got here, he just poured into us. He let us know everything and I miss having him in the room. It's definitely a hole in the wall without him. ... He's my brother from another mother. And, you know, I love him."

title: Easton's Keenan steps down as coach
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton's Keenan steps down as coach

 June 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 826
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Dennis Keenan's answer came as it so often did — wrapped in humor."So, how long have you been thinking about stepping down coach?"
"Since I started," Easton High's boys head lacrosse coach of 26 years answered dryly before a slight laugh.
The winningest coach in program history who led the Warriors to their only state championship in 2015, Keenan stepped down at the end of this past season, citing a desire to watch his two youngest sons play in the collegiate ranks.
"When Ethan was playing the last two years in college, some of the games conflicted (with Easton's)," Keenan said of his son Ethan, who will be a junior eligibility-wise next season at Lebanon Valley College in Pennsylvania. "I want to watch his games. He's only got a couple years left."
Keenan, who led the Warriors to a 6-7 mark this season, said he also wanted to have time to watch his youngest son, Colin, possibly play at Anne Arundel Community College next spring.
"I think I put the program in a good position for the next guy," said Keenan, 57, who will continue teaching special education at the high school. "I had a lot of fun over the years with the players and the coaches. We had a lot of success, and I'd like to see it keep going. I'll still be around it. I offered to help when I could for whoever comes in to transition them."
Keenan, who played defense and was a backup goalie at New England College in New Hampshire, was a volunteer assistant at Easton in 1998. One year later, the Long Island native succeeded Andy Burke as Warrior head coach, a position he held with the exception of 2017 — when he had to sit out the season. The 2020 season was canceled due to COVID.
Over his 26-year run, Easton became one of the Bayside Conference's stronger programs, winning four regional titles, one Bayside Conference crown (2023) and the Class 2A-1A state championship in 2015 with an 8-4 come-from-behind victory over Southern of Anne Arundel.
"It's always a game you have to prepare for because he's the type of coach that's preparing for you," said Kent Island head coach Bobby Woolley, whose team's last North Bayside loss came against Easton in 2023.
According to Laxnumbers.com, Keenan moved into 20th place all-time for career victories among high school coaches in Maryland this spring, and retires with a record of 237-149.
Despite that record, Keenan often redirected praise toward his assistants through the years, which included Will Schmidt, Steve Hurley, Billy Murdoch, Kevin Parks, Bill Keswick, Joe Gamble, Scott Haddaway, Arlie Marshall, Irv Phillips, Bill Kirwan, Lenox Trams, Keith Berry, Tom Torrence, Walt Marciniak and David Baker.
"I had a bunch of great coaches and players," Keenan said. "They all made me look good."
And Keenan seemingly always looked to make the game fun.
"He's got a great sense of humor. He coaches with a sense of humor, and I think the players can relate to that, and respond well to that kind of coaching style," said Schmidt, whose had two coaching stints with Keenan covering close to 10 years. "He just has a great rapport with them and knows how to motivate them through humor without necessarily being a screamer."
But Keenan, who's been known to jokingly tell people of his brutal daily commute to work — he lives across the street from the high school — admitted the humor may not have been as prevalent when he began.
"When I first started coaching I was like, 'We got to win. We got to do this stuff,'" Keenan said. "And then you realize the success you have is basically on the kids. That old saying you hear at the coaches' clinics, 'It's the Jimmys and Joes, not the x's and o's.' That humbles you a little bit and lets you know not many guys are going to play college lacrosse. So this was going to be the best time they were going to have, so we might as well have fun while we do it."
While one of the top 20 winningest high school coaches in state history, Keenan served on the Maryland Public Secondary School Athletic Association's state boys lacrosse committee, was an MPSSAA regional representative for 2A boys lacrosse, the Eastern Shore representative for the Maryland State Lacrosse Coaches Association, and the C. Markland Kelly Award coordinator for the best player in the state.
"He's done a remarkable job not just with the program, but with overall representation of the Bayside Conference pertaining to the Maryland State Lacrosse Coaches Association, the all-state selections, making sure kids get recognized for their hard work," Woolley said. "He's always been a leader in that regard."
Schmidt agreed.
"I don't think people realize how much Dennis contributed over there," Schmidt said. "I'm sure they do from a coaching perspective, all the time on the field and everything. But all the stuff he did at the state level. ... Pretty impressive. He's going to be definitely missed."

title: Competitors have a ball with Chestertown big bocce tournament
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Competitors have a ball with Chestertown big bocce tournament

 June 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 364
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With the weather warming up, it was perfect timing for some heated bocce ball competition.The Italian team sport where you aim to toss your ball closer to the target ball for points is big in Chestertown ever since founder of Ye Olde Towne Bocce League, Frank Hurst brought it to the area in 2013.
On June 14 at Wilmer Park, the League held their annual tournament for the spring season, drawing a generous crowd of onlookers and players.
The last two teams remaining out of the 50 competing on Tuesdays and Thursdays were the Scalawags (Tuesday's reigning champ) and Pour Decisions (Thursday's champ).
In the end, winning 17-14 due to a skilled roll of the ball by Judge Anthony, the Scallawags took the trophy for the spring season.
Pour Decisions fought to the very end, nearly causing an upset, being down at one point, 5-10, before chipping away at the Scallawags lead.
"We almost had them," said Pour Decisions player DeLia Shoge, enjoying the moment with her team.
The tournament lasted for about two hours and the crowd enjoyed ice cream, cold beer and the musings of Zane Carter providing the play-by-play.
"Everyone young and old can join in play. It's a great social game," said Stu Cawley watching with amusement from the sideline.
The rules are easy and accessible for anyone interested. In bocce, teammates take turns throwing their ball towards a pallino — a 'bullet' or 'little ball in Italian — the target ball and the first one in play.
Next, both teams try to underhand roll or throw their ball closest to the pallino. Only the team that gets their ball closest, scores for that frame or round.
When it is too difficult to tell who got closest with the naked eye, judges with measuring tapes determine that. This happened often during the tournament.
Jim Mason, commissioner of the League thanked everyone for coming out, and invited anyone interested in participating to the fall season.
And why should you come out? Because if you are a Chestertown resident, the odds are good that somebody you know is already playing, said an enthusiastic crowd member.
So come be a part of the sport that took over the town before the pickle ball craze hit.

title: Queen Anne's girls wrestling team honored for second state championship
author: DOUG BISHOP
content:
Queen Anne's girls wrestling team honored for second state championship

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DOUG BISHOP | Section: Local News 
 
 477
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — On the evening of May 17, the Centreville American Legion, Jeff Davis Post 18, hosted the Queen Anne's County High School girls wrestling team for a banquet celebrating their second consecutive state championship. The team, along with their coaches, was presented with state championship rings for the second consecutive year.The 2024 state tournament was the first-ever state championship tournament for girls wrestling in Maryland, and Queen Anne's County High School won the inaugural title. The team graduates only two wrestlers this year, just as they did in 2024. Winning consecutive state championships is a rare feat in any sport, underscoring the strength of the coaching staff and the team's commitment.
The banquet, prepared by the Legion's Auxiliary members, and the championship rings were made possible through donations from the community.
Each of the 20 girls on the team received a championship ring. The players included seniors Ally Conley and Kaylynn Bryant; juniors Linda Vail, Lilly Hammond, Faith Connolly, Addie Dickens, Bree Conard, Maggie Rooney, Morgan Morris, Lilly Tyree, Cora Fellows and Shayla Watson; sophomores Annalise Michael, Celeste Molina, Bevyn Branham, Adyson Kendall, Emmy Falcone and Emma Coppage; and freshmen Sophie King and Bella Voss.
Girls head coach John Waters, boys head coach and founder of the girls team David Stricker and assistant coaches Rondell Bryant, Frank Conley, Tasha Jackson, Dawn Schipul Kelly, Kendra Kofffee, Kai Richards, Jimmy Swindell and Wendy Zottarelli also received rings.
Waters credits the team's success to his assistant coaches, noting that having nine assistant coaches is exceptional for any school team. The possibility of continued success next year was discussed during the banquet. While no one mentioned another state championship, the coaches expressed pride in the team's achievements. With 10 juniors and six sophomores returning, the potential for a third consecutive state championship is strong. Achieving this will depend on goal-setting, offseason work and the passion to excel individually.
Coach Dawn Schipul Kelly, introduced by Waters as the daughter of the late Andy Schipul, a prominent figure in Queen Anne's County wrestling, offered an inspiring message.
"I saw our team become a family during the season, as we all cheered for each other's success," she said. "I remember a wise man, my father, saying this: 'In the face of adversity, your success comes down to yourself, your family and your community.' I saw each of you dig deep, grow as a family, and become champions. Ladies, hold your heads high with what you accomplished."
The success of girls' sports at Queen Anne's County High School has been remarkable in recent years. Four years ago, the girls' softball team won the state championship. The following year, the girls' field hockey team made it to the state championship match. Last year, the girls' wrestling team claimed the title, and earlier this school year, the girls' soccer team took home the state championship. Now, girls' wrestling has done it again.

title: Cassell, Palmer, Femi lead all-star cast
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Cassell, Palmer, Femi lead all-star cast

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1738
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Brian Femi's mind was made up."I said before the season, he's going to be the best hitter we face all year," St. Michaels High's longtime head baseball coach said of Easton senior Dylan Cassell. "I think some people were a little skeptical. He is the best hitter I think in the North Bayside. I just felt that."
After watching Cassell take a pair of potential extra-base hits away from Connor Wheeler during the Saints' 7-1 victory over Easton on April 14, Femi may have also felt Cassell was one of the best right fielder's his team faceD this year.
"The two catches he made are as good as any I've ever seen in high school baseball," Femi said after the game. "I mean they were unbelievable. He kept them in the ball game.
"I didn't have knowledge of how good a defender he was," Femi continued. "We always had trouble getting him out. And now you put these defensive plays on top of it. Just a complete player. I hope he continues to play somewhere because he's just a talented player. But on top of that he is a first-class young man."
That combination helped Cassell earn the North Bayside Player of the Year as voted on by division coaches.
"Probably the best offensive season I've seen in a while," Easton head coach Albert Pritchett said of Cassell. "And I think he made one error. The ball went to right field, we knew it was going to get caught."
The last of the Cassell brothers to come through Easton's program, Dylan led the Warriors (11-7) in almost every offensive category this season, including hits (29), runs scored (28), home runs (three), triples (five), RBIs (33) and slugging percentage (.757). He was second on the team in hitting with a .414 average, shared the team lead for doubles (five) with Dustin Blue, and finished with a .429 on-base percentage.
"It's his ability to swing the bat as hard as he can and make contact," Pritchett said of Cassell's success at the plate. "Lot of kids swing hard and lot of kids miss the ball. He didn't swing and miss a lot. When he swung he hit."
Femi noted a few other elements in Cassell's approach at the plate.
"I think his pitch selection is really good," Femi said. "He doesn't chase balls out of the zone. And to be a good hitter, you've got to keep the barrel in the zone for a long period of time. Two people that just come to mind when I think that are he and (St. Michaels') Will Sherwood. Their barrels stay in the zone so long, it gives you like a margin of error. And you're still going to get the barrel on it because they get in the zone early and they stay in the zone. And that's what makes them tough."
Among those making life tough on hitters this season was Queen Anne's County's Noah Palmer. Named the North Bayside's Pitcher of the Year, Palmer helped the Lions go 12-9 overall, 7-1 North Bayside en route to their first division title since 1980.
"A lot of times from a junior to a senior, I've seen it where they just don't feel like they have the same drive that they did going into their junior season," Queen Anne's head coach Rick Sutch said of players. "But he (Palmer) kept pretty much the same intensity level from his junior season all the way up through this year."
A senior right-hander, Palmer went 5-3 with a 2.07 earned-run average. He allowed 14 earned runs and 32 hits over 47 1/3 innings, struck out 49 and walked 31.
"He pitched against every team that was a big factor in our conference or outside our conference," Sutch said of Palmer, who is headed to Chesapeake College. "I think he was 5-1 in conference with a .83 ERA. Everything in 2A he pretty much dominated."
Palmer beat Easton during the regular season, and went five innings in the Lions' 8-4 victory over the Warriors in the 2A East Region II semifinals.
"Got ahead early, threw strikes early," Pritchett said. "Didn't walk anybody. Challenged hitters when necessary. I thought his cutter-slider was probably one of the better out-pitches that I saw all year. Hard thrower but also a smart pitcher."
Palmer finished the year batting .339 with 20 hits, including five doubles and two homers. He drove in 17 runs and had a .477 OBP.
Femi was chosen Coach of the Year after leading St. Michaels to a 16-6 mark and a 10th appearance in the 1A state championship, where the Saints lost 6-2 to Allegany.
"We thought we had a chance to make a little run," Femi said. "I didn't anticipate going as far as we did. But this team just kept getting better. As the year went on they just kept progressing.
"And we got a little break there with Colonel (Richardson) getting knocked out and us getting the number one seed (in the 1A East I Region), which meant they had to throw a pitcher," Femi added of the postseason. "We got lucky and didn't have to throw one. The cards fell for us."
The Saints were bidding for their sixth state title, but were denied by Allegany.
Here's a look at this year's all-North Bayside teams:
First Team
Jordan Regulski, Col. Richardson
Sr., RHP/Shortstop, First Base
Regulski capped an impressive high school career with a 5-1 record and a 1.42 ERA, striking out 80 over 44 1/3 innings. He batted .396 with 15 hits, including four doubles, three triples and one home run while helping Colonel to a 12-7 record. Drew 19 walks and stole 17 bases. Regulski is headed to Wake Forest University.
Kayden Webb, Easton
Sr., RHP/Center Field
Batted .400 and finished with 20 hits, including two doubles and three triples. He scored 26 runs, drove in 12 runs and had an .587 OBP. The ace of the Warriors staff went 4-2 with a 2.944 ERA, striking out 28 and walking 20. Bound for Salisbury University, Webb is set to play for the South squad in the Brooks Robinson High School All-Star Game on July 13 in Camden Yards.
Blake Bramble, North Dorchester
Sr., Third Base
Helped Eagles on a late-season five-game win streak that was ended by St. Michaels in the 1A East I final. Led North Dorchester in slugging percentage (.619), RBIs (11) and triples (four). Batted .333 with 14 hits, six runs, four doubles and a .356 OBP.
Travis Sutch, Queen Anne's
Sr., Left Field
Led the Lions in batting average (.418), hits (28), doubles (six) and RBIs (19), and shared the team lead for home runs with fellow first-team pick Nathan Procopio with three. Also had one triple, 17 runs, a .481 OBP and a 1.153 OPS. Plans to play at Chesapeake College.
Will Sherwood, St. Michaels
Sr., Right Field/RHP
Saints ace went 6-2 with a 1.48 ERA, yielding 11 earned runs over 52 innings. Sherwood logged four complete games, struck out 43 and walked 17. He led St. Michaels in hits (27), RBIs (25) and home runs (two). Batted .386 with 21 runs scored, six doubles, a triple and had a .522 OBP. Sherwood, who is headed to Chesapeake College, will also play for the South in the Brooks Robinson All-Star Game.
Connor Wheeler, St. Michaels
Jr., Center Field
Wheeler's nine doubles were a North Bayside high. He shared the team lead for stolen bases with 20, and finished the season with a .362 batting average, 25 hits, 18 runs, 14 RBIs and a .500 OBP.
Jack Grossi, Kent Island
Jr., Shortstop
Proved a steady for the Bucs (8-10) at short and the plate. Batted .370 and totaled 22 runs and 22 hits, including six doubles, three triples and a home run. Set a school record with 27 walks and finished with a .696 slugging percentage and .595 OBP.
Jacob Clough, Queen Anne's
So., Third Base
Another key part of the Lions' division title run, Clough played a solid hot corner and was one of the North's top closers. He finished the season batting .409 and was second only to Sutch with 27 hits. Hit five doubles, a triple, drove in 17 runs, and finished with a .500 OBP.
Wyatt Offutt, Kent Island
Sr., RHP/Outfield
Posted a 2-2 record with a 2.14 ERA. He recorded 40 strikeouts over 32 2/3 innings and notched a save. He was also a solid contributor at the plate, hitting .308 with five doubles, a home run, 10 RBIs and a .410 OBP. Slated to play at Wilmington University in Delaware.
Jack Walls, Col. Richardson
Jr., First, Third Base
Finished the season batting .349 with 15 hits, including four doubles, a triple and one homer. Drove in 10 runs and scored 25. Drew 13 walks and swiped 20 bases.
Austin Frank, North Caroline
Sr., Left Field/RHP
Frank went 2-0 during the regular season, allowing just two earned runs over 23 1/3 innings. He finished with 26 strikeouts and an 0.60 ERA. Was on the mound when the Bulldogs handed Bayside champion Stephen Decatur its first loss of the season, beat St. Michaels, and earned a postseason win against Kent Island. Is headed to Chesapeake College.
TJ Leonard, North Dorchester
Sr., Catcher
One of the conference's steadiest catchers, Leonard batted .367 with 11 hits, two doubles, 10 RBIs and seven runs. Had a .523 OBP.
Kashton Thomas, North Dorchester
So., Center Field
Led Eagles in batting average (.435), hits (20), runs (15), doubles (five) and OBP (.527). Thomas also drove in eight runs and posted a .543 slugging percentage.
Nathan Procopio, Queen Anne's
So., First Base/RHP
Batted .393 with 22 hits, one double, one triple, three home runs, and a team-high 19 runs. Finished the season with 17 RBIs, and OBP of .507, and a 1.114 OPS.
Second Team
Cambridge-SD: Tanner Coulbourne, Jr., RHP; Col. Richardson: Derrick Mitchell, Jr., LF; TJ Wenger, Sr., CF; Easton: Michael O'Connor, Sr, 1B; Chase Raab, Sr., LF; Kent Island: Derek Grossi, So., C/RHP; Brady Hart, Sr., 1B; Traise Woolford, Jr., OF; North Caroline: Lewis Higgs, Jr., CF; North Dorchester: Peyton Bleyer, So., LF; Manny Reyes, Jr., SS/DH; Queen Anne's: Dulin Clark, Sr., C; Noah Cramer, Sr., 2B/RHP; St. Michaels: Pearson Greenwood, Sr., C; Brock Grow, Jr., RHP/2B; Ethan Royer, Jr., SS; Blake Wheatley, Fr., 3B.
Honorable Mention
Cambridge-SD: Noah Marshall, Sr., C; Easton: Dustin Blue, Jr., SS/RHP; Colin Mooney, Sr., C; Kent County: Tanner Beck, Sr., SS/RHP; Kent Island: Logan Baierlein, Jr., OF/RHP; Aiden Bonds, Sr., 3B; Kevin Coe, So., 2B; Paul Horner, Sr., RHP; North Dorchester: Sutton Dukes, Sr., RHP; Queen Anne's: Chance Hegedus, So., SS; Brendan Parsley, Sr., CF; St. Michaels: Jack Brennan, Sr., Utility; Brennan Dean, Jr., 1B; AJ Dove, Fr., OF; Brandon Toadvine, Fr., 1B/LHP; Eli Wallace, Jr., RHP/DH.

title: Easton's cradle king stood for more than wins and losses
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton's cradle king stood for more than wins and losses

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1153
 Words 

 Read News Document

 He never won a title or set any records. And not once in three seasons on Easton High's wrestling team did he qualify for the regional or state tournament.But then wins and losses weren't what made Darren Foxwell stand out.
"The thing with Darren is he's such a unique person," Adonis Schmitt, a wrestling teammate, said of Foxwell, who died Wednesday, June 18, from injuries sustained in a single-car accident the day before.
That certainly fit the way Foxwell decided to briefly quit the wrestling team early this past season.
Easton's starter at 167 pounds, Foxwell didn't just stop coming to practice without explanation. He didn't try dodging head coach Jason Biringer or attempt to find a new way to class in an effort to avoid passing Biringer's room like he had every morning.
Instead, the 18-year-old sought out Biringer during his planning period in the teacher's lounge. He told his coach face to face he just couldn't do it anymore, and just wanted to enjoy his senior year.
Before leaving the lounge, Foxwell handed Biringer six envelopes. One was for Biringer. The other five were for Easton's assistant coaches. Each envelope contained a hand-written letter from Foxwell thanking Biringer and assistants Steve Culver, James Gardner, Chris Danels, Jason Perez and Josh Valdez for all they had done for him.
"It caught me off guard," Biringer said. "I was shocked when he gave it to me. Then I read it, and I was like, 'Oh my God. What does that tell us about him? What an outstanding kid.' He wrote how much I helped him and how much of an impact I had on him. A lot of times kids just ghost and disappear. You see them in the hall and they're like, oh, they don't want to confront you."
Not Foxwell. Maybe that's why a few days later, Biringer sought out Foxwell and pulled him from class.
"I was like, 'Darren, what's going on? Just talk to me,'" Biringer recalled. "He said he didn't know if he had the passion for it anymore and it was a lot of work. I was like, 'Well, what got you into wrestling, or what did you like about it that made you come back for three years?' He said how he felt when he would go out on the mat and win, bonding with his brothers on the team. I said, 'You really want to give it up?' And he said, 'I don't know if I really do coach.'
"I said, 'Well, would you want to come back because I know we need a senior on our team with the affect you have. You're someone who's always trying hard and showing, not telling, kids what to do. They follow your lead.'"
Less than a week later, Foxwell was back on the team going through the grueling and exhaustive two-hour practices.
He was again having his face shoved into the mat, perhaps with the help of a forearm on the back of his head or neck. He was again running the risk of having his ears shaped into cauliflowers. He was again drilling, working on takedowns and escapes. He was again leaving the room drenched in sweat.
And he was again trying to help everyone around him.
"He could be having a bad day, a good day, it didn't matter," said Schmitt, who along with Foxwell accounted for the two seniors on the team. "He came to practice. He practiced hard. Those that he practiced with, and everybody around him, he lifted up. He made them better. No matter if it was a little bit, a lot, he made each and everyone of us better."
Biringer noticed and a little over a month after his return named Foxwell captain.
"He came back, and he was just so committed," Biringer said. "That was one of the things we pointed out at the awards night, just how he came back. He was just so motivated. He was just a positive presence honestly. The other wrestlers looked up to him. He has such a good, gentle demeanor that he was just very well liked. And kids loved to interact with him and that made him a good leader.
"Even off the mat," Biringer said. "Every morning he would walk past my room and he was like, 'Morning coach.' He just had one of those infectious smiles that your'e like, 'It's always good to see Darren.'"
Foxwell had earned the title of captain. He'd also earned a nickname along the way — cradle king, for his knack for using his 6-foot-3 frame to catch the neck of an opponent with one arm while wrapping the other arm behind the opponent's knees, creating a nice bundle.
"Just during practice, randomly, out of nowhere," said Schmitt, who along with teammates Esteban Velesquez and Wahaab Popal slapped Foxwell with the moniker. "He'd be in the craziest position and he'd just strike cradle. Like you'd be ready to go live (in practice). The next thing you know, you're on your back, pinned by cradle by the one and only cradle king."
Biringer laughed.
"He could be down 12-0 and then all of a sudden he would just lock a kid up and pin him," Biringer recalled. "And you'd just be shaking your head, saying, 'Oh, my gosh.' I remember James (Gardner) the first time this year we were in a match and he's getting beat. James is like, 'Don't worry.'"
Foxwell went 16-14 this season. After a loss, his unique side often resurfaced. The senior captain wouldn't storm off the mat in a rage or see if he could make history by trying to become the first to throw his headgear through a wall. Instead, Foxwell would check his disappointment, hit a quick reversal and return to encouraging his teammates in the matches that followed.
"He didn't like to lose," Schmitt said. "Over time it did get to him to a point where I know he was considering leaving. But he didn't leave. He stayed for the sake of the team. He stayed for the sake of the bond. He stayed for the sake of his peers and everybody that looked up to him."
Teammates weren't the only ones that looked up to Foxwell.
One of the requirements for Easton wrestlers is to help with the youth program that includes wrestlers ages 6 to 13. But Biringer noticed Foxwell lingering more and more after practice.
"I started noticing Darren hanging around.," Biringer said. "I was like, 'What are you doing?' He was like, 'I'm going to stick for these little guys.' And he stayed pretty much every youth practice just on his own volition, and he would work with these little kids.
"He wouldn't be able to stay all the time, and the kids were like, 'Is Darren going to be here?'" Biringer added. "I was like, 'No, he had to go home and do something.' And they were like, 'Awe, man.' So he obviously bonded with these little guys."
Those were the things that made Darren Foxwell stand out.

title: AN UNEXPECTED PATH ENDS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
AN UNEXPECTED PATH ENDS

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 846
 Words 

 Read News Document

 He'd played a handful of sports.There was T-ball, which naturally progressed into Easton Little League baseball. He was a member of the inaugural FC Tred Avon Rec Soccer League in 2016 and eventually went on to play two seasons with G.R. Cannon's Shore FC group. He even took a swing at tennis.
Once he was at Easton High though, wrestling became Darren Foxwell's primary sport.
Lacrosse?
Well, yeah he was raised in Talbot County, where many grew up with a rattle in one hand and a lacrosse stick in the other. And yes, he'd heard his father, Len Foxwell, former Easton Little League president, rant plenty of times about how the lacrosse fields at the North Easton Sports Complex were literally on higher ground than the baseball fields, which required so much more preparation after a good rain.
Darren came to lacrosse late. He made Easton's lacrosse team but lost his sophomore season after suffering a season-ending knee injury wrestling. He was back on varsity his junior and senior seasons, but he saw little playing time as a backup long-pole defenseman.
But in February of this year, lacrosse — college lacrosse that is — came to Darren via an out-of-the-blue phone call.
"I'll never forget this as long as I live," Len Foxwell said. "I was out having dinner with friends and Darren texted me and said, 'Hey, do you have a second? I want to run something by you regarding college.'
"I didn't know what he was talking about," Len continued. "I'm thinking, has he decided he doesn't want to go to Chesapeake (College) or Wor-Wic? Because that was the plan. He was going to go to community college and then eventually transfer probably to Salisbury."
Len pardoned himself from his dinner guests, stepped outside, took his son's call, and couldn't believe what he was hearing.
"'Dad, I have gotten an offer to play lacrosse at Bethany College,'" Darren told his father, adding he was going to receive financial assistance from the Division III school in West Virginia.
Len initially sensed a prank.
"I said, 'Darren, whatever number they called you on call it back and see who answers,'" Len said. "'Cause I thought it was a joke. Darren said, 'No. It's real. I've been talking to this coach (Bethany's Harold Palone III).'"
Len still wasn't convinced. Struggling to digest everything, he decided to make a direct call to Palone, who was entering just his second year as Bison head coach.
"We're talking, he's going a mile a minute, talking about his plans for Darren, 'How we need a long pole. This guy has left.' And I finally just said, 'Coach, just hold on for one second. I don't want this to be taken the wrong way, but why have you recruited Darren? He didn't get a lot of playing time,'" Len said.
What the senior defenseman did get though was a favorable report from longtime Easton head coach Dennis Keenan, who loved Darren's sense of humor.
"I think he was funnier than he actually thought he was," Keenan said. "The things he would say would just crack me up."
But Keenan also thought Darren had possibilities.
Coaching his final season, Keenan noted Foxwell's 6-foot-3 height. He added Darren had the wingspan of a pterodactyl and that he had gained upper body strength from being on Easton's wrestling team for three years. Keenan filed all that in the report he submitted on FieldLevel, a national athletic recruiting network that helps athletes and coaches find the right fit for potential prospects. A report that started Palone on the recruiting trail for Darren.
"'The only thing he lacks is experience and refinement,'" Foxwell recalled Palone saying during their phone conversation. "'And we can teach that. He's got the raw tools we need.'"
Darren committed with Bethany in March.
"He was getting better each day," Keenan said of Darren. "You could see flashes of brilliance. He was just a late bloomer; just a late starter. He had a bright future ahead of him."
Len felt the same way.
"This was a way to fuse those mental and physical attributes," Len said. "He had finally found his athletic path."
That path ended fatally just three weeks after Darren had graduated from Easton.
In the early morning of June 17, Darren sustained injuries as a passenger in a single-car crash outside Trappe. He was transported to Shock Trauma in Baltimore for treatment of life-threatening injuries. One day later, Darren Foxwell died. He was 18.
Len Foxwell last saw his son alive on Father's Day when they had lunch together. As he pulled up in front of Darren's home, Len noticed the corrugated sign out front that read, "Bethany Bound" and remembered an earlier conversation.
"I had been so focused on getting him to the next step, somehow getting him prepared for college," Len said. "And I said, 'Darren, these next four years at Bethany are going to be the best of your life.' And he said, 'These are the best years of my life right now at Easton High School. I have my friends here. I have it pretty good.' He cherished everything about his high school experience and being with his friends and brothers."

author: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
111 kids start Fourth with a bang at triathlon

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Dorchester 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge is known for its triathlons. On the Fourth of July, children as young as 6 years old participated in their own triathlon, the Gerry Boye Firecracker Kids Triathlon.The event saw 111 children from 6 to 15 years old competing in swimming, cycling and running, just like in the full marathon. For the Firecracker, the distances were greatly pared down for the young athletes who competed in five groups based on their age.
The swim was done in the YMCA pool with 6 and year old swimming 25 yards, the length of the pool; 8 and 9 year olds swimming 50 yards; 10 and 11 year old swimming 100 yards; 12 and 13 year olds swimming 150 yards; and 14 and 15 year old swimming eight lengths of the pool, 200 yards.
All athletes competed in a 2-mile bike ride that also allows for training wheels the youngest competitors. The triathlon capped off with a run of 1 kilometer for 6 to 10 year olds and a full mile for the older competitors.
There were 35 volunteers who helped set up the course, provide traffic control and assist the young athletes in each event.
"It truly takes a village to make it happen each year, and we are deeply grateful to the dedicated volunteers who make it possible," race director Lynn Stewart said.
Proceeds from the event go to scholarships for graduating high school students. This year scholarships were awarded to:
Kevin Banda-Perez, North Dorchester High School.Rodney Harris, Cambridge-South Dorchester High School.Isabelle Hughes, Cambridge-South Dorchester High School.Camryn Russum, Cambridge-South Dorchester High School.
According to Stewart, the Gerry Boyle Firecracker Kids' Triathlon was launched in 2012 by Cambridge Multi-Sport to give local children a fun, confidence-building introduction to the sport. The late Gerry Boyle — who served as race director for both Ironman 70.3 Eagleman and Ironman Maryland and was instrumental in bringing races to Cambridge in 2014 — was a passionate supporter of the Firecracker.
As a comparison to the Firecracker triathlon, the Ironman covers 140.6 miles, comprising a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike ride and a 26.2-mile run.
Since his death in 2019, the Firecracker race has carried Boyle's name and honors his legacy, she said.
