title: New pickeball courts open in Hurlock amid ongoing tension
author: Lily Tierney
content:
New pickeball courts open in Hurlock amid ongoing tension

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 288
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — After much contention between pickleball and tennis players ultimately culminating in the vandalization of the Glasgow Tennis Courts in Cambridge, Dorchester County's Recreation and Parks Director Duc Trieu is seeking to solve the problem by creating a new space for pickleballers in Hurlock.After the Dorchester County Council received numerous requests to provide more pickleball courts, the county allocated funds to resurface three tennis courts at the Hurlock Athletic Center.
Two courts have been transformed into four dedicated pickleball courts while the third tennis court has blended pickleball lines and portable nets, according to Dorchester County Recreation and Park's official Facebook page.
While residents online say this is a major win for pickleballers in Hurlock, those in Cambridge are still hoping for dedicated courts in the near future.
"This is great…hoping we can get dedicated pickleball courts in Cambridge one of these days. So happy for Hurlock residents!" Karen Lewis Tecce said in a reply to Dorchester County Recreation and Park's post.
The Glasgow Tennis Courts currently do not allow pickleball due to a stipulation from the United States Tennis Association and the James G. Busick Tennis Foundation who funded the project. Under the grants guidelines, pickleball playing will not be allowed for at least five years on the resurfaced courts.
Some pickleballers took this personally, and in May of this year, vandalized the repaved courts with permanent marker and rocks.
The pickleballers of Dorchester pushed back at County Council meetings demanding outdoor court space.
"We are very mindful of that," County Manager Jerry Jones said. "We're not dismissive of what their concerns are."
Trieu said he appreciated that the County Council is trying to be proactive in finding everyone a space to play.
The new pickleball courts opened to the public on July 1.

title: Rockwell, Fisher net North's top honors
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Rockwell, Fisher net North's top honors

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1081
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Lexi Rockwell had always set goals."But I feel like she didn't realize how high she could set them early on," St. Michaels High head tennis coach Jordan Miller said of his No. 1 girls player. "And once she did it felt like she could do anything."
Well, the senior raised the bar higher than ever before this spring, wanting to earn player-of-the-year honors and win a state championship.
She did both.
Rockwell went undefeated in singles play, then slapped an exclamation point on her season by teaming with Tom Weller to win the Class 1A state title in mixed doubles, giving St. Michaels its first state tennis crown en route to earning the All-North Bayside Girls Player of the Year, as selected by the division coaches.
"She wanted to be player of the year and she wanted to win a state title," Miller said. "And she accomplished all those things by determination and hard work. She put in the hours, doing some extra running before and after practice, to make sure she was in good physical condition."
Rockwell also put a lot of time in playing against members of the Saints' boys team to give her more of a challenge during the year. The results were a 15-0 singles record and a 12-3 slate in doubles.
Her and Weller went 3-0 to win the Class 1A East Region I mixed doubles title, leading St. Michaels to a fourth straight regional team title. Rockwell and Weller then went 3-0 at states, which included a 6-1, 6-2 victory over Mountain Ridge's Marissa Greg and Aiden Pirolozzi in the final, earning the Saints' their first state crown of any sort in tennis and a runner-up finish in the team standings.
"She's very much an all-around player," Miller said of Rockwell, who finished the season 33-3. "One of the stronger girls' serves in the Bayside (Conference) for sure. Rock-steady from the baseline. Just never missed. Hit with good pace and depth. And she had a game plan that she executed every single time. It was start to the backhand, open up the court, and then hit the opposite way. And it worked very, very well."
Miller thought that game plan was one of the key pieces that gave Rockwell an added edge this season.
"She's been hitting a good ball since she was a freshman," Miller said. "Last year she did have a lot of good results," (which included reaching the 1A state girls doubles final with Lila Jones). "But I felt like she didn't really have her game plan. This year when she went out there, she knew what she was going to do. It didn't matter what the other person did across the net."
Named the North Bayside Coach of the Year, Queen Anne's County head coach Dee Fisher's objective for the season was vastly different than Rockwell's.
"My goal going into the season was to play 10 girls at every match, and to get all of my 28 players match time," Fisher said. "Twenty-five people actually played against another school, (some in) exhibition matches. And there was at least six or seven times where we had 10 different girls playing at a varsity match. That was my goal."
The Lions were also playing with a different label than any Fisher-led team had worn in his 25 seasons as head coach — defending Bayside champion.
"Nothing changed," Fisher said. "We just went out and they played. I always talk with my captains about what our lineup should look like because a lot of teams only play six people. They have their strongest four, they play doubles and singles, and then that's it. But a lot of times we change our lineup up. So we may have our top four players just play singles, and then everybody else play doubles. Or our top four play doubles and people play singles. It was more of a team effort."
No matter what the lineup, the Lions won, going 18-0 to win their second consecutive division and conference titles, and pushing their record to 35-1 over the past two seasons.
Fisher, who has forever preached to his players, "Just have fun and play," admitted he didn't feel any pressure this season until the tiebreaker of the Class 2A state girls doubles final, when sisters Lucy and Meg Taylor earned a 3-6, 6-3, 11-9 victory over Poolesville's Kyra McGlinchey and Pranahitha Kanuparthi, giving Queen Anne's its first-ever state title.
"This year we had so many people coming back, and I knew we were going to go all the way," Fisher said of winning the conference title. "It was never a question if we were able to win every match because I know how strong the girls were, and how great leaders they are."
Here's a look at the rest of this year's all-North Bayside teams:
First Team
Lucy Taylor, Sr., Queen Anne's
Went 9-6 at No. 1 singles and joined younger sister Meg to go 11-2 in doubles. The Taylors gave Queen Anne's its first state tennis title, winning the 2A state girls doubles championship. That was the first state title in girls doubles for a Bayside team since Cambridge-South Dorchester's Heidi McWilliams and Abby Messick won their second straight in 1991, ending the conference's longest drought in the state's five brackets.
Meg Taylor, Jr., Queen Anne's
The other half of Lions state doubles championship tandem, Meg compiled a 9-5 mark at No. 2 singles before going on to make school history with Lucy.
Maddie Tobat, Sr., North Dorchester
The school's valedictorian who also played lacrosse, Maddie went 14-1 in singles and doubles. Her and twin sister Jules won the Class 1A East Region II girls doubles championship, and came within a win of giving the Eagles their first state tennis title, falling in the 1A finals.
Jules Tobat, Sr., North Dorchester
North Dorchester's salutorian, Jules also played lacrosse and joined her sister to win the regional title in girls doubles before reaching the 1A state finals. Finished the year 14-1 in singles, 13-2 in doubles.
SECOND TEAM
Amy Wanex, Sr., Cambridge-SD; Taryn Brandt, Sr., North Caroline; Tess Weller, Jr., St. Michaels; Parker Jimenez, Jr., Easton; Hayden Legg, Sr., Queen Anne's.

title: Easton's Hershey named player of the year; St. Michaels Miller selected coach of the year
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton's Hershey named player of the year; St. Michaels Miller selected coach of the year

 July 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1326
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Easton High's Jake Hershey wanted another shot at the champ."Yes. He felt like there was a little unfinished business, and he knew he wanted to get back and have another chance at the same young man," Warrior boys head tennis coach Aaron Hutt said.
Hershey came within a win of becoming the first boys singles player to win a state title in school — and North Bayside — history a year ago, only to be denied by Poolesville's Andy Wu in the Class 2A final.
Carrying an 18-0 record into this year's state tournament, Hershey was on course for a rematch with Wu. That second chance was foiled though, when Hereford's Harry Smith defeated Hershey, 7-5, 6-2 in the semifinals.
With his hopes for a rematch and a state title gone, the recently-graduated Hershey could have easily packed his bag and made the long, slow drive back from the Wilde Lake Tennis Club in Columbia to Easton in heavy Memorial Day weekend traffic. Instead, the senior fell back on the family, friends and teammates that watched him play May 23.
"I owe a lot of that to my family and the people I was there with; my teammates," Hershey said of moving forward. "(Teammate) Clay Nagle, similar situation happened to him and his partner, Parker Jimenez (who lost in the mixed doubles semifinals). We went back (to the hotel), had a nice relaxing night. I think that's where the team aspect comes into it in moments like that, where they help you get yourself together when you might not be exactly where you want to be mentally."
Hershey returned the following day and defeated C. Milton Wright's Xavier Moaddel, 6-0, 6-4 in the third-place match, capping a 20-1 season in singles play that earned him the North Bayside's boys tennis player of the year as voted on by the division's coaches.
Nagle and Jimenez also rebounded from their semifinal loss, defeating Wilde Lake's Jakob Bluemner and Jillian Davis, 6-0, 6-0 in the third-place match in 2A mixed doubles.
"There's an old saying: You can let it go to your heart for a moment, but you can't let it go to your head," Hutt said of the disappointment that comes from a loss. "And he was able to compartmentalize that loss, granted being very upset. But after a few hours, he put it together and said, 'OK, next challenge.' It's a testament not just to his resilience, but the experience he's gotten from traveling and playing some pretty high-level tennis."
That experience helped Hershey go undefeated during the regular season in singles, compile a 14-1 record in doubles, and win a third straight Class 2A East Region II singles title. And though he did not get a second crack at Wu — who went on to win a third straight 2A state title — Hershey showed growth through the season.
"I think he matured, and his ability to not be his own worst enemy was apparent," Hutt said of Hershey, who was 57-2 over four years in the regular season, and intends to continue playing at Catholic University. "Last year, and past years, something might not go quite right and he internalized it automatically, forgetting that the other person has something to do with it as well. And that's kind of what greatness does. It looks at what it needs to do initially, and then it realizes, it's not just what I need to do, it's what I need to do to stop them as well. He got very good at that. Not only that, but being able to play every game as its own little match. He only lost a handful of games let alone sets."
St. Michaels' boys team didn't lose a match this season until the Bayside Conference championship, where it fell 4-3 to Stephen Decatur. But that was the lone blemish on a season of firsts for St. Michaels tennis, earning 11-year head coach Jordan Miller the North Bayside boys coach of the year.
"I knew we were going to be a very strong team," Miller said. "I worked with throughout the year most of the players that we see. So I know what we have. And I also know what everybody else has. I knew our guys were putting in a lot of work. And that was going to be very helpful."
One year after falling shy of the division via a 4-3 loss against North Caroline, St. Michaels dominated its North competition with an 18-1 overall record, winning 14 matches by 7-0 scores, and three others by 6-1 margins. The Saints not only won their first division title and reached the conference championship for the first time, they earned a fourth consecutive 1A East Region I crown.
St. Michaels wasn't quite finished though.
Lexi Rockwell and Tom Weller teamed to win the school's first state tennis championship, when they won the 1A mixed doubles crown. That effort, coupled with Sean Kline and Miles Fox finishing third in boys doubles, and Tess Weller placing fourth in girls singles, helped the Saints take runner-up honors in the 1A team competition at states — another program first — by just one point.
"It was definitely a good feeling," Miller said.
It may also prove to be good motivation for next season.
"I talked with my assistant (Casey Capute)," Miller said. "We didn't like coming home with the second-place trophy as a team for states. And we didn't like coming home with a second-place (at Baysides). I hate for us to be, 'OK, we got a state championship and we're happy with that.'
"Prior to coming back (as head coach), I never knew what we were capable of," added Miller, a St. Michaels graduate. "But the more I coached, the more I saw opportunities for us, if we could just get a few kids to really buy in. And now we've got quite a few more than a few kids that have bought in. And I think we're going to be able to hopefully maintain that for many years to come.
Here's a look at the rest of the this year's teams
FIRST TEAMSebastian Cousineau, So., Kent County
Became the first in school history to reach a state championship, where he lost in the 1A final to Boonsboro senior Hunter Liao, who became the state's first four-time state champion in boys singles. Cousineau was 13-2 in singles — his only other loss coming against Easton's Hershey — and 6-4 in doubles. The sophomore beat Colonel Richardson's Jeffrey Lin, 6-2, 6-4 to win 1A East I title.
Miles Fox, Jr., St. Michaels
Fox was 14-2 in singles, which included a win against Decatur at Baysides. Teamed with Sean Kline in doubles, posting a 16-0 conference record, and a 21-1 overall mark. The tandem beat Decatur at Bayside, won the 1A East I boys doubles title with a 6-0, 6-0 sweep of Perryville's Holden Coe and Tyler Loss, and reached the state semifinals. Defeated Southern Garrett's Ben Nazelrod and Shane Sisler, 6-1, 6-2 in consolation final.
Sean Kline, So., St. Michaels
Kline posted a 13-3 singles mark during the regular season, losing only to Hershey, Cousineau and Queen Anne's County's Tyler Olah — all first-team all-North picks.
Lost singles match against Decatur at Baysides before he and Fox won the boys doubles title at regionals and took third at states.
Tyler Olah, Sr., Queen Anne's
The Lions' No. 1 went 14-5 in singles, 8-5 in doubles. He won the 2A East I singles championship with a 6-2, 6-3 victory over North East's Brady Dvorak. Lost in 2A state quarterfinals to Poolesville's Wu.
SECOND TEAMTom Weller, Sr., St. Michaels; Clay Nagel, Sr., Easton; Christian Chase, Jr., North Dorchester; Bjorn Birkmire, So., Kent County; Will Taylor, Fr., Queen Anne's.

title: St. Michaels' Sherwood, Easton's Webb set to play in Robinson all-star game
author: Bill Haufe
content:
St. Michaels' Sherwood, Easton's Webb set to play in Robinson all-star game

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 805
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Neither has chased the dream of playing major league baseball."I've always loved the game of baseball," St. Michaels High graduate Will Sherwood said. "But I never thought of it as like big leagues. Maybe when I was real, real young. But I've always just loved to play. As long as I'm out there I don't really care what happens."
Easton High grad Kayden Webb echoed Sherwood's sentiment.
"It wasn't really something that I was trying to pursue," Webb said of a potential professional career. "Never really thought about that. I just kind of like playing the game of baseball."
Sherwood and Webb will be playing again this Sunday — only this time in a big-league park — as members of the South team in the annual Brooks Robinson High School All Star Game at Oriole Park at Camden Yards in Baltimore. The game is scheduled to start after Sunday's Orioles-Miami Marlins game.
"Awesome. Never thought I'd be playing there," said Sherwood, whose older brother Josh played in the 2022 all-star game. "Just happy to get the opportunity to play in a game like this."
"Just excited," said Webb, the first Easton player chosen for the team since 2021, when Max Vener was selected as an alternate. "I just feel like I'll let it all in when I get there."
Sherwood and Webb each played in the Maryland State Association of Baseball Coaches' Prospects Game as freshmen, which is factored in as part of the selection process for the Brooks Robinson game. Both played in the MSABC Futures Game as sophomores. Webb played in the Futures Game again last year, while Sherwood played in the Classic Game.
This year's MSABC Classic game, which offered players another chance to showcase their talents, was rained out. That left Sherwood and Webb uncertain if they would be selected, and somewhat surprised when they learned they had made the team.
"I thought about it my freshman year, just kind of working towards it," Webb said of possibly being picked for the Robinson game. "It was pretty cool to see that happen."
"I knew there was a chance, but I wasn't sure because of the people picking the team," Sherwood added.
Sherwood, who pitched and played right field, led St. Michaels to a 16-6 record this season and a 10th appearance in the Class 1A state championship, where the Saints lost 6-2 to Allegany. The right-hander was 6-2 and led the North Bayside in wins and innings pitched (52). His 1.48 earned-run average was second only to Colonel Richardson senior standout Jordan Regulski (1.42), who is headed to Wake Forest University. Sherwood finished the year with four complete games, 43 strikeouts and 17 walks.
"If you took him off our team, we'd probably lose five or six more ballgames," St. Michaels head coach Brian Femi said of Sherwood. "It's not a question in my mind. He pitched every big game we had. And then he hits."
Sherwood, who is headed to Chesapeake College to play, batted .386, leading St. Michaels in hits (27), RBIs (25) and home runs (two). He also had six doubles, a triple, 21 runs scored, and a .522 on-base percentage.
"He basically, and I haven't had a kid do this in a long time, he put our team on his back," Femi said. "He was the most unbelievable leader. You just can't measure it. He took all the young kids, he made them feel welcomed. Our team chemistry was as good as it was when Adam (Parks) and those guys were there (in 2010-11). You had that kind of leadership. Not many other coaches would have seen the leadership that he had because they weren't present."
One year after struggling with an injury to his right arm, Webb emerged as Easton's ace, posting a 4-2 mark with a 2.944 ERA, 28 strikeouts and 20 walks. When he wasn't on the mound, Webb was in center field and finished the season batting over .400 with 20 hits, two doubles, three triples, 12 RBIs, 26 runs, and a .587 OBP.
"He's worked hard his four years," Easton head coach Albert Pritchett said of Webb, who is playing for the Baltimore Chop of the Maryland Collegiate Baseball League this summer before heading to Salisbury University to play. "He showed up every day, every practice. I think over the four years he developed into more of a leader by example, as well as his verbal contributions. He was just a pleasure to watch develop. Strong player. Very athletic. Left us as an even better player. Kind of kid you want to play with. Calm on the outside, fire on the inside. Made every team he was on better."
Sherwood and Webb are listed as outfielders, but could possibly pitch Sunday.
Femi will be on the South coaching staff Sunday. Washington High's Dawson Daniels also made the South team, giving the Bayside Conference three players on the roster.

author: Bill Haufe
content:

 649

 Read News Document

 The Washington Nationals are at a pivotal point in their rebuild to relevance, owning the No. 1 overall pick in Major League Baseball's amateur draft that begins on Sunday night in Atlanta.There are multiple intriguing prospects they can choose from, including prep shortstop Ethan Holliday, the son of seven-time All-Star Matt Holliday and brother of Jackson Holliday, the No. 1 overall pick in 2022 and is now in the majors with the Baltimore Orioles.
Washington this week fired longtime general manager Mike Rizzo and manager Dave Martinez.
Bold choice.
The Nats' head-scratching move — more for the timing than the actual decision — injected another layer of uncertainty to a draft that might be one of the most unpredictable in recent years. The first three rounds of the 20-round draft will take place on Sunday with the rest of the selections on Monday.
Washington promoted Mike DeBartolo to interim GM and he'll supervise the team's selections. He was previously the team's assistant general manager and has been with the franchise since 2012.
DeBartolo said he'll lean on the evaluations of the team's scouting department but also has his own opinions about the process and will be the decision maker. Money will also be a factor, as teams have to work within their bonus pool.
The Orioles are at the high end this year with more than $19 million to spend. The Yankees — who don't pick until No. 39 — are at the bottom with roughly $5.3 million.
"They've been working hard for this moment, almost even before the last draft ended," DeBartolo said. "So, I'll bring my own voice to that process, and I'll work collaboratively with them, and take what they have to say and ultimately be responsible for making the picks."
There is little consensus about whom the Nats might select at No. 1, though some of the top prospects are a pair of left-handed pitchers — LSU's Kade Anderson and Tennessee's Liam Doyle — along with Oregon State shortstop Aiva Arquette and prep shortstops Holliday and Eli Willits.
"There are several really talented players that are going to be in the mix for us," DeBartolo said. "We have to decide how to strategize with our bonus pool money and what the player bonus pool demands are and run through all those scenarios over the coming days."
After the Nationals, the Los Angeles Angels have the No. 2 selection. The Seattle Mariners, Colorado Rockies and St. Louis Cardinals round out the top five.
LEFTIES LEAD PACKSeveral of the top prospects are left-handed college pitchers, including Anderson, Doyle and Florida State's Jamie Arnold.
Anderson helped LSU win the College World Series title last month, throwing a complete-game shutout in Game 1 of the championship series. He finished 12-1 with a 3.18 ERA with 180 strikeouts in 119 innings.
Anderson had Tommy John surgery in high school.
Doyle rocketed up mock drafts with a terrific season for the Vols, finishing 10-4 with a 3.20 ERA and 162 strikeouts in 95 2/3 innings. Arnold was a breakout star for Florida State in 2024 before regressing a bit last season, but he still finished with 8-2 with a 2.98 ERA and 119 strikeouts.
"Obviously, college left-handers are kind of a premium right now," Mariners vice president of amateur scouting Scott Hunter said. "There's a few of those at the high end of the draft."
CORONA STARSCorona High School — about 45 miles from Los Angeles — could have three players drafted in the first round.
The prep powerhouse is led by right-handed pitcher Seth Hernandez, regarded as a potential top five pick. Shortstop Billy Carlson is also expected to be selected early in the first round.
Third baseman Brady Ebel isn't quite as highly-regarded — he's the No. 64 prospect according to MLB.com — but there's potential that he could still sneak into the opening round.
A fourth Corona player, Ethin Bingaman, is a two-way player committed to Auburn but could be drafted in the top five rounds.

title: State, local officials announce return of Fair Hill Races
author: Erik Halberg ehalberg@chespub.com
content:
State, local officials announce return of Fair Hill Races

 July 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Erik Halberg ehalberg@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 643
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FAIR HILL — State and county officials have announced the long-awaited return of the Fair Hill Races to Fair Hill on Aug. 30, along with promises of future racing events to be held at the track."The Fair Hill Races are back in Cecil County," Cecil County Executive Adam Streight said. "We're bringing back a tradition that has bonded us together. And we intend to keep it here."
Last occurring in 2019, the Fair Hill Races are a longstanding Cecil County tradition stretching back nearly 90 years, and their absence has been a subject of public inquiry throughout the six-year gap. With the Maryland 5 Star becoming an annual event at Fair Hill's race track, officials said that the return of the races will usher in a new era for Cecil County's equine community.
"A renaissance of racing starts today," said Del. Kevin Hornberger, who has been heavily involved in legislating the Fair Hill Special Event Zone and its use.
The official announcement of the races' return comes in the wake of a $2.85 million dollar partnership between Cecil County and the Sport and Entertainment Corporation of Maryland that was approved by the county council last October.
State officials thanked local and state partners and acknowledged the feedback from Cecil Countians as a major impetus for the return of racing to the track.
"This is clearly a place Cecil County loves," Maryland Department of Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz said. "Our responsibility as the steward is to reflect what Cecil County wants and what Cecil County needs."
Other officials agreed with Kurtz, saying that Cecil Countians' calls for the return of the races have been heard.
"We couldn't let another year go by without racing at Fair Hill," said Sport & Entertainment Corporation of Maryland President Terry Hasseltine, noting that the races' return has been "a long time coming."
This year's race will be free to the public and is planned to be a one-day event held on Aug. 30. According to Hasseltine, the number of races in this year's event is still being determined.
While the reborn Fair Hill Races are the only event on the docket for the remainder of 2025, Hasseltine also said that there are already plans to hold another racing event next Memorial Day, as well as discussions about races on other dates.
"[Fair Hill] is globally significant when it comes to the equine community," said Kurtz.
Officials noted that the horse racing industry and economy has a multi-billion dollar impact on Maryland, directly employing approximately 22,000 workers throughout the state.
Local organizations expressed their pleasure that the races will finally be making their return to Cecil County.
"The Board of Directors is delighted by this morning's news from Maryland Department of Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz that racing will return to Fair Hill on August 30," Fair Hill Foundation President Charles C. Fenwick Jr. said. "It has been gratifying to work with his dedicated team, the Sport and Entertainment Corporation of Maryland, the Cecil County Breeders Fair, and Delegate Kevin Hornberger to make this long-anticipated outcome a reality, and we are immensely grateful for all the hard work on the part of so many people. We look forward to our continued work together to realize Mr. du Pont's vision for Fair Hill as one of the world's leading venues for equestrian sport."
With events like the Maryland 5 Star and the Cecil County Fair already making use of the site, Streight noted that his administration expects that the addition of the races and future events will show returns not only economically — with an emphasis on the benefits to small businesses — but culturally.
"We expect an economic boom," Streight said. "[And also] a return to pride in what Cecil County has to offer."
Streight also pointed to the history of the races and their value to Cecil County's identity.
"This is a tradition that goes back decades," said Streight. "That bonded us together."

title: Federalsbug starts, ends hot
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Federalsbug starts, ends hot

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 AMERICAN CORNER — It's a pretty basic approach."It's all how you begin and how you finish," Federalsburg head basketball coach Tyrin Hammond said.
Well, Federalsburg didn't need a big finish Wednesday night, as it scored the game's first 21 points en route to a 78-57 victory over Centreville to cap a perfect regular season in the Colonel Basketball Association Summer League at Colonel Richardson High.
Federalsburg (6-0) will be the No. 1 seed and have a first-round bye for next week's playoffs.
"They're playing great," Hammond said of his defending league champions, who were led by Ja'Zir Dickerson's game-high 34 points. "We're working on defense, having better ball movement, and having fun."
Makiah Batson (26 points) drilled a 3-pointer and scored a layup, watched Robbie Cunningham drain a three-ball, then splashed another trey for a quick 11-0 Federalsburg lead that ballooned to 21-0. Centreville (4-2), which entered the game tied for second place with Seaford, finally got on the board with 1 minute, 49 seconds remaining in the first quarter, when Jared Robinson connected on a 3-pointer.
Federalsburg, which is made up mostly of Colonel Richardson High players, carried a 24-6 lead into the second quarter. Batson canned a 3-pointer and scored a pair of layups to restore Federalsburg's 21-point cushion at 31-10 with 7 minutes left in the first half.
DeRodney Smith (team-high 21 points) sandwiched a pair of 3-pointers around a follow-shot that helped pull Centreville within 35-20 with under a minute left in the first half.
"You're going to have little mess-ups during the game," Hammond said. "But if you start out hot, end off hot, you're going to come out with a great game."
Centreville trimmed its deficit to 37-24 at halftime, but Leshaun Allen, Batson and Dickerson each scored on drives, starting Federalsburg on an 8-3 burst to open the third. An Amari Baynard 3 and three consecutive buckets by Dickerson capped a 19-9 Federalsburg run that extended the lead to 56-33.
Centreville scored the final 10 points of the third quarter to draw within 56-43. But Baynard (nine points), Dickerson and Batson accounted for all their team's points in a 19-4 fourth-quarter run that gave Federalsburg a 75-47 bulge in the closing minutes.
"A lot of not maximum effort," Centreville head coach Rocky Harris said of his team. "Lot of not being sure of themselves. And Colonel (Federalsburg) looked like the better basketball team.
"At times we were able to find a group of five players that were (playing well together)," added Harris, who got 11 points from Bryson Marsh and nine from Dontell Guy. "But then Colonel kind of went on a run. They're making their layups. They're making better passes. And they were making their shots."

title: Ravens' Hamilton voted NFL' s top safety
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Ravens' Hamilton voted NFL' s top safety

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 498
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kyle Hamilton has quickly proved that he can be a jack of all trades on Baltimore's stellar defense, thriving in the slot, the box or as a deep safety.But it was the decision to move Hamilton to free safety midway through last season that helped eliminate the big plays and boost the Ravens' defense.
Hamilton's talent and versatility helped him earn the honor of being voted the top safety in the league by The Associated Press.
A panel of eight AP Pro Football Writers ranked the top five players at safety, basing selections on current status entering the 2025 season. First-place votes were worth 10 points. Second- through fifth-place votes were worth 5, 3, 2 and 1 points.
Hamilton got five first place-votes, one second and one third to claim the top spot. Detroit's Kerby Joseph got the other three first-place votes and finished second.
Green Bay's Xavier McKinney, Detroit's Brian Branch and Derwin James of the Los Angeles Chargers rounded out the top five.
Atlanta's Jessie Bates, Tampa Bay's Antoine Winfield Jr., Miami's Minkah Fitzpatrick, Denver's Brandon Jones, Arizona's Budda Baker and Houston's C.J. Gardner-Johnson also received votes.
1. KYLE HAMILTON, Baltimore Ravens
Hamilton has been the most important piece on Baltimore's defense thanks in large part to his versatility. He has the ability to stop the run, excel against the pass and rush the quarterback and was voted a first-team All-Pro in 2023 and second-teamer last season. Hamilton played the majority of his snaps starting in Week 11 last season as a free safety and the Ravens went from allowing 4.7 pass plays of at least 20 yards per game to 1.6 after the switch.
2. KERBY JOSEPH, Detroit Lions
Joseph emerged as a big-time playmaker in his third season, leading the NFL with nine interceptions to earn first-team All-Pro honors. His 17 career interceptions are the most for any safety in his first three seasons since Hall of Famer Ed Reed had 21.
3. XAVIER MCKINNEY, Green Bay Packers
McKinney made a major impact on Green Bay's defense in his first season after signing with the Packers as a free agent. He was at his best in pass coverage as a deep safety. McKinney had eight interceptions last season and allowed a 56.4 passer rating when targeted in coverage, according to Pro Football Focus.
4. BRIAN BRANCH, Detroit Lions
Branch has become an immediate impact player on Detroit's defense since being drafted in the second round in 2023. He led all safeties with 16 passes defensed last season and was tied for third with eight tackles for loss as he performed at a high level both in the run and pass game.
5. DERWIN JAMES, Los Angeles Chargers
James bounced back from a down 2023 season to earn second-team All-Pro honors in his first season in coordinator Jesse Minter's defense. James is one of the most versatile safeties, getting extensive time working in the slot, as a box safety, a deep safety and even as a pass rusher, where he had the second-most pressures of any safety last season.

title: Denton Little League Major All-Star team wins district championship
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Denton Little League Major All-Star team wins district championship

 July 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Denton Little League Major All-Star baseball team won the District 6 championship over South Caroline 10-4 on Saturday.This is the first time since 1999 Denton has won the district championship. Denton Little League President Kyle Bringman recalled when the 1999 team won.
"The last time we won the district championship, I was an 11-year-old in Denton Little League," Bringman said. "I remember the boys that won it that year and the level of competitiveness that they had, and the skill that they had. This team reminds me of the teams that Denton used to have when I was a kid that could go up there and compete at this level."
The all-star team is selected from the four Denton Major teams for players aged 10-12. The coaches pick the best 12 players out of the four teams to create the team.
"It's a lot of talented 12-year-old kids who have been playing ball with us for a very long time, and it's neat to see them get to this level of winning the district championship," Bringman said.
Denton head coach Joe Amalfitano applauded his players' hard work for making it to the state tournament.
"I really have to credit the players because they put in a lot of work in the offseason and a lot of them hang out together and practice, even on their own time, not just on practice time," Amalfitano said.
According to Denton Little League Facebook, the team went 4-0 in the tournament, outscoring its opponents 71-13.
Amalfitano said the team is a close-knit group and has a confidence that shows on the field.
If Denton wins the state title, it qualifies for the regional tournament and a chance to play in the Little League World Series.
Amalfitano said the team doesn't think about what can happen in the future. They have a one-game-at-a-time mentality.
"We preach one game at a time," Amalfitano said. "I've always told them we don't even look ahead. We just look at the game in front of us."
Denton is scheduled to play South Baltimore this Saturday at 2:30 p.m. at West Salisbury Little League.

title: Scheffler storms into lead
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Scheffler storms into lead

 July 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News 
 
 933
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PORTRUSH, Northern Ireland — The rain pounded Royal Portrush right when Scottie Scheffler poured in a birdie putt on his first hole Friday in the British Open. No matter. Nothing stopped the world's No. 1 player on his way to a 7-under 64 to build a one-shot lead going into the weekend.Scheffler made eight birdies on another wild afternoon of weather at Royal Portrush, and his 15-foot birdie attempt on the 18th stopped inches short for another.
The result was a one-shot lead over former U.S. Open champion Matt Fitzpatrick, who made four straight birdies to start the back nine until he cooled on the home stretch and had to settle for a 66.
The rain was heavy at times but never lasted long. The wind was breezy but never at strength that can cause fits. The scoring was lower, nearly two shots easier than the opening round.
Except for a few chasers, Scheffler made it look like it wasn't enough.
He was at 10-under 132 as he chases the third leg of the career Grand Slam, having won the PGA Championship by five shots in May.
Brian Harman got the best of the weather — surprising sunshine — and took dead aim in his hunt for another claret jug. Harman played bogey-free for a 64 that left him only two shots behind, along with Li Haotong of China, who had a 67.
Everyone else was five shots behind or more.
That includes Rory McIlroy, who went around Royal Portrush in his native Northern Ireland with plenty of cheers but only a few roars. McIlroy had a 69 but lost a lot of ground because of Scheffler, Fitzpatrick and Harman.
He started the second round just three shots behind. He goes into the weekend seven shots behind the top-ranked player in the world.
Fitzpatrick was at his lowest point just four months ago when he changed his caddie and coach and began pulling himself up. And now he takes that into the weekend against Scheffler.
"He's going to have the expectation to go out and dominate. He's an exceptional player. He's world No. 1, and we're seeing Tiger-like stuff," Fitzpatrick said. "I think the pressure is for him to win the golf tournament. For me, obviously I hope I'm going to have some more home support than him, but it's an exciting position for me to be in given where I was earlier this year."
Fitzpatrick was rolling along until a pair of short putts he missed, from 5 feet for par on the 14th and from 3 feet for birdie on the 17th. Even so, he holed a 25-foot par putt on the final hole and assured him being in the last group at 9-under 133.
Scheffler was sharp from the start. He hit eight of the 14 fairways — compared with three in the opening round — though his misses never left him too badly out of position. But he is seeing the breaks on smoother Portrush greens, and he looks confident as ever.
None of his eight birdies were closer than 7 feet. Five of them were in the 10-foot range and then he threw in a 35-foot birdie on the sixth. His lone bogey came on a drive into deep grass on the 11th that kept him from reaching the green.
The statistics led to a shrug.
"Overall, I'm hitting the ball solid," Scheffler said. "The tournament is only halfway done. I got off to a good start."
Harman was called the "Butcher of Hoylake" when he won the claret jug at Royal Liverpool two years ago because the British press was fascinated by the Georgia native's love for hunting. Now it's about his golf, and it was superb.
Harman played bogey-free, only once having to stress for par as Royal Portrush allowed for some good scoring in weather that again did not live up to its expectation.
Not that anyone was complaining. Temperatures were warm, at least by Irish standards. The breeze was noticeable without being overly punishing.
"They're very different golf courses, but the golf is similar," Harman said. "You've got to be able to flight your golf ball. You've got to know how far everything's going. Then you can't get frustrated. You're going to end up in funny spots where it doesn't seem fair, and you just have to kind of outlast that stuff."
The group at 5-under 137 included Harris English (70), Harman's former teammate at Georgia; Tyrrell Hatton of England (69) and Chris Gotterup (65), who wasn't even planning to be at Royal Portrush until winning the Scottish Open last week.
Also still around is Bryson DeChambeau, who made a 13-shot improvement from the first round with a 65. Still, he was 11 shots behind.
McIlroy wasn't at his best in the opening round and was pleased to be only three behind. Now he has a real mountain to climb. But at least he's still playing, unlike in 2019 at Royal Portrush when he shot 79 and then had a terrific rally only to miss the cut by one shot.
"I didn't have this opportunity six years ago, so to play an extra two days in this atmosphere in front of these crowds, I'm very excited for that," McIlroy said. "I feel like my game's definitely good enough to make a run."
That was before Scheffler began to run away from so many except a small collection of challengers. But this is links golf. And this is the Emerald Isle, where the weather seems to have a mind of its own.
Still, Scheffler has gone 10 tournaments without finishing out of the top 10 and would appear to present a challenge every bit as daunting as Royal Portrush.

title: Amalfitano, Peris combine for 3-hitter as Denton extends stay
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Amalfitano, Peris combine for 3-hitter as Denton extends stay

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 492
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SALISBURY — Denton manager Joe Amalfitano thinks his team could be sticking around Salisbury for a few more days.If it continues playing like this, he may be correct.
Amalfitano watched his son Joe combine with reliever Gabe Peris for a three-hitter Monday, as Denton rolled to a 13-1 five-inning victory over Chesapeake City in the Maryland State Major Little League (10-12) baseball tournament at Pemberton Little League Park.
Denton (2-1) was scheduled to play South Baltimore (2-1) Tuesday at Pemberton. Denton defeated South Baltimore, 14-2, in Saturday's opener but lost 6-1 to Montgomery County on Sunday.
Monday's loss eliminated Chesapeake City.
"We feel confident," manager Amalfitano said. "We're going to play a few more games this week."
Chesapeake City took a 1-0 lead in the bottom of the first. Eli Jackson hit a clean leadoff single to right field. Three batters later, Kade Pierce dropped a sacrifice bunt in front of the plate that scored Jackson. But Amalfitano wouldn't let another Chesapeake City runner to reach second, retiring the final six batters he faced. Denton's starting right-hander allowed just the one run and hit, walked none and struck out four.
Peris came on in relief to start the fourth and retired the first two batters he faced. Bryson Smeyda singled to center but moved no further, as Peris handled Pierce's come-backer for the final out of the inning.
Down 13-1, Chesapeake City tried to avoid the 10-run slaughter rule with a small rally in the fifth. With one out, Tyler Graf walked, stole second, and moved to third on Tony Zaun's double to right. Ryder Corrigan worked a walk to load the bases. But Peris escaped the jam, as Eric Thompson lined out to shortstop Isaac Hansley, who quickly stepped on second base for a game-ending unassisted double play.
"Pitchers pitched well," manager Amalfitano said. "That's what we needed; threw strikes. And we've got a good defense. We knew our defense could make the plays if we threw strikes."
Denton scored all the runs it needed in the top of the second. Ashton Buckius, Ethan Lee and Trey Rinaudot III each drew walks. Jackson Weishar greeted reliever Smeyda with a single to right, scoring Buckius and Lee for a 2-1 Denton lead. Peris bounced a single through the middle that plated Rinaudot. Weishar scored on Miles Moczulski's sacrifice fly to right, pushing the lead to 4-1.
"Some days they swing at the first pitch," Amalfitano said of his team's patience at the plate in this game. "We told them, "Be a little patient tonight. Work the pitch count.' Felt like they did that."
Denton widened its lead to 8-1 in the third, capitalizing on errors and another RBI single from Peris.
That lead ballooned to 10-1 in the fourth, as Amalfitano hit an RBI single and eventually scored on Nicholas Newman's groundout. Denton added three more runs in the fifth for a 13-1 cushion.
"They made some errors," Manager Amalfitano said. "But good things will happen if we can put the ball in play."

title: Caroline outlasts Talbot for state bid
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Caroline outlasts Talbot for state bid

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 891
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — Austin Frank didn't know how many pitches he threw.And after getting buried under an avalanche of red, white and blue-clad teammates after a second nine-inning victory, he may have temporarily forgotten where he was — cloud nine or the infield at the American Legion baseball field in Hurlock.
What Frank did know was where he and his teammates were headed this Friday afternoon.
"We're going to Hanover. We're going to Joe Cannon Stadium," Frank said of this year's American Legion state baseball tournament site.
Frank pitched 7 2/3 innings of shutout baseball over two games, then stroked a two-out single to score Hayden Diefenderfer with the winning run in the bottom of the ninth inning Tuesday night, giving Caroline Post 29 a 3-2 victory over Talbot Post 70 and a sweep of the best-of-three Eastern Shore North Division playoff series.
Winners of five straight division titles, Caroline is slated to play Eastern Shore South Division champion Ocean City at 4 p.m. Friday in the first round of the state tournament.
"Austin loves baseball," said Caroline first-year manager Travis Breeding. "He knows the game inside and out. You can always count on him to come through and rise to the situation."
Boy, did Frank rise to the situation.
Game 1, which was suspended last Thursday with the score tied 4-4 after seven innings, remained knotted until the top of the ninth. Caroline's Gavin Whitby hit a leadoff single to center field, moved to second on an error, and scored when Wes Thomas ripped a double to left field off Talbot's Couper Barletta for a 5-4 lead.
Frank, who retired Post 70 in order in the eighth, struck out the side in the ninth to seal the 5-4 Game 1 victory.
Frank remained on the mound to start the second game, which became a scoreless pitcher's duel between Post 29's right-hander and Talbot lefty Cullen Murphy. Frank surrendered no runs, three hits, three walks and struck out seven over 5 2/3 scoreless innings before reaching his pitch limit with two outs in the sixth.
"I had most of my stuff with me today," Frank said of his fastball, slider and change-up. "They all looked good. They all felt great. I could just locate really well. I felt like I could put the ball where I wanted it."
"He's a tough, tough pitcher," Talbot manager Albert Pritchett said of Frank.
Murphy was equally tough, yielding no runs, two hits, six walks and striking out eight over 5 2/3 innings.
"Cullen did a great job of holding us in it," said Pritchett, whose southpaw reached his limit after fanning the first two batters in the sixth.
Talbot broke the scoreless stalemate in the top of the eighth.
Anthony Massaro lined a leadoff single to center off Caroline reliever Chase Hitchens. Jesus Crespo singled through the right side, pushing Massaro to third. Pearson Greenwood then skied a single down the right-field line, scoring Massaro for a 1-0 lead. Ethan Royer followed, doubling into the right-center field gap to plate Crespo for a 2-0 Post 70 lead.
Talbot (5-3-1) appeared on the verge of widening its lead when Jordan Langrell walked, loading the bases. Gavin Murphy singled into shallow left, but Frank, now playing left field, fired a strike to the plate to get the force on Talbot's pinch-runner for the inning's first out. Hitchens then induced an inning-ending double play, keeping Caroline's deficit at 2-0.
Still, Post 70 looked ready to force a Game 3 — which was slated to be played at the conclusion of Game 2 — as reliever Nathan Spurry retired the first two batters of the eighth. But Derrick Mitchell reached on an infield single. Whitby walked. David Saathoff lined a sharp single to left, loading the bases. Johnny Radcliff then smacked a 2-2 delivery into center field, plating Mitchell and Whitby for a 2-2 tie. Spurry intentionally walked Kenton Robbins to reload the bases in hopes of a force at any base, before notching an inning-ending strikeout.
Hitchens set Post 70 down in order in the top of the ninth.
Colton Maans began Caroline's game-winning rally in the ninth, reaching on a one-out infield single with no one covering first base. Diefenderfer came on to pinch run, was balked to second base and advanced to third on Trent Breeding's groundout to second. Frank followed, hitting a 1-2 pitch up the middle to score Diefender with the winning run.
"He went first-pitch slider and then went slider again," Frank said of Spurry. "Then he went fastball so I knew he was going to come back to it. I was sitting slider and he threw it and I got a good swing on it."
Frank touched first base, raised both arms to his sides in celebration. Mitchell reached Caroline's hero first, quickly hoisting him upward before a steady wave of teammates sent both tumbling to the ground.
"Big shoes to fill definitely with the success the program had had," Travis Breeding said of succeeding former skipper Neil Lambert. "They really are a good group of guys. You saw how they clawed and fought back. I was like, 'Here we go. We're going to be here until the lights go off, trying to get another game in to be the decider.' They just battled back. I can't say enough about their fortitude and how they stayed in the ballgame when they could have got down. They're just determined. They were determined to win."

title: Hurlock's surprise run falls shy
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Hurlock's surprise run falls shy

 July 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 695
 Words 

 Read News Document

 AMERICAN CORNER — One game.That was the grand sum total of victories for Hurlock during the Colonel Basketball Association Summer League's six-game regular season.
Hurlock earned a pair of postseason victories though, and narrowly missed a third Wednesday night, before Enoch Dupri's free throw with 1.3 seconds remaining lifted Seaford (Delaware) to a 48-47 victory in the league championship at Colonel Richardson High's Merrill Morgan Gymnasium.
"We've come a long way this summer," said Hurlock head coach John Ridenour, an assistant for North Dorchester High's varsity. "I mean we won one game before the playoffs started and we came out and won two, and took Seaford to the brink. It would have been nice."
Like Stevensville and Saints Peter and Paul, Hurlock finished the regular season 1-5, but earned the fifth seed for the playoffs based on its margin of victory in its one win. Hurlock knocked off No. 4 seed Ridgely on Monday, then upset unbeaten top-seed and defending league champion Federalsburg, 47-38, in Wednesday's first semifinal.
Seaford reached the final via its 54-34 win over third-seeded Centreville in the second semifinal. The Blue Jays looked ready to turn the title game into a waltz, building a 17-7 lead after the first quarter, and stretching that edge to 39-25 midway through the third.
But Hurlock steadily began whittling its deficit, starting with Tajir Pritchett's bucket with 4:30 left in the third. Wyatt Barone (12 points), who plays for St. Michaels High, scored on a follow. Tyrone Smith (game-high 16 points) scored on a drive then hit 3 of 4 foul shots, capping a 9-0 quarter-closing run that pulled Hurlock within 39-34 heading into the fourth.
"To be honest, we came in here with the expectation of playing Colonel Richardson (Federalsburg) in the championship game," Seaford head coach Vince Evans II said. "I think once we realized it wasn't them, I don't think we played up to our expectations and kind of went through the motions. If we do that during the (high school) season that's going to cost us."
It almost cost Seaford on this night.
Smith sank a free throw and scored on a finger roll, trimming Seaford's lead to 39-37 early in the fourth. Seaford's Taj Bacon hit a 3-pointer. But Barone, who seemingly got stronger and stronger on both the offensive and defensive boards as the game progressed, scored inside, getting Hurlock within 42-39 with 7 minutes left.
Brendan West converted a Vince Evans feed to nudge Seaford's lead to 44-39. Again Barone, who netted eight fourth-quarter points, responded inside. Sammy Robinson's follow restored the Blue Jays' five-point lead at 46-41 with 2:40 left. Barone made a put-back and Smith scored on a drive, drawing Hurlock within 46-45 with 2 minutes to play.
"The guys just fought," Ridenour said. "They played hard and that's all I asked of them is give it their all."
Ridenour also acknowledged having played the first semifinal allowed his players to rest while Seaford started its second game about 10 minutes after its semifinal victory.
"We got a break in between games," Ridenour said. "To be honest I think it helps sometimes having a smaller seven; seven, eight guys. It's easier to maneuver and you can see what rotations are working a little better."
Dupri (team-high 12 points) converted one of two from the foul line for a 47-45 Seaford lead with 56 seconds left. Barone's turnaround jumper tied it at 47-all with 37.3 seconds to go. Seaford called timeout with 15.6 seconds left. Dupri was fouled in the chaotic closing seconds and hit the first of two free-throw attempts with 1.3 seconds left.
Confusion about how much time was left ensued and officials decided 2 seconds should be put on the clock. But Jayden Turner's three-quarter court desperation heave hit a ceiling beam, ending the game.
"Credit to them because they played hard," coach Evans said of Hurlock. "They struggled throughout the league, but hats off to North Dorchester for playing hard, for knocking off Colonel. And they should have beat us. They played a lot harder than we did."
Notes: Evans, the coach's son, finished with 10 points for Seaford, which ended the season 8-1. … Hurlock finished 3-5. Federalsburg, which was minus some key players Wednesday, finished 6-1.

 EASTON — Special Olympics Maryland athletes joined with police officers on Tuesday to carry the torch through Easton.Beginning on Dover Street, a group of around 100 athletes, families, law enforcement officers and community members participated in Talbot County's leg of the Law Enforcement Torch Run, an annual tradition to raise money for the Special Olympics. They brought along the Special Olympics torch, called the Flame of Hope, as they traversed the downtown streets of Easton.
Officers from the Easton Police Department and Talbot County Sheriff's Office, as well as local officials such as Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Talbot County Council member Dave Stepp, participated in the event. Some local organizations stood outside to cheer on the athletes, including employees from the Town of Easton offices and Rauch Inc.
Walking down Harrison Street, athlete Hannah McNiece beamed with joy alongside Easton officer Cordero Proctor, as the two each placed a hand on the torch and led the entourage of athletes to the finish line at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department.
Some officers and athletes took a running route through town and caught up with the walkers toward the finish.
Jill Garvey, management assistant for the Easton Police Department, helps organize the torch run. She said it means a lot when the athletes interact with law enforcement and build relationships with the officers.
Other counties across the state participate in the torch tradition. Also on Tuesday, Queen Anne's County police officers joined with Kent Island High School students for the Law Enforcement Torch Run.
"This event is about more than a run, it's about promoting inclusion, dignity, and respect for every athlete," said Queen Anne's Sheriff Gary Hofmann in a press release. "We're honored to be part of this tradition and proud to stand alongside our partners and students in support of such a meaningful cause."
The Summer Games for Special Olympics Maryland athletes is set to take place this weekend at Towson University from Friday to Sunday.

title: Ticknor has a stellar bowling performance at Junior Gold Nationals
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Ticknor has a stellar bowling performance at Junior Gold Nationals

 July 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WESTON, WI — 12-year-old bowler Abigail Ticknor of Millington stays in her lane, then dominates in it. Even if that lane is at a national championship youth bowling tournament held in Northeast, Wisconsin.On July 14-19, she was the first ever bowler from Kent County to compete at the USBC Junior Gold Championships, an annual bowling tournament for the top male and female youth bowlers in the United States.
The competition was fierce and Ticknor, according to WBAY, a local news source in that area, competed against the top 3100 bowlers in the nation for nearly half a million dollars in scholarship prizes and a chance to be on the Junior Team USA.
She did not get to be one of the top 16 to go to the finals, but Ticknor placed 51rst in the nation in a field of 107 U12 girls at the 2025 edition of Junior Gold Championships.
Ticknor finished her 16 qualifying rounds with a total score of 2,222 for an average of 138.88, roughly a pin better than her league average from this past season.
Junior Gold, her father Phil Ticknor said is a challenging event, consisting of four four-game qualifying rounds, then an advancer and final rounds on a different sport-shot oil pattern each round.
"Sport-shot patterns force bowlers to make adjustments to how they usually bowl and each pattern plays differently," Phil pointed out, being present and cheering his daughter on.
Ticknor began qualifying play with a 493 (142-111-113-125) four-game round at Ashwaubenon on July 14, which put her in 85th place.
The next day, she moved up to 61th, after a 555 (122-156-134-143) at Dale's Weston Lanes in Weston.
Then at Ashwaubenon for round 3 she moved her up to 49th place before settling into 51rst with a 528 (143-103-127-155) at Dale's on July 17th.
Phil said, the highlight for Ticknor at the tournament came the night of July 16th when she opened her four-game qualifying round at Ashwaubenon.
"Those were two of the best games of her life on any type of oil pattern," Phil remarked.
Ticknor opened the evening with a five-strike, three-spare performance en route to a 177 game. In game two she topped that, opening with a turkey (three consecutive strikes) and finishing with five strikes and three spares, this time putting a 190 on the board. That score tied her highest-ever game on a sport-shot pattern and tied her fifth-highest ever score on any lane condition.
After bowling a 126 in game three, she finished the night strong with a 155 in the fourth and final game. Her total score in the round was 648 (162 average), giving her by far her best-ever single-day sport-shot performance.
Phil was thrilled with her very first performance on the national stage.
"I went in thinking her being in the 70s or 80s would have been a great success for it being her first time and where she is as a bowler — making top half was great!"
Ticknor had earlier earned her spot at Milford Bowling Lanes on Sept. 22 finishing third place in a co-ed field of a dozen U12 boys and girls in the first Delaware-sanctioned Junior Gold Qualifier of the season.
She bowls in the varsity division of the Doverama Dragons Youth League in Dover, Delaware.
Competing and doing well inspired her. When she got back home, the new ball her family purchased for her was tried out.
"She threw nine practice games with it at Doverama yesterday and two of them were a 232 and 230, the highest games she has ever thrown, if you count practice."
Proof Ticknor is just getting the ball rolling.

title: Governor's Cup race returns to St. Mary's College
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Governor's Cup race returns to St. Mary's College

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 554
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Sailors of all types and experience levels will hope they are on even keels and that they have fair winds this weekend as they take part in the 52nd annual Governor's Cup sailing race.The St. Mary's College of Maryland tradition, which is the oldest overnight race on the Chesapeake Bay, features a 68.6 nautical mile race from Annapolis to the college.
There are also two other satellite races, each of which is about 48 miles in length.
"I'm always excited for the Governor's Cup to return," said Race Director Rick Loheed, who is also the St. Mary's College associate director of the waterfront.
Boats departed Annapolis beginning 3 p.m. Friday and, depending on winds and other variables, are scheduled to arrive at the college early Saturday morning.
"There's something special about sailing back to the college you graduated from," said Michael Woolen of Baltimore, who graduated from St. Mary's College in 2014 and has taken part in the race about five times. "And there's something special about sailing overnight, assuming the conditions are advantageous."
Other options include the Potomac leg, which runs from Dahlgren, Va., to the college.
"They will sail to a marker at the mouth of the Potomac where the river is widest and then come all around to the 'SM' marker," Loheed said, adding that heading up the St. Mary's River is "a completely different challenge than sailing down the bay."
There is also a Solomons leg which has three entries this year.
"The Annapolis [leg] is more challenging because of the bigger distance and more water," Loheed said, "but they're all challenging and you're sailing at night."
There are 81 boats competing this year, which Loheed said "is on par with post-pandemic years."
Loheed will be pulling double duty as he will be sailing in his third Governor's Cup aboard his 35-foot Poor Richard, which will depart from Annapolis and compete in the CRCA Class.
"The more crew you have, the more righting movement you can have because they can all sit on the rail," Loheed said. "Many of these boats have heavy weighted keels. But by adding weight to the windward rail you help the righting moment of the boat fight against the sails trying to tip it over, so you're able to use a little more of that sail power to propel you forward a little faster."
Crew members will serve as bow, main trimmer, jib trimmer, helmsman and sewer guy, which is so named because they pack up spinnakers down in the cabin. Loheed will be the tactician.
"It's a challenging, grueling race," Loheed said. "A lot of times those faster boats overtake us and sometimes that happens during the day, but it also happens at night. The whole race is a challenge. You're constantly watching the Automated Identification System for other boats and as you go down the bay you have to make sure you're aware of the ships. They are much faster than most people realize."
He said the secret to having a successful race is "don't make any mistakes."
Woollen, who is planning on competing in the Annapolis leg aboard Jester in the PRFA Class, said that "most of the time sailing the rhumb line (the shortest point between A and B) is the fastest way in my experience. I think only one year has that not been the winning recipe."
For more information on the race, visit smcm.edu/signature-events/governors-cup-yacht-race/.

title: Springer 'doing all right' after fastball to his head
author: Staff Writer
content:
Springer 'doing all right' after fastball to his head

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 262
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE — George Springer twisted his head, absorbed the full impact of a fastball near the ear flap of his helmet, and dropped to the ground in a heap.As Toronto's designated hitter lay prone at the plate, the raucous crowd of 20,176 at Camden Yards immediately became silent. Quite suddenly, Baltimore's seven-run ninth-inning lead over the Blue Jays on Monday night became of secondary importance to the condition of Springer, who was essentially motionless in the dirt.
After several anxious moments, Springer slowly lifted his head. He mouthed the word "Wow!" before walking to the dugout with aid from a man on each side.
Whew.
"He's doing all right," manager John Schneider said afterward. "Kind of got him on the shoulder and then the helmet. Thankfully he was able to turn a little bit, too."
It was as good a result as could be expected after the 96 mph pitch from Kade Stroud struck Springer in the head in the Blue Jays' 11-4 loss. Stroud crouched behind the mound, a worried look on his face as he watched, waiting and desperately hoping for Springer to get up.
"That's the worst part of baseball for any side, when a pitch gets thrown that high," Schneider said. "You don't think about baseball. You think about the human. It's scary. It happens. It sucks."
Schneider was among the first to know that Springer was not in a life-threatening situation.
"He was alert the whole time," Schneider said. "He was kind of talking to me ... which is a good thing. But you hate seeing that happen to anyone at any time."

title: Orioles sending nearly $8.5 million to teams involved in trade-deadline deals
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Orioles sending nearly $8.5 million to teams involved in trade-deadline deals

 August 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 855
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Baltimore will be sending nearly $8.5 million to four teams as part of five deals made ahead of the trade deadline.The Orioles will give San Diego $3,324,300 along with All-Star first baseman Ryan O'Hearn and outfielder Ramón Laureano, who were dealt last week for right-handers Tyson Neighbors and Tanner Smith, left-hander Boston Bateman, infielders Brandon Butterworth and Cobb Hightower and infielder/outfielder Victor Figueroa.
O'Hearn was owed $2,537,634 of his $8 million salary and Laureano $1,268,817. Baltimore will pay two installments of $1,662,150 on Sept. 15 and 30, according to trade details obtained by The Associated Press. The money reduces San Diego's expense to $482,151, which comes to a prorated share of the $760,000 minimum for each.
Baltimore will send Detroit $2,758,065 on Sept. 30 as part of the trade that sent right-hander Charlie Morton to the Tigers for minor league left-hander Micah Ashman. Morton was owed $4,758,064 of his $15 million salary, and the cash reduces his cost to the Tigers to $2 million. In addition, the Orioles will send the Tigers $100,000 on Aug. 15 as part of the trade to acquire left-hander Dietrich Enns.
The Orioles also are sending Toronto $1.75 million on Sept. 30 as part of the July 29 trade that sent right-hander Seranthony Domínguez to the Blue Jays for minor league right-hander Juaron Watts-Brown — a deal announced between games of a doubleheader between the teams. Domínguez had $2,645,161 left from his $8 million salary at the time of the trade.
Baltimore is giving Houston $520,000 along with infielder Ramón Urías, who was dealt for minor leaguer right-hander Twine Palmer. The money is due in equal payments on Sept. 15 and Oct. 15. Urías was owed $1,016,129 of his $3.15 million salary.
Money in the five trades totals $8,452,365. Baltimore opened the season with a $169 million payroll, 15th among the 30 major league teams.
Minnesota is paying $33 million to Houston in the July 31 trade that returned All-Star Carlos Correa to the Astros for minor league left-hander Matt Mikulski, by far the largest amount among 14 deadline trades involving cash transactions. That covered a significant portion of the $103,419,355 remaining in the contract of the three-time All-Star, who left the Astros to sign with the Twins ahead of the 2022 season. Houston gets $3 million this year and $10 million each in 2026, 2027 and 2028, with installments due each Dec. 15.
Arizona will pay Milwaukee $5,258,000 as part of the July 31 trade that sent right-hander Shelby Miller and left-hander Jordan Montgomery to the Brewers for a player to be named or cash. Arizona will send the money in four installments of $1,314,500 on Aug. 15, Aug. 31, Sept. 15 and Sept. 30. Montgomery was owed $7,137,097 of his $22.5 million salary and Miller $317,204 of his $1 million salary.
Milwaukee is sending San Diego $2,169,000 as part of the trade that sent left-hander Nestor Cortes and minor league infielder Jorge Quintana to the Padres for outfielder Brandon Lockridge. That offsets part of the $2,410,753 remaining from Cortes' $7.6 million salary. The Brewers will send $361,500 each on Aug. 15 and 29, Sept. 12 and 26 plus $723,000 on Oct. 10.
Cincinnati is paying Pittsburgh $1,935,484 as part of the July 30 trade that sent left-hander Taylor Rogers and minor league shortstop Sammy Stafura to the Pirates for third baseman Ke'Bryan Hayes. The cash covers half the $3,870,968 Rogers was owed from his $12 million salary, and the Reds paid $435,484 on Aug. 1 and owe $500,000 each on Aug. 15, Sept. 1 and Sept. 15.
Rogers was dealt the following day to the Cubs for outfielder Ivan Brethowr, and Pittsburgh agreed to give the Cubs $1,903,226. That offset half the $3,806,452 then left on Rogers' salary after the $64,516 he earned during his one day with Pittsburgh, for whom he never threw a pitch. The Pirates pay $423,226 on Aug . 15 and owe $500,000 installments on Aug. 31, Sept. 15 and Sept. 30.
San Francisco will give Kansas City $1,934,100 as part of the trade that sent outfielder Mike Yastzemski to the Royals for right-hander Yunior Marte. Yastzemski was owed $2,934,140 of his $9.25 million salary, and the Giants will make four payments of $483,535 on Aug. 15. Aug. 31, Sept. 15 and Sept. 30.
Tampa Bay is sending Milwaukee $1.1 million in the July 28 trade that sent catcher Danny Jansen to his hometown Brewers for minor league infielder Jadher Areinamo. Jansen was owed $2,833,333 of his $8.5 million salary. The Rays will make six payments of $183,333, on Aug. 1, 15 and 29, Sept. 12 and 26, and Oct. 10. Tampa Bay agreed to send an additional $500,000 if a $12 million mutual option for 2026 is declined, which carries a $500,000 buyout.
St. Louis agreed to pay Atlanta $2.28 million as part of the July 27 trade that sent right-hander Erick Fedde to the Braves for a player to be named or cash. Fedde was owed $2,455,645 from his $7.25 million salary. The Cardinals will make equal payments of $1.14 million on Aug. 11 and Sept. 22.
Detroit will pay Texas $100,000 on Aug. 15 as part of the trade to acquire right-hander Codi Heuer.

title: Sharp Road Park basketball court update sends nod to first responders
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Sharp Road Park basketball court update sends nod to first responders

 August 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 555
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Sharp Road Park in Denton is expected to see major improvements within the next couple of years. The first major improvement will be unveiled this week.When the park's revamped basketball courts reopen to the public, they will feature a bright design of interlocking shapes created by local artist Shelton Hawkins.
The new mural on the basketball court honors first responders with the colors red for firefighters, navy blue for police and light blue for emergency medical services. Terae Warner, a local business owner and JV basketball coach at North Caroline High School, helped with a great portion of the design.
"I feel like the design aspect itself brings people together off the court and on the court as well," Warner said. "Off the court, it's going to be something that integrates different lifestyles, types of people, and on the court, the same thing. Just in the last few days, when it's been done, I've had a lot of people ask me about the court."
Warner first brought his idea to improve the courts to the town in 2019. The town loved his idea but didn't have any money left over in the budget to complete the project.
Five years later, the town administrator called Warner and said they had the funds. Warner called Hawkins to help, and the project was underway.
"I think it was just really for us we wanted to make sure that it was colors, large shapes, and a lot of movement," Hawkins said. "... So, this one, I think, kind of challenged us design wise, but I think it came out really dope."
Hawkins has worked on over 60 basketball court murals, with nine on the Eastern Shore and, most notably, the LeBron James I Promise School basketball court mural in Akron, Ohio.
The mural will be complete on Wednesday in time for an event Warner holds for local basketball players each summer.
"We call it the largest high school basketball showcase in the state," Warner said of the event taking place Saturday. "So basically the concept is we want to get the top players from the Eastern Shore of Maryland, and we give them an opportunity to play in an All-Star-type game. So, each year all the kids get a free uniform that's provided by our sponsors, our brands that we work with.
"We also hold a free one-hour clinic at the beginning of the event with two different age groups. All those kids get free one-hour training from high school coaches, college coaches, they get a free t-shirt, they get to scrimmage a little bit."
Warner has been holding the Napday Invitational for the past three years. The games give players a chance to showcase their talent and a chance for exposure.
Improvements like those made to the courts in Denton help preserve places where everyone has access to basketball, Warner and Hawkins said.
"It's like the biggest reward," Warner said. "For me, it's always been about showing the kids that you can be somebody from here. It doesn't matter where you come from, you can literally be anything and do anything. So, I feel like me being from here born and raised and to be able to go through all these different avenues, phases, changes and be able to do something like this for the next generation is kind of should be inspirational. I hope it is."
